Sonos has a new app. Stop me if you’ve heard this one before.
The smart speaker company, long a darling of the audio industry, undid much of the goodwill it earned with its multiroom speakers through a bevy of software updates that broke its app in 2024. Almost all app users hated it, citing the loss of features like volume control and accessibility tools meant to help blind people use the wireless speaker system. Sonos eventually owned up to the mistake, considered bringing back the old app again, then booted its CEO and marched its new leaders out to apologize profusely to win back the company’s furious customers.
Now, Sonos says it has a brand-new app update, infused with lots of generative AI features. The company also announced a new soundbar and its second pair of over-the-ear headphones. Sonos representatives say it doesn’t want to be seen as a speaker company anymore, but as something bigger and more holistic.
“For years people have been seeing us as a speaker company,” says Brandon Holley, the interim hardware lead at Sonos. “What we actually are is an audio operating system.”
The company is calling that operating system Sonos 27, and it manifests in a few ways. First and foremost: updates to the Sonos app.
Sonos 27 App
Sonos knows that the words “new Sonos app” might strike fear in the hearts of its users.
“When I say that out loud, I know exactly what comes to mind,” Sid Patel, vice president of software at Sonos, tells WIRED. Patel says the app was developed with a “customer-centric feedback listening approach” that involves reaching out to the community and being active in forums like Reddit. New features to make the app easier to use will include improved tab navigation, better room sorting, and changes to volume knobs on the app itself. In the fall, Sonos will release system health views that let you diagnose connection issues for each product.
The big feature is Sonos 27voice, the company’s generative AI integration, which is being released in early access. It lets you talk to the speakers like you would Amazon’s Alexa or a Google Home speaker, allowing you to request music based on your mood. It also has a Model Context Protocol, which can connect to your AI service of choice if you want to ask ChatGPT to play music on your speakers.
The company is highlighting its Sonos Custom Agents, which let users customize their agents to do various tasks throughout the system, like triggering speakers in a certain room at a certain time. You can also change the voices used if maybe you’d like the AI in your kitchen to sound like a fancy French chef, or have your bathroom speaker talk to you like a pirate.
“Obviously AI is something that's very hot these days, clearly,” Patel says. “So we have integrated various pieces of AI into our system.”
When asked what products Sonos 27 and its AI features would work with, a Sonos representative wrote via email that Sonos 27 will work in Sonos’ S2 app, but not the S1 app—the version that controls some older Sonos equipment. So owners of older Sonos hardware won't be able to access these new AI features.
“Sonos 27 is designed to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities, so not every product will support every new feature,” the representative wrote. “We want to be transparent about those limitations while continuing to support products with security and ongoing updates for as long as the hardware allows.”
Despite the stated effort to be transparent, Sonos says it won’t release details about compatibility or upgrade paths for each product until “a later date.”
Sonos Fabric
Sonos has an official name for the network its products use to sync across rooms: Sonos Fabric.
“Sonos Fabric is the name of the magic that has existed for what Sonos was built on,” Patel says. “The idea of, you have one speaker, two speakers, three speakers, and how they magically work together in a home theater setup or a bonded setup or group.”
Two new features are coming to that newly christened technology. One is what Sonos calls portable surround, which enables users to take devices from one room to another and have them sync there. So if you have a main soundbar by your TV but want to bring in another couple of speakers from other rooms to act as surround sound speakers for movie night, the Sonos products can detect their location and moderate which audio to play where.
Second is the ability to switch audio between the speakers and headphones, which Sonos calls Headphone Linking.
Sonos Ace Ultra
Sonos’ first pair of over-ear headphones arrived in 2024, right during the height of the Sonos app woes. The Sonos Ace were very good, except the headphones didn’t work within Sonos’ speaker ecosystem. Sonos wants to fix that problem with its follow-up headset, the Sonos Ace Ultra.
It has 35 hours of battery life and can connect to devices via USB-C and 3.5 mm. More importantly, it can connect to other Sonos speakers via Wi-Fi. The Ace Ultra runs on Sonos Fabric, which means it can connect to your wider Sonos system and let you switch playback between speakers and the headphones
“With a single push of a button, you'll be able to suck music into your headphones,” Patel says.
Sonos Beam Ultra
Sonos introduced a new soundbar, called the Beam Ultra. It’s an upgrade of the company’s existing Sonos Beam with nine drivers, four more than the past Beams. They’re also upward-firing drivers that bounce the sound off your ceiling for better acoustics. The Beam Ultra has AI-enabled features, like AI speech enhancement that aims to make dialog more discernible in loud scenes. The Beam Ultra can connect via Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and wired HDMI eARC.
This is a lot of change for Sonos, something the company hasn’t always handled gracefully. Sonos’ home systems already aren’t the easiest to set up, sometimes requiring separate apps for older products. The company may be rejiggering itself as an “audio operating system,” but its software has long been the source of its troubles with getting its products to work right. Will AI smarts fix that? Maybe for its newer devices. But anyone with an existing system may still struggle.
The AI features on products and in the Sonos 27 app will be opt-in, meaning you can avoid them entirely. “That really is our new approach to our app release,” Patel says. “We're going to bring our customers along. We're going to listen more.”
That would be a good plan. Sounds like Sonos’ speakers will be listening more, too.

The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Wednesday wrapped up a key meeting in Ayodhya, announcing several changes to its organisational structure, including the appointment of Govind Dev Giri as the Trust’s General Secretary. Giri succeeded Champat Rai, who had stepped down taking moral responsibility in connection with the alleged Ram Temple donation theft case. In a statement, Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) international president Alok Kumar congratulated Giri on his appointment as general secretary, saying that his leadership would provide guidance to everyone, as per PTI. Swami Govind Dev Giri Maharaj, earlier known as Acharya Kishoreji Madangopal Vyas, was born on January 25, 1949, in Belapur village of Maharashtra’s Ahmednagar district, according to Bhishma School of Indian Knowledge System. His followers popularly refer to him as “Swamiji”. Coming from a family with a long tradition of spiritual learning and religious practice, Giri was introduced to India’s ancient spiritual traditions from an early age. He completed his primary schooling in his native village before joining Tatvagyan Vidyapeeth, an institution founded by Pandurang Shastri Aathavale, who pioneered the socio-religious movement known as “Swadhyay”. Giri later earned a bachelor’s degree in Philosophy under Aathavale’s guidance. He subsequently spent years delivering religious discourses and became a prominent spiritual figure. His association with the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust began in 2020. As a trustee, he was entrusted with overseeing the collection and management of funds for the construction of the Ram Temple. The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust appointed retired Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra as its first Chief Executive Officer (CEO) as part of a major organisational restructuring following allegations of donation theft. Mishra, who led the Indian Air Force’s Western Air Command during Operation Sindoor, was chosen from a final shortlist of three candidates after the Trust’s selection committee evaluated 5,585 applications for the newly created post. The Trust also appointed Mahesh Bhagchandka as treasurer and expanded its governing body by inducting three new trustees — Madan Mohan Pandey from Ayodhya, Bhagchandka from Delhi and Dr Nirmala Yadav from Shikohabad. After his appointment, Mishra thanked the selection committee and the Trust for entrusting him with the responsibility. He expressed confidence that he would be able to fulfil the duties associated with the post. Mishra, who is from Uttar Pradesh’s Deoria district, served in the Indian Air Force for several decades and held senior command positions. His service record includes multiple military honours, including the Yudh Seva Medal. Saif Ali Khan recently interacted with fans during his first-ever Instagram Live session, joining through his official fan account. The actor, who does not have an official Instagram account, took time out from the promotions of his upcoming film Haiwaan to answer questions about the project and his experience of working on the crime thriller.
Saif Ali Khan hosts first Instagram Live session ahead of Haiwaan premiere; reveals why he thought his character was ‘really cool’
During the interaction, Saif was asked what prompted him to come on board the film. The actor revealed that the opportunity to collaborate with director Priyadarshan and the uniqueness of his character were among the key reasons behind his decision. In Haiwaan, Saif plays a visually impaired character who is also capable of taking on action sequences.
"The role and working with Priyan sir. Having this kind of blind character, that does action. Can you imagine? Can you imagine like a visually impaired person who has special abilities and can fight and do all kinds of things? So I thought that was really cool," he said.
The film also marks the reunion of Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar after 18 years. The actors were previously seen together in Tashan, which released in 2008. Their return to the screen together has become one of the talking points surrounding Haiwaan.
Speaking about the film and his experience of working with Akshay once again, Saif said he is looking forward to the thriller's release. "I'm very much looking forward to. it's nice thriller. (I) got to work with Akshay (and I am) playing a blind character. So it was challenging and lots of fun," he said.
Haiwaan is co-written and directed by Priyadarshan and is produced by KVN Productions and Thespian Films. The film is a remake of Priyadarshan's 2016 Malayalam crime thriller Oppam, which starred Mohanlal in the lead role.
The upcoming Hindi adaptation features an ensemble cast comprising Akshay Kumar, Saif Ali Khan, Boman Irani, Shriya Pilgaonkar and Saiyami Kher. The film is expected to blend crime, suspense and action, with Saif's visually impaired character forming an important part of the narrative.
Haiwaan is scheduled to release in theatres on September 11. The film also marks the final screen appearance of veteran actor Asrani, who passed away in October 2025.

Shares in the fast-fashion brand Shein slumped by as much as 10% as the China-founded company made its long-anticipated trading debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
The Singapore-headquartered company, once valued at almost $100bn (£74bn), went public on Tuesday pricing shares at HK$48.56, valuing the business at just over $26bn.
However, minutes after the flotation, which raised HK$13.6bn, the stock fell as much as 10%, pushing the online retailer’s valuation below $25bn. Shein’s share price recovered some ground to be 4% below its offer price by the end of trading, at HK$46.62.
“Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion,” said Leigh Gui, Shein’s chief financial officer, after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading.
The lacklustre launch as a publicly listed company comes after one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings in recent years, after plans to list in New York were blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns.
Shein also considered a £50bn flotation in London but faced similar questions about its supply chain from campaigners, MPs and investors.
Nevertheless, the company has become one of the world’s biggest listed fashion groups, with a valuation around the same as the Swedish retailer H&M. The Zara owner, Inditex, has a market capitalisation of about $213bn.
Shein reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world at the time. The plunge in its value since has been driven by regulatory changes around the world that threaten its business model of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods.
The company swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the US removed its “de minimis” import duty exemption on small packages, hitting its sales in the country.
The EU is also cracking down on the loophole, introducing a €3 (£2.56) duty on small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc in June, and intends to phase it out, while the UK has said it will do the same by October 2028.
On Tuesday, France began imposing penalties on some fast-fashion items to curb the surge in sales of cheap products sold by retailers such as Shein and its Chinese rival Temu.
Paris passed a fast-fashion law in June to address concerns about overproduction, with the penalties calculated using a formula that factors in the number of products sold, their prices and repairability.
The penalties, which are set to increase in 2030, range from €0.25 for a pair of boxer shorts or socks to €12 for a coat, with the amount capped at 50% of the product’s pre-tax sales price.
China’s commerce ministry has called the French law discriminatory and a trade barrier and said it could be in violation of World Trade Organization principles.
Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at about the start of 2022, a move viewed by analysts as designed to avoid increasing scrutiny of Chinese companies.
After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.

Blue Origin wins NASA contract for telecommunications on Mars
Can you hear me now?
NASA announced today that it has awarded Blue Origin the contract to develop the Mars Telecommunications Network. The company has taken a deal worth potentially $700 million to create a high-performance Mars telecommunications orbiter for the agency by December 31, 2028. Once operational, the orbiter will transmit "science data, imagery, navigation information, and critical mission communications for spacecraft operating on and around the planet."
The space agency is using its Artemis program to explore the moon. Progress has been slow but resulted in a successful human crewed mission earlier this year, and those missions will serve as preparation to eventually send astronauts to Mars. NASA will need more data as it continues to work toward that goal, so having a reliable way to send that information from the Red Planet to the Blue Dot will be essential.
Blue Origin has already worked with the space agency, securing a contract to build lunar landers at the start of this year. In May, the company's New Glenn rocket program took a setback after a launchpad explosion, and although Blue Origin's CEO claimed repairs on the launchpad would be done by the end of 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman projected it would be out of commission until 2028.

Pune-based startup Minimac Systems has raised ₹30 Cr ($3.2 Mn) in a fresh funding round led by Zerodha’s investment arm Rainmatter as it looks to scale its lubricant recycling and circularity infrastructure across India. Minimac plans to deploy the fresh capital towards research and development (R&D) of miniaturised fluid-treatment infrastructure, fleet automation and fluid analytics. Some of the funds will also help in deepening its recycling technology and expand its doorstep services footprint. Founded in 2012 by IIM Indore alum Anshuman Agrawal, Minimac Systems focuses on lifecycle management of lubricants. The startup operates across three areas of lubricant circularity. While nano circularity offering focuses on monitoring lubricant condition and contamination while the oil remains within industrial equipment, it restores recoverable lubricant by removing contaminants under micro circularity. Meanwhile, its ‘Recycling on Wheels’ offering deploys mobile treatment systems directly at industrial plants, allowing companies to assess and restore lubricants onsite instead of transporting the oil to a treatment facility. “This investment lets us bring advanced restoration and circularity infrastructure within reach of many more industrial plants across India,” Agrawal said. India is the world’s third-largest lubricant market, trailing only the United States and China, and consumes more than 5 Mn tonnes of lubricants and greases, annually. However, the country imports more than 60% of its base oil requirements, with its annual base oil import bill exceeding $2.7 Bn. The startup expects the demand for lubricants is expected to grow between 4-5% annually over the next five years. Minimac claims to have deployed more than 2,500 miniaturised fluid-treatment systems with a combined installed processing capacity of over 3 Lakh liters per minute. The startup claims to have worked across more than 2,200 industrial assets and kept over 14 Mn litres of lubricant in productive use across India and international markets. Its customers include NTPC, Adani Power, JSW Steel, Tata Steel, Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum, Hindustan Petroleum, Reliance Industries, Shell and ExxonMobil, among others. The startup aims to help abate 860 gigagrams of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions by 2034.

South Africa reappoint Mosimane as head coach
- Published
Pitso Mosimane has been reappointed as head coach of South Africa's men's national team.
The 62-year-old previously served as Bafana Bafana boss between July 2010 and June 2012.
He replaces Hugo Broos, who stepped down after five years in the role when his contract expired at the end of July.
The Belgian led the side to a third-placed finish at the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) and the last 32 of this year's World Cup, when South Africa returned to the finals for the first time since hosting in 2010.
The decision to rehire Mosimane was approved by the South Africa Football Association's executive committee on 8 August, but the former Mamelodi Sundowns boss was unveiled to the media in Johannesburg on Tuesday after finalising his contract and technical team.
The length of his deal has not been announced.
South Africa failed to qualify for the 2012 Afcon during Mosimane's first stint in charge after mistakenly believing a draw in their final group game against Sierra Leone would be enough to secure a spot at the finals.
He parted company with Bafana Bafana in June 2012 after a 1-1 home draw against Ethiopia in their first qualifier for the 2014 World Cup.
Since then he has enjoyed club success with Sundowns and Egyptian giants Al Ahly, winning the African Champions League three times.
More recently he has had spells managing in Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Iran.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

Mumbai/New Delhi:
 The future of Rohit Sharma and the shape of India’s ODI team for the next World Cup cycle are set to dominate discussions when the BCCI’s top brass meets in Mumbai on Thursday for a wide-ranging performance review.
While recent defeats in Ireland, England and Sri Lanka will be assessed, board officials are understood to be more concerned about the lack of a clearly defined ODI roadmap at a time when preparations for the 2027 World Cup should be taking shape.
BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia, president Mithun Manhas, head coach 
Gautam Gambhir
, chief selector 
Ajit Agarkar
 and Centre of Excellence chief VVS Laxman will attend the meeting, with ODI and Test captain 
Shubman Gill
 and T20I skipper Shreyas Iyer also expected to be present.
At the centre of the discussions lies the most sensitive issue facing Indian cricket: Rohit’s future. Though there is immense respect for the veteran opener’s stature and achievements, selectors and members of the team management are increasingly aware of the need to prepare for a post-Rohit era.
According to sources, one option under consideration is to evaluate Rohit’s role on a series-by-series basis rather than committing to a long-term plan through the entire World Cup cycle.
“It’s very tough on a young captain like Shubman Gill when there is no clear direction. The dressing-room environment in the ODI team hasn’t been the best, especially when it comes to dealing with stalwarts,” a BCCI source said.
The uncertainty around Rohit reflects a broader concern. Of India’s three national teams, the ODI side is regarded as the least settled. Injuries and workload management have prevented selectors from identifying a stable core, leaving several key positions unresolved.
The fast-bowling allrounder’s role remains a particular headache. Hardik Pandya continues on a managed workload programme after recurring fitness issues, while Nitish Kumar Reddy is yet to receive full clearance following rehabilitation.
“Hardik, at the moment, has been cleared to bowl six overs in a day. Reddy is still to clear his fitness tests. The ODI team doesn’t have even half of the core ODI team ready. It has to be a joint effort between the CoE and the team management to zero in on players and formulate a roadmap to get them all on the park as soon as possible,” the source said.
The review was initially planned after the Ireland and England tours but was postponed because of the subsequent Sri Lanka assignment. It will now cover India’s performances across multiple tours, including Zimbabwe and Sri Lanka.
India’s 2-0 T20I series defeat in Ireland and the 4-0 drubbing in England raised alarm bells, with the 125-run loss at Nottingham viewed internally as one of the team’s poorest performances in recent years. Gill’s ODI side also lost the England series 2-1.
However, officials insist the exercise will focus on solutions rather than assigning blame, with particular emphasis on recurring issues in preparation, selection and execution.
Fitness management is expected to be another major talking point. Jasprit Bumrah missed the Sri Lanka tour after aggravating a knee problem, while Washington Sundar, Nitish Kumar Reddy and Harshit Rana remain in line for fitness assessments at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru on Sept 9.
With a two-Test tour of New Zealand scheduled for Nov and a packed calendar ahead, the board wants tighter coordination between the medical staff, strength-and-conditioning team and national selectors to ensure greater player availability.
New role for Laxman
The meeting could also have significant administrative consequences. Laxman is being considered for an expanded role, with discussions continuing over a possible Director of Cricket position overseeing coaching, selection and player-development pathways. Agarkar’s tenure as chief selector, which ends later this month, will also come under review, with a one-year extension among the options being discussed.
Board President’s XI fixture vs visiting teams may be back
Meanwhile, BCCI is also examining the possibility of reviving the traditional Board President’s XI match before home series, following a recommendation from Manhas. The fixture, which historically featured leading domestic performers and Test hopefuls against visiting teams, has often served as a stepping stone for future India players while providing valuable match preparation to touring sides.

Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan on Wednesday (September 2, 2026) sought the support of the Union government and the Coconut Development Board to establish a Coconut Value-Addition Park in the State for modernising the coconut sector and ensuring increased incomes for the farmers.
The Chief Minister was addressing the World Coconut Day celebrations organized under the aegis of the Coconut Development Board here. Mr. Satheesan underscored the need to restructure coconut farming in Keralam through a shift from traditional methods to scientific and planned plantation models. It is important that productivity is increased through scientific management and effective disease control, he added.
Agriculture Minister T. Siddique, who presided, said the government intended to implement a ‘Coconut Rejuvenation Plan’ with the support of the Union government and the Coconut Development Board. He said the Agriculture Department will submit a ₹500 crore project to the Coconut Development Board. The project will cover all aspects of coconut farming right from the production of planting material to marketing, he said. In the first phase of the programme, the department intends to take forward the activities with ₹500 crore as the board’s share and ₹41 crore as the State government share, he said.

A case back in focus: All you need to know about Disha Salian's death case as HC orders CBI probe
Disha Salian died on June 8, 2020, after she fell off the 14th floor of a residential building in Mumbai's Malad area.
The Bombay High Court on Wednesday ordered the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to launch a probe into the death of Disha Salian, a former manager of actor Sushant Singh Rajput. Ordering the CBI investigation, the court slammed the Mumbai Police for treating the celebrity manager's death as an accident for six years and said there were "glaring discrepancies" in their probe.
"In the present case, the investigation went on for about six years. The investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers. Therefore, an investigation by the CBI is necessary in this case," PTI quoted the high court.
ALSO READ: CBI to probe Disha Salian case, HC says ‘no one can be made accused unless...’
Salian's demise eventually led to a massive clamour about foul play as Rajput died less than a week after she fell to death. The case also gained national attention as it included big names from the entertainment industry as well as the political world.
Here's all you need to know about Disha Salian's death case:
- Disha Salian died on June 8, 2020, after she fell off the 14th floor of a residential building in Mumbai's Malad area. At the time, Mumbai Police registered an Accidental Death Report (ADR).
- Salian had briefly worked as Sushant Singh Rajput's manager before her death. Rajput died six days later, on June 14, 2020. His death was separately investigated, including by the CBI, which subsequently filed a closure report concluding that he died by suicide. The court concerned is yet to decide on that report.
- The death of Disha Salian, investigated by the Malvani police, was treated as suicide. According to the police, which filed an affidavit in the Bombay High Court in July 2025, Disha Salian had jumped off the window of a flat, and the postmortem report revealed no signs of sexual and/or physical assault on the dead.
- Disha's father, Satish Salian, had approached the Bombay High Court seeking a CBI investigation in March 2025. He alleged that his daughter had been raped and murdered and claimed there had been an attempt to cover up the circumstances surrounding her death. He also sought an FIR against Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray.
- A bench comprising Justices Sarang Kotwal and Ranjit Sinha Bhonsale on Wednesday criticised the manner in which the investigation had been conducted. The court observed that the police investigation "raises more questions than answers" and said a case investigation cannot continue for an inordinately long period without reaching a proper conclusion.
- The High Court noted that despite the passage of approximately six years, the police had not registered an FIR for a cognisable offence. "In this case, we are of the opinion that the police had sufficient opportunity to investigate the offence, but they have not registered the FIR and have not carried out the investigation of a cognisable offence," the court said.
- The judgment referred to several alleged shortcomings, including the delayed spot panchnama. The court also questioned the absence of blood at the location where Salian reportedly fell and raised doubts about the injuries recorded on her body.
- The High Court has directed the CBI to register an FIR and record the statement of Satish Salian. It also ordered Mumbai Police to hand over all relevant case papers to the central agency immediately. A suitably experienced and senior officer is to lead the investigation.
- The court did not hold any individual responsible for Salian's death. "Nobody shall be treated as an accused unless in the opinion of the investigating officer there are sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against him depending on the material collected during the investigation," the HC said. The court also refrained from making any remarks against Aaditya Thackeray or any other person.
- The responsibility now lies with the CBI to examine the evidence and establish whether a criminal offence occurred. If the investigation finds sufficient evidence, the agency can submit an appropriate report before the competent court. If no offence is established, the CBI must file a summary report.

This fall, clinicians and researchers around the world will gather at conferences to discuss the future of psychiatric care, including the next edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), expected in 2030.
It will be the first revision since 2013, when TikTok didn’t exist and generative AI wasn’t a source of health information. That same year, Facebook retired its old ranking system and moved to a machine learning model built to predict what would keep someone scrolling. The way algorithms now shape how people think about food, their bodies, and themselves would have seemed like science fiction in 2013.
Clinicians already routinely assess family dynamics, trauma history, and substance use when evaluating someone for an eating disorder. At a time when social media has become one of the primary ways many people encounter messages about bodies, food, and exercise, a patient’s digital environment deserves the same scrutiny. The next DSM should encourage clinicians to assess algorithmic exposure as part of a comprehensive eating disorder evaluation.
The DSM focuses on observable symptoms and diagnostic criteria rather than offering a theory of etiology. It addresses context separately through descriptive text, explicitly considering external influences, including environmental, genetic, physiological, and temperamental risk factors, as well as cultural and gender-related issues, and the development and course of a condition. These sections provide clinical context rather than a definitive account of why a disorder develops. For example, in its discussion of eating disorders, the DSM can describe factors associated with increased risk while leaving the underlying causes open to multiple biological, psychological, and social explanations. This structure allows the manual to acknowledge influences of a disorder without taking a firm stance on etiology.
Within that framework, social media algorithms could be considered a modern environmental influence added to those already addressed by the DSM. Algorithm-driven exposure may contribute to the onset, maintenance, or exacerbation of eating disorder psychopathology by increasing repeated exposure to body comparison, restrictive eating content, compulsive exercise messaging, and appearance-focused social reinforcement.
In May of this year, the National Eating Disorders Association surveyed nearly 2,700 people — including those who have experienced eating disorders, clinicians, and caregivers — about social media’s effect on body image. Eighty-two percent said social media had triggered eating disorder thoughts or behaviors. Clinicians described patients in treatment constantly bringing up GLP-1 content unprompted. People in recovery described specific ads and videos triggering relapse.
None of that proves social media causes eating disorders, which remain complex conditions shaped by biology, psychology, and environment together. However, it does show that digital exposure now belongs in the same category as the other environmental factors clinicians are trained to ask about. That’s the gap the DSM-6 could close.
For many adolescents and young adults, an algorithm-driven feed may be as psychologically influential as their in-person peer group, while remaining largely invisible in the clinical interview. Recognizing digital reinforcement as a clinically relevant maintaining factor wouldn’t require changing a single diagnostic criterion. It would simply bring the manual into closer alignment with what clinicians are already seeing in practice.
There’s also a related piece that current diagnostic language mostly misses: the emotional response to digital exposure. Feelings of guilt, inadequacy, and anxiety after viewing triggering content are not incidental side effects. For someone with an eating disorder, those responses can be part of the cycle through which symptoms are reinforced and recovery becomes more difficult. A DSM revision could direct clinicians to assess that loop of exposure, emotional response, and symptom reinforcement as part of a comprehensive evaluation, rather than relying on it to surface during treatment.
From its first edition in 1952 to the current DSM-5-TR, the diagnostic manual has shifted alongside major changes in psychiatry’s understanding of mental illness. DSM-I reflected the dominant psychodynamic thinking of its era, while later revisions moved toward standardized, symptom-based diagnostic criteria designed to improve reliability across clinicians and research settings. Over time, the DSM expanded its attention to cultural considerations, risk factors, prognostic factors, and the broader context in which disorders develop and persist. That history matters because it demonstrates that the DSM was intended to evolve as the world around it changed. We are in just such a moment.
Many will point out that the manual isn’t designed to explain every cause of every mental illness, and they’re right. But it is designed to give clinicians the context they need to assess patients accurately. Right now, a clinician following the DSM to the letter has no structured prompt to ask a patient with an eating disorder about their digital environment, even when that environment may be actively reinforcing the illness.
By 2030, when the next manual arrives, the platforms will look different, and so will the content on them. What shouldn’t change is the expectation that clinicians ask about it. In the next four years, DSM-6 has a chance to make that expectation explicit by recognizing digital environments as part of the broader clinical context in which eating disorders develop, persist, and recover. It should take it.
Jessica Scheer is CEO of the National Eating Disorders Association. Riley Nickols, Ph.D., is a sports psychologist and clinical adviser for the National Eating Disorders Association.

The story so far: A ‘peptide party’ scheduled for August 29 in Koramangala in Bengaluru was cancelled after Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration officials shut down the gig. It was an invite-only biohacking event that was advertised only online, offering — among other party staples like music and networking — ‘peptide tasting’. This immediately triggered pushback from the medical community, and State health regulators sprung to the act to put an end to the event.
What are peptides?
Peptides are the fundamental building blocks of proteins, shorter chains of amino acids. Proteins, on the other hand, are typically long, complex chains of 50 or more amino acids. Peptides are smaller, often containing anywhere from two to 50 amino acids. They serve as biological signalling molecules and instruct cells, including being the starting point for functions including hormone production, tissue repair, immune response and metabolic regulation.
The key point is that the human body naturally produces many peptides; common ones in the public domain include insulin and endorphins. Synthetic proteins have also been created in laboratories for therapeutic uses — even these are quite common — synthetic insulin and more recently, GLP-1 receptor agonists popular as weight-loss drugs.
Peptides as biohacks
Peptides have suddenly assumed centre stage as part of the orchestrated global longevity and wellness movements. Spread by online influencers and some wellness companies, this trend has crystallised into off-label units that are reportedly able to help rapid muscle recovery, aid muscle growth and fat loss, improve sleep, and, above all, act as anti-ageing agents. Biohackers use specific synthetic or medical peptides to mimic natural hormones, boost muscle development, or speed up healing. These seldom fall within the ambit of prescription drugs, nor are the risks and benefits discussed in proper consultation rooms.
In a paper in Cureus in June this year, Kirubel T. Hailu et al discuss Unregulated Peptide Use in the Age of Biohacking: Digital Promotion, Gray-Market Access, and Emerging Public Health Risks. They write: Unregulated peptide use is emerging as a digitally mediated public health concern. Although peptide-based medicines have important therapeutic roles when developed, prescribed, manufactured, and monitored through regulated pathways, online biohacking and wellness spaces increasingly promote experimental or weakly evidenced peptides for fat loss, recovery, aesthetics, cognition, performance, and longevity.
What was planned in Bengaluru?
Media reports say that the planned peptide party in Bengaluru was to be an intimate gathering (around 50 attendees), bringing together people from all walks of life interested in ‘biohacking’. While biohacking operates on the principle that one needs to alter one’s lifestyle to live longer and live healthy, it also implies a belief that the human body is ‘editable’. Promotional material circulated online hyping up the meet to be the start of the ‘next wave of science’, offering testing samples of peptides.
The event was called off after doctors raised red flags about the unsupervised distribution of medical compounds, saying this would pose serious risks to health, including severe “allergic reactions, hormonal imbalance, and organ strain.” They also warned that misdosing or overdosing can lead to severe complications for individuals.
The Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration team stepped in, issuing a formal notice to the organisers, demanding proof of the exact composition of the products, manufacturing sources, Drug licenses, evidence for health claims, and the proposed arrangements for medical supervision during the party.
The organisers said they intended only to educate participants about biohacking, not to cause harm, but they couldn’t immediately provide the comprehensive documentation required to meet human-use safety standards. They officially cancelled the meetup.
What’s the future?
Constant vigil and monitoring of online trends as biohacking grows is absolutely essential in order to not cause harm from completely experimental techniques like peptide parties. If anything, the shutdown of the Bengaluru event has only highlighted the need for tight regulatory boundaries to curb unlicensed wellness ventures.

Few visual patterns in contemporary art are as immediately recognizable as Yayoi Kusama’s polka dots. They have covered pumpkins, rooms, trees, handbags and entire buildings. Even after her death at 97 was announced last week, her dots will remain the visual shorthand by which millions know her work.
The dots are playful enough to delight children and unmistakable enough to function as a global brand. Yet they came from a darker place: the hallucinations, obsessive thoughts and fear of self-obliteration that Kusama described as following her from childhood.
When I interviewed Kusama in 2016 for the Swedish newspaper Svenska Dagbladet, ahead of a major Scandinavian retrospective at Moderna Museet in Stockholm, I asked what the dots meant to her. The interview was published in Swedish; her original answers quoted here have not previously appeared in English.

Harlequins have signed Zimbabwe winger Edward Sigauke.
The 22-year-old has played 12 times, scoring eight tries, for his country, having made his international debut in 2024.
Quins head coach Jason Gilmore said: "Eddie is a player we've been tracking and we're really pleased to get his signing over the line.

Variety will honor Joel Crawford, the DreamWorks Animation filmmaker behind the Oscar-nominated “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish” and the upcoming “Forgotten Island,” with the Creative Impact in Animation Award at this year’s SCAD AnimationFest.
The honor will be presented Sept. 25 at SCADshow in Atlanta, where Crawford’s latest feature “Forgotten Island” will screen. The festival runs Sept. 23 through 25. Past recipients of the award include Chris Miller, director of “Smurfs”; Nick Park, director of “Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl”; and “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” directors Joaquim Dos Santos, Kemp Powers and Justin K. Thompson.
“SCAD is honored to partner with Variety in presenting the Creative Impact Award in Animation to Joel Crawford,” says Christina Routhier, senior executive director of SCAD theaters and festivals. “Joel’s work reflects a rare balance of technical mastery and heartfelt storytelling and we’re excited to screen his latest project ‘Forgotten Island.’ For our SCAD animation students, his career is a powerful example of how bold creative risks and a deeply personal point of view can shape the future of the medium. We are thrilled to celebrate his contributions to animation at SCAD AnimationFest.”
Popular on Variety
Crawford recently completed “Forgotten Island,” which he wrote and directed alongside longtime collaborator Januel Mercado. The film features the voices of H.E.R., Liza Soberano, Dave Franco, Jenny Slate, Manny Jacinto and Lea Salonga, and Universal Pictures releases it in theaters Sept. 25.
The recognition caps a fast climb through the studio system. Crawford married his love of the spaghetti western with a taste for absurdist comedy on “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” the DreamWorks Animation and Universal hit starring Antonio Banderas and Salma Hayek Pinault that drew Oscar, BAFTA and Golden Globe nominations and amassed nearly half a billion dollars at the global box office. He made his feature directorial debut on “The Croods: A New Age,” and after serving as head of story on the 2016 musical “Trolls,” he directed the animated “Trolls Holiday” special for NBC.
Crawford joined DreamWorks Animation in 2006 and became an integral part of its story department, contributing to “Trolls,” “Shrek Forever After,” “Rise of the Guardians,” “Bee Movie” and all three “Kung Fu Panda” films. His earlier story credits include “The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge Out of Water” and “Alvin and the Chipmunks: Chipwrecked.”
A native of Southern California by way of Hawaii, Crawford attended the California Institute of the Arts and worked as a caricature artist at Six Flags Magic Mountain before joining Nickelodeon. He is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and ASIFA-Hollywood. The SCAD honor marks a full-circle moment. In 2023, the university awarded him an honorary Doctorate of Humane Letters for his contributions to animation.

Antonio helps young Ghanaians chase Premier League dreams
- Published
In the heat of rural Leicestershire, the Samba Stars are chasing their dream.
Head coach Freddie Okyere has just finished a shooting exercise and allows the squad to catch their breath.
The teenagers from the Ghanaian academy, which is backed by former West Ham and Nottingham Forest forward Michail Antonio, have spent two and a half months in England with one goal - impressing clubs and earning a contract.
While scouts do visit west Africa, it is rare for academies to travel to the UK to put their players directly in front of professional clubs.
"The talent the lads have is incredible," said Antonio.
"We created Samba Stars Academy to give young players in Ghana access to elite coaching, shape them as players and create real avenues into the pro game and show how much talent Ghana has."
Based in Kumasi while building a new facility in Bompata, just over 100 miles north of Ghana's capital Accra, the Samba Stars' tactic has paid off.
Bournemouth, Everton, Manchester City, Charlton, Preston, Barnsley and Peterborough have all taken players on trial this summer.
"The first two or three weeks it hadn't sunk in, but then they saw the facilities we'd be [using] and the teams we were playing," said Okyere.
"They want to go and show what they can do. They are hungry, they really want it. I'm hoping there will be so much interest because we have so much talent here.
"With the facilities we will have in Ghana we feel we will be top two, top three [academies]. We hope we can bring the best of Ghana to Europe."
There are other success stories, with midfielder Listowell Lord Hinneh joining Middlesbrough in February after a trial., external
The 18-year-old has trained with the first team after swapping west Africa for England's north east.
"When I came in January, it was so cold. Experiencing something like that for the first time was tough," he told BBC Sport.
"Moving was a big milestone. It just makes me feel the dreams I've been having, thinking of trying to find myself in Europe to become a professional footballer.
"I feel the kind of dreams that I want, I'm on the verge. I'm on the way [to] becoming who I wanted to become."
Hinneh - whose sister Groovy lives in Leeds - met with the Samba Stars squad on their trip, offering advice.
"[I told them] what you've been dreaming about the future, it starts from here," he said.
"Don't just try, be so passionate. You need to play and enjoy it because you can have the success in whatever you're doing. You have to just put your heart in it."
'I'm seeing a different side of professional football'
All but one of the 20-strong visiting group initially had their visa application denied before eventually being admitted after re-evaluation.
Since arriving in the UK, they have been hosted by Brook House College in Market Harborough and trained at Harborough Town, who play in the National League North.
"The football [here] is very detailed," said 17-year-old goalkeeper Joshua Tetteh Tuwor.
"In Ghana we have the same passion but I'm seeing a different side of professional football.
"We are grateful to have such opportunities to train with elite coaches."
Rob Newman, formerly West Ham's head of recruitment and Manchester City's international scouting and recruitment manager, spent time with the academy in Ghana earlier this year and has helped coach them in Harborough.
"Hopefully clubs can see the potential," said the ex-Bristol City and Norwich defender.
"Nothing will give me greater pleasure in six months [than] going to see these boys playing in a first team in Europe. I believe they are two or three months away from being able to do that."
The Stars have played a series of games against youth teams from the EFL and non-league.
They started with a 9-0 thumping of Dorking Wanderers and also beat Under-21 sides from Sheffield Wednesday, Luton and Peterborough.
There were draws at Sheffield United and Barnsley while their only defeat came 3-2 against Preston's U21s.
Antonio watched them thrash Peterborough U19s 6-0 last month.
"You can see from what they've done since they've been in the UK - the results against top teams - that they have what it takes to play pro level," said the 36-year-old.
"It's great to help knock down barriers and give these lads a real chance."
'Back home everyone is depending on you'
Ghana have reached five of the past six Fifa World Cups - having never qualified before 2006 - and made the quarter-finals in 2010.
At this year's tournament, where they exited in the last-32 against Colombia, eight members of the squad were born overseas.
The Black Stars may not have come to rely heavily on diaspora talent, unlike some other African nations, yet the Ghana Football Association has made noises about widening its global search - something which could potentially impact home-grown talent.
"You have to have a tough mentality," said Sherif Mashud, an 18-year-old striker who has already had a trial with Hungarian top-tier side Zalaegerszegi thanks to his involvement with Samba Stars.
"Back home everyone is depending on you, everyone is looking up to you to succeed, to come and help them, your friends, your family. Everyone is praying for you."
The new English season has begun with six Ghana internationals on Premier League books: Mohammed Kudus at Tottenham, Antoine Semenyo with Manchester City, Brighton's Ibrahim Osman, Ipswich's new signing Abdul Fatawu and Coventry's Brandon Thomas-Asante and Caleb Yirenkyi.
The first to play in the English top flight was striker Nii Lamptey when he joined Aston Villa in 1994, while midfielder Michael Essien has made the most appearances, winning two titles with Chelsea.
Only two other Ghanaians have lifted the Premier League trophy - Jeffrey Schlupp and Daniel Amartey when Leicester stunned the world in 2015-16.
"Back home we've got people you grew up with and you might miss them, but that doesn't kill the dreams I'm here for," said Hinneh, who lists Kudus as his biggest inspiration and hopes to follow his heroes into the top flight after Boro missed out on promotion in last season's Championship play-off final.
"I'm trying to figure out what the reality is, what the future holds for me and then just chase the dreams."

Brentford sign £40m defender Diouf from West Ham
- Published
Brentford have signed West Ham defender El Hadji Malick Diouf in a deal worth up to £40m.
The 21-year-old Senegal left-back has joined on a five-year contract, with the club having an option to extend it by a further year.
The move sees Brentford paying an initial £35m for the player, with a further £5m in add-ons.
Diouf played in West Ham's Championship opener against Burnley, but was excluded from the matchday squads of the Hammers' following two games as a deal was worked on.

Diouf is returning to the Premier League after suffering relegation with the Hammers last season.
And his sale represents a big profit for West Ham on a player they paid Slavia Prague £19m for a year ago.
Diouf played 34 times for West Ham last season, providing five assists.
"He's a player that fits our ideal age profile, with lots of room to still develop," Brentford head coach Keith Andrews said.
Diouf said Andrews had convinced him he could continue to improve at the club.
And when asked about his ambition upon joining his new club said: "Why not win the league?"
He is Brentford's fifth summer signing of the summer after the arrivals of striker Callum Wilson, midfielder Mamadou Sangare, centre-back Jannik Schuster and winger Jaidon Anthony.
After breaking into the Senegal side last year, Diouf played four times at the World Cup this summer.

Brentford began their season on Saturday with a 3-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur and play Leeds on Sunday in their next league game.

A 27-second long video has gone viral on social media over the past week. The clip shows a mob, predominantly comprising men, kicking and attacking a woman in the middle of a busy street, while police personnel in the vicinity do little to nothing to prevent the attack.
The X user, Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst), posted the clip on August 31, claiming that a female Hindu teacher had been attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh. At the time of this article being written, the post had been reshared over 3000 times. (Archive)
Female Hindu teacher attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh pic.twitter.com/DQnvCjN8FK
— Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst) August 31, 2026
Pokhariyal later posted a reply to his tweet, attempting to correct his earlier claim. “Correction: The woman was reportedly assaulted by shopkeepers and salesmen after she complained about the shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law,” the tweet read.
Another X user, Deepak Sharma (@SonOfBharat7), posted the same clip, with a seperate claim that in Bangladesh, a Dalit teacher had allegedly offered water to an upper-caste Muslim child, following which she was chased down in the streets and thrashed. (Archive)

— Yati Sharma (@yati_Official1) August 31, 2026
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claims surrounding the viral clip, Alt News broke it down into keyframes. A reverse image search on one keyframe led us to a news report published by the Bangladeshi news portal BD News 24 on August 30.
According to the report, the incident took place at Bangladesh’s Rajbari clothes market, on August 29. The victim in the video is reportedly a female shop owner, who managed her own clothing shop in the market for 12 years. She had allegedly found that one of her female employees had started working in a different shop on August 22. In response, she dismissed the worker from her role at the shop and asked her collect payment in the following month.
Further, another news report published by The Dhaka Tribune on August 30, identifies the female shop owner as one Zakia Sultana, and the ex-employee as Shahana Parveen Bristy. In another report by the outlet Ajker Patrika, Sultana accused Bristy of turning up at her shop with 15-20 men on August 23 and intimidating and verbally abusing her.
This prompted Sultana to launch a protest at the clothes market on August 29 afternoon, along with her female employees. Enraged by this, several shop-owners from the Rajbari clothes market then attacked her, in the presence of police officers who had turned up at the spot to offer her protection, the report states. However, in the video it is visible the that men continue to kick and attack Sultana despite police presence.
We also found a video report from BBC News Bangla, uploaded on August 31, which shows recorded evidence of the attack.
News reports from Bangla TV, Views Bangladesh, and Jago News 24, dated September 1, also reveal that three people have been arrested in relation to the violent attacks on Sultana, as recorded in the viral video.
In conclusion, the viral clip which shows a woman being violently attack is indeed from Bangladesh, but the woman seen in the clip is Muslim, thereby refuting any allegation of a communal angle at play.
Further, the reason for the attack arises from a business dispute as reported by several credible news outlets, thus the aforementioned claims, including that Sultana is a Dalit teacher who was beaten up for offering water to a Muslim child or that she complained about the other shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law, are false and misleading.

Dan Driscoll’s Parting Shot
The Army secretary told Trump about problems in the Army and his friction with Hegseth, then resigned.
During a White House meeting last week, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll brought his concerns about the future of the Army under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directly to President Trump—a sign of how far tensions between the two Pentagon leaders had escalated, and of the dysfunction inside the building, four people familiar with the conversation told us.
Trump was surprised when Driscoll told him how many generals and other top officers had been fired, pushed out, or passed over for promotion under Hegseth, one of the people said. Driscoll argued that the Army could not transform itself the way it needs to, because of the departure of so many leaders, this person said, adding that Trump expressed concern about the deep cuts to the Army’s senior leadership. Driscoll informed the president of his intention to resign—and by today, Driscoll was on his way out.
Hegseth’s purge of the military has been so dramatic that with Driscoll gone, the military’s largest service is left without a top civilian leader, a Senate-confirmed top general, a confirmed Army general in charge of operations, or a confirmed commander of Army troops in Europe. Because of all the firings across the service over the past year, the Army, with more than 450,000 active-duty soldiers positioned across the globe, has fewer generals than at any point in recent history. Driscoll’s personal appeal to Trump just days before his exit was the most direct articulation of high-level concerns among Pentagon leaders about the strains facing the force—including Hegseth’s intervention in Army personnel decisions and the mounting demands of the Iran war.
The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that Driscoll had been “highly effective” in improving soldier readiness and advancing other administration priorities. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” Kelly wrote in a statement, using the administration’s preferred term for the Department of Defense.
Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment, and Driscoll did not respond to a call seeking comment. But a person familiar with his resignation told us that Driscoll had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” Hegseth did not have an immediate response to Driscoll’s departure.
Since his arrival at the Pentagon early last year, Hegseth—a former Fox News host who appealed to Trump loyalists by deriding a “woke” military and advocating for leniency for troops charged with war crimes—has sought to reshape the Army. He has placed like-minded generals in positions of influence, intervened to stymie the promotions of lower ranking-officers, and gutted diversity initiatives. The result was an Army depleted of leaders, and an Army secretary and a Pentagon chief at constant odds. Hegseth has ended dozens of Army careers, all without any clear explanation. He now has driven out the secretary of the Army.
Driscoll’s departure puts the Pentagon even more firmly under the control of Hegseth and his MAGA agenda. Driscoll is a confidant of Vice President Vance, a relationship that gave him access to the West Wing, and at times Driscoll served as a counterweight to Hegseth’s impulses, but only up to a point. Some current and former defense officials told us they believe Driscoll’s enmity toward Hegseth actually had the unintended consequence of broadening the purge of the uniformed ranks. And yet Driscoll’s departure, which had been expected for months, and the prospect that he will be replaced by someone more politically aligned with Hegseth are already raising fears inside the Army. “What happens then? Generational damage,” a defense official told us.
Driscoll arrived at the Pentagon in February 2025, a third-generation Army soldier who shared several things in common with Hegseth, his new boss. Like Hegseth, Driscoll joined the military in the most muscular years of Washington’s post-9/11 wars. Both men served in Iraq in a company-grade role. (Hegseth, a National Guardsman, also deployed to Afghanistan.) Both returned with sharp criticisms of America’s overseas adventures and the military’s hidebound ways. Both attended Ivy League schools: Hegseth, Princeton and Harvard; Driscoll, Yale Law, where he befriended the fellow veteran Vance. Both Driscoll and Hegseth have made unsuccessful runs for political office. Both have also eyed a return to politics. As Army secretary, Driscoll frequently reminded people that he had a direct line to the vice president, people familiar with the matter said, and told others that he had ambition to someday run for president himself—an ambition that Hegseth is also said to harbor.
But the two men differed starkly in temperament and style. Hegseth, who required an unprecedented tie-breaking Senate-confirmation vote from Vance after failing to win any Democratic support, is one of Trump’s most reliable MAGA warriors. He has publicly boasted about firing “woke” generals, dared military dissenters to quit, and demonized the mainstream media. Driscoll also supported administration policies but has done so in a more genial way that appealed to many lawmakers more than Hegseth’s combative approach before Congress. And unlike Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who has echoed Hegseth’s scornful and partisan tone on social media, Driscoll has steered clear of endorsing Hegseth’s most controversial actions or most of his culture-war priorities. Unlike Hegseth, Driscoll is friendly with the press, cultivated ties with lawmakers of both parties, and courted technology leaders as he promoted the Army’s sprint to transform how it wages war. That served him well in the administration, earning him additional responsibilities as director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and later as an unofficial mediator for the war in Ukraine. None of that sat well with Hegseth.
Army personnel appointments were a particular point of friction. Hegseth has not hesitated to push aside or promote officers as he sees fit, in many cases in ways that have irked others in the Pentagon. Driscoll advocated for General Randy George, the Army chief of staff whose name appeared on a list circulated before Trump’s return to office of senior officers who should be fired due to perceived transgressions against the MAGA agenda. Although Driscoll may have bought George time, Hegseth ultimately fired the general in April. Chris Donahue, the four-star general who headed U.S. Army Europe and Africa, followed several months later.
The Army has been without a top commander since George’s firing. General Christopher LaNeve, who was picked by Hegseth as the No. 2 officer in the Army, has been acting in that role, often going straight to Hegseth for decisions, bypassing Driscoll, according to defense officials. Hegseth is expected to nominate LaNeve to lead the Army, but Capitol Hill is already signaling that LaNeve would struggle to be confirmed, because of many lawmakers’ antipathy to Hegseth. “We are not going to reward Hegseth for what he did to the Army,” one congressional staffer told us.
The Army has long prided itself on representing the diversity of the country, but under Hegseth, minorities and women have been pushed out or barred from promotion. The military has long sought to be apolitical, but under Hegseth, troops are measured not by combat experience but by their perceived loyalty to the administration. Among the generals fired have been some of the most experienced and decorated in the service. Each departure marks the loss of decades of investment in that soldier and raises questions about how future troops can rise through the ranks.
Although Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal is expected to take over in the near term, many Pentagon officials fear that the administration will nominate the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, another Army veteran, to replace Driscoll. Parnell, who previously made a failed bid for U.S. Senate in Pennsylvania, shares Hegseth’s pugilistic spirit and interest in culture and personnel issues. Like Hegseth, Parnell has no experience managing a large organization and would face a contentious confirmation hearing. A new Army secretary who is more politically driven—and likely less experienced and less well connected than Driscoll—could keep the service embroiled in cultural fights rather than focused on the long-term planning that Driscoll and others believe it desperately needs.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

Dolly Parton’s most enduring contribution to science, from a public point of view, is probably Dolly, the cloned sheep. Though that was a reference to her prominent mammaries, a fact she reacted to with her characteristic good humour, despite the controversy, but the whole story is that Dolly Parton, singer, celebrity, and philanthropist, who died at 80, after a short battle with cancer, also stood solidly on the side of science.
Her contributions have been eulogised after her death last week, following a battle with cancer, and as a result, more people than ever know about her vast contributions provided specifically for the advancement of healthcare. In fact, Tedros Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, wrote on X, of her passing: “Today is a sad day as we mourn an exceptional artist, a true champion of kindness, and ambassador of science and public health.”
Her contributions to developing the COVID-19 vaccination have not received as much publicity as they deserve. In a tribute, Nature recorded that at least 37 research papers credit the Dolly Parton COVID-19 Research Fund with support. In March 2020, she gave $1 million to Vanderbilt Medical Centre in Nashville, Tennessee, to promote vaccine research. Nature also mentions that the “the money helped to fund the ‘critical’ early stages of research into a then-experimental messenger RNA vaccine eventually produced by Moderna, a biotechnology firm based in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The fund is acknowledged in the first published report of a phase I trial of the vaccine, which appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine in July 2020.”
But, that was not all. She posed while getting a COVID-19 vaccine injection, quipping: “I’m old enough to get it, and I’m smart enough to get it.” She went on to rewrite the lyrics to her famous song Jolene to promote vaccine uptake. “Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I’m beggin’ of you, please don’t hesitate” she sang, to do her bit to push people to take the shot.
This was not her venture into healthcare philanthropy though. When HIV research was in its early stages, in 1994, she contributed a version of You Gotta Be My Baby to the charity compilation Red Hot + Country, produced by the Red Hot Organization to raise funds for HIV/AIDS awareness and research. This was one of the standout songs in the album and was also significant in setting her on the path of philanthropy that was to become a life-long commitment.
U.S. media, since her death, have reported that Parton donated $1 million to Monroe Carell Jr. Children’s Hospital, Vanderbilt, to the pediatric cancer programme after her niece survived leukemia there, helping fund clinical trials and research into pediatric cancers. Later, she followed it up with another $1 million to advance research into pediatric infectious diseases. In January 2026, she released a new version of her 1976 song, Light of a clear blue morning, to celebrate her 80th birthday. The entire proceeds went to benefit paediatric cancer research at Monroe Carell. The East Tennessee Children’s Hospital in Knoxville was renamed the Dolly Parton Children’s Hospital in recognition of her continuing contributions.
She also contributed, through fund raising concerts and direct donations, to help build the LeConte Medical Center in Sevier County, Tennessee, where she grew up. The hospital opened in Sevierville in 2010 with the 30,000-square-foot Dolly Parton Center for Women’s Services, which includes the Dolly Parton Birthing Unit.
As Parton has departed, rhinestones and wigs and good humor et al, what she has left back on earth remains truly a shining example to good science and genuine philanthropy.

The plot to disrupt mail-in voting
A new whistleblower report warns that Trump’s mail-in voting requirements could cause chaos in the midterm elections.
It took the US government two years to roll out HealthCare.gov, nine months to pilot a direct tax-filing tool…and just 11 weeks to build a new system for processing Americans’ absentee ballots.
Before you cheer this rare instance of bureaucratic efficiency, however, please allow the other shoe to drop: That figure comes from an alarming new whistleblower report that foretells potential chaos in this fall’s midterm elections.
According to the whistleblower, the US Postal Service has rushed out a janky, error-prone processing system in its mad dash to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots. That order, currently paused, would require states to comply with new rules for preparing, tracking, and mailing ballots. Several states have since sued to stop it.
If the order does go into effect, however, the Postal Service has to be prepared. So the agency scrambled to hack together its new system — forgoing standard testing procedures and adding requirements that are likely to hold up thousands of outbound ballots, the whistleblower says.
According to the report, multiple USPS officials have described the system as “a shit show” that, as of late August, was apt to “completely crash.” “Move fast and break things” is actually not a great look for governments.
Go a little deeper
But the issue goes far beyond one IT meltdown at the post office, or even many IT meltdowns at many post offices. As my colleague Ian Millhiser has covered in depth, Trump’s March executive order could effectively end mail-in voting in several states by imposing a slate of last-minute requirements that election officials don’t have time to implement.
Let’s just take the narrow issue of ballot envelopes. Trump’s executive order directed the post office to issue new rules about the design of those envelopes, which the post office did…on August 21.
The new rules required that ballot envelopes bear a unique barcode and a logo that the Trump administration claimed would “facilitate proper handling” of election mail. But by that point in the season, a number of states were already preparing to mail their midterm ballots.
North Carolina starts mailing general election ballots this week, for instance. More than a dozen other states post theirs by late September. And even in the unlikely case that these states could design, order and distribute millions of compliant envelopes in the next few weeks…it’s not clear the post office could process them.
Under the new system, the Postal Service must individually scan every outbound ballot as it heads to voters, a process that the Trump administration says will take “less than a minute” each. Across millions of ballots, however, “less than a minute” adds up: potentially to more than 380,000 hours, in California’s case.
That’s enormously concerning, Ian writes. Should courts allow Trump’s order to go into effect, the states that can’t comply won’t be able to do mail-in voting this year. And there are a number of states — including Oregon, Washington, Hawaii, Colorado, Utah, and California — where the entire election is basically vote-by-mail.
”I think it is more likely than not that SCOTUS does not back Trump’s play here. But you can never rule anything out with this Supreme Court,” Ian said.
One link for later
➨ Listen to “your true self.” In one social science experiment, researchers found that participants who were asked to make an arbitrary decision based on their “true selves” — as opposed to their “rational” brains — were much happier with their choices in the end. So the next time you face a tough decision or a moment of personal ambiguity, you might also consider asking: “What would my true self do today?”
