Trump’s Economy Goes to the Polls
Trump wants Republicans to run on his record in the midterms. Democrats do as well.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the policies of the party in power; President Trump is hoping that Republicans steer into the skid. Last week, my colleagues reported that the president—dogged by the war in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and an economy that has Americans dipping into their savings for groceries and daily expenses—hopes that Republicans seeking to win reelection or gain seats will use his time in office to sway voters.
But that strategy could play directly into the hands of Democrats hoping to take back both chambers of Congress. My colleagues the Atlantic staff writers Michael Scherer and Ashley Parker join me this week to discuss Congress, the economy, and the midterm elections.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Ashley Parker: At the end of the day, one thing that President Trump is great at is getting people to sort of remember and understand what it is he ostensibly cares about, right? Whether that’s “Drain the Swamp” or Space Force. And Democrats need to find a way to signal—need an elevator pitch that voters can say, I’m voting for the Democrats because I know that my interest rate will go down to 3.875 percent.
[Music]
Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and this week, we need to think about the midterms.
The House of Representatives is back on Capitol Hill this week as the nation turns its attention to the general election. It’s the last opportunity for lawmakers to show they are working for their constituents.
Meanwhile, President Trump is trying to convince congressional Republicans to run on his record. But amid a war with Iran driving up the price of everyday items and a burgeoning trade war with Canada, Americans are feeling the pinch of the president’s agenda.
And Democrats, on the heel of bitter primary races around the country, are hoping to seize upon the president’s unpopularity, and they’re banking that Americans want something different. The question is: Are they right? I’m joined by my colleagues Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer to discuss.
Ashley, Michael, welcome to the show.
Michael Scherer: Thanks for having us.
Parker: Thanks for having us.
Harris: Ashley, I want to start with you first. Congress is back this week, and one of the first things that they must do is to fund the government, right? Do you think that Congress is more likely to get this done in a timely manner than we’ve seen in some of these previous spending cycles?
Parker: Yeah, I mean, a lot of these stopgap measures end up being incredibly fraught and going up to the last minute. This one is looking like it’s going to be less controversial, in part because what House members really wanna do is get back to their districts to campaign for the midterms. And so there’s a few things in there that might raise some eyebrows, but the sense right now is that they’ll be able to, they hope, push this through pretty quickly.
Harris: Speaking of kind of getting back to the districts for the midterms, right, this is a very important cycle. I feel like every cycle we say, It’s, you know—
Scherer: —most important election of your lifetime.
Harris: Exactly. The most important one of the lifetime. But this one is a pretty important cycle, particularly for Democrats hoping to stop the president’s agenda and for Republicans hoping to continue with the president’s policies moving forward.
Oftentimes, parties don’t like to make this a referendum on the presidency. I’m reminded of [Barack] Obama saying, I’m not on the ballot, but these policies are certainly on the ballot.
And you both have reported that Trump is planning to roll out a series of TV ads that are touting his personal record leading up to the midterms in November. What does this ad blitz say about the administration and how they’re feeling about the election prospects, Michael, and the president’s image?
Scherer: Yeah, so there’s a formula for midterm elections. It’s always a referendum on those in power. So the in-party—the people who hold the presidency, and if they also hold the House, the Senate—try their best to make it a choice, not a referendum, to basically put the opposing party in the spotlight, say, Look, they’re terrible and bad and have done all these awful things, and if you give them back power, it’ll be terrible. And they’re always fighting an uphill battle, because voters don’t see it that way, and voters tend to just, you know, say, I’m happy or I’m pissed off. And you know, for the last four decades, they’re almost always pissed off when it comes to a midterm.
This cycle is a little different because of voting patterns and the appeal of President Trump.
[It] used to be that Republicans turned out more than Democrats in midterms. Now that’s kind of reversed. Democrats are more likely to turn out in midterms. [It] used to be that presidents don’t really have much impact on who turns out in midterms, for the reasons I just said—you know, it’s a referendum, and people are upset. Republicans are betting on this idea that their biggest problem is motivation, that they have the voters out there, that if they can get those voters to the polls, they can stem their losses, they could actually overperform expectations.
But the polls right now show, you know, they’re not that excited. Like, a Fox News poll a few weeks ago asked, Are you extremely motivated to vote? Democrat voters were like 70 percent saying they’re extremely motivated; Republican voters, like 60 percent saying they were extremely motivated. And so the White House solution to that, the president’s solution to that, is to say, We’ve got the magic man on the stump here. We’re going to make this about President Trump, which really undermines the pattern I just described. You know, the Republicans and the Democrats now are in some way saying, We’re gonna make this a referendum on the president.
Parker: And to be clear, everything is always about President Trump. That’s just the rule of President Trump. And so as much as this strategy that Michael and I and our colleague Yvonne reported last week seems counterintuitive and is legitimately frustrating to some Republicans, the White House thinking and the president’s thinking is, It’s always about Trump, right?
And he likes it being about himself, and so if it’s gonna be about him, we might as well put him front and center and tout what we believe are his accomplishments.
Harris: Yeah, if he’s gonna be there, why run away from him? Might as well steer into the skid, right?
Scherer: The problem is that the more you’re talking about Trump and trying to convince people that he’s, you know, improved everyone’s lives when the polls show people don’t feel like he’s improved their lives in the last year and a half, the less you’re talking about Democrats.
And so, you know, that’s the choice they’re making. It’s not that it’s a terrible idea to be talking about the president.
You know, another pattern is, like, Obama would go out on the stump and, you know, [Joe] Biden went on the stump in his midterm elections, [George W. ] Bush went on the stump in his midterm elections, and would obviously talk about their own records. So it’s not like presidents don’t talk about themselves. The difference here is putting money on TV and digital media about the president.
Normally, the in-party only wants to talk about how terrible and bad the out-party is. And, you know, that’s especially true for super PACs. The president’s talking about spending. He’s got $400 million we know about. He may have hundreds of millions more in sort of dark money, basically independent money he’s collected. Normally, that money is just used to ravage the other side and just tear them apart. And the idea that the president’s gonna put some significant part of that behind convincing people that no tax on tips, or the stock-market highs, or the closed border have really done them well is what’s so controversial.
Harris: And how are congressional Republicans feeling about this? How have they sort of responded to the president trying to have his name sort of be more forward in the campaign?
Parker: In general, if they’re speaking candidly, which they don’t really do in public, because they’re fearful of the blowback from President Trump, they find him generally unhelpful in this moment, right? A lot of the things he says and does just further the sense that he and his party don’t care about voters like them.
So there’s some stuff he said. He was recently at a rally in South Carolina for Darline Graham, Lindsay Graham’s sister, who’s running to replace him, where he said, I know my economic numbers are bad, but they should actually be at 100 percent. I’m doing such a great job. That makes people—who, you know, are going to maybe two or three grocery stores right now to use their coupons to get the best deals on what they can—feel like, He has no idea what my life is like. That’s, like, a very clear one where he’s talking about the economy.
But some of his other favorite topics are the ballroom, the new construction of the helipad on the South Lawn. And among all the various controversies that Trump has, these are physical, tangible things that voters really latch on to that Trump loves to talk about. At his core, it’s, like, cool to be president, but he’s sort of more animated by being a developer, you know, and a construction magnate. And so when he is talking about the marbling or the gilding or the slope of the helipad, even though that has nothing to do with the economy, that’s sort of the problem. That reminds voters, Look, this guy is focused on things for himself and his rich friends that again have nothing to do with me.
So Republicans privately will say, This is a nightmare. But at the end of the day, he’s their president, he’s what they’ve got. They know now, in sort of our 12th, 13th year of Trump, he’s not gonna change, and so this is the landscape they live in.
Scherer: And the biggest issue right now is not what the president is saying; it’s what the president has done. He won election very clearly in ’24 on the idea that he would lower prices and sort of reverse the economic squeeze that had emerged under Biden. And if you go back to February, March, White House was saying, like, This is how we’re gonna message this. This is our plan: Gas prices are down; interest rates are down; homeownership’s more affordable; generally, prices, inflation is stabilizing and dipping down.
All that’s been reversed by the Iran war. And so the biggest issue is not what the president’s saying or not saying. It’s that on Sunday night, the U.S. again had kinetic strikes against Iran. And we talked to a bunch of Republicans last week, and every one of them said, Well, it’s gonna be okay because we’re gonna have less actual violence in the Middle East over the next couple months. Every time another bomb goes off in the Middle East, it’s a hit to Republicans at this point.
Parker: And which, by the way, Michael is talking about the president promising to lower prices. His other big promise was no more foreign wars, right? So the thing that is contributing to prices is another very clear broken promise.
Harris: Well, I wanted to ask: What are hearing about the administration’s strategy, current strategy in the war, right? As you mentioned, Michael, the bombings resumed over the weekend. Are we actually trying to get out of this war, and how are Republicans up for reelection talking to their constituents about it?
Scherer: What the White House and the political advisers want is basically a cease of violence right now for the next couple months. I mean, that’s their desire, and they want to keep squeezing the Iranians. The Iranians are not in a great position economically, so they can keep squeezing them. The problem is the Iranians have enormous leverage on Trump, as we’ve just been describing. And the Iranian position is: We control the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. position is: You don’t control the Strait of Hormuz. So there’s, like, this deadlock at the center of the conflict. So every time, you know, the Iranians re-mine the Gulf or fire at another ship and the U.S. feels tempted to retaliate, it’s undermining the strategy the president has. And right now, the president doesn’t have control over that.
Harris: When we come back, Ashley and Michael on the burgeoning trade war with Canada and the Democrats chances in the midterm elections.
[Music]
Harris: So, Ashley, we have this actual war with Iran, but we also have this developing trade war with Canada. And it feels like the culmination of something that Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, said in January at Davos about the ways that countries with smaller economies needed to start renegotiating and looking out for themselves a little bit more. And there’s been a lot of tension between him and President Trump.
But I guess the thing that I keep coming back to with this trade war with Canada is: How did we end up back here? Why are we in this trade war with Canada?
Parker: Well, it’s the South Park truism of “Blame Canada,” right? Like, it’s just an easy thing to know. I mean, Trump likes tariffs. That’s clear and that’s true. And he’s very frustrated with Canada, in part because, as he said, you know, on the one hand, he’s sort of ready to get to trade-war footing with our neighbor to the north, and on the other hand, he’d happily make Canada a 51st state.
But therein is kind of the rub. If you hear Trump talk about it, he sort of says, Canada is getting all of the advantages of being a state, right? We’re subsidizing them to the tune of $200 billion. That’s not an accurate number, but that is what he says. And the thing that bothers Trump more than anything else is sort of, in his view, when people are taking advantage of him, profiting off of him. And, you know, that goes to, you know, former aides writing best-selling books from their time in the White House, to countries he believes sort of should be showing more deference to the United States than they are.
And then on the flip side, you mentioned Mark Carney’s speech to Davos, where he said what we’ve been hearing publicly a bit, and especially privately from a lot of our other especially European allies, which is: Originally, after Trump’s first term, they sort of thought it was, like, a fever dream that they could PTSD black out when Biden returned to the scene. And I remember going on Biden’s first foreign trip—I can’t remember if it was like a G7 or a G20—but that was literally his message. It was like, America, the America you know, the America you love; we’re back.
And then when Trump came back to power, the view, especially from our allies, was like, Maybe Biden was the aberration, right? And even though we know, you know, allegedly Trump was not gonna run for a third term, like, the allies’ thinking is, We have no idea if a new Trump, if a J. D. Vance, or if a populist on the Democrats’ side is gonna come in. And we kind of have to—we can’t count on the U.S., and these tacit deals we used to make with the U.S. (and by that I don’t mean a trade deal, but sort of that, like, We show deference to the United States because they are a bigger, more powerful, and ultimately benevolent force in the world)—we’re willing to take that; we’re willing to subjugate ourselves a bit.
They’ve decided, like, We’re not gonna do that anymore. So you also have a changing stance from our allies being much more willing to stand up for the United States and say, like, I’m not gonna bend my knee, because I can’t count on the United States. And by the way, I could agree to the worst trade terms with this president possible, and that might only placate him until his next Truth Social post.
Harris: Yeah, you know, actually, to that point of sort of the deference that was shown, we’ve also seen the ways that the president has sort of out-and-out attacked allied nations in recent weeks, from South Korea, thinking about some of the threats towards places like Oman.
And these aren’t small things, right? Even the fact that you mentioned something like the president saying that he’s not gonna run for a third term—to even to even think about a third term is sort of moving into an uncharted territory. Where does that leave the sort of long-term view of American responsibility as a world player?
Scherer: I mean, I think everybody’s just waiting out Trump to see what happens next. And I think what you’ve seen in Canada is their conclusion. I mean, exactly how that fell apart is, you know, there’s conflicting stories. But it does seem pretty clear that Canada views its maximum point of leverage as being right now. I mean, if they threaten to withhold electricity from the United States before midterm elections, that obviously it could have huge impacts on Trump. If they threaten to withhold electricity in early January, when Trump’s a lame duck, it may not have the same import.
I think the rest of the world is just coping with Trump. I mean, he’s so unpredictable. We don’t know how the last two years of his term will go. There’s just been a lot of preparation around the world to figure out how to reorient their own, you know, foreign policy to not depend on the U.S. going forward.
Harris: Yeah, we’ve talked about Republicans. I want to talk about the Democrats for just a moment. And Ashley, you’ve done some reporting on the Democrats and how they’re thinking about the midterms.
How much does the infighting of the primary, sort of the bitterness of the campaigns between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens in Michigan, races in Wisconsin, Florida, Maine, et cetera, sort of matter now to Democrats? And do Republicans sort of see an offset with the unpopularity of the president and the sort of discord that they might see among the Democrats?
Parker: I mean, it’s not helpful, right? One thing, when you talk about these races and you talk to people on both sides, and it’s always true, it’s like it’s a national referendum, but at the end of the day, candidates matter, districts matter, the dynamics of states matter, right? And so, you know, Susan Collins is someone who has great name recognition in Maine, fits the state very well. I’ve talked to Democrats who don’t vote for her, but they’ve told me, they’ve been like, I have to say, she has amazing constituent services, right? You know, when I was DOGEd, like, she was in constant contact with me.
And so, you know, for a state like that, or in Michigan, right, like, if you’re the Democrats, you want the best possible candidate for a general election. And there’s a sense among Democrats and Republicans that in some of these states and districts, they’ve done that, and in some of these states and districts, because of contentious primaries, they haven’t. That’s the first thing.
And it’s interesting: Republicans in many ways should be doing even worse than they seem poised to do, and when you kind of drill down on that a bit, one of the things you hear is, at the end of the day, every election is a choice, right? And Democrats have a pretty bad brand, universally.
Someone even said to me, Look, people don’t like the economy right now, what they’re feeling. And voters have short-term memories, but they still remember the Biden economy. And Democrats, again, individual candidates are doing things that are very compelling. But as a party, if I asked you, What is the Democratic Party plan to make this economic pinch better, to lower inflation, to cut prices?, almost no voter could tell you, because there doesn’t seem to be a bite-size talking point, cohesive, catchy, snappy Democratic plan.
Harris: People have pushed back against sloganeering and things like that, but not having a sort of digestible plan, not sort of having that digestible slogan, can also be an issue for voters who don’t necessarily see the big picture, right?
’Cause if you say, Well, we have a policy for supplemental nutrition benefits, and then we also have a policy for this and for this, it doesn’t sort of capture an economic picture. So how much does that sloganeering matter?
Parker: It’s Already I’m asleep, right?
Harris: Yeah.
Parker: I was talking to someone who runs focus groups among swing voters, and this person told me, You know, in a lot of these states, they will hold up the picture of the two Senate candidates running against each other in an election that’s now two months from now, and the voters can’t identify who either candidate is. And I don’t say that—I’m not making fun of voters. It’s a reality that like people are dealing with other things, right? Including the high cost.
So if you don’t even know the names of the candidates, the idea that you’re gonna remember like the third policy platform of an economic plan, it has to be something that—and I get the sloganeering and this kind of cheesiness about that. But at the end of the day, one thing that President Trump is great at is getting people to sort of remember and understand what it is he ostensibly cares about, right? Whether that’s “Drain the Swamp” or Space Force. And Democrats need to find a way to signal—need an elevator pitch that voters can say, I’m voting for the Democrats because I know that my interest rate will go down to 3.875 percent. To dream.
Harris: Yeah. Michael, Republicans have a lot of money going into this election. How are they spending it? Sort of putting the president’s TV ads aside, how are they currently spending that money, and will that have an effect, right? Will that matter?
Scherer: Yeah, normally, the last decade or so, Democrats go into midterms, even they go into presidentials, with pretty substantial financial advantages. This is reversed this time. So there’s a lot of speculation.
What is also very clear is: They have not done the typical thing you do when you have a huge financial advantage, which is to go up early and spend money in the spring or, you know, even in the summer to sort of lay the groundwork when your opponents can’t afford to be up on the air, you kind of have the airwaves to yourself. They haven’t done that, really. So there’s a lot of suspense, I think, about how that’s actually going to play out in the final months.
Harris: I’m gonna ask both of you to sort of open your reporter’s notebooks and think about sort of the threads that you’re going to be following this week. So, Ashley, I’m gonna go to you first. Sort of open your notebook. What are you thinking about in this week ahead?
Parker: Sure, I mean, I alluded to it a bit before, but the bottom, by all accounts, should have fallen out for Republicans in this midterm cycle. Harris: And Michael, same question to you.
Scherer: Another thing Ashley and I’ve been looking at is Cabinet travel. My first encounter with a Prop 65 warning was on the back of my TV.
I was selling it on Facebook Marketplace, and when the buyer arrived to pick it up, he spotted a warning I had never noticed. “California Proposition 65 Warning: This product contains chemicals known to the state of California to cause cancer and birth defects or reproductive harm.” Neither of us had seen such a label before, and for a moment, he didn’t want the TV anymore. We did what anyone would do in this situation: We Googled it. He ended up taking the TV. I kept Googling.
California’s Proposition 65, officially called the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act, applies to a dizzying range of products, from food and cosmetics to electronics and household goods. Passed in 1986, the law turns 40 this year, yet that ominous little label still confuses the average consumer.
So, should you steer clear of all products with a Prop 65 warning? Not necessarily. Here’s what you need to know before you panic-buy a new TV.
Proposition 65, Explained
In November 1986, California voters approved Proposition 65 by a landslide margin of about 63 percent to 37 percent. It’s a right-to-know law, meant to inform Californians about potential exposure to chemicals that may cause cancer or reproductive harm over a lifetime.
It doesn’t ban those chemicals; instead, it requires businesses to provide a warning when their products could expose people to a listed chemical at levels above specific thresholds.
“At that time, it was part of a broader effort to address a growing concern that the public had about toxic chemical exposure,” says Megan Schwarzman, environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health.
The idea is that consumers can use that information to make their own decisions. A warning might prompt someone to choose an alternative, use a product less frequently, or take other steps to reduce their exposure. Prop 65 also gives businesses an incentive to reformulate products or change manufacturing practices to avoid issuing a warning that may deter customers.
And because California is such a massive consumer market, products often need to comply with Prop 65 requirements even when they’re manufactured or sold by companies elsewhere. Some large retailers, such as Target and Amazon, also require their vendors to comply with Prop 65 warning requirements.
Prop 65 Is Everywhere
Prop 65 covers a broad range of products and potential exposures. You can find warnings on fortified foods, smartphones, and appliances. The law is concerned with exposure, not simply whether the chemical is detectable. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) establishes the so-called safe-harbor levels for many listed chemicals. Generally speaking, a warning is required when anticipated exposure exceeds these levels.
The Prop 65 list contains both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals that California has determined are known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Supplements, for example, can contain trace amounts of naturally occurring or environmental contaminants, including lead, cadmium, and arsenic. The list is updated at least annually, and chemicals can also be removed from the list as scientific evidence evolves.
Chemicals can be added to the Prop 65 list through four mechanisms: through California’s Labor Code; through evaluations from California’s Carcinogen Identification Committee (CIC) or Developmental and Reproductive Toxicant Identification Committee (DARTIC); through identification by certain authoritative bodies, like the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA); or through identification by a state or federal agency.
Mariana C. Stern, cancer epidemiologist and member of the CIC, says the committee includes epidemiologists, toxicologists, molecular biologists, and cancer scientists who review the available literature before deciding whether a chemical belongs on the list.
“We may spend the whole day trying to dissect one chemical,” Stern says. “It’s not uncommon that we end up deciding we don’t have enough evidence to add this compound to the list.”
But seeing a warning doesn’t necessarily mean a product contains a dangerous amount of a chemical, or even that the product itself has been tested. According to Schwarzman, “some companies have opted to warn rather than test or reformulate, but from our research, I believe that is much less common than when companies post a warning because of the actual presence of the chemical above a certain threshold.”
From a consumer standpoint, the ubiquity of Prop 65 labels also means that it can be harder to prioritize which ones actually warrant attention. “We definitely have a concern with over-warning,” says Tina Cox, section chief of the OEHHA’s Proposition 65 Implementation Program. “Any unnecessary warnings do make it difficult for consumers to identify where the real exposures are, and it does dilute the value of Prop 65 warnings.”
As a result, California has started trying to make them more useful by requiring short-form warnings to name at least one chemical, rather than relying on the generic “may cause cancer or reproductive harm” language. Businesses have until January 2028 to fully comply with the new requirement. The state is also conducting more outreach to help companies understand when a warning is required and when it is not.
The Warning Isn’t a Verdict
Prop 65 was meant to inform consumers, not to tell them which products to buy. By the same token, a product without a warning isn’t necessarily free of hazardous chemicals.
“You’re never going to be zero exposure, even if you avoid all Prop 65 labels,” says air pollution scientist Shahir Fouad Masri. “If you have a product that doesn’t have a label, it’s one of two things: It was tested and it didn’t exceed Prop 65, and therefore it’s safe, or simply nobody ever sent it to the lab.”
That said, a Prop 65 warning is still useful information, and there are ways to reduce your exposure to these harmful chemicals. “Everybody has different risk tolerances and different priorities,” says Schwarzman. Consider how frequently you use the product and at what dose.
“Exposure from that one product, in many cases, is not going to cause cancer,” adds Cox, “but maybe over a lifetime of exposure, or exposure to similar products that have the same chemical, will increase your risk for cancer or reproductive toxicity.”
One example is holiday lights. Flexible plastic components can contain phthalates, which are added to PVC (polyvinyl chloride) to make it more pliable. Those chemicals migrate out of the plastic and come into contact with your hands or enter household dust. “My own choice around that is to handle them briefly and wash my hands,” says Schwarzman. “I don’t have my kids handle them, and I do make a different decision about that than something I’d be consuming on a daily basis.”
On a similar note, if you’re concerned about a warning on a tool, Masri suggests wearing gloves to reduce direct skin contact. There’s also a difference in dermal absorption rate. The skin on your hands, for example, is generally thicker and more calloused than the skin on your face, which means less absorption. So you might think differently about a screwdriver you occasionally handle with gloves than an LED mask you put directly on your face every day, where the potential for absorption is higher.
TL;DR
If you’re considering a product with a Prop 65 warning, don’t fret. Instead, look for more information.
- Determine what chemical triggered the warning, if identified.
- Check whether the manufacturer provides testing or contaminant information. Look for credible third-party certification, where appropriate.
- Consider how frequently you’re using the product and how extensively. Occasional exposure is different from using something every day.
- Don’t assume the absence of a Prop 65 label means the product is free of contaminants.
- For consumers who want to dig deeper, P65warnings.ca.gov has information about individual chemicals and ways to reduce exposure. There’s also a dedicated Help Desk for Prop 65, along with an email and phone line for specific inquiries.
- If you’re pregnant, trying to become pregnant, taking medications, or managing a medical condition, talk to a qualified health professional.
Prop 65 is a right-to-know law meant to raise awareness and ensure that we, as consumers, have an impact on the type of products we’re exposed to in our daily lives. As Schwarzman puts it, “I want to encourage us all not to feel like the toxic things are inevitable, and there’s nothing we can do, because there often is something we can do.”
Meet the Experts
- Tina Cox, senior environmental scientist (supervisory) and section chief of the Proposition 65 Implementation Program at the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)
- Mariana C. Stern, PhD, a cancer epidemiologist and professor of preventive medicine and urology at the University of Southern California, Keck School of Medicine
- Megan Schwarzman, MD, a physician and environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health
- Shahir Fouad Masri, ScD, an air pollution scientist at the University of California, Irvine

If you were trying to identify the spiciest policy affecting the fewest Americans, you’d struggle to do better than New York City’s pied-à-terre tax.
This spring, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul agreed on a plan to target extremely valuable homes. As of this fiscal year, homeowners will have to pay up to 6.5 percent tax on condos and co-ops assessed at more than $1 million; and up to 1.3 percent on multifamily houses assessed at more than $5 million. The out-of-town owners of a $10 million single-family home would pay $80,000 a year, on top of standard property taxes, for instance. Although the new fee is expected to hit only about 11,000 of the city’s 3.7 million housing units, it has dominated nightly newscasts and fronted tabloids (PIED-A-TERROR, HOLD IT RIGHT TERRE!) for weeks. A city-council hearing on the policy stretched for hours, with resident after resident complaining that it was confusing, unfair, invasive, confiscatory.
New Yorkers have every right to criticize the rollout, which left a lot to be desired. Still, this controversy is a tempest in a walk-in closet. The pied-à-terre tax is a sound progressive option for a city with an excruciating housing shortage and obscene wealth inequality. More than that, it is a policy meant to make the city a city—populated by, enjoyed by, and built for people.
Right now New York does not always feel that way. The brutal cost of housing has strained or wholly priced out many artists and care workers, retirees and young parents, blue-collar types and entrepreneurs.
When wealthy families actually live in the units they own, they invest in the city in many ways. They pay income taxes. They buy bacon-egg-and-cheeses at the deli down the block. They volunteer at nonprofits. They eat at restaurants. They put their kids in school. If they don’t live in their units, they pay property taxes without making extensive use of city services. Still, they contribute to rising housing prices without paying income taxes, spending at local businesses, or filling classrooms with children. They turn homes into safety-deposit boxes, “zombifying” their neighborhoods. No vacancies, no residents—it’s not a great scenario for a city as wonderful and in demand as New York.
Local legislators have kicked around the idea of taxing pieds-à-terre for years. At first glance, the structure seems to hit apartments owned by members of the upper middle class harder than it hits brownstones owned by billionaires. In reality, the different rates are meant to equalize the burden. The city values houses by looking at comparable sales, yet state law prevents it from valuing apartments the same way; instead, buildings are appraised by estimating the amount of income they would generate if their units were rented out. The calculation tends to work out to a fraction of the actual market value, particularly for expensive units, hence the higher tax rate and lower threshold. (A condo that sold for $4 million would likely be assessed at about $800,000.) In two years, the city is expected to update its assessment system and apply a uniform set of rates.
It’s confusing, and the complex tax has gotten a baffling rollout. The city’s Department of Finance published a roster of close to 1 million properties, along with their estimated market value and owner’s name. Anna Wintour, Cynthia Nixon, Deepak Chopra, Darren Aronofsky, and two city-council members were on the rolls. So were tens of thousands of middle-class homeowners, some of whom felt like Mamdani had personally doxxed them—even though property records were already public and city hall was legally obliged to publish the list.
The DOF then sent 17,000 homeowners a letter asking them to prove that they were residents or to get ready to pay up. At the city-council hearing, an Upper East Side retiree described getting a notice saying that he might owe $52,000 on top of his current property-tax bill next year. “I filed an exemption,” he said. “The point is the government is assuming that I’m guilty unless I can prove myself to be innocent.”
He has a point. To prove residency, the city is asking homeowners to furnish a federal or state tax return, a valid driver’s license, or a voter-identification card. These are records the government already has. Then again, filing for an exemption isn’t exactly hard. It certainly isn’t as hard as registering a kid for school, applying for food stamps, or purchasing a $5 million townhouse. And if city residents do not manage to get their paperwork done by the September exemption deadline, they will still be able to file an appeal with the tax commission at any point in the next six months.
Concerns about the validity of the law have snuck through the turnstile along with concerns about the technicalities of the law. At the city-council hearing, a former union leader praised the politicians for asking the super-rich to pay their fair share. Still, he said, he worries about a friend who had purchased a townhouse four decades ago, and is now retired and living in the South. The friend “kept his brownstone here so that he can keep in touch with his kids and his grandkids,” he said. “It’s not only billionaires that are concerned. It’s the everyday, hardworking New Yorkers who’ve dedicated themselves to making this city work.”
But, remember, the tax on brownstones applies exclusively to homes valued at more than $5 million. Is this friend really a hardworking New Yorker who had the good fortune to buy low? Or is he a millionaire who actually lives in Boca and thus might benefit from Florida’s homestead exemption? Such policies reduce or eliminate property taxes on primary residences, and may also protect them in bankruptcy proceedings. They’re exceedingly common. And they’re an analogue to New York’s pied-à-terre tax. (This specific kind of fee is sui generis in the United States, as far as I can tell, but popular, in both senses of the word, in foreign jurisdictions. Vancouver and Paris are among the cities imposing them, without obvious ill effect.) Plus, the former union leader’s friend does not necessarily have to pay the tax. He can reside in the brownstone. He can let one of his kids or grandkids live there. He can rent it out. Or he can sell it to someone who wants to live here.
Any of those choices would benefit New York, in the form of tax revenue, foot traffic, consumer demand, housing supply, or community investment. That’s the thing about the pied-à-terre tax. Instead of approaching the city as a collection of investments and assets, the policy treats the city as a collection of people—Chanel-clad couples, T-ball-playing preschoolers, subway breakdancers, financiers, socialist politicians, and high-net-worth investors—who are welcome to be part of the city too.

Swiss rave shooting suspect has 'psychological problems': prosecutor
A Swiss man in custody after a rave shooting that kills an Italian woman and wounds five suffers from “psychological problems” and stays silent, prosecutors say.
ZURICH: The man suspected of shooting dead an Italian woman at a rave party in Switzerland is suffering from "psychological problems" and has remained silent in custody, prosecutors said Wednesday (Sep 2).
Gunfire erupted in the early hours of Sunday morning as an annual rave was winding down at the racecourse in Aarau, capital of Switzerland's northern canton of Aargau.
The attack left a 22-year-old Italian woman dead and wounded five others.
A 43-year-old Swiss man handed himself in to police in Delemont, in northwestern Switzerland's Jura canton.
He is suffering from "psychological problems" and has maintained his silence since his arrest on Monday, the Aargau cantonal prosecutor Christoph Ruedi told a press conference.
The Aargau police said that two pistols and an AK-74 assault rifle were found in the suspect's vehicle.
Police chief Michael Leupold said the motive for the attack remained unclear, adding that the suspect was not previously known to the police and had no known links to extremist movements.
SHOOTER ACTED ALONE
The police said the shooter acted alone and fired around 40 rounds before fleeing in his vehicle.
Evidence from the crime scene suggests that the shooter fired indiscriminately at the festival site from various positions outside the grounds, they said.
The five survivors hit by gunfire were four Swiss men and a German woman, aged between 24 and 31. They were taken to hospital.
The police said Wednesday that two of them were still in hospital, but their lives are no longer in danger, and they should be able to be discharged in the coming days.
Another person has since come forward who sustained a minor injury, possibly from a ricocheting bullet, they added.
And at least one bullet hit a car containing four people as it was driving away.
"All indications suggest that all these people were random victims," the police said.
Public prosecutors have opened a criminal investigation.
Shootings are rare in Switzerland, despite widespread gun ownership.
The rave organisers said they were "devastated", saying on their website that "the insidious attack on the guests at the Aarauer Rave has broken our hearts."
"A rave should always be a place of joy and love. Never a place where people are killed, injured or left in fear."

Amazon customers are taking aim at the e-commerce giant over its email etiquette.
Earlier this summer, some Amazon customers started seeing generic descriptions instead of exact ones in receipts and other order-related emails. An engine air filter for a car, for example, might now appear in the emails as an "automotive item" and require the reader to check Amazon's website or app for more details about the order.
It's a change that has drawn ire from some Amazon shoppers. Amazon made a similar change to its emails in 2020, but eventually rolled it back.
One Reddit post, for instance, has attracted 450 comments over the last two months, including many from Amazon users who take issue with the new system.
"I just noticed this today and I HATE IT," one commenter wrote. "I order things both for work and home, on two different cards. Now I have to click through to see which is which when things ship? Lame."
Other posters pointed to reasons that the change mattered to them, from managing businesses to budgeting apps that pulled the product information from Amazon's emails.
Amazon made the change for privacy reasons, the company told Business Insider. It's also designed to "direct customers to our app and website for the latest information on their orders," a spokesperson said.
The change "reduces customer information shared outside the Amazon app and website to further improve customer privacy," the spokesperson said.
Some customers have pointed to other possible reasons for the change.
Information about what customers buy online has long been a treasure trove for advertisers. It's also become useful for training AI. Last month, for instance, Google agreed to pay $10 million for anonymized employee data, such as work emails and messages, from Spirit Airlines — information that could be valuable to the search giant, experts told Business Insider.
"I'm wondering if this is because they don't want AI tools to be able to easily scrape sales data?" wrote one Reddit user on a post about Amazon's change that attracted 162 comments.
The Amazon spokesperson said the change was intended to "help protect customer information" when asked whether the company was trying to limit what third parties could scrape from its emails.
One poster on a Github forum posted a message from an Amazon customer service representative, who said that the change was meant "to minimize the risk of package theft by not disclosing the specific contents of your shipment in publicly visible communications."
The posted message, which Business Insider verified, also said that the less-informative emails "maintain confidentiality for gifts, surprises, or personal items you may not want others in your household to see."
An Amazon spokesperson declined to comment on the contents of the message.

How Thailand’s notorious Pattaya was transformed from fishing village to sin city
Thousands of US sailors set to descend on a city with international reputation for sex tourism
After a long deployment in the Middle East, a US navy aircraft carrier is set to dock in Thailand’s infamous resort city of Pattaya, triggering a hasty crackdown on prostitution.
Nearly 5,000 American sailors and marines are set to arrive on the USS Abraham Lincoln and two accompanying vessels on Wednesday after more than 200 gruelling days at sea during Donald Trump’s war with Iran.
Five days of rest and recuperation will come as a relief following weeks of mounting reports of dire conditions on board the carrier, including food shortages, water contamination and the deteriorating mental health of staff.
But while the visit is expected to bring a much needed $3 million to the local economy, law enforcement officials say they will have difficulty policing the visit.
The Independent looks at how Pattaya earned its status as an international ‘Sin City’.
Pattaya transformed from fishing village to tourism hotspot
Pattaya is today a metropolis of some 350,000 people renowned worldwide for its long beaches and nightlife. But that was not always the case.
Until the second half of the 20th century, Pattaya was a fishing village on the east coast of the Gulf of Thailand, some 150km southeast of Bangkok.
That began to change with the arrival of American soldiers on leave during the Vietnam War.
A large group of U.S servicemen arrived in 1959, renting houses at the beach’s south end and that has become what is known as its strip.
Word soon spread of the local hospitality and by the late 1970s, Pattaya had been granted city status.
High-rise condos and investment into a burgeoning tourism industry flowed through the 1980s, and even as the war wound down, the city retained its appeal with westerners.
Pattaya today remains popular with British tourists, with occasional headlines in the UK press recording bar brawls, police raids and shootings.
It also played host to Manchester boxer Tyson Fury’s latest professional fight.
The heavyweight beat Mariusz Wach in Pattaya’s Max Muay Thai Stadium in July.
The local authorities are working to shed the city’s image as a hotspot for vice and debauchery, investing in family friendly attractions and child-friendly hotels.
But Pattaya’s Walking Street, brightly lit with neon signs, remains a busy centre of restaurants and parties, pressed together with an array of brightly lit nightclubs and sex shows.
While prostitution remains illegal in Thailand, the sex industry is openly visible in major tourism hubs, including parts of Bangkok and Pattaya.
And this year has also seen a number of tragic incidents in the city.
In February, Quentin Griffiths, a co-founder of online fashion retailer Asos, died after falling from a high-rise condominium in the city, police said.
Thai police said Griffiths, 58, a British passport holder, fell from the 17th floor of his apartment building.
Authorities last month said that a 17-year-old girl whose body was found in a suitcase near a railway in June died from suffocation.
Pattaya City police chief Anek Srathongyoo told the BBC: "She also suffered some brain injury but that was not the cause of death.
"It could have happened after she died as the accused moved her body in a suitcase before dumping it."
US soldiers bring needed boost to economy
Nearly 5,000 American sailors and marines are set to arrive in Pattaya following a record long deployment aboard a troubled US aircraft carrier.
The Abraham Lincoln is due to dock on Wednesday at nearby Laem Chabang. Shore leave is typically staggered, meaning not all personnel will step off the vessels at the same time.
The local government is hoping that each sailor could spent around 1,000 to 3,000 baht per day ($30-91) depending on how long they stay ashore and whether they stay overnight, according to mayor Poramet Ngampiches.
After meeting with American officials Monday, Poramet shared that the service members will be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and marijuana use. Medical cannabis was legalized in Thailand in 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities.
Pattaya brings in around 28 million tourists annually but has been struggling in recent years, in part due to travel disruptions and rising costs linked to the war in the Middle East.
Lisa Hamilton, president of the Pattaya Nightlife Business Association, said the arrival was a “source of hope” for the community after what she said had been the slowest year for business in two decades.
But money could also flow into the unseemly part of Pattaya's entertainment industry, so massive that the FBI described it a decade ago as "one of the world's leading sex tourism destinations."
"The risk to health and safety, as the influx of a large number of customers may increase the likelihood of sexual exploitation and the spread of sexually transmitted diseases," said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor at Bangkok University's School of Humanities and Tourism Management.

Queen Elizabeth II met Paul Keating “alone, to her credit” in what the prime minister was informed was her great-great-grandmother, Queen Victoria’s, favourite room at Balmoral Castle.
“And I took some pleasure in explaining the furniture to her,” Keating recalls, an old elan breaking through.
“It was made of Karelian, Russian Karelian birchwood. She had kept all the green-and-blue tartan carpets, all worn, so the room had something going for it. But the thing is, what had nothing going for it was any relativity to Australia.”
Keating was in the UK to deliver his monarch a message, that Australia, Australians, “did not need her any more”. Australia should, must become a republic.
“She said to me in this conversation, rather plaintively, ‘my family and I do our best for Australia’, whereas what I was really offering was a way out.”
A file note written by Keating following the meeting re-affirmed his belief in Australia’s independent future.
“The hereditary nature of the queen’s position, the remoteness from any contemporary mandate, struck me at that moment, at that proximity, as so banal, even sad.”
Keating, Australia’s 24th prime minister, is in conversation Wednesday night with Sydney University professor of modern history, James Curran, author of Grand Ambition: Paul Keating’s Global Vision for Australia.
It is an adroitly drawn portrait of a past leader – Keating lost power 30 years ago – but one who remains firmly convinced his vision is still very much this country’s future. An Australia that finds its security in, rather than from, Asia, that will be a republic, that will finally walk the path to reconciliation with its indigenous history.
‘Timidity is like a virus’
“My view of the country was bigger than the country’s view of itself, but the vision will never deteriorate,” Keating says.
This evening, Curran reminds his audience (gently) that his interlocutor is no longer a young man, a child of the second world war (born 1944), who was just 25 years old when he entered parliament in 1969. Who cut his political teeth during the height of the cold war, and whose time as leader coincided with its end (once held up as the “end of history”).
Keating’s first remarkable month as prime minister took in the fall of the Soviet Union; the arrival on Australian shores for the first time in three decades of a US president (George HW Bush, whom Keating wanted to “put in a headlock” to get something from him – the result was Apec, now still a key leaders’ meeting on the multilateral calendar, deep in its fourth decade); and a visit from Her Majesty (still yet a couple of years from their awkward meeting at Balmoral).
Keating’s age is apparent.
The voice is a little weaker, raspier; the pauses – formerly used to such dramatic effect on the floor of the Reps – are a little longer; the quotes once-remembered now come through an aide-memoire.
But there is still the killer line, the rapier wit, blunted a little, but still penetrating.
“Timidity,” he tells Curran in their interviews for the book, “is like a virus in the bloodstream.”
Curran writes: “Keating’s central theme over the years is that the country has become afraid, and that its leaders have refrained from articulating a bigger idea of the place.
“Instead of long-term strategic thinking about the kinds of issues coming down the national and international track, he sees frenzied activity. His retort? ‘Busyness is not substance.’”
Australia suffers no shortage of political autobiography, for better or worse. Keating, famously/notoriously, has never put pen to paper in his own defence.
Recollections of a Bleeding Heart, a memoir by his speechwriter, Don Watson, was said to have wounded him. He saw it as a betrayal. In response to what he saw as yet another Hawke biography, Keating delivered a veiled threat: “If I get around to writing a book, I will be telling the truth; the whole truth.”
It never eventuated.
But throughout this conversation, and throughout Grand Ambition, it is apparent that Keating has always kept an eye on legacy, on his place in history, and on grand ambition, his own and the country’s.
‘Trump wants to do is avoid world war three’
He keeps, Curran writes, meticulous records of the policies he considers the signal markers of his time in office, “the pillars of his political legacy”.
For a historian of Curran’s forensic eye, exclusive access to these files is manna from heaven.
“Each folder contains the relevant primary cabinet documents and diplomatic cables and, where applicable, briefings to and from his advisers and department, records of what other ministers thought or wrote, details of critical conversations with other leaders, and a carefully selected array of newspaper articles.
“They are all stamped ‘PJ KEATING PERSONAL COLLECTION’, arranged in precise chronological order and stapled at top left. The stamp itself is a statement about more than just the provenance of the documentary record; it is asserting, in its own way, Keating’s ownership of that past.”
To end the evening, Keating is asked for his message for young Australians, and the future they will encounter and make. The key themes are still there: a republic, indigenous reconciliation, a fairer Australia “making housing more affordable is a great thing to be doing. And if we’ve lost 10 or 15% in house values, so what?”.
But there are still surprises too. Keating’s proclaimed support for the foreign policy of the current occupant of the White House – “what Trump wants to do is avoid world war three” – his existential concern over the rise of artificial intelligence: “which I think is going to be the greatest agency of change since the discovery of electricity”.
Keating is taken to a speech he gave at Kokoda. On Anzac Day in 1992, as prime minister, he had fallen to his knees and kissed the base of the memorial to fallen Australian soldiers, describing the PNG highlands village as “the place where the depth of the soul of the Australian nation was confirmed”.
“It is important for all of us, but particularly and especially young Australians,” Keating said that day, “to believe in an independent Australia, beholden to nobody. We can’t deny young Australians their birthright to a past with meaning for them and a future without meaning: it has to be a future with meaning.”

The Best Folding Phones
Featured in this article
You may be scoffing as you read this. The best folding phones? Really? Aren’t those just gimmicks? I'm here to tell you they're pretty darn useful. And yes, there are quite a few now, so you have options. Folding phones are an evolution of the traditional single-screen slab of glass we've all been using for nearly two decades—and we might even see a folding iPhone in 2026.
They largely come in two forms: a folding flip phone or a folding book-like phone, enabling you to either relive the glory days of small phones or expand your multitasking options while on the go. A folding phone is a personal decision—arguably even more than a traditional smartphone, since it hinges (heh) on what style you prefer. We have tested almost all of them, and these are our favorites.
Check out our other mobile buying guides, including the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Best Google Pixel Phones, Best Motorola Phones, Best Phones With a Headphone Jack, and Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US.
Updated August 2026: We've added the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Motorola Razr Ultra (2026), Motorola Razr (2026), Honor Magic V6; mentions of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Flip8, Motorola Razr Fold, Motorola Razr+ (2026), and Oppo Find N6; removed some older devices; and updated prices.
Other Folding Phones to Consider
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: The Z Fold8 Ultra is a refined release with a 6.5-inch cover display that opens to an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side. It's fast and smooth, with a 5,000-mAh battery, but it's the camera that earns it the “Ultra” title. It's an impressive combo, including a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Sadly, it lacks Qi2 support for magnetic wireless charging, and the camera module makes it rock when lying flat on a surface. But the main reason it misses out on a place above is that the smaller Fold8 is so much easier to handle.
Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 for $1,200: We haven't had a chance to spend much time with the Flip8 yet, but based on what we have seen, it's a close second to Motorola's Razr Ultra. It is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world with a redesigned chassis. It has a 4.1-inch cover screen, and it flips open to become a 6.9-inch candy bar. It's also more durable than ever and boasts the same excellent chipset and performance as Samsung's larger Fold models. The 4,300-mAh battery is solid, but the camera system is relatively basic, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide.
Motorola Razr Fold for $1,900: The first book-style foldable from Motorola is good, but not great. The front screen feels very much like a normal phone, and you can open it to enjoy the vast 8.1-inch display inside. Sadly, the Razr Fold lacks the top-end processor of the year, which is disappointing at this price. The highlight is the massive 6,000-mAh battery, which can stretch to nearly three days of use. Thankfully, it does come with seven years of software updates (unlike Motorola's Flip family). Motorola has also added a telephoto lens to the capable camera, though it can't compete with Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
Motorola Razr+ 2026 for $1,100: The awkward middle child in the Razr lineup lacks the bells and whistles or top-notch specs of the Ultra, but still costs more than $1,000. You can get very close to the same experience from the cheaper Razr and save hundreds. Even battery life is unimpressive, because it has the smallest capacity of the Razr family. The cover glass isn’t the ceramic glass mixture as on the Razr Ultra. I found out the hard way after dropping the phone once, roughly a 4-foot drop onto asphalt, and the front screen shattered. Get a screen protector!
Oppo Find N6 for $1,929: With an 8.12-inch internal display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its promise of being creaseless, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it when the screen is on, though you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide. The global model can use familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import it, as this phone won’t officially be released in the West.
Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold for $1,799: The only reason to consider the Pixel 10 Pro Fold right now is if you see it on sale. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is superior, but the 10 Pro Fold isn't far behind this year's release. It's still a reasonably slim device with a large front screen that feels like a normal phone, an excellent 8-inch inner screen, and a triple-camera system that delivers great results, though not as great as the Pixel 10 Pro series. Read our Best Pixel Phones guide for more.
Xiaomi Mix Flip for $899: Xiaomi’s first flip phone has a lovely design with excellent displays inside and out, long battery life with fast charging, and flagship-level performance, which makes a nice change, as flip phones often have middling specs. It also boasts a solid dual-lens camera, opting for telephoto instead of ultrawide alongside the capable main shooter, which is more useful for most folks. The software lets the party down a little; there’s no IP rating, and it is pricey, but I had fun with this flip phone.
Things to Know Before Buying
Folding phones are more fragile than normal phones. Folding phones have more parts than a traditional smartphone, not to mention a hinge. Companies advertise how many folds these devices have been tested for—usually around 200,000 or 500,000 folds—but a single drop can be incredibly damaging. They are not as dust-resistant, and some aren't as water-resistant (only the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is IP68-rated in the US), so you'll want to be especially careful. Use a case, and it may be worth investing in the manufacturer's device care policy.
Don't remove the built-in screen protector. Most of these folding phones have a film over the inner screen. You might be tempted to remove it, but don't—it can damage the display. The packaging usually includes instructions not to remove it and how to care for your device.
There's a small learning curve to the software. Flip-style folding phones are fairly straightforward, but book-like folding phones that double as tablets have new multitasking tricks that will take some getting used to if you want to make the most of them. I recommend taking some time to run through these features so you understand how they work.
They're expensive. Do you need one? Nobody needs a folding phone. If you think you'll benefit from one, know they're frequently discounted during big sale events like Black Friday, and you can also knock a few hundred dollars off if you trade in an eligible device.
Which Type of Folding Phone Is for You?
Folding flip phones are for people who want a compact device. Think of a normal phone you can fold in half. That's pretty much what you get, plus a screen on the front to monitor widgets and texts. This does mean you can flip the phone to answer a call and flip it shut to end one—super cool. You can put the phone at a 90-degree angle, and some apps will adapt to show controls on the bottom and important details at the top, like in video calling apps or when watching videos on YouTube, though this depends on the phone. Folding flip phones typically have mediocre battery life, and their cameras aren't as good as their non-folding counterparts.
Folding book-like phones are for people who want the big-screen experience. Are you constantly watching full-length movies on your phone? Or do you always find yourself jumping back and forth between two apps? Then these are for you. They have good battery life and better cameras (though not as good as non-folding phones), but they're far more expensive. These include the short-lived triple-screen folding devices like Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold. They're thick and heavy, though we're seeing newer models that are surprisingly thin. Still, you may have a hard time fitting them in your pockets.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
If you're team Android, this is a good time to buy. Samsung and Google just updated their foldables, and Motorola released its first big foldable in the summer and won't announce the Razr 2027 lineup until the spring. For folks outside the US, we probably won't see new foldables from Honor or Oppo until the spring, too.
If you're considering an iPhone, Apple is likely to unveil a new folding phone soon, so you might want to wait and see what it looks like.
My Favorite Folding Features
Whichever style you go for, my favorite feature of folding phones is the ability to see the viewfinder on the external screen and snap a selfie with the high-quality rear cameras—just set the phone down slightly folded so it stays upright, and there's usually a button you can click in the camera app to send the preview to the external screen. You can usually trigger the shutter hands-free with a palm gesture. (Motorola's Razr Ultra lets you start and stop video recordings with hand gestures, too!) It's excellent when traveling if you want to take a photo of yourself next to a point of interest.
Many of these phones offer similar functionality with translation—Samsung and Google, for example, let you show your words translated on the external screen so the person you are speaking to can see it, and then they can tap a button on the screen to have the phone start translating their words, which you'll see on the internal screen. It's a much nicer system than using Google Translate on a candy bar phone.

US Treasury issues $1 coin with Trump's face on it
A new US$1 coin bearing Donald Trump enters circulation as the US marks 250 years of independence, despite a federal bar on living presidents appearing on currency.
WASHINGTON: The US Treasury on Wednesday issued $1 coins featuring the face of President Donald Trump, the latest move in an unprecedented campaign by the Republican billionaire to put his personal stamp on national institutions.
The coins were minted to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States, celebrated this year.
A roll of 25 $1 coins was available for $61 - a markup of 144 per cent - with a 100-coin bag available for $154.50.
When the Treasury announced the plan, it was unclear if the coins would have monetary value or would be purely commemorative, but on Wednesday the US Mint said the coins were "also in circulation."
The move to put Trump's countenance on a coin with monetary value runs counter to federal law that says no living president may appear on US currency.
Trump has aggressively defied precedent and legal challenges in his push to remake US institutions in his second term, putting his name on the Kennedy Center for the Arts and demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make room for a new ballroom, among other moves.
The new coin features Trump's face on one side, with the words "Liberty" and "In God We Trust." It also features the dates 1776-2026, marking 250 years of US independence.
The other side of the coin features a version of the US presidential seal, depicting an eagle clutching arrows and an olive branch, while covered by a shield that says "250."
This is just the latest in Trump's campaign to put his face and name on US currency.
In May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department was pursuing a plan to issue a new $250 bill with Trump's face on it.
He conceded that the move would require Congress to change the law barring living persons from appearing on currency.
The US Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether the new $1 coin violates that law.
In March, the Treasury announced that US paper money would soon bear Trump's signature - another first for a sitting US president.

Uber to lay off 10% of staff in biggest cuts since COVID
Uber cuts about 3,300 jobs, or 10% of staff, as it overhauls management and braces for rising robotaxi competition.
SAN FRANCISCO: Uber Technologies UBER.N will lay off about 3,300 employees, or 10% of staff, in its largest cuts since the COVID-19 pandemic, to better navigate the rise of robotaxis encroaching on its ride-hailing business.
The cuts will flatten management layers, reducing organisational complexity that was built during a period of rapid growth, but is now proving a hurdle to decision-making, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in a note to employees on Wednesday (Sep 2).
Unlike several tech executives, Khosrowshahi did not blame the cuts on AI, even as a push to adopt the technology and the efficiencies it can unlock have driven large cuts in the industry this year, with tracking website layoffs.fyi putting the overall number at over 123,000 across nearly 390 companies.
"A leaner organisation will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years," Khosrowshahi said.
Uber shares rose nearly 2%. The stock has underperformed the S&P 500 and rival Lyft LYFT.O this year, with a near 8% decline driven by worries about growing competition.
DoorDash DASH.O, Instacart CART.O and local delivery platforms have been putting pressure on Uber Eats, forcing the company to turn to deals such as its $14.8 billion Delivery Hero DHER.DE acquisition to build scale and compete better.
GROWING ROBOTAXI COMPETITION
Some of the concern stems from reports of growing tension between Uber and Waymo, the biggest US robotaxi operator, which runs its cars through Uber's app in Austin and Atlanta.
Waymo has also been expanding into new markets without Uber, while rivals such as Tesla double down on robotaxis, feeding fears that a growing fleet of driverless cars could erode Uber's lucrative role as the middleman between vehicles and riders.
To defend its position, Uber plans to put more than $10 billion into robotaxis in the coming years, backing the companies developing autonomous-driving systems and positioning itself as a go-to marketplace for driverless rides.
"As AV tech and relationships grow and expand, there is a different type of employee needed to scale that business than one built around human drivers and all the cost to serve entailed with that, including management layers," said Adam Ballantyne, analyst at Uber shareholder Cambiar Investors.
As part of Wednesday's overhaul, Uber will reduce the number of employees positioned seven or more reporting layers below the CEO by 20% and cut the number of teams with only one or two direct reports by nearly half. It will also combine some teams and concentrate much of its staff presence around key hubs.
It will also limit fully remote roles to about 1% of staff, while maintaining its three-day office policy.
The layoffs, first reported by Bloomberg News, are Uber's largest since May 2020, when a pandemic-driven collapse in demand forced it to shed 6,700 jobs, nearly a quarter of its staff.
The company is also grappling with AI costs after employees used up their entire 2026 budget for the technology in just four months, according to media reports.
Uber had about 34,000 employees globally at the end of last year, according to its annual report.

In a strategic retreat in the fight against climate change, the United Nations has acknowledged that Earth has lost its chance to prevent some of the worst of global warming's harms. So now the world must figure out how to get temperatures below the danger zone and back to safety, officials say.
Earth is soon going to exceed the safe temperature threshold agreed upon by the world in the 2015 Paris climate accord because of warming from the burning of coal, oil and gas, according to a bleak first-of-its-kind report issued by the United Nations Environment Programme Wednesday (September 2, 2026).
Instead of giving up, scientists and UN officials recommend trying to limit excessive warming and then bring the temperature back down to the agreed-upon threshold. But it still will mean decades of increased weather-related disasters, rising seas, extinctions and melting ice and glaciers.
“Humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe,” United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said.
After a period of over-the-limit warming, the new strategy envisions getting back below the limit by ending fossil fuel use and developing some kind of way to suck industries' carbon dioxide out of the air.
“It's a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world,” said report co-author Richard Betts, a climate scientist at the University of Exeter. “But there's still a lot we can do to limit warming.”
Passing the longtime warming threshold
After the Paris climate accord, the United Nations ordered its climate science arm to study different warming limits. A goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above mid-19th-century temperatures became generally accepted after scientists found dramatic impacts that affect people and the planet at 2 degrees Celsius (3.8 degrees Fahrenheit) but not at 1.5 degrees.
The world is now at 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, some scientists have calculated. The measure is based on a 20-year average, rather than a single year's temperatures.
Despite experts saying there's no way to limit warming to 1.5 degrees, U.N. officials long maintained the 1.5 window was still open. Wednesday's (September 2, 2026) report finally admitted that the world will cross the 1.5 threshold “in the next few years.” The report said the most optimistic scenario has warming peaking at 1.8 degrees (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) around mid-century if countries pursue ambitious climate goals, but that governments' current policies should push temperatures to 2.6 degrees (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
So instead of preventing warming of 1.5 degrees, now the UN said it wants policymakers to “prepare for and navigate a future'' in which the globe crosses that limit and then corrects course and cools temperatures. The report envisions that global temperatures will pass 1.5 “within the next few years,” follow a hump-shaped path of more warming, peak, then gradually cool to below the 1.5 mark, ideally by the end of the century. The report and experts call it “overshoot.” “Let's be very clear, the 1.5 target is still the goal. But now we need to approach it differently from above,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.
The 1.5 limit is not “some magical climate cliff” where it's just game over, said University of Victoria climate scientist Andrew Weaver, who wasn't part of the study. “Every tenth of a degree we avoid still means less damage.”
Limiting how high temperatures go past threshold is key
It's most important to limit the new peak temperature and then reduce the amount of time above 1.5 degrees, Andersen said.
But the world likely will be in that overshoot period for “many, many decades,” Mr. Betts said.
Every five years of delay in reducing emissions adds at least a tenth of a degree to peak warming, said report co-author Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at Imperial College London.
“If we act now we can limit overshoot,” the report said. “Not a safe world, but safer than remaining above 1.5 degrees for the long term”.
“This is among the bleakest U.N. climate reports I have read. It carries the unmistakable tone of desperation, frustration and urgency — but not resignation,” Mr. Weaver said.
Climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, said that “although UNEP does a good job of describing the hole we've dug ourselves into, it does a poor job of showing us that there's a way out.”
Adapting to a deadlier, hungrier, thirstier world
Governments need to increase efforts to adapt to worsening warming, which hits the poor hardest, “because some impacts simply cannot be avoided,” Mr. Andersen said.
The report calls this phase “coping and containment.” During this overshoot period, more people will die or get sick because of the worsening climate change and its extreme weather, the report said. Food production will drop, people will go hungry, water shortages will worsen, economies will be hurt, and species like coral will go extinct, the report said.
Although the triggers behind the recent deadly Nepal flooding that came as part of a Himalayan glacier dislodging are complex, Mr. Betts said: “Unfortunately, we do expect to see more of such things, and this is exactly why we need to limit peak warming.” The report warns of “tipping points” with irreversible and cascading effects, including the loss of the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the loss of the Amazon rainforest and the shutdown of the Atlantic Ocean circulation system that keeps much of Europe warm.
“Some locations might become more or less uninsurable or even uninhabitable,” the report said.
The last phase in overshoot is cooling the planet by removing carbon dioxide from the air and storing it somewhere. The report said the traditional approach to this is planting more trees, but it says planting trees could, at most, shave a tenth of a degree off global temperatures. So the authors said more novel carbon removal approaches will be needed.
Other scientists called that unreliable and expensive.
“We were unable to stop the runaway train of global emissions to avoid 1.5 C of warming,” said Stanford University climate scientist Rob Jackson, who wasn't part of the report. “Now overshoot scenarios require us to stop the train quickly and to back it up. Is it our best hope? Absolutely. Is it likely? Absolutely not.”
