Bank of Canada says inflation risk rising, holds key interest rate at 2.25%
Next rate announcement is scheduled for Oct. 28.
The Bank of Canada held its benchmark interest rate steady on Wednesday at 2.25 per cent, in a move widely expected by economists.
Canada’s central bank has been on hold since December 2025, with Wednesday’s announcement marking its seventh consecutive decision to leave its trend-setting policy rate unchanged.
In its decision, the bank said recent data confirms its prediction for a "broadening recovery" in the economy. However, policymakers also said the risks of higher inflation have increased — citing new U.S. tariffs and the escalating U.S.-led war with Iran.
"With the Middle East conflict still ongoing, and little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz, upside risks to the bank’s inflation forecast have increased," bank officials said on Wednesday.
"The longer that high oil prices and elevated refinery margins persist, the greater the risk of spillover to the prices of other goods and services."
U.S. benchmark oil prices have soared about 13 per cent since the bank’s last announcement in July. The U.S.-led war in Iran has intensified in recent weeks, resulting in slower tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime passageway for oil to reach global markets.
At the same time, the Canada-U.S. trade war has escalated significantly since the bank's prior meeting in July.
Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian products. Starting Sept. 8, Canada will match those levies with dollar-for-dollar tariffs on $27.6 billion of comparable U.S. goods.
Last week, the federal government rolled out a $7.5-billion expanded economic relief program for impacted workers and businesses. The new supports are on top of the nearly $25 billion in tariff support it implemented over the past 18 months.
'Uncertainties over trade'
CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld said Wednesday’s hold was no surprise “amidst the fog of a trade war.”
“Newly heightened uncertainty over trade relations clouds that picture too much to be definitive about what lies ahead,” Shenfeld wrote in a research note published after the decision.
“The bank did judge that the direct impact of the latest tariff round would not be large, but cited the uncertainties over trade as being a further drag,” he added.
“It didn’t mention the downside implications of a failure to lower the existing tariffs on autos, metals and lumber that most economic projections were assuming would take place.”
A Reuters poll of economists taken on Aug. 22 found all 35 participants expected policymakers to leave the bank's key rate in place.
The Bank of Canada’s next rate announcement is scheduled for Oct. 28.

Arrest warrants issued in Mexico for duo accused in alleged condo scam
Ontario couple put $280K into plan to flip condos in Playa del Carmen
A Mexican court has issued arrest warrants against the man and woman accused of defrauding a Canadian couple of their retirement savings through an alleged condo-flip scheme, CBC News has learned.
The warrants for Harry Robinson, a British national, and Jacqueline Herrera Herrera, a Mexican national, were issued in late July by a Quintana Roo state court judge.
Both are now before a Mexican federal court seeking to toss those warrants, according to copies of court records.
The criminal case against them, which is being heard at the state level, won’t be impacted by the federal court process around the arrest warrants, however.
Robinson and Herrera are accused by the state prosecutor's office of committing fraud through deception.
The Canadian couple — Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown, of Curve Lake, Ont. — sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by a Robinson and Herrera who promised big returns on a condo flip in Playa del Carmen that never materialized.
"It is not something that leaves your mind because you’re always worried about what’s going to happen, what’s next," said Thompson this week.
Quintana Roo is a popular vacation and investment destination for Canadians, and also home to Cancun and Tulum.
Thompson and Brown filed a criminal complaint against Robinson and Herrera earlier this year.
The case stems from late 2024 when Thompson, searching for possible real estate investments in Mexico, came across the web page for XMEX Investments which was run by Robinson.
She eventually met Robinson and Herrera in Playa del Carmen. Herrera pitched her on buying a one-bedroom condo and Thompson sent $170,000 in two installments, but never received the keys.
Robinson then convinced Thompson to move her money, with an additional $110,000 from Brown, into a deal to flip seven condos, saying via WhatApp it was looking "to be 100 per cent profit."
Thompson and Brown’s money then vanished.
A federal court judge granted a stay on Aug. 27 against the warrant seeking Herrera’s arrest, but the process to have it tossed continues, according to court records.
A hearing on Robinson’s application is scheduled for Sept. 8 in Cancun, according to court records.
Herrera has claimed in WhatsApp messages that Robinson took some of the money. Robinson filed a criminal complaint against Herrera in late 2025 alleging she stole all the money.

Expanding its footprint beyond India, streaming giant JioHotstar today said that it is launching its services in the UK, Canada and Singapore. The move marks a significant shift for the India-focused streaming giant, which will now also target the South Asian diaspora and wider audiences in the three nations. In a statement, JioHotstar said that it will roll out 1.6 Lakh hours of content across 12+ languages in the new markets. The content lineup will include webseries, TV shows, films and regional programming. JioHotstar also said that it will add over 30,000 hours of fresh content every year to expand its library for these new geographies. The streaming giant has also introduced region-specific pricing for the three geographies across two tiers – quarterly and annual. Users in the UK will have to shell out £19.99 (₹2,562) for the quarterly plan and £69.99 (₹8,972) for the annual plan. Meanwhile, customers in Canada will be able to avail its quarterly and annual tiers for CAD 19.99 (₹1,365) and CAD 49.99 (₹3,415), respectively. The subscription plan in Singapore starts at SGD 29.98 (₹2,235) for three months and SGD 69.98 (₹5,217) for a year. “... South Asian audiences have a deep connection with Indian entertainment across languages, generations and households. At the same time, audiences globally are increasingly seeking stories and cultures beyond their own. We see an opportunity to build for this broader, underserved global audience - not simply export an Indian streaming service to new markets,” said JioStar’s head of international business Amit Malhotra. JioHotstar said that it is betting on product experience, technology, dubbed content and the demand for vernacular content among the Indian diaspora to power its international foray. The platform is using a mix of new originals, iconic franchises and early TV access to attract subscribers in these three markets. In Singapore and Canada, popular daily soaps will be available before TV, while key shows will stream simultaneously with their TV broadcast in the UK. With this, JioHotstar appears to be trying to convert cultural affinity into a sticky streaming proposition in the three markets. The launch is also expected to act as a test bed for tracking the demand for JioStar’s products. This comes nearly two years after Disney and Reliance officially signed agreements to create a joint venture (JV), merging Viacom18 with Star India Private Limited. Since then, the combined JioStar entity has become one of the biggest entertainment giant in the country, with more than 100 channels under its belt. Streaming arm, JioHotstar, has also grown alongside. The platform currently claims to have a library of more than 3 Lakh hours of programming and 50 Cr monthly average users. In its Q1 FY27 results, Reliance had also said that its newly launched microdrama vertical Tadka crossed 10 Cr active users within two months of launch. JioHotstar’s international foray comes amid intensifying competition in the Indian OTT space. From Netflix and Amazon Prime to Zee5 and SonyLIV, streaming platforms are aggressively rolling out new content slate and offering lower subscription tiers to woo and retain users in India. Just last month, rival Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said that India is central to the company's global strategy and launched a new programme to train and support creators across animation, visual effects, gaming and comics (AVGC). Homegrown Zee5 also recently locked both TV and digital rights for the now-over 2026 FIFA World Cup to capture the on-demand sports segment. At the heart of all this is the Indian OTT streaming ecosystem, which is being driven by affordable mobile data, widespread smartphone adoption, 60 Cr OTT users and the demand for vernacular content. As per reports, the homegrown OTT market is expected to become a $27 Bn opportunity by 2033.

Whenever Dyson enters a new product category, a ripple effect usually follows, with the buzz growing so loud that competitors are forced to react. The company did this with stick vacuums and premium hair dryers. Now it's aspiring to upend the oral care business.
On Tuesday, Dyson announced the CameraJet, a two-in-one electric toothbrush and flosser, to help you clean those pearly whites. It's not the company's first hybrid experiment (that would be the short-lived Dyson Zone air-purifying headphones), but as a pairing of two technologies, this makes far more practical sense—even if the word camera isn’t one you’d typically expect in the name of an oral device.
The CameraJet is an electric toothbrush with an embedded flosser that shoots liquid into the gaps between your teeth as you brush. How does the device know when the brush head is right above a gap that needs blasting? A built-in endoscope camera analyzes 28 images per second, shooting bursts of rinse as you move the device over your teeth.
Dyson calls this the Gap Optical Targeting system. The company says it’s powered by a macro-lens camera and a machine learning algorithm trained on 470,000 dental images that Dyson collected during the six years it spent developing the product. Dyson says the magic happens within 100 milliseconds—the camera sees the gap and flushes it with a mouth rinse, all while you brush normally.
The fluid jet itself has some interesting engineering. Dyson notes that it's a conical jet, which the company claims removes plaque more effectively than the “needle-type jets” used by competing stand-alone water flossers. Dyson says its cone-shaped jet of fluid can remove plaque over a wider area using less pressure, making the brush gentler on gums and enamel.
For testing this, Dyson created its own proxy plaque in collaboration with the National University of Singapore's Faculty of Dentistry. This allowed the designers to iterate and test the brush’s plaque-removing prowess in the lab without running a clinical trial after every minor change.
Right below the brush is a tank where the gadget stores 12.5 milliliters of alcohol-free mouth rinse. A diaphragm pump and pressure chamber ensure the jets shoot out no matter how you hold the brush, which Dyson claims gives the CameraJet an edge over its peers, which it says lose performance when tilted. A docking station refills the toothbrush with mouth rinse in three seconds with the touch of a button. It also recharges the CameraJet and gives it a nice resting place on your sink. There's a travel case for packing the whole thing up.
Finally, we get to the bristle brush head. Dyson says it's contoured precisely to reach a “greater proportion of the tooth's surface,” with firmer inner bristles and softer outer bristles. A radio-frequency identification (RFID) tag inside measures how many cleans it has completed, so you'll know exactly when to replace the brush head. There's also a softer version of the brush head for people with sensitive teeth and gums.
Don't forget the sonic oscillation! That's a normal part of an electric toothbrush, where it vibrates side to side to clean your teeth. Dyson's CameraJet uses variable sonic oscillation, which varies the angle of oscillation as you brush. The company says this design prevents the bristles from stalling under pressure.
All of this brings us to the CameraJet's biggest claim: that it “removes up to 69 percent more plaque than market-leading premium electric toothbrushes in hard-to-reach areas.” (Dyson's small print says this is based on laboratory tests in the brush-only variable mode in hard-to-reach areas.)
The CameraJet connects to your phone over Bluetooth (there's also Wi-Fi support), where it will show up in the MyDyson app. You don't need to open the MyDyson app to use the toothbrush. But if you do use the app, you can look through the brush’s camera in real time and watch the device shoot liquid into your tooth gaps. If you're worried about putting a camera in your bathroom, Dyson says not to worry; the camera is active only when you open the live view through the MyDyson app or when the brush is automatically scanning your teeth to find the places to shoot those rinsing jets. The company says it does not record or store images locally on the CameraJet or in the cloud.
If you decide to use the app, you can get personalized feedback, coverage mapping to make sure you're cleaning all your teeth, and even a guided cleaning mode. Also, if you don't want the CameraJet to shoot its jets automatically, you can use the manual jetting mode.
There are two more things you should consider before bringing this tech into your bathroom.
Dyson products command high prices, and the CameraJet will unsurprisingly cost you a pretty penny: $499. It comes in blue and pink, and each CameraJet comes with a refill dock, two regular brush heads, and a charging cable.
The final catch is that you cannot use any old toothpaste and mouth rinse. Dyson has a proprietary “non-foaming” toothpaste coming soon, which is crucial, because foam will block the camera. The “low-foaming” rinse is also specifically designed to work with the entire system. You'll be able to sign up for a Dyson subscription to get toothpaste, rinse, and replacement brush heads on a recurring basis. However, you can use any third-party rinses and toothpaste if they are sodium lauryl sulfate–free, as that substance causes foaming.
Around one in three adults in the US reports flossing daily, and multiple studies show that people often spend less than a minute brushing instead of the two minutes recommended by the American Dental Association. By combining brushing and flossing, Dyson is pitching that its product condenses two steps into one, though we'll have to see if its camera-equipped brush can successfully blast those jets into just the right spots.

There are, by various estimates, several trillion planets within what is known as the Local Group of galaxies—our closest galaxy neighbors, including our own Milky Way. Many of these planets are within the habitable zone of their stars. So if life finds a way, where are the alien civilizations?
This is the crux of what is known as the Fermi paradox, which posits that if life is fairly common in the Universe, humans should have collected credible evidence for the existence of extraterrestrial civilizations by now. People who think about this paradox believe there may be some “filter” that limits or entirely prevents an advanced civilization from sending out probes or even life-bearing spacecraft to nearby stars.
Philip Johnston is someone who thinks a lot about the Fermi paradox. A mathematician and physicist from the United Kingdom, Johnston has gained some notoriety lately in the space community as one of the biggest proponents of orbital data centers. He co-founded Starcloud in 2024 to develop such data centers, and the company is presently valued at $2.3 billion.
Johnston is in the midst of scaling up Starcloud, working through technical issues, and raising hundreds of millions of dollars. So he’s pretty busy. But Johnston also wants to send a mission to the nearest star to our Sun and investigate the Fermi paradox.
Meet the Fermi Explorer
On Tuesday, Johnston and a handful of other entrepreneurs announced the “Fermi Explorer” mission. In concept, it is simple. They seek to raise $15 million to build a small spacecraft, carrying a 1 kg payload, and launch it to Alpha Centauri such that it reaches that system in fewer than 80,000 years. Why? In conversations about the Fermi paradox, Johnston realized such a mission would knock two “filters” off the list: Species won’t want to send spacecraft beyond their home star, or species will find that interstellar transit is too difficult.

After country music legend and philanthropist Dolly Parton died in August 2026, rumors spread online about supposed public spending cuts to her Imagination Library, which sends free books to children until their 5th birthdays.
Posts online claimed that Missouri or Indiana Republicans cut funding for the child literacy program. Some claims were vaguer, merely stating that "Republicans" ended financial support for the Imagination Library. Readers asked us whether the Imagination Library was "defunded" after Parton's death or in the past year and whether U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, Congress, Republicans or other various entities were the culprit.
Here's the truth: In about two dozen states, the Imagination Library receives state government funding. In the year before Parton's death, two states with Republican-controlled governments — Indiana and Missouri — and two with Democrat-controlled governments — Maine and Washington — ended or reduced financial support for the Imagination Library.
At least one state with a Republican governor and Democrat-controlled Legislature, Nevada, also did not renew several grants that supported local partners of the Imagination Library.
The federal government does 
Dollywood Foundation spokesperson Tracy Long declined via email to answer any questions about funding for the Imagination Library; The New York Times reported on Aug. 25 that the Imagination Library was overwhelmed following Parton's death.
At least one state, Oregon, passed bipartisan legislation in 2026 that codified the Imagination Library as an official state program.
According to the Imagination Library's website, 
Here's everything we know about the Imagination Library's funding and why some states and other organizations stopped providing 
How is the Imagination Library funded?
The Imagination Library uses a mix of private and public funding at the state and local levels. The organization itself covers all of the administrative and overhead costs. Local partners who work with the Imagination Library are asked to enroll children in the coverage area and pay an average of $2.60 per child per month toward wholesale books and mailing costs, according to a 2024 infographic from the library.
(Imagination Library)
According to Courtney Vashaw, director at a New Hampshire library that partners with Parton's foundation, in at least some cases, like hers, the Imagination Library pays for the books, too.
"Where does local funding come into it? The postage," she said in a phone call. "There has to be some kind of partnership that allows for that money to be raised."
As of June 2026, the Imagination Library has full coverage in 21 states, according to a fact sheet the organization released. State governments often support those statewide programs through a 50/50 funding match, where the state pays for half of the local partners' costs.
Many of the Imagination Library's local partners — which are all nonprofit organizations — also heavily rely on federal or state grant funding.
Did state Republicans cut funding?
Missouri and Indiana Republicans cut funding after reportedly facing budget deficits. Kentucky lawmakers also reportedly considered cutting funding but reversed the move after public backlash.
Missouri
In November 2023, under Republican Gov. Mike Parson, Missouri became the first state to cover all costs for the Imagination Library. (Tennessee, Parton's home state — which Republicans control — was the first to introduce a statewide program involving partial public funding support.)
In lieu of local nonprofit partners, Missouri had school districts partner with the initiative, and the schools did not have to pay for the books or postage.
But in June 2026, under Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers cut state funding for the program for the upcoming fiscal year — reportedly from $6 million to $2 million.
"The Governor is a strong supporter of children's literacy. Given the seriousness of Missouri's budget imbalance, tough decisions are being made to restore responsible spending across the entirety of state government," Gabby Picard, Kehoe's spokesperson, said in an email.
According to the Missouri Department of Education, the planned cuts mean it can't support adding more children to the program. However, Missouri children already enrolled in the program will continue receiving books "as funding allows."
Indiana
Indiana began supporting the Imagination Library statewide through the 50/50 funding match model in 2023 under Republican Gov. Eric J. Holcomb, who championed the program. Lawmakers allotted $6 million to the program over two years.
In 2025, under Republican Gov. Mike Braun, GOP lawmakers cut the funding from the state budget entirely. Facing public backlash, the Indiana governor tasked his wife, Maureen Braun, with fundraising for the state-level match.
"In March, Mrs. Braun announced that fundraising for the state-level match for the program through June 30, 2027 is nearly complete," Griffin Reid, a spokesperson for Indiana's governor, said in an email. "The program is successfully delivering books to young Hoosiers in all 92 counties in Indiana."
According to the Indiana Capital Chronicle, the program was on hiatus while Maureen Braun fundraised.
News outlets have reported that the governor's office has consistently declined to share how much the first lady has raised. Reid also did not respond to our questions asking for specific numbers.
Did state Democrats cut funding?
Yes, in Washington, which was facing budget issues, and Maine, for unclear reasons. Nevada, which has a Republican governor but a Democratic state Legislature, also failed to renew several grants to help fund local partners of the Imagination Library.
Washington
Washington established its statewide program in 2022 through bipartisan legislation under Democratic leadership. The state also used the 50/50 match model.
In 2025, while facing a $12 billion shortfall, Washington cut all state funding to the Imagination Library under Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson and a Democrat-controlled Legislature.
State Superintendent Chris Reykdal, a Democrat, kept the program running through "limited discretionary funds" until June 2026. Reykdal has called on the Legislature and Ferguson to restore funding.
On July 31, 2026, the Imagination Library of Washington announced grants from two private foundations "expected to ultimately restore access for approximately 40,000 children and return the program to full statewide coverage."
Ferguson's office did not return an inquiry about restoring state funding.
Maine
Maine's Imagination Library program launched in late 2023 using the 50/50 match model after the Democratic state Legislature approved a $200,000 proposal from Democratic Gov. Janet Mills.
During Maine's budget process for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, both Mills and the Maine State Library requested funding to continue operating the program and to expand it into all of Maine's counties, according to emails from Beth Crist, director of special projects at Maine State Library, and Ben Goodman, a spokesperson with Mills' office.
The final budget the Legislature approved provided only $100,000 a year, however, which was not enough to expand the program, nor to support the existing nonprofit partners who administered it across seven counties at the time, Crist and Goodman said.
Maine's budget chairs, both Democrats, did not return an inquiry as to why the Legislature did not fully fund the program. Crist said the Legislature did not provide an explanation to Maine State Library.
Some chapters still operate in Maine without state funding.
Nevada
Nevada does not have a statewide Imagination Library program. However, in October 2025, Storied, a local partner serving Clark County, announced that the Nevada Legislature did not renew a grant that started in 2023, as the Nevada Current reported (and Storied confirmed).
Meredith Helmick, executive director of Storied, said in an email that the organization was able to resume its program in July 2026, "but on a much smaller scale."
"Kids will start receiving books in September," Helmick said.
Helmick said Storied spent the 10-month hiatus applying for local and state grants and receiving donations from local private foundations and individuals. She hopes to "find a path towards statewide coverage or to at least bring the program in Clark County back to its previous levels."
The Nevada Independent also reported that United Way Northern Nevada and the Sierra, a partner in Nevada's Washoe County, lost state grant funding in 2025.
However, a United Way Northern Nevada and the Sierra spokesperson, Daniel Amaya, said in an email that it was "changes in federal funding and resources being allocated elsewhere" that resulted in a pause in its partnership with Imagination Library.
"The loss of federal funds to the State of Nevada directly impacts the amount of money the state can allocate," Amaya said.
According to the Imagination Library's website, Washoe County no longer has an operating Imagination Library presence. United Way is seeking donations to resume the program.
"Our hope and goal is to restart Dolly Parton's Imagination Library in Northern Nevada as soon as we secure the funding needed," Amaya said. "We look forward to the day we can turn the page and begin this important work again."
Did Trump or the federal government cut funding?
Federal funding indirectly provided support to local partners who worked with the Imagination Library, even though the federal government doesn't directly fund the program.
Aside from Washoe County in Nevada, the Trump administration's 2025 cuts to federal grant funds affected at least one other area: New Hampshire's North Country, which is effectively the top half of the state.
Whitefield Public Library — the Imagination Library's local partner in the North Country — first launched the program in 2025 after months of work, said Vashaw, the director of Whitefield Public Library.
Part of that work involved finding a financial partner who could cover the local partner costs for the program: an organization called the Education Alliance for New Hampshire.
After just a "handful of months" of that group running the program, however, the Trump administration rescinded federal grant funding that the Education Alliance relied on. The Education Alliance closed down.
"Their doors were shuttered, their programs closed with very little notice and that meant we had no funding," Vashaw said. "We literally weren't sure we were going to be able to pay the bills come January."
The Department of Education declined to answer questions about these funds on the record.
After emergency fundraising, the Whitefield Public Library was able to keep the program going. As of this writing, 620 kids are enrolled, Vashaw said.
Vashaw said private fundraising isn't on track for 2027. However, she's hoping a bipartisan effort from New Hampshire lawmakers to make the Imagination Library available statewide will help keep the program going.

Five years after the Taliban seized full control of Afghanistan, forcing the US-led NATO forces to move out of the country in 2021, Kabul is now trying to improve bilateral ties with Washington. The Taliban-led government is now offering American investors access to the vast mineral wealth that the country has to offer. In return, Kabul is urging Washington to ease sanctions and release billions of dollars in frozen Afghan assets. Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi told The Financial Times that Afghanistan’s Taliban-led government was “absolutely” willing to welcome US investment in sectors such as mining, infrastructure, agriculture and trade. In an interview published Monday (local time), Muttaqi said, "Relations between Afghanistan and the United States should not be assessed through the lens of the past 20 years of war, but rather on the basis of future co-operation." He added that the country’s economic policy remained open. The Taliban-led government is reportedly hoping that such proposals could pave the way for Washington to agree to lift international sanctions and unfreeze Afghan assets. However, Muttaqi did not clarify whether the proposal had already been presented to the White House. Geological assessments conducted by the US and the former Afghan government indicate that Afghanistan holds at least $1 trillion worth of largely untapped mineral resources, including deposits of copper, iron ore, niobium, cobalt, gold and lithium. US President Donald Trump has shown little to no willingness to establish ties with the Taliban. Previously, he called for the return of Bagram Air Base, a demand that Muttaqi rejected, stating that all military and civilian facilities were assets of the country. After the Taliban takeover in 2021 led to the withdrawal of US and Nato forces and the collapse of the US-backed Afghan government, the US president called the episode the “most embarrassing thing in the history of our country.” Muttaqi has also urged Washington to reopen the US embassy in Kabul, stating that security at the site has been ensured. According to Iran International, Muttaqi, in a separate interview with Japan’s Kyodo News, called on Washington to abandon what he described as a confrontational approach towards the Taliban administration. Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban has stepped up efforts to attract foreign investment and has signed mining contracts worth more than $7 billion, including deals involving gold, precious stones and chromite. These contracts have been signed with countries such as China and Iran. In recent years, Kabul has expanded its diplomatic outreach, with countries such as China, India, Iran, Qatar and several other Central Asian nations opening channels with Afghanistan and Taliban officials. Last year, Russia officially recognised the Taliban government. In May, it also entered into a military cooperation agreement with Afghanistan. Separately, in June, the European Union (EU) held talks with Taliban representatives in Brussels over the potential return of migrants. - Rockstar is taking a more tactical approach to GTA 6's gunplay and combat.
- Australian creator TGG revealed that GTA 6 will disable auto-aim by default.
- He also noted that GTA 6's weapons will have more recoil and crisper sound design.
Rockstar is making major changes to GTA 6, including a more tactical gunplay system than in previous GTA games. Australian creator TGG has revealed new details about GTA 6’s gunplay and combat after a two-hour preview at Rockstar North with studio co-head Rob Nelson.
According to TGG’s preview analysis, GTA 6 will have auto-aim disabled by default, placing greater emphasis on free aiming while allowing players to adjust the aiming settings to their preference. Unlike in Red Dead Redemption 2, you will not be able to hold the left trigger and have Jason or Lucia automatically lock onto an NPC.
However, you can adjust aim stickiness via the game’s settings. Additionally, TGG also revealed that GTA 6’s weapons have significantly more recoil, kickback, and a crisper sound design than in Grand Theft Auto 5. For example, assault rifles require more controlled bursts and tap-firing for better precision due to the recoil.
Speaking of the gunplay, you also need to be careful with your exposed weapons when you’re free-roaming the GTA 6 map. On this topic, the Australian creator states that NPCs won’t mind if you have a long weapon on your back. However, if you aim the weapon at them, the situation will escalate, as they will try to flee or call the cops.
Shoulder switching also returns from Red Dead Redemption 2, giving you more control over your aim with Jason and Lucia, further refining GTA 6’s combat gameplay compared to the previous instalments. Jason and Lucia can also swap weapons if one of them runs out of ammo.
We saw plenty of Jason’s gunplay in the GTA 6 Extended Look, and it looked more tactical, fluid, and crisper than GTA 5’s gunplay. With GTA 6’s improved gore and dismemberment system, shooting will definitely be a highlight in the highly anticipated title.
So, what do you think about GTA 6 taking a more tactical approach to the gunplay? Tell us in the comments section below.

Nintendo's surprise free update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe on Switch 2 includes eight-player split-screen
The nine-year-old game that keeps giving.
You'd be forgiven for thinking Nintendo had already squeezed every remaining drop of juice out of Mario Kart 8 Deluxe. After starting its life as a Wii U title in 2014, the already expanded Switch version of Mario Kart 8 that arrived three years later went on to receive even more new tracks and features, keeping it in the US sales charts for almost the entirety of the console's lifespan.
The Switch 2 launched last year with Mario Kart World, which looked like the end of the (Rainbow) road for its staggeringly successful predecessor, but Nintendo apparently isn't done just yet. Completely out of the blue (shell — OK I promise to stop now), the company has just rolled out a meaty new free update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe specifically aimed at Switch 2 players.
You can now play with up to eight players in split-screen in local multiplayer, provided you have enough controllers to go around (original Switch controllers are also supported). Nintendo has also added CameraPlay support, so if you have an official Switch 2 camera or compatible USB-C camera connected to your console, you can see your friends' very own Luigi death stares when you overtake them. You can also use CameraPlay online via GameChat, just like in Mario Kart World.
Loading times are also now shorter, and you'll be getting "enhanced visuals" when playing in docked mode. Obviously this assumes you have a 4K TV that can take advantage of the Switch 2's improved output. Mario Kart 8 Deluxe could already output at 1080p in handheld mode via 'Handheld Mode Boost' but can presumably now do so natively thanks to the new update.
Exactly why Nintendo is adding all these features to an old game instead of pushing even more people towards Mario Kart World is anyone's guess. The company has also been gradually improving the Switch 2-exclusive entry through updates, but by now a lot of people were hoping to have heard about DLC plans, given how many new tracks we got over the years in Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.
Mario Kart World is still included in one of the recently revamped Switch 2 bundles, which costs $50 more than the same bundle did at launch but now also comes with a three-month Nintendo Switch Online membership.

Zee Group founder Subhash Chandra on Wednesday opposed the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)’s decision to constitute a five-member bench to hear his personal insolvency case afresh, questioning the legal basis for expanding the bench after three members gave differing views on his repayment plan. Chandra’s counsel argued that Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, which deals with differences of opinion among tribunal members, did not give the NCLT the power to constitute a five-member bench. “The scope of Section 419(5) is very limited… It does not give power to the NCLT under the IBC or company law to form a five-member bench”, Chandra's counsel argued. Chandra’s counsel also opposed the move to hear the entire case again. He argued that the earlier order approving the repayment plan could not be set aside. He also questioned the order of the third member, Nilesh Sharma, who had stayed the proceedings against Subhash Chandra. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) kept the creditor's challenge to Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan pending. The appellate tribunal decided not to dispose of the appeal for now, allowing the lenders to keep their challenge alive as the NCLT is hearing the matter afresh after constituting a five-judge bench. After hearing the arguments, NCLAT decided to hear the matter on October 7. On Tuesday, a newly formed five-member NCLT bench led by president Justice Anupinder Singh Grewal clarified that the order of member Nilesh Sharma, delivered on 25 August, could not be given effect because it did not constitute the majority view of the tribunal. A day earlier, the appellate tribunal had agreed to hear an urgent plea by several creditors challenging the NCLT Delhi bench’s approval of the repayment plan proposed by Zee Group founder Subhash Chandra. Minutes after the NCLT special bench proceedings ended, solicitor general Tushar Mehta appeared before the NCLAT for creditors including LIC Housing Finance, HDFC Bank and Union Bank of India. Mehta asked the NCLAT to consider whether its intervention was needed now that the NCLT had stayed the earlier order. The case concerns Chandra’s liability as a personal guarantor for loans taken by companies linked to the Essel Group and the Zee Group. In February, a two-member bench of the NCLT differed on whether his repayment plan would be binding on dissenting creditors. Sharma, who was brought in as the third member, approved the plan and held that it would be binding on dissenting creditors. Government officials told Mint earlier that about ₹2,574 crore of the claims were related to loans for which Chandra had given personal guarantees when they were taken. Chandra has said he did not personally borrow the money and that his ₹31.79 crore net worth formed the basis of his repayment proposal. There is also a dispute over the voting process. A creditor alleged that the resolution professional had wrongly admitted the claims of five entities—Veena Investments, Direct Media Distribution Ventures, World Crest Advisors, Lemonade Capital Advisors and Corpcall Capital Advisors—which together held 61.78% of the voting share and helped approve Chandra’s repayment plan. Tugboat sinks off South Korea's southern coast, leaving 1 dead and 6 missing
A tugboat capsized and sank off South Korea's southeastern coast, leaving one crew member dead and six others missing
SEOUL, South Korea -- A tugboat capsized and sank off South Korea's southeastern coast on Wednesday, leaving one crew member dead and six others missing, the coast guard said.
The 286-ton tugboat was carrying eight crew members when it departed Wednesday morning to tow a merchant vessel in the waters off South Korea's southeastern city of Busan, the coast guard said in a statement.
After the tugboat overturned, one crew member, an Indonesian, was rescued by the merchant vessel. Another of the crew, a South Korean, was discovered unconscious by coast guard rescuers before being sent to a hospital on the mainland and declared dead there, the coast guard said.
The coast guard and the navy sent vessels, aircraft and other assets to rescue the six remaining crew members who are still missing, according to the coast guard. President Lee Jae Myung ordered authorities to mobilize all available resources.
The coast guard said the tugboat eventually sank at around 3:30 p.m. (0630 GMT) about two hours after the capsizing was reported. The cause of the capsizing wasn't immediately known.

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.
The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.
Flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41 to 46 feet (12 to 14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.
Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.
“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”
South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.
Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”
Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.
“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.
Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

Five moments that shaped Taylor's legendary career
- Published
On Saturday, Katie Taylor steps through the ropes at an 82,000-capacity Croke Park to face France's Flora Pili in her farewell fight.
Victory on the hallowed Dublin turf would write one final fairytale chapter - a chance to bow out as undisputed light-welterweight champion and put the seal on a career that has revolutionised women's sport.
There have been countless moments that have shaped the 40-year-old's journey.
From a childhood letter to a Twitter direct message, these are five sliding doors moments in the making of an Irish icon.
The letter to Deirdre Gogarty
Long before Taylor became Olympic champion, she was a 10-year-old girl in Bray who simply wanted to box.
There was nowhere for her to go though. Women's boxing was unsanctioned in Ireland, absent from the Olympic programme and devoid of any clear professional pathway.
But there was Deirdre Gogarty. Having relocated to the United States, she became Ireland's first female professional world champion in 1997 when she defeated Bonnie Canino for the WIBF featherweight title in Louisiana.
"How did you do it when everyone tried to stop you?" a 10-year-old Taylor asked in a letter sent to her hero.
"If you keep working at it and keep showing your skills, somebody's going to say 'we've got to let this girl box'," Gogarty replied.
Reflecting on the letter years later, Gogarty added: "It's mind-blowing. Especially when she wrote, 'maybe one day they'll let us box in the Olympics'."
Had that letter never been written, Taylor might still have found her way to the top, but Gogarty offered hope when none seemingly existed.
Heartbreak at Rio 2016 and the leap into the unknown
When the International Olympic Committee was undecided on including women's boxing at the Games, Taylor was brought in for showcase events in front of sceptical officials in Chicago. Her dazzling displays dismantled every argument.
"Katie won't say this, and I've been holding back from saying this, but single-handedly, Katie Taylor got women's boxing into the Olympics," her manager Brian Peters says.
Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at the London 2012 Games and Taylor claimed lightweight gold.
Four years later in Rio, however, that amateur journey ended when a split-decision quarter-final defeat shattered Taylor's title defence. She was at a crossroads - rebuild for another Olympic cycle or turn professional in an era where women's pro boxing was still neglected.
"It was probably the worst year of my career," Taylor later admitted. "I needed a change. I needed a new mindset."
Had she secured a second Olympic gold, the motivation to dive into the pro ranks might have evaporated. Instead, the sting of defeat forced reinvention.
Hearn's DMs & Taylor's loyalty
Turning professional was one thing, but securing both the right team and commercial backing was another challenge.
First came manager Peters, who initially stepped in out of concern for her future.
"I only took her on not to see her end up with people who didn't know what they were doing," Peters says.
On 4 October 2016, Taylor sent Matchroom's Eddie Hearn a direct message on Twitter, now known as X, asking if he would consider promoting her. Hearn replied 24 hours later, inviting Taylor, Peters, and her mother Bridget to a London restaurant. Hearn even borrowed his father's car to impress Taylor.
The charm offensive worked and Taylor made her debut at Wembley Arena a month later.
In a sport notorious for fractured relationships and bitter splits, Taylor's core team has remained the same from day one with Peters, Hearn and trainer Ross Enamait.
"In a business full of egos, she's stayed loyal to everyone around her and remained the most humble person you could ever meet," Peters says.
Had Hearn dismissed that DM - or had Taylor lacked the enduring loyalty that kept the same tight-knit team in her corner for a decade - the promotional engine that transformed women's boxing might never have started.
MSG & the Serrano test
By April 2022, Taylor was the undisputed lightweight champion. She had already survived a razor-thin majority decision against Delfine Persoon at Madison Square Garden (MSG) three years earlier to unify - a night when many felt her aura of invincibility was almost cracked.
Returning to MSG to face seven-division title winner Amanda Serrano presented a different magnitude of threat.
Their blockbuster marked the first time two women headlined the storied New York venue. In front of a sellout crowd of 19,187, Taylor claimed a split-decision victory in what was widely hailed as the fight of the year.
Had one scorecard leaned the other way or had the bout failed to deliver on its enormous hype, the momentum behind women's mega-fights would have stalled.
Instead, the victory spawned a record-breaking rivalry. Their 2024 rematch drew global viewing figures on Netflix on the undercard of Jake Paul v Mike Tyson, before Taylor sealed the trilogy at the Garden in 2025.
Taylor v Pili
Saturday, 5 September
Croke Park, Dublin
Coverage on Radio 5 Sports Extra from 19:00 BST, then 5 Live from 22:00. Ringwalks for main event expected between 22:00 and 22:30.
Cameron II: Legacy on the line
Taylor's first professional defeat came in May 2023 at Dublin's 3Arena when she was outpointed by Chantelle Cameron for the undisputed light-welterweight belts.
At 36, questions around retirement surfaced.
In the ring immediately following the defeat, Peters says he told his fighter to congratulate Cameron and ask for the rematch.
Six months later, Taylor delivered a masterclass in grit, claiming a majority decision to become a two-weight undisputed champion.
"The pressure was immense," Peters says.
"For all she had done, her legacy was suddenly questioned. Had Chantelle won the rematch, who knows what would have happened?"
The final pay-off - Croke Park
Croke Park is not really a sixth sliding door but rather the final pay-off.
After beating Serrano in last year's trilogy decider, Taylor quietly decided she was done.
"She actually retired that night," Peters says. "She said, 'We convincingly beat Serrano - where do we go from there?' I said I'll agree on one condition."
That condition was Croke Park or nothing.
"Croke Park - no disrespect to Wembley - is the greatest stadium in the world," Peters says. "You cut an Irish person and they'll bleed Croke Park."
Peters insists there will be no change of heart - no Cameron trilogy and no comebacks.
"When Katie gives her word, that is it," he says.
Regardless of Saturday's result, Taylor will be remembered as a pioneer who kicked open the door for women's boxing.

Matte gold, sloped, and steering-wheel-free, the Tesla Cybercab seems designed to catch the eyes of looky-loos. Now rubberneckers may have more opportunities: Tesla is set to host an event on Thursday at its Austin, Texas, headquarters to debut the Cybercab.
Tesla first rolled out a prototype Cybercab at a flashy event on the Warner Bros. lot in 2024. This week’s unveiling will likely mark the vehicle’s official introduction to the electric-auto maker’s small ride-hail service. It has operated a pilot program in Austin since last summer, and has since expanded to a handful of other cities in Texas and Florida, with permits to launch in Arizona and Nevada. (A “robotaxi” service in the San Francisco Bay Area is not legally permitted to operate without drivers behind the wheel.) Before the event, Tesla added 51 Cybercabs to its fleet of vehicles registered to operate in Texas (263 Model Ys are also registered).
“The streets won't be the same anymore,” Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, posted last month on X. When an X user asked whether the Cybercabs would “flood Austin,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk, with his characteristic moth-to-the-flame tendencies toward hyperbole, responded with a simple “Yes.”
Details on the event are still scant, and the basic business model for the Cybercab is in question—are the vehicles just for ride-hail operations, or meant to be sold to individual drivers? States regulate autonomous vehicles, and some tightly control permits and data collection. However, Musk still insisted this year that Tesla will sell Cybercabs directly to consumers before the end of 2026.
Either way, the physical Cybercab slated to be shown off in Austin on Thursday may be the easiest lift in Tesla’s deeply ambitious plan to shift from a company that builds cars to one entirely focused on autonomous vehicles and robotics. Manufacturing a car isn’t easy. But neither is running a functional autonomous vehicle service, nor building the software to power it. Tesla hasn’t yet proven that it can do either at scale.
“Longer term, the software is the most important piece,” says Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst for Morningstar who follows Tesla. “This is a very important step, to put the Cybercab in production, but ultimately, it only matters if the software can allow a car to navigate safely.”
Musk has promised for nearly a decade that the Teslas sold to everyday consumers are just a software update away from driverless capabilities, but that has yet to come true. (Musk admitted earlier this year that some vehicles will need a hardware upgrade to get the capability.) The company’s critical thesis is that a car can drive on complicated, chaotic public roads with only inexpensive cameras, which could allow it to deploy self-driving robots much more cheaply than the competition. Waymo, the US industry leader, took a direct swipe at Tesla last month, writing in a blog post that “cameras are incredible, but they aren’t enough.” Waymo’s more expensive setup uses lidar and radar along with cameras.
Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) product, available to drivers for a $99 monthly fee, currently does many driving tasks, including changing lanes and stopping at red lights. But the company warns in its manuals that drivers must pay attention and be ready to intervene at all times. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the US’s top auto safety regulator, opened an investigation into crashes involving FSD in 2024 following concerns that the system falters in situations with poor visibility. That probe is ongoing.
Tesla began testing its steering-wheel- and pedal-free Cybercab on Austin streets in late June 2026. Based on videos posted online, much of the testing occurs with a safety monitor in the front passenger seat, ready to intervene if something goes wrong.
Success in the robotaxi game also has a lot to do with balance sheets and spending. “These AV companies are spending so much money getting this technology in place, but in order to scale up the business, the economics come down to utilization," says J. D. Alexander, the founder of AVFleetTech, a consultancy focused on AV fleet operations.
Companies need to wring all they can out of their investments on wheels, making sure their vehicles are on the road and picking up passengers as much as possible. Efficiency comes down to how, when, and where the robots get charged, cleaned, and fixed—and making sure that the humans hired to do those things are well trained and motivated.
The nitty-gritty operations are complicated enough that other firms with robotaxi services and ambitions have partnered with several other companies to get it done. In Dallas, the rental company Avis manages fleet logistics, maintenance, charging, and depots for Waymo; Hertz is slated to do the same for Uber self-driving cars. Waymo also works with the fleet manager Moove in Arizona, Florida, and, soon, London, and with Lyft’s Flexdrive service in Nashville.
Tesla likes to do everything on its own, and it has clearly started to think about where and how it wants to stage its robotaxis. In new markets, Cybercabs might first operate out of Tesla service centers, where employees already repair and clean its electric cars. Tesla is tinkering with the cleaning part too. A Texas state architectural permit application the company filed in June 2025 indicated that the company’s main robotaxi hub would have a “cleaning robot” on the premises. However, Tesla hasn’t released details on that tech beyond a promotional video posted last year.
The physical Cybercab, then, is just a start. As more of the gilded cars “flood” the streets, it should be easy to watch them go.

Worms found crawling in khichuri served to children at West Bengal anganwadi
White worms were found in khichuri served to children at an anganwadi centre in Cooch Behar. The incident reportedly left two children ill and sparked a village protest.
White worms were found crawling in khichuri prepared for children at an anganwadi centre in the Kuthibari area of Dinhata in Cooch Behar, West Bengal. Two local children reportedly fell ill after eating the meal.
The incident came to light on Wednesday morning and led to anger among villagers in the area. Residents gathered at the anganwadi centre to protest over the food served to the children.
VILLAGERS LOCK ANGANWADI CENTRE
During the protest, villagers locked the door of the anganwadi centre. The action reflected their anger over the alleged presence of worms in the khichuri prepared for the children.
The incident was reported from Kuthibari under Putimari-2 Gram Panchayat in Dinhata. It has caused a stir among residents in the area.
SIMILAR INCIDENTS IN BIHAR
In a separate incident in Bihar's Nalanda district, at least 40 students fell ill after detergent powder was reportedly served instead of salt with their mid-day meal at Parasi Middle School. The students complained of stomach pain and vomiting and were taken to Hospital. Bihar Rural Development Minister Shravan Kumar visited the hospital and assured strict action against those responsible.
In another case in Arwal district, worms were reportedly found in a soybean dish supplied by an NGO to 75 schools in the Sadar block. Headmasters stopped the food from being served and informed the Education Department. District Education Officer Asgar Ali said the matter was being investigated and action would be taken against the NGO if negligence was established.

Man Utd and their calculated left-back gamble
- Published
As 23:00 BST ticked by on 1 September and the suspicion became reality, many Manchester United fans thought the same thing – what about a left-back?
Since the 2025-26 season ended, and United's summer transfer strategy started to be debated, it seemed obvious the club would move to address a perceived weakness in Michael Carrick's squad.
Luke Shaw is their only senior orthodox left-back. He started all 38 Premier League games last season, which given his previous injury record was phenomenal.
But as back-up Tyrell Malacia had unsurprisingly been allowed to leave when his contract expired at the end of June, and it is widely accepted 31-year-old Shaw will not be able to play repeatedly in a new campaign that could stretch beyond 60 games, a reinforcement was expected.
Various targets were identified, including Newcastle's Lewis Hall, Barcelona's Alejandro Balde and Racing Santander's Jorge Salinas. Finally, it came down to an attempt to get Rayan Ait-Nouri to cross the great Manchester divide by joining on loan, but City said no.
For that move to have progressed, United would have had to include an obligation to buy at a later date, but have instead chosen to bide their time for their first-choice targets.
Now the deadline has passed and, at least until the winter window opens in January, United and Carrick must stand or fall by what has to be viewed as a calculated gamble.
- Man Utd fail in attempt to sign Ait-Nouri from Man City 
  - Published15 hours ago
Will Man Utd try to sign Hall in 2027?
Firstly, it must be acknowledged Manchester United really like Lewis Hall.
Had they been able to do a deal with Newcastle for him, they would have done.
However, raided by Premier League rivals for their star men this summer, it became obvious in discussions around the highly-rated 22-year-old if Newcastle were to be persuaded to strike a deal, the transfer fee would be huge.
Manchester United's summer transfer budget was finite.
Faced with the reality of the situation, they opted to maintain their focus on the 'priority' midfield area and eventually committed £70m to bring in Carlos Baleba from Brighton.
Hall, it was concluded, is someone they are prepared to wait until next summer for.
United would have been prepared to take Balde on loan. Barcelona would only sell him. Salinas had a relatively low release clause, but Atletico Madrid were favourites to sign him. By the time they moved on to Argentina defender Nicolas Tagliafico, who they missed out on anyway, United had moved on themselves.
Their decision to belatedly act on an initial approach made by an agent around Ait-Nouri was an admission they are not totally certain of the path they have chosen.
Effectively that is Shaw as first-choice left-back, with Noussair Mazraoui as back-up, in a position he admittedly plays in for Morocco, supported by Diogo Dalot, who has switched flanks before, and Harry Amass.
Right-back role for Yoro and when does Amass play?
The Amass case is a strange one. A natural left-back in United's academy, who did well in a loan spell at Sheffield Wednesday last season, then got injured straight after switching to Norwich in the winter window, Amass, 19, impressed many observers with his performances during pre-season, when he shadowed Shaw.
Yet, for some reason, United were willing to let him leave.
In the summer of 2024, then manager Erik ten Hag opted not to pick the teenager in his squad for the Community Shield, even though Amass had given a creditable account of himself up against Mo Salah in a pre-season game in the United States just a week earlier.
Ten Hag felt, physically, Amass was not at the level required. In theory, the two years that have elapsed since then should have made the defender bigger and stronger.
There have been multiple expressions of interest in Amass. Even heading into deadline day, his omission from United's Premier League 2 game against Leicester on Monday reinforced a widespread belief he would leave, probably on loan.
But that has not happened and it is not clear what his role will be within the senior squad.
The willingness to view Mazraoui as a left-back option was helped by the performances of Leny Yoro in pre-season.
Signed from Lille for £52m in 2024 as a central defender, Carrick used Yoro mainly as a right-back this summer.
Against Ipswich on Sunday, that was the slot Yoro was introduced into as a replacement for Dalot, at the same time as Mazraoui was coming on for Shaw.
At just 20, Yoro has plenty to learn about the right-back role. However, he has pace, is strong and is good on the ball. United supporters only have to look at how Josko Gvardiol has adapted to the full-back role at Manchester City after signing as a central defender to realise switching positions can have a positive outcome.
That is the calculated risk United have taken.
What they absolutely did not want to do, having taken a hardline stance all summer on the fees they were willing to pay, and a refusal to spend more than they thought a player was worth, was end up making a signing like Alex Telles, or Matteo Darmian, or Sergio Reguilon, who all arrived in recent years but were evidently short of the standard required.
It makes sense. It is probably the right call.
But that is a view taken away from the emotion of matches and the rollercoaster of results. And the reality is they will be the deciding factor in whether it was a good decision or not.

In Summary
- Instagram has announced a new feature for its app, called First Draft. Available only for iPhone users at the time of writing, it trims and blends selected videos, converting them into a reel within seconds.
- Although First Draft’s editing is on the basic side, it is nevertheless extremely useful for those newcomers (or even veterans) who are not comfortable with editing videos.
- Experts might find First Draft to be very basic, but its ease of use and speed make it perfect for content creators who feel held back by their lack of basic video editing ability.
Instagram has just rolled out a new feature, which it claims is going to make creating Reels easier. As its name suggests, First Draft basically gives users a quick “first draft” by turning all the video clips that they have selected into a quick Reel. The feature is an iPhone exclusive for now and only available on the main Instagram app, and not on Edits (the Reels editing app by Instagram), but an Android release is likely to follow soon.
Given all the AI hype and how much Meta is focusing on it, you might think First Draft is a new AI feature, but Instagram has confirmed that First Draft does not use Artificial Intelligence. Nevertheless, it has made people wonder if its ease of use could actually reduce the role of conventional, “manual” editing in the Reel world. Well, we have used the feature for a short while, and here is what we think.
How to use Instagram First Draft
Using First Draft is a pretty simple affair. Just follow these steps:
- Open the Instagram app on your iPhone (do remember to update it to the latest version), then tap on the “+” icon present on the top left side of the app to add new content.
- From there, swipe to Reels on the panel on the lower part of the app.
- Tap on the camera to record footage or select an existing video from your gallery, which will be displayed.
- Once you have selected all the clips you wish to add, look for the First Draft option, which will appear on the panel at the lower part of the app – it appears the moment you select a video. Tapping it will open a First Draft box, with a “Try it” button. Tap on this button.
- Hitting the button puts the selected videos into a processing phase where the app analyses the clips, identifies highlights, trims clips, and reduces the length.
- In a matter of ten seconds, the feature will present a pretty basic edited version of your videos, trimming them and cutting out awkward pauses, with preview frames beneath the result, which you can move back and forth to reorder.
- If you like the results, tap on the Next button in the bottom right corner of the app to go to the Instagram Reels posting page (you can also take your results to Edits), make more changes, if need be, and hit Publish.
How First Draft works
Instagram has stressed that the new editing feature is just a “starting point” on which creators can then build their final Reel. The social media platform says the feature can identify silences, awkward pauses, and other such moments. It then removes these moments, trims the video, and gives a first draft that highlights what it assumes are important parts of the video. It allows creators to select or record, edit, and share all without leaving Instagram.
Instagram has been ensuring that users know that all that is done by the feature is reversible, and does not come as an attempt to replace a creator’s creativity, but actually offers ‘early video trimming’ so users can move their focus from the technical part of editing to its creative part. Instead of using AI (which comes as a surprise), First Draft actually uses internal processing and audio detection to find moments of silence in selected videos. We have fiddled with the feature for a short while and can say that it actually works,serving up a very basic edit of videos (or of a single long video), even while leaving the “creative work” to the user.
Going by our first encounter with First Draft, it cannot really replace manual editing. It is not a very creative feature and only offers what can be termed as the ‘bare-bones’ of what your edited Reel might look like. We found the feature does eliminate pauses and silence, but when it trims videos, there seems to be no method to its madness, which basically means you can end up with some of the important bits removed from the video. In its current form, it might come in handy for people who create piece-to-camera video formats, but you would still need to revise and re-edit the whole thing on your own.
Also See: Instagram Edits vs CapCut: Best Video Editing App for You
First Draft: Who is it for (and who might not like it)
It is rather basic, but those who are new to creating videos and struggle with editing might find First Draft useful. It offers a very quick, hassle-free edit of videos. This can be helpful for creators who are not as skilled when it comes to editing their content, or are intimidated by the task. First Draft can be a very simple, quick-fix solution for them. But it is unlikely to appeal much to those creators who have been in the game for a while, are good at editing, and have their own style and flair in the editing field. We can already see them skipping this new feature.
But given that a large number of Instagram users do not really know much about video editing, First Draft seems to be an extremely handy tool, especially for those who do not want to get into the hassle of going through all their videos one by one and trimming out stutters and pauses. The fact that one can do so right from within Instagram, without having to open an additional app, is a huge bonus. As mentioned by the platform itself, First Draft is just a starting point and nothing more. Even in its current form (and we think it will get better in clip selection), it will help new creators start their content journey and feel more comfortable without getting knee-deep in editing hassles from the get-go.
Experts might shake their heads at how basic the feature is, but then remember how DSLR photographers shook their heads at 0.3 MP cellphone cameras? First Draft might be the first step to breaking down the editing barrier that holds back many content creators, and if it gets better (maybe with even options to automatically choose background audio or add subtitles in other languages, and so on), who knows, even experts might find it a handy tool to save them some time. But that’s in the future (and we bet AI will come into it at some stage). As for now, First Draft is mainly for Instagram newbies who want Reel creation with zero hassles. And that actually is a bigger deal than some of the pros might admit.

OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman are facing 30 new lawsuits that accuse them of providing “substantial assistance and encouragement” to the suspect in Canada’s Tumbler Ridge school shooting, as reported earlier by TechCrunch. The new wave of lawsuits was filed in a California federal court on Wednesday by the students, teachers, and the principal in the school at the time of the shooting.
OpenAI accused of ‘aiding and abetting’ Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in dozens of new lawsuits
The lawsuits accuse OpenAI of providing ‘substantial assistance and encouragement’ to the Tumbler Ridge shooting suspect.
Similar to the lawsuits filed by Tumbler Ridge victims’ families in April, these lawsuits claim OpenAI failed to take action after its automated review system flagged conversations that the alleged shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, had with ChatGPT about gun violence. While its safety team recommended that OpenAI contact Canadian authorities, the lawsuits allege OpenAI chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, was involved in a decision to stay silent out of concern for the company’s “reputational and financial standing.”
Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, responded to the lawsuits in a post on X, saying they contain “false claims” about its safety teams. He adds that it’s “completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.” OpenAI is also facing a lawsuit from the state of Florida, which accuses the company of aiding and abetting mass shooters, including the suspect who carried out an attack at Florida State University last year.
The new Tumbler Ridge lawsuits also allege that OpenAI allowed the suspect to continue using ChatGPT by “deactivating” their account rather than issuing a system-wide ban. This allegedly allowed the suspect to regain access to the AI chatbot by signing up with another email. “Providing the Shooter with continued access to this tool constituted substantial assistance in itself,” the lawsuit alleges, claiming OpenAI’s “substantial assistance was a key factor in causing the Shooter to plan and carry out the attack.”

'Moonies' church leader jailed for two years over bribery offences
- Published
The leader of the controversial Unification Church has been sentenced to two years in prison for bribing South Korea's former first lady and other political funding offences.
A court found that Han Hak-ja's church gave Kim Keon Hee, the wife of ousted president Yoon Suk Yeol, two Chanel bags and a diamond necklace, together worth 80 million won ($57,900; £42,500).
Earlier this year, Kim was sentenced to 20 months in jail for accepting bribes from the church.
Han, the 83-year-old widow of the Unification Church's founder Sun Myung Moon, had repeatedly denied the allegations, calling them "false".
A special counsel team appointed to the case said Kim received the luxury products from the church between April and July 2022, in exchange for business and political favours.
The prosecutors said the probe was the first time the authorities have confirmed the church's attempt at buying influence in politics, and released photos of $19m (£14m) worth of cash found in Han's personal safe.
South Korea's former first lady admitted to receiving Chanel bags, but said she later returned them without using them.
Kim made a public apology when she appeared for questioning last August: "I am truly sorry that a nobody like me has caused concern to the people."
The Unification Church, known formally as The Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, was founded in South Korea in the 1950s by Moon Sun-myung, who proclaimed himself the messiah.
The church is probably best known for the mass weddings where thousands of couples were married by Han and her late husband and founder Sun Myung Moon in a stadium.
Critics have described the group as "cult-like". Lawyers have accused it of coercing devotees, known colloquially as "Moonies" after its founder, to donate large sums of money. "Moonies" is a term used by critics that many church members find offensive.
The Unification Church had come under the spotlight in Japan after the assassination of the country's former leader Shinzo Abe. The alleged assassin blamed the group for bankrupting his family and held a grievance against Abe for allegedly promoting it.
The church has boasted extensive links to politicians in Seoul, Tokyo, and even in Washington. Various politicians sent video message to its 2021 event congratulating the church's new think tank.
The list included US President Donald Trump, former US Vice-President Mike Pence, Shinzo Abe, as well as the mayors of Seoul and Busan.
The group is banned in parts of the world, including Singapore. In Japan, it has been ordered to dissolve.

Tencent Holdings’ strategy of using its vast product ecosystem to train its new Hy4 preview model gives it an edge in developing AI agents and brings its flagship model suite back into the top tier of open-source offerings, according to analysts.
