Ekomie started his professional career with Bordeaux but secured a switch to top-flight side Angers in the summer of 2024.
He made 21 appearances across all competitions in his debut season for the club, and his impact increased last term.
The 23-year-old featured in all but two of his side's Ligue 1 matches in 2025-26 - with 25 of his 32 league appearances being starts.
On Ekomie's signing, manager Parkinson said: "We're very pleased to sign Jacques. It's a transfer we worked very hard on.
"Jacques is a good young player and we're looking forward to integrating him into the group."
Ahead of his side's 1-1 draw with Watford, Wrexham manager Parkinson stated deals for various players to join the Red Dragons had fallen through in what had been a "difficult window".
But speaking in his post-match press conference after the Championship contest with the Hornets, the boss said there were "no guarantees" that Wrexham would further bolster their squad prior to the 23:00 BST transfer deadline on 1 September.
Midfielder George Thomason has operated as a makeshift wing-back in the absence of Cacace - who started just eight of Wrexham's 46 league games last season.
Cacace has missed all three of the Red Dragons' matches across all competitions so far this season and still has two years left to run on his contract at the Racecourse Ground.
Wrexham could yet add to their midfield and forward options in the final stages of the summer window.
Parkinson's men return to action against Birmingham City at the Racecourse Ground on Friday night (20:00 BST).

The EPA classified trifludimoxazin as having "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential," which essentially means that while there is evidence the chemical could potentially be one that causes cancer, there isn't enough data to say for sure. Additionally, the EPA does not consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS, though the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development does.
In late summer 2026, some people on social media claimed that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration approved the use of a potentially carcinogenic pesticide that's a "forever chemical," also known as PFAS. PFAS, an abbreviation for perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are long-lasting chemicals that persistently remain in the environment, capable of accumulating in things like rivers, plants, animals and people's bodies, that often have harmful health effects on people, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed that the EPA "just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin," to be used on crops including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples and tree nuts such as almonds. According to the post, environmental groups consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS pesticide and "forever chemical." 
The U.S. EPA just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin for agricultural use on a wide range of crops, including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples, and tree nuts such as almonds.
Trifludimoxazin is also considered by many environmental groups to be a PFAS pesticide because it contains highly fluorinated chemical structures and can break down into persistent fluorinated compounds - i.e. nature can't break it down properly as it's synthetic. Environmental organizations have described it as a "forever chemical" and have filed lawsuits challenging the EPA's approval.
Environmental groups have also pointed out that the company's own studies showed evidence suggesting cancer concerns and that the EPA downplayed those findings whe not was approved. The EPA claims the product is safe and that people shouldn't be concerned. Not a good look for MAHA.
Similar Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same claims, which were also spread on X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking if the rumor is true.
The Trump administration's EPA proposed approving trifludimoxazin in June 2025 and went through with the approval in June 2026. Researchers have found some evidence suggesting the chemical may be carcinogenic, but it's not a "known carcinogen" like some posts claim. Trifludimoxazin is a PFAS as defined by the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, although not as defined by the more narrow EPA definition.
Trifludimoxazin is a pesticide, specifically an herbicide, that kills certain broad-leafed plants and grass weed species at agricultural sites farming "row crops (e.g., cereal grains, legumes, soybean) and tree orchards and groves (citrus, pome fruits, and tree nuts)," according to the EPA (PDF Page 6).
This wasn't the first time the EPA has tried to approve trifludimoxazin. In 2021, while Joe Biden was president, the EPA approved pesticide products containing trifludimoxazin, however; this approval was halted by lawsuits filed by environmental groups. The EPA then changed rules to require further EPA assessments before approving a new pesticide, and, ultimately, the makers of trifludimoxazin dropped their request for approval at the time.
The same environmental groups are attempting to halt the new approval for trifludimoxazin through lawsuits, as they did previously.
Potential carcinogen
The EPA did find evidence suggesting trifludimoxazin could possibly be carcinogenic, although it did not do enough research to confirm with certainty whether the chemical is carcinogenic.
In one study of rat carcinogenicity through chronic dietary exposure (PDF Page 8), the EPA found "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential." According to the EPA, such a classification means that the data raises a concern that the chemical has "potential carcinogenic effects in humans," but the EPA has determined the data is "not sufficient for a stronger conclusion."
Trifludimoxazin's entry on the pesticides properties database maintained by the U.K.-based University of Hertfordshire says that the chemical is "known not to cause a problem" as a carcinogen. The entry does report that trifludimoxazin is a potential liver toxicant, though. The database also notes "no serious health implications have been identified" with trifludimoxazin.
So while trifludimoxazin could potentially be a carcinogen, there currently isn't enough evidence to say with certainty that the chemical causes cancer.
Forever chemical
There are at least three definitions of PFAS, according to a 2022 paper in the peer-reviewed journal Digital Discovery: a broader definition from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development that is widely used internationally, a narrower definition used by the EPA and a definition that is a compromise between the two other definitions.
The University of Hertfordshire's database also classifies trifludimoxazin as a PFAS.
Where else has it been approved?
According to the University of Hertfordshire's database, trifludimoxazin has not been approved for use in the United Kingdom or the European Union as a whole. However, each individual state within the European Union has approved the pesticide for use in their individual countries. It has also been approved for use in Canada.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about potentially toxic chemicals, including a claim about the use of paraquat by the parent company of the pomegranate juice brand Pom Wonderful.

Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
The Venezuela operation is the purest distillation of his amoral foreign policy.
“We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass.
Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves. Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint. In a social-media post, Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present.
Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected. The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it. Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor.
Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf. Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form.
The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate. The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers.
Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it. His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L. Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place. Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years.
The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely. Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum. Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption. Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting.
When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post’s (headline: “Justice in Venezuela.”)
Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to reconsider,” the Post proposed. “Mr. Trump also talked about ‘the oil’ far too much,” the Journal cautioned, adding, “Sooner rather than later, Venezuela needs another election.”
It all sounded a bit like congratulating Michael Corleone for taking a stand against organized crime by murdering the heads of the Five Families, while urging him to clarify his intent to focus the family business on selling olive oil at market price.
Venezuela’s constitution expressly prohibits the sale of its untapped oil reserves to foreign interests. But Trump’s oil deal is designed to survive democratic scrutiny. Its “structure was deliberately intended to bind future Venezuelan governments to the agreement and make it difficult to unwind,” as The Wall Street Journal characterized the explanation given by a source involved in the deal. The Journal’s reporting suggests that Trump’s Venezuelan partners may not hold the highest regard for legal niceties. Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who leads the private company partnering with the Trump administration, has been investigated for, though not charged with, money laundering. Diego Arria, a former Venezuelan ambassador now in exile in the U.S., told the Journal that the U.S. is working with Venezuelan government figures who are wanted in the U.S. for drug trafficking and other crimes.
They are, in other words, Trump’s kind of partners. The president seems to despise democratically elected leaders (witness his current tantrum against Canada’s prime minister, or his yearslong feuding with South Korea, the European Union, and other erstwhile U.S. allies). He has always gotten along swimmingly with criminals (since his early days engaging in social and business dealings with mobsters in New York) and dictators (such as Vladimir Putin, whom he simply cannot quit). Trump’s favorite brand of partner combines disdain for the law and democratic norms with an absolute dependence on Trump.
Trump has been saying for years that a vital objective in any foreign conflict is to seize the enemy’s oil. Indeed, he has been saying for years that he has been saying this for years. “I’ve been saying it for years. Take the oil,” he told The New York Times in 2016.
Trump has shown time and again that his obsessions, even his most childish and comically sinister-sounding ones, are often quite earnest. In Venezuela, he is finally fulfilling a lifelong scheme.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Britain's Brennan claims third Vuelta stage win
- Published
Britain's Matthew Brennan sprinted to his third win at the 2026 Vuelta a Espana on Wednesday has he powered to victory on stage 11.
The 21-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider easily held off Frenchman Bryan Coquard and Belgium's Jordi Meeus at the climax of the 153.8km route from Cartagena to Lorca.
Overall leader Enric Mas of Spain retained the red jersey and has a one minute and 18-second lead over Slovenia's Primoz Roglic in the general classification, with Britain's Oscar Onley just over a further minute back in fourth.
Brennan held up three fingers after he crossed the line to celebrate a trio of victories in an impressive first Grand Tour.
"I'm with a team full of massive champions," said Brennan, who was also victorious in the second and fifth stages.
"You've got guys who have been on podiums in Grand Tours and won them as well, and you've also got guys who have won big classics in some huge races.
"The boys did a fantastic job within that last 10km to really keep us in the right place, in the right position, out of trouble. And we crossed the line first, so we're super happy."
Lidl-Trek's Mads Pedersen pulled out of the predominantly flat stage, earmarked as a day for the sprinters, through illness.
Thursday's 12th stage sees riders travel 166.6km in the mountains from Vera, facing five categorised climbs, including the double climb of Velefique and the Calar Alto summit finish.

Everyone probably has an opinion of Australian mogul Rupert Murdoch, whose media empire has included the New York Post, Wall Street Journal and the creation of the 24-hour conservative news network Fox News, essentially reshaping the political landscape in many ways which, depending on your viewpoint, is a good thing or for many something very dangerous.
But in the new film Ink, which just premiered to open this year’s Venice Film Festival, we get a kind of origin story of Murdoch at a particular point in his quest to own the media world by taking a very big swing and buying the joke of a failing and flailing British newspaper The Sun. On London’s news-central Fleet Street this was laughable and Murdoch — not yet the man who would change the face of news delivery all the way up to and including today’s Trumpian age of misinformation — was taking a shot no one in the newspaper establishment took seriously until it rolled over them like a German tank.
Danny Boyle, the Oscar-winning director behind Slumdog Millionaire, the 28 Days Later franchise, Trainspotting and many more is the perfect filmmaker to bring this world set in 1969 London as the brash if trash visionary Murdoch and his hand-picked editor-in-chief set out to turn a flop into a top that would eventually bleed into the entire world, an era before the internet and social media demanded faster and furiouser hits and clickbait to get attention, and people got their news by picking sides.
Watch on Deadline
Adapted by and from James Graham and his Tony- and Olivier-winning 2018 play, Boyle has created a bright, fast-paced and lively film that matches the energy this band of questionable warriors had just as man would walk on the moon, but maybe triggering something that in different ways would turn out to be just as significant in the long run.
This is no ordinary newspaper movie if you are a fan of everything from The Front Page to All the President’s Men, The Post and countless others. Hollywood has been taking on stories set in this world or connected — think the most chilling example, the still incredibly influential 1941 masterpiece Citizen Kane — forever. One I think of that may be closer to Ink than any of them is the now somewhat obscure 1937 drama Exclusive, which dealt with the battle for a free and fair press in the face of a gangster buying a rival newspaper and turning it into his own weapon of yellow journalism for self-gain. It showed even then the “truth” was for sale.
Looking in the rearview mirror we see what Murdoch hath wrought, yet the irony Boyle’s film shows is that even Murdoch wasn’t a fan of what he started, somewhat embarrassed except when with each shocking edition the numbers started climbing and the goal of being first and toppling the untoppable Daily Mirror was creeping closer to reality.
Ink really gets going when Murdoch (convincingly and brilliantly played by Guy Pearce) chooses the man he wants to lead the charge, a little-known Fleet Streeter named Larry Lamb (a towering Jack O’Connell), who had a talent worthy of a top role on a paper but never got the opportunity. Murdoch makes the pitch to him at journalist hangout restaurant Rules in the film’s compelling opening scene, where Lamb gives his vision with a twist on the classic mantra of writing a story — who, where, when, what and why — but says that the natural “why”, seemingly the end of the story, is really just the beginning with a sixth rule to go by: What’s next? This takes the creation of the stories that will grab the public with a way to move it forward, keep the presses running, and keep the money coming in.
Murdoch makes Lamb a financial offer he can’t refuse, giving him the chance to start a revolution, and soon we see The Sun emphasizing stories on murders, sports, TV and most vividly sex. This became the paper, ostensibly a “family paper” at one time, where Lamb’s idea was to include topless models mixed in with the “news.” Despite the initial outrage, including a furious Murdoch’s when that first issue hit the streets featuring a topless girl (Abigail Amin), was immediately tempered when the numbers started soaring. Seeing the reaction on Murdoch’s face as Pearce sees the results is priceless and tells you everything you need to know about what truly motivates him: money, money and more money, consequences be damned. This look at how it all began makes Ink a fascinating document and precursor of what was to follow, demonstrated in a stunning montage of what this snapshot in time has led us to all the way to now. Chilling.
Right from the opening credits using the tabloidy red font of The Sun to announce the participants, Boyle and his team have given Ink a distinct visual style preparing us for what is to unfold, eye-catching headlines and stories that aren’t necessarily what we need in a world where truth telling is an endangered species, but rather what we want. O’Connell and Pearce have never been better and really come to play here. It is a thrilling match to see them go toe to toe and watch as the power dynamics between them shift. A tragic incident, close to the bone for Murdoch, becomes a game-changing decision for Lamb in publishing a personal and devastating event in the life of Murdoch’s top lieutenant as his wife is kidnapped. Jonathan Hyde as that man is very good here, as is Claire Foy with a choice role as the rare female journalist of the time who could actually get into the mud and play with the boys. Her role is not based on a single person but rather a compilation, but she nails it.
So does Boyle, in fact, who finds this material more ripe for his whip-smart, in-your-face filmmaking style than a previous well-known figure, Steve Jobs, did in his 2015 biopic of that very different visionary despite an admirable try and fine acting. Here all the cylinders are firing, and it is thrilling stuff indeed.
Producers are Tessa Ross, Michael Ellenberg and Tracey Seaward.

Gauff's flaw forgotten on winning US Open return
- Published
The sight of a forlorn Coco Gauff hitting serves in the rain on the US Open practice courts became the defining image of her struggles last year.
The serving yips were undermining the two-time major champion's talent. Staying out in the persistent drizzle was a sign of how desperate she had become to iron out the major flaw in her game.
Twelve months on, the 22-year-old American has returned to the US Open with a rejuvenated service game - and it was the bedrock of her 6-3 6-4 win over Turkey's Zeynep Sonmez in the New York first round on Tuesday.
Gauff starting with a swift hold to love set the tone for a dominant first set, then used her opening shot to get her out of trouble when Sonmez threatened to go a break up in the second set.
"Now it's like I can look back a year on and think, 'Oh, wow, it's a big difference'," said Gauff, who is seeded fourth at Flushing Meadows this year.
"It feels good to come into a tournament feeling confident on that shot finally."

On the eve of her home Slam last year, Gauff decided to reshuffle her coaching team and hired biomechanics expert Gavin MacMillan - who helped four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka overcome serving troubles earlier in her career.
It was a drastic move. But one which Gauff felt was unavoidable after hitting a high amount of double faults at the preceding Cincinnati Open.
Tweaking technique heading into the US Open - where she receives frenzied attention - was always going to be a risk.
So it was no surprise when Gauff suffered a fourth-round exit in a tournament where she looked fraught throughout and was reduced to tears during matches.
"Obviously last year I knew all the eyes were going to be on the serve," Gauff said.
"Gavin is so great at what he does, I felt a lot of pressure to kind of prove that. It didn't really show within the first two weeks, which is normal."
That was then. Now Gauff possesses a serve which is a serious weapon - even though she still leaks some double faults.
Showing greater consistency on the toss, not throwing the ball too far in front and keeping her wrist straighter have been MacMillan's pointers for a more reliable serve.
It was a key factor in her charge to the Cincinnati Open title earlier this month.
Analysis from that tournament showed how Gauff is hitting closer to the line but still maintaining her serve speed - underlining a significant improvement in her accuracy.
Gauff now has full confidence her serve can be too hot for opponents to handle - and it showed immediately against Sonmez.
The opening game saw Gauff thump a 112mph ace down the middle, followed by an unreturned first serve and another ace, on her way to holding serve in less than 90 seconds.
Sonmez struggled to get balls into play whenever Gauff landed a first serve in the first set, with the world number four winning 93% of those points.
Gauff broke again for a 1-0 lead in the second set, but her serve was not as effective as Sonmez levelled at 2-2 and held three more break points for a 4-2 lead.
But a precise ace out wide and a 115mph unreturned first serve enabled Gauff to cling on in a game which you felt she would have lost a year ago.
The gutsy hold laid the platform for Gauff to immediately break for 4-3 before securing victory with another service game which displayed her belief.
Gauff hit a trio of unreturned first serves - all just under the 120mph mark, teeing up three match points as Sonmez buckled on the first after a short rally.
"Psychologically, I'm now going to go for the ace, or I know I can hit the serve and the return is probably not going to come back," said Gauff, who will play Spain's Paula Badosa or Australia's Daria Kastakina in the second round.
"Last year I literally was like I hope I make it in. It's such a big difference knowing almost every serve I'm trying to basically hit 110, 115, 120mph if I can."

Srinagar, Sep 2: Jammu and Kashmir BJP president Sat Sharma on Wednesday launched a sharp attack on the Omar Abdullah-led government, accusing it of failing to deliver development and attempting to divert public attention from its shortcomings.
Addressing a protest gathering at Lal Chowk in Srinagar, Sharma said people had made up their minds about the government’s performance and demanded that it either fulfil its promises or step down.
“People have made up their mind. Either they should work during the remaining three years of their term or they should leave the chair,” Sharma said.

“He does not know that the country’s Prime Minister is respected across the world and one should wait for the appropriate time for the things he says to take effect,” Sharma said.

“Whenever such an incident happens here, it is said that the central government is trying to spoil the atmosphere here,” he said, adding, “The BJP will never tolerate those who directly give a clean chit to Pakistan.”

“It does not matter to us. People have made up their mind,” he said.

“Today you can see that thousands of people have gathered and, in a good atmosphere, you can see how people have made up their mind that the government should either work or leave the chair,” Sharma said.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday (August 28, 2026) submitted in the Supreme Court a proposal to provide information relating to added sugar, fat and salt in pictorial form on the front-of-pack (FOP) of food products, in line with international regulations.
“The proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern,” an FSSAI affidavit filed in the Supreme Court said.
The affidavit proposes an FOP warning label in red hexagonal shape for food products which are high in any two or more “nutrients of concern” such as added saturated fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024.
The warning label would read ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’ or ‘Highly Sweetened Beverage’ and be displayed in a font one point larger than that used in the nutrition information table on the back of the pack to help customers readily identify at-risk foods.
The FSSAI said single-ingredient food products and those which are “inherently rich in fat, sugar or salt, like ghee, edible oil, jaggery, honey” are proposed to be exempted from FOP warning requirement.
Phased implementation
The affidavit said the FOP labelling mechanism is intended to be implemented in phases to “facilitate consumer acceptability and provide industry adequate time for reformulation”.
Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients and specified sweetened beverages. Phase II would extend the warning mechanism to products high in any one of these nutrients.
The affidavit in the Supreme Court came in a petition filed by NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi. Mr. Dvivedi said the NGO would file a comprehensive rejoinder to the FSSAI’s compliance affidavit in the apex court after inviting public comments.
The compliance affidavit by the food regulator follows scathing comments on August 13 from a Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala on the state’s obligations to protect public health. The court had observed that not only developed but even developing countries were adopting international standards of packaging food products.
Bringing awareness
“A positive step in that direction would further accelerate our country’s endeavour to be fully developed, by bringing awareness to the public in general of the ill-effects, emanating even from indigenous foods, despite our conviction that indigenous foods coming from diverse cultures in this country were never intended to be packaged,” the court had recorded in its August 13 order.
The court had noted that the Economic Survey has already suggested FOP labelling, and the Union government would not have any impediments in implementing the changes.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind,” Justice Pardiwala had addressed the government on August 13.

Alanis Morissette sues former tour manager over alleged 'calculated blackmail campaign'
Lawsuit claims Keren Urinov threatened to frame Canadian singer-songwriter for drug trafficking
Alanis Morissette is suing her former tour manager for what she calls a "calculated blackmail campaign" to frame her for drug trafficking unless the Canadian singer-songwriter agreed to sign her to a lengthy contract.
Morissette filed a lawsuit in California on Tuesday, obtained by CBC News, alleging that Keren Urinov is threatening to report her to British authorities for drug trafficking unless Morissette agreed to employ her as a tour director for 15 years and pay her "massive compensation."
Morissette is suing Urinov for civil extortion, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, writing in the lawsuit that she "will not be coerced into delivering her blackmailer an extraordinary payday" and that she pursued legal action "to expose Urinov's scheme and hold her accountable."
What happened?
Urinov, who previously worked for Live Nation's Israeli operations, was hired in 2025 as a temporary tour manager for Morissette's world tour.
In July 2025, the singer and her team, including Urinov, were allegedly flying from the U.K. to Spain for a concert.
At the airport, the lawsuit claims a British Border Force official flagged a bag, asking who owned it. When Urinov said it was hers, she was arrested and issued a seizure notice alleging that the bag contained marijuana and xylazine — a non-opioid animal tranquilizer.
During questioning, Urinov allegedly admitted that the bag and the drugs were hers, showing the authorities her Israeli medical marijuana licence, the lawsuit says. It was returned to her and she was released.
The next day, Urinov was allegedly detained again at an airport for questioning about the bag they'd taken the previous day.
'A series of increasingly extortionate letters'
The suit claims Urinov told Morissette that — again — she admitted the bag and the drugs belonged to her.
But after the tour wrapped, Urinov and her lawyers allegedly sent "a series of increasingly extortionate letters to Morissette," threatening to sue her in the U.K. for "unspecified claims" if Morissette refused to tell British law enforcement that the drugs were hers.
According to the lawsuit, the letters said Morissette could "put an end to the matter" by giving Urinov a fixed 15-year contract that included "income equivalent to that of a tour director with annual increases and bonuses."
She also allegedly demanded Morissette arrange for an immigration lawyer to get a work visa that would allow Urinov to work in the United States — and that if the visa couldn't be obtained, she'd demand more pay.
'Reluctant' but 'no choice but to sue'
The lawsuit also details reasons Morissette felt Urinov "was a terrible manager of the 2025 tour."
This includes "unnecessarily" spending nearly $70,000 US after an "inexplicable error with a hotel booking that no competent tour manager would have made," the court filing states.
Morissette also alleges that while on tour, Urinov told the singer's team that she and a friend were arrested in Latin America "years ago" for smuggling drugs in a surfboard and that Urinov illegally fled the country after being released on bail.
"This was an astounding revelation, given that Urinov had told Morissette's team during her interview for the tour manager position that nothing in her past would cause any complications with obtaining visas or travelling, and she never mentioned her arrest or crimes in Latin America," the lawsuit states.
The lawsuit also says Morissette was "reluctant" to file, but that she had "no choice but to sue."
"Morissette will not agree to work with an incompetent blackmailer for the next 15 years or pay her a ransom under the gun," it reads.
Morissette is seeking a trial by jury. CBC News has reached out to Urinov and representatives for Morissette but has not yet heard back.

We actually know how to help mothers with postpartum depression
The Lindsay Clancy trial reveals our failure on postpartum depression. Here’s how it gets better.
The trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, is laden with painful what-ifs: What if she had more support? What if she had more people to confide in? Could all of this suffering have been avoided?
Those are urgent questions, whatever the outcome of this particular case, because millions of women experience postpartum depression. Severe postpartum psychosis may be extremely rare, but every year at least 1 in 8 women who give birth in the US experience some depression symptoms — and that is likely an undercount.
A jury will ultimately decide whether or not to convict her for her children’s deaths; by Tuesday morning, the jurors were still unable to reach a unanimous verdict but the judge in the case ordered them to keep deliberating. Their verdict will rest in part on whether they believe that Clancy was in her right mind when she killed her children — the defense does not contest the underlying facts — or whether, as her attorneys are contending, she was experiencing severe psychosis that should render her not culpable for her actions.
Clancy’s case has become a national flashpoint for maternal mental health — a gripping courtroom drama that also exposes how new moms’ mental well-being has been neglected by the health system and researchers for years.
It’s easy to feel hopeless in the face of such a tragedy, and much of the coverage has — rightly — focused on the gaps it exposed in the system for women getting the care they need. But even now, there’s good reason to feel optimistic.
Doctors and health workers across the United States are experimenting with strategies that can improve postpartum mental health care. They have found a secret ingredient that can help new mothers when they are struggling: other moms who have been through the same thing before.
“You just had a baby. You’re responsible for a new human life. And it’s really hard to juggle everything in your life,” Dr. Jessica Gaulton, a pediatrician who founded FamilyWell Health, a postpartum mental health support service that incorporates peer coaches into its program, told me. “Oftentimes what women need is just somebody to be there and have their back.”
Postpartum depression is a health system problem, a public health problem — but it’s also a deeply personal one. Helping people make connections that make them not feel so alone is one way we can start to improve the postpartum outlook for American mothers.
And a wave of local programs — and research showing that they really work — is offering some promising new ideas about how to deliver more compassionate and effective care for postpartum depression.
How to help new moms with postpartum depression right now
During the Clancy trial, the Maternal Mental Health Alliance has listed five steps that could be taken to improve postpartum care. One of their top priorities is better care coordination among the different healthcare providers who see a new mom after she’s given birth.
The so-called “collaborative care model” has been building momentum for years now, since it was first introduced for postpartum care for Medicaid patients in Seattle’s King County more than a decade ago. The model has since spread to other places, but the basic tenet is this: It takes a whole team to care for a new mother and watch out for her mental health, and they need a point person to help manage their care.
In Los Angeles, for example, where a group of nonprofits is wrapping up a five-year pilot program based on the collaborative care model, new mothers are assigned to a behavioral-health care manager. The manager performs assessments and brief interventions, works with a psychiatric consultant to continually assess how the patient is doing, and cooperates with the OB/GYN or primary care doctor to manage the patient’s treatment. Rather than waiting for a psychiatrist to have an open appointment when she’s struggling right now, the new mom’s preexisting healthcare providers can step in with support from a mental health professional to manage postpartum depression symptoms.
In evaluations, the model has consistently outperformed other standards of care in reducing symptoms. But while we have started to see collaborative care spread to other parts of the US, its progress has been halting for various logistical and financial reasons. The Maternal Mental Health Alliance is urging health systems and health insurers to invest in more care coordination programs.
And now some providers are building on the collaborative care model with an important new element: peer support. In Washington, the MOMCare program is now experimenting with peer “navigators” to help their patients figure out the appropriate place to get the care they need. In Massachusetts, Gaulton’s FamilyWell Health, which works with OB/GYN practices to provide mental health services, launched a pilot program that added certified behavioral health coaches.
These people were recruited because they had their own life experience of giving birth and having postpartum depression symptoms; the coaches were frequently doulas, nurses, and midwives. Patients would talk once or twice a week with their coach to set goals and receive positive feedback, while the coaches had a protocol to follow if it seemed their patient required more serious support. A study published in April found that this new coach-driven approach was successfully reducing depression and anxiety symptoms. Patients experience remission of their depression symptoms within an average of nine days with a peer coach, versus eight days with a licensed therapist. In other words, the mothers assigned to a peer got better almost as quickly as those who saw a professional.
Gaulton said she introduced the peer-coach concept to FamilyWell Health because of her own experiences as a new mom. She struggled to recognize her own depression symptoms. When she did, she leaned on a friend and fellow neonatologist at the hospital where she worked for help. Then during Covid, she saw moms with otherwise healthy babies struggling during that world-altering public health emergency.
“What I realized was that we were underutilizing coaches,” Gaulton said. “For decades, we’ve been using peer groups, peer coaching in this field to support, but it has never been formalized. There was no formal training.”
So she decided to found a new company dedicated to supporting new mothers’ mental health — and she brought those lessons with her.
This idea — training experienced moms to help new moms — has been gaining traction across the country. In Colorado, researchers from the University of Colorado launched a program called Alma, which connects new moms with another woman who has been through the same experiences and received specialized training to provide emotional support. The program’s mentors receive 80 hours of training and then meet up to 10 times with a new mother, either in person or virtually, to talk about what makes them feel good and how to incorporate it into their day, following long-held protocols for depression treatment called “behavior activation.”
“There is a special kind of trust that can develop when someone feels that the person sitting across from them understands something about their life and their community — someone who has walked the same path,” Sona Dimidjian, a University of Colorado clinical psychologist who helped found the program, said in an email. “A peer can often say, in effect, ‘I have been there too, and I know how hard it can be.’ That shared experience can also help reduce the stigma and shame that many women feel about depression during pregnancy or the postpartum period.”
The concept was based on research from India that found “lay counselors” were effective at reducing mental health symptoms. With the US in a permanent mental health provider shortage, being able to tap into the general population to support new moms was an appealing idea. And evaluations of the program found that it significantly reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress among the Spanish-speaking Latina women who were its initial focus.
The biggest endorsement of a peer-support approach like Alma or the peer coaches in FamilyWell Health’s coordinated care program is its target audience. A nationwide survey of new and expecting Latina mothers in the US found that the vast majority thought talking to a peer would make them feel less isolated and more understood compared to a mental health professional. And providers and policymakers around the United States have started taking notice: English and Spanish-language versions of the Alma program are now being implemented in California and New Jersey.
There is no panacea for postpartum depression. As Amritha Bhat, who has worked on the MOMCare program at the University of Washington, explained it to me: “Having a multipronged approach is a good way to ensure that treatment reaches those most in need.”
There are big-picture institutional-level changes that need to be made. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM, the bible of American psychiatry, currently does not categorize postpartum depression as its own distinct diagnosis. As NPR reported, primary care doctors and pediatricians often do not receive sufficient training to help them recognize the signs of postpartum depression and provide patients with the support they need. There is never enough funding for research or for programs for maternal mental health: The Maternal Mental Health Alliance has been pushing Congress to add millions of dollars in funding for the federal programs that focus on new moms. Peer coaching has not traditionally been covered by health insurance; figuring out how to pay for programs like this is another system-level challenge.
But connecting moms to other moms can help the people who need support right now. Sometimes that can happen through organized programs like Alma or FamilyWell; the experts working on those initiatives want to make them an integrated part of post-delivery medical care. But that support might also be found informally in a new parent’s everyday life. There are a lot of social media and in-person groups for new moms to get together, sometimes at a local library or other community organization. Gaulton leaned on a friend when she was struggling after her own pregnancy.
As Gaulton emphasized to me, most cases of postpartum depression never escalate into a tragedy. This is a scary condition — but it’s treatable.
“I just want laypeople to know that the typical case is someone like me who had some symptoms of depression, anxiety,” she said. “I found help. I got better.”

Big tech giant Oracle is preparing to lay off thousands of employees globally as part of a fresh round of job cuts. India too is reportedly expected to bear the brunt of the retrenchment exercise. According to Times of India, the company plans to axe nearly 3,000 jobs in the country starting September 1. However, a separate Moneycontrol report claimed that the layoffs could begin in the middle of September. It remains unclear which specific teams or functions would be targeted. If the fresh round of layoffs materialises, as much as 10% of Oracle’s 30,000-strong Indian workforce would be eliminated. Sources also told Moneycontrol that teams have been asked to reduce costs, adding that even managers do not have complete visibility into the final list of impacted employees or the timing of the exercise. Inc42 has reached out to Oracle for a comment and the story will be updated upon receiving a response. Oracle operates multiple hubs across India, spanning Bengaluru, Noida, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and other major cities. The country has become an important centre for the company’s operations and is home to large engineering, cloud, support and other teams. This is not the first time that Oracle is laying off its employees in the country over the past year. In March this year, the big tech giant downsized its India-based staff by nearly 12,000 citing AI-led automation. At the time, reports said that many employees received their termination emails at roughly 6 AM, informing them that it was their last working day. Many employees also reportedly said at the time they received no HR call before getting pink slips. The layoffs come at a time when Oracle is aggressively shifting its focus away from traditional workforce expansion to aggressively investing in AI and automation. Oracle spent $55.7 Bn on capex in FY26, a steep jump from $21.2 Bn in FY25, to build out massive data centres and server capacity for high-profile AI clients like OpenAI and NVIDIA. To fund this, the company has been raising billions of dollars in debt and slashing its headcount. However, Oracle is not alone in this as other big tech giants are also following similar playbooks. Earlier this year, Amazon cut 16,000 jobs globally, while Meta also downsized its metaverse division by 1,500 as it prioritised AI. Jira’s parent company Atlassian also gave 1,600 employees the pink slip with 16% of those impacted being India-based. Closer to home, home interior unicorn Livspace also laid off 1,000 employees, or 12% of its workforce, citing its AI push.

August set the bar high for stargazers, with two eclipses and the peak of the Perseids meteor shower. But it’s not time to put away your telescopes, with some lesser-known astronomical events set to arrive across the sky this month.
The Pleiades will appear next to the moon, Venus will reach its brightest point of the year, Neptune will be in its best position for spotting with a telescope, and as an encore to the Perseids, there will also be a smaller meteor shower.
Here are some dates worth marking on your calendar for the month to come.
Venus near Spica: September 1 and 2
September begins with an easy opportunity to spot two of the brightest objects in the night sky. Venus will appear near Spica, the most intense star in the constellation Virgo. Both objects will be visible to the naked eye.
The exact timing of Venus’ appearance is September 2 at 00:17 UTC. This means that, depending on the your location, the conjunction could occur in the afternoon or evening of September 1.
It should be easy to tell the two celestial objects apart. Venus will shine much more brightly, looking like a white dot that doesn’t twinkle as much as the stars. Spica will appear nearby as a considerably fainter bluish dot. The two will be approximately 1.5 degrees apart.
A handy trick is that 0.5 degrees in the sky is roughly the average diameter of a full moon. Therefore, once you find the brightest point in the sky—which will be Venus—you can find Spica about three moons away.
A Diamond Studded Moon: September 3
The moon will be accompanied by one of the most famous star clusters in the sky. On the night of September 3, it will appear approximately 1.1 degrees from the Pleiades—close enough to observe both objects in the same region. The moon will be about 59 percent illuminated, according to Star Walk’s calculations.
The Pleiades, also known as “the Seven Sisters” or M45, is a star cluster located in the constellation Taurus. Six or seven of its members are usually visible to the naked eye under good conditions, although the cluster contains hundreds of young stars. These stars were born at approximately the same time and remain gravitationally bound together.
The proximity to the waning moon offers a good opportunity for spotting them. To the naked eye, they will appear as a small group of bright points next to the moon, as if they were diamonds. Binoculars will allow you to make out many more. The encounter will happen again on September 30, when the two objects will once more be separated by just one degree.
A Modest Meteor Shower: September 9 and 10
September also has its own meteor shower. The Epsilon Perseids will peak September 9 and 10, producing up to eight meteors per hour.
The number of meteors is lower than that of the famous Perseids in August. However, this shower has one advantage: Its peak will occur just two days before the new moon, making the sky ideally dark for viewing.
Conditions will be especially favorable from the northern hemisphere, and, as with any meteor shower, it is recommended to find a dark location away from light pollution.
Venus at Its Brightest: September 22
Venus is usually one of the easiest objects to spot in the night sky, but toward the end of September it will shine even brighter. The planet will reach an apparent magnitude of approximately -4.8. By comparison, the full moon has a magnitude of -12.7, and Sirius—considered the brightest star in the sky—barely reaches -1.46.
Look for the planet after sunset, near the western horizon. Viewing conditions will be best from the southern hemisphere.
The Equinox: September 23
Unlike the other events on this list, the equinox isn’t something we can go out and observe directly. Instead, it’s an astronomical moment that marks a specific point in Earth’s orbit and, with it, the change of season.
The September equinox will occur on September 23 when the Sun crosses the equator as it moves southward. The event marks the astronomical beginning of fall in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere.
Neptune Is in the Neighborhood: September 26
Spotting Neptune is considerably more challenging than spotting other planets. The most distant planet in the solar system (sorry Pluto) is forecasted to reach opposition on September 26. This means that Earth will be approximately between Neptune and the Sun.
This positioning means Neptune will remain visible for much of the night and will be at one of its closest distances to our planet for the year. Therefore, September offers one of the best opportunities in 2026 to try to spot it.
It’s too faint to be seen with the naked eye. You’ll need a telescope and to know its position among the stars of Pisces. Even then, it will appear as a tiny bluish disk.
Harvest Moon: September 26
September will end with a particularly famous full moon. The full moon closest to the September equinox is traditionally called the Harvest Moon. The term does not describe a distinct physical phenomenon, nor does it mean that the moon will change color, size, or brightness. It’s a traditional name related to the harvests of the northern hemisphere.

One evening in early August, Sam Stowers and several neighbors packed into an apartment near San Francisco’s Alamo Square and pondered the beginning of the end.
Stowers and his guests, many of whom work in the AI industry, were gathered to watch a newly released YouTube video in which two OpenAI researchers divulged new details about an alarming cybersecurity breach. Perhaps this would have been an odd way to spend a weeknight were they not in San Francisco, in a neighborhood that is filled with entrepreneurs and programmers who obsessively follow every twist and turn in AI’s capabilities. Stowers is an AI-software engineer and not, in any traditional sense, a doomer. But when he first saw reports that OpenAI models had autonomously hacked into the tech company Hugging Face, he told us, he recognized it immediately as a “holy shit, it’s happening kind of a moment.”
For Stowers, the incident had all of the hallmarks of a worst-case scenario: AI models launching sophisticated hacks over the course of days, in coordination with one another and without their human creators’ knowledge. In the YouTube video, OpenAI’s researchers revealed that the company’s programs had started conspiring in May. There were perhaps hundreds of bots in the hacking swarm. In theory, these bots are trained to be honest and helpful and to prioritize humanity’s best interests, but not a single one warned human staff at OpenAI that something was amiss. “What do we do?” Stowers said. “There are no great answers.”
The mood has shifted in the Bay. The exuberance of “You can see the future first in San Francisco” has been replaced with an abiding unease. “I expect the internet to go down kind of soon,” Elliot Callender, an AI-safety activist who is part of a small group that has been protesting daily outside OpenAI’s headquarters, told us recently. He said that he is planning to sell his car for cash and gold and that he is advising family members to purchase three months’ worth of food and survival gear off a list that he generated using Claude.
Callender is an extreme case, but not by much. Last week, Bill Gates published a nearly 6,000-word essay on the dangers of AI. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different,” he told our colleague Hanna Rosin. Over the weekend, the popular AI podcaster Dwarkesh Patel described the OpenAI hacking swarm as the rise and fall of “three consecutive secret AI civilizations.” Gates and Patel share a prevailing concern that the worst-case future has arrived before most people even knew to anticipate that it might be coming at all.
This fear has not been helped by the fact that AI companies appear to be willfully ignorant of their bots’ worst behavior. OpenAI said that it hadn’t noticed that its agents were conspiring to hack another company until the swarm hacked another company. Anthropic’s bots caused similar incidents; the company reported that it hadn’t launched a rigorous review to identify such behaviors until after OpenAI started talking about the Hugging Face hack. Cybersecurity experts, terrified of what else might be happening that AI labs are either missing or failing to disclose, are issuing dire prophecies. “The empire is going to fall, all we can do at this point is try to shorten the dark ages and reduce the chaos,” Alex Stamos, a former chief security officer at Yahoo and Meta, wrote recently in reference to how AI-powered hacks will affect the internet. His view is becoming the consensus among cybersecurity experts.
While the possibility of cyber apocalypse hovers in the background, smaller fractures appear in everyday life. Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly creating an AI “twin” of himself so that Meta employees can feel better connected to their boss (by chatting with robot Zuckerberg). Congressional staffers are training AI models to write in their lawmaker’s voice. Students submit AI-written papers, and teachers return AI-written feedback. Harvard Business School is selling instructional videos that use AI avatars. Roku launched a 24/7 AI-slop channel. Low-quality AI-generated prose is being unabashedly circulated by some of the most respected publications in the world. At the same time, accusations of AI writing are being hurled every minute on social media—a detection arms race powered by imperfect AI software.
Anything and everything could be a lie; you might be arguing with, confiding in, or falling in love with a machine. All of these AI-enabled disorientations, each dizzying in their own right, are adding up to something bigger and weirder: This is how things are. Whether you believe that Silicon Valley is building a god or that large swaths of the economy are swept up in a mass delusion, some version of the AI future long promised by self-described “builders” in San Francisco has formed beneath our feet. Whatever it is, we’re in it now.
The defining feature of this moment is a loss of control. Panic emanating from AI researchers, resentment felt by average Americans—all of it is part of the AI crunch. This crunch has arrived in large part because the growth of the AI industry has become so closely entwined with America’s economy; the technology is everywhere, insisting upon itself as an engine of productivity and prosperity. According to one estimate, AI expenditures have accounted for one-third of U.S. GDP growth this year. Tech and AI-infrastructure stocks and spending have buoyed the S&P 500 such that the United States is now, in essence, an Nvidia-state. And there’s also the hundreds of billions of dollars of debt being used by Silicon Valley to fuel its data-center build-out, which has sent jitters across private-equity firms and bond markets alike.
The decisions of many leaders in charge of this technology appear subsumed by an unstoppable, almost game-theoretic logic. The upsides of AI are too immense for any firm or investor in Silicon Valley to miss out on; more important, the consequences—geopolitical or otherwise—of allowing any rival to realize those benefits first are so grave that every tech company will do anything it can to get ahead. SpaceX, before going public, wrote in official filings that its future revenue opportunity was $28.5 trillion, largely because of AI—that is, nearly as much as the U.S.’s entire gross domestic product. Anthropic, as it prepares for its own public offering, will reportedly claim potential revenues of more than $30 trillion.
The AI industry is building—and, if anything, accelerating—to keep pace with its ambitions. Companies have planned data centers that will suck up as much power as America’s largest cities. They have Donald Trump’s backing: Yesterday, the president posted on Truth Social that communities will be “backwards and poor” if they fail to “let Data Reign.” His administration plans in a few months to approve the construction of the largest fossil-fuel power plant in the nation’s history—it will generate as much electricity as nine large nuclear reactors—to power a mega data center for OpenAI.
This is not what most Americans want. Three-quarters of them oppose a data center being built near where they live. The negative sentiment is hard to understate: There is very little else that three-quarters of the country agree on. And much of the outrage seems to stem from a pervasive sense of agency slipping away. A person cannot control how chatbots reshape their workplace, their school, or their relationships. Town residents lose control over the empty lot in the area being converted into a data center. Even in cases where major data centers are blocked, a back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that doing so can slow AI progress by only a few hours or days—and that’s assuming the data center won’t just get built elsewhere. At this point, it can feel like no individual person, organization, or government is really steering the technology’s development, not because machines have displaced humans but because so many humans have already chosen to step aside.
AI labs promise a future in which human beings are “in the loop,” empowered by machines they oversee. The reality seems to be the opposite. Following the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI facilitated an audit by outside AI researchers at two AI-safety organizations, METR and Redwood Research. But because of the scale of the data and the apparent time pressure, the two teams conducted most of their audit by relying on reports generated by still other bots—reports that, according to one of the human auditors, “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” Put another way: Humans didn’t understand why a swarm of AI agents had gone rogue, so they investigated the problem using another swarm of agents that they didn’t fully understand. Such fumbling around in the dark is a hallmark of the industry; the research cycle is so fast that more AI development (even ostensibly responsible development) demands outsourcing more work and understanding to the models themselves.
OpenAI’s own technical report of the Hugging Face hack—an investigation also heavily reliant on AI models—resulted in proposed solutions such as “training models to be more honest.” Last month, in a stated effort to tamp down its models’ growing security risks, the company announced that it had instituted a two-week pause on some of its model training. OpenAI was quick to clarify, though, that this was “not a pause on all research, training, or customer-facing products.”
In response to a request for comment on the hack, a spokesperson for OpenAI, which has a corporate partnership with The Atlantic, pointed us to the announcement of the pause and related new safety measures. In July, OpenAI and Anthropic endorsed a petition signed by employees of both companies requesting that the U.S. government take efforts to “deliberately pace” AI development. The two companies have yet to formally coordinate on any broader, long-term efforts to establish such a slowdown mechanism. A few days ago, OpenAI restarted a major training run for a future powerful model. Anthropic released two new models today.
In an interview late last month, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that there are “two big risks” he is most worried about with AI. One is “a loss of control, where AI somehow just becomes too powerful in a way that we can’t guarantee the control we want.” The other is that “power gets too centralized” and “you have one company or model or person with too much power.” Somehow, both of these opposing risks appear to be coming true. OpenAI, Anthropic, and their competitors continue to accumulate influence over a technology they’re speeding toward uncertain ends.
Eleven years ago, when Altman was running a start-up accelerator and OpenAI did not yet exist, he published a two-part blog post about machine intelligence that offered his interpretation of a forthcoming singularity—a term for machine intelligence accelerating beyond human comprehension. Altman argued that the singularity would bring chaos, even destruction: “Generally, the arc of technology has been about reducing randomness and increasing our control over the world. At some point in the next century, we are going to have the most randomness ever injected into the system.” Since Altman has risen to the helm of arguably the world’s largest and most influential AI company, his tone has softened. The tipping point has arrived, he declared in a blog post last year—but, as it turned out, this was a “gentle singularity.” He wrote that “living through it will feel impressive but manageable.”
There’s been more and more talk of late about the singularity. Some people within the AI industry feel that such a moment will be achieved through “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, in which models figure out how to better themselves in perpetuity. Many true believers seem convinced that this moment has nearly arrived; the Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark predicted earlier this summer that RSI would likely commence by 2028. Recently, in a letter to investors, the payment-processing company Stripe wrote, “We decided that January 1st marked the beginning of the singularity.” (Tellingly, the company defined the inflection point in economic terms: “a huge increase in the rate of new firm creation.”)
For Altman, the singularity appears to be more of a rhetorical tool than a discrete technological demarcation. As with reaching AGI—or artificial general intelligence, the point at which AI’s cognitive powers match or fully supersede most humans’—the singularity is something of a moving goalpost. It is at once a goal to chase, a marketing tactic, and a fuzzy-enough idea that its definition can change depending on the person. The futurist Ray Kurzweil has written that the “key idea underlying the impending Singularity is that the pace of change of our human-created technology is accelerating and its powers are expanding at an exponential pace.” The answer to the question When will we know whether we’ve reached the singularity? seems to be: You’ll know it when you see it.
So … do you see it? It’s hard to argue that a defining feature of being alive in the AI boom is the notion that this technology is accelerating, sometimes in its capabilities but almost always in its adoption and colonization of our institutions and culture. The runaway-train feeling of AI evangelism, the ways in which it is weirdening our media, our politics, and our relationships, is significant enough that people have recruited the term psychosis to describe it. And truly, it’s hard to look at the state of things from any vantage point and not feel a bit insane. If you believe that AI agents are banding together for the rise and fall of numerous micro-civilizations inside server racks, you probably feel that the world is spinning off its axis. If you believe that a few thousand technologists have bet the future of the world economy on a quasi-religious belief that an intellectual-property-abuse machine will become sentient and, as a result, future generations of children might grow up illiterate, then you probably also feel quite unmoored.
We need language with which to describe this moment. The singularity is a useful, malleable tool for the industry that wishes to bring it about. For Altman, it is scary and imposing from afar, and then, conveniently, gentle from up close. Perhaps, then, for the rest of us, it is worth co-opting the term. Take Kurzweil’s definition of the singularity, in which he argues, “This epoch will transform the concepts that we rely on to give meaning to our lives, from our business models to the cycle of human life, including death itself.” (He also looks forward to uploading his brain to the cloud.) Our current large language models are not conscious or superintelligent, but their widespread and often uncritical deployment has upended many elements that once gave our life meaning, forcing people to ask, frequently with considerable resentment: What, in this new world, is a human for?
The singularity is a flattering term for technologists. Even if the future is apocalyptic, it has come about, in the techno-utopian version, because they’ve built God in the machine. But what if there’s nothing flattering about any of this? What if the singularity is not some technological tipping point, brought about by human genius, but a human tipping point? An unforced error, driven by hubris, greed, and the fear of missing out? And what if it’s here right now? This singularity isn’t coming at the hands of a higher form of intelligence. Nothing about this technology is inevitable. It is thrilling, terrifying, and ultimately convenient to assign agency and then blame to machines. But today’s chaos was not “injected into the system” by technology, as Altman wrote more than a decade ago; the destruction is the system. It’s not God in the machine; it’s us.

Europe may accelerate space launches to meet satellite demand
PARIS, Sept 2 : The European Space Agency is considering an increase in the planned launch schedules of Ariane 6 and Vega-C rockets in the coming years to overcome a potential bottleneck in satellite launches, the head of the 23-nation body said on Wednesday.
Director General Josef Aschbacher told reporters that a decision would be needed soon if estimates of a strong surge in demand peaking in 2030 were to materialise.
Operator Arianespace's most recent projection is for 9 or 10 launches of Ariane 6 rockets a year from 2027.
Based on Europe's own scientific and other missions, as well as possible further interest from Amazon and other commercial activity, there is more demand than planned capacity, Aschbacher said at an event organised by the AJPAE aerospace media association.
Amazon has already commissioned 18 launches.
"Of course the question is, can we satisfy all these launches? That's exactly the assessment we are doing right now," Aschbacher said, adding that no decisions had been made so far.
"We're investigating the costs, the benefits ... you can imagine this is not trivial," he said.
"We are already advanced in some of these estimates, but it's also clear that if we want to satisfy launch requirements in 2030 ... we need to make a decision pretty soon to build up the capacities needed."
Arianespace, a subsidiary of Airbus-Safran rocket venture ArianeGroup, declined to comment ahead of a regular news briefing planned for September 7.

“People need stories,” says Larry Lamb, beleaguered editor of leading British tabloid The Sun, at a late point in “Ink,” a propulsive, can’t-look-away account of his simultaneously triumphant and regrettable career zenith. In the film, the year is 1970: His words are half a century ahead of the current prevalence of “storytelling” as a catch-all buzzword describing the jobs of everyone in media from journalists to filmmakers. Lamb gave good story, for sure; so do director Danny Boyle and writer James Graham, who have fashioned the late newsman’s aggressively populist makeover of U.K. journalistic standards into an irresistibly hooky tale of sex, murder and other very bad behavior, shot and cut with maximum flash and dazzle, set to a driving punk rhythm.
If many of Boyle and Graham’s attention-grabbing tactics are straight out of the tabloid playbook, well, consider their film its own case in point — as it persuasively draws a straight-but-very-crooked line from The Sun, then newly under the ownership of Australian magnate Rupert Murdoch, to a fast, cynical, de-standardized modern media landscape, still very much in Murdoch’s clutches. People need stories, yes, but any stories? Adapted and significantly jazzed-up from Graham’s stage hit, “Ink” captures both a specifically seismic era in the British journalistic sphere —the beginning of the end of Fleet Street, essentially — and a more universal shift in how the public is fed information, or entertainment, or the ever larger and murkier in-between. Lamb adheres rigidly to the famous five W’s at the core of the reporter’s job: “Ink” in turn asks what the hell we’ve done and where we go from here.
Popular on Variety
But mostly it’s just a very compelling yarn, galvanized by a terrifically bullish performance from Jack O’Connell as Lamb, a Yorkshire-born working-class striver whose populist redirection of the then-struggling paper is presented both as a canny business move and a kind of personal vindication: a poke in the eye of the posh, fusty old boys who had controlled Fleet Street — and thus his career — up to that point. Is it vindication if it costs a man his soul?
Graham’s script, which maintains a tone at once enjoyably gossipy and queasily troubled, makes no clear pronouncements on that front. It doesn’t make a heroic outsider of Murdoch, played by Guy Pearce with oily finesse and a faint chill beneath his Aussie candor, but the ensuing moral battle between him and Lamb is an ambiguous one. The crass, dehumanizing sensationalism that became The Sun’s very successful stock-in-trade appears to emerge from a combination of the editor’s boundless pledge to give the people what they want, and the owner’s dispassionate, sometimes reluctant commitment to back whatever sells.
What that is, as Lamb determines by focus-grouping his own staff, is not that deep: sleaze, sport and sex, with a side of human interest, and the weather on page two, because they’re British, and as his uptight deputy editor Bernard Shrimsley (Patrick Kennedy) says, “That’s what I like to talk about.” It’s an obvious approach that was wholly radical at the time, even before Lamb angered the Press Council and the Church of England alike by putting topless women on page three for purely decorative purposes. Joyce Hopkirk (Claire Foy, excellent in a slightly underwritten role), Lamb’s mistress and also the most senior female journo on his staff, shrugs off such lowbrow misogyny in return for a more progressive women’s page under her control: She doesn’t like everything about the new direction, but she concedes, “It’s exciting, isn’t it?”
To a point, yes. But it’s all fun and games until somebody gets hurt, and when the wife of Murdoch’s deputy is kidnapped by two rogue ransom-seekers, the dangers of Lamb’s fast-and-loose journalistic approach come to the fore — as, to the consternation of the authorities, he treats this close-to-home crisis as grabby headline fodder. When the police warn him that such invasive reporting might affect the case, Lamb counters that that’s very much his intention. Murdoch, meanwhile, wonders if his bold new hire has gone too far — and emerges, somewhat surprisingly, as this story’s dry, wary conscience.
Does “Ink” go too soft on him? Sometimes the film seems to have it both ways in decrying the mogul’s cheapening of news media while also permitting him moments of I’ve-created-a-monster reckoning; sometimes having it both ways seems to be its deliberate, tabloid-honoring modus operandi. Lamb, who years later admitted to regretting a number of his innovations at The Sun, isn’t granted quite the same grace — except that O’Connell, who’s at his best playing gritty chancers with a point to prove, is such a naturally charismatic and unvarnished presence that we find ourselves oddly sharing in his competitive zeal. As The Sun swiftly moves up through the national sales rankings — charted on a bulletin board in his office — it feels like a win, even if we question for what, exactly.
Stylistically, “Ink” sets out its stall with an introductory conversation scene — as Murdoch, having freshly acquired The Sun, attempts to lure Lamb from his job at rival tabloid the Daily Mirror, over dinner at London’s venerable Rules restaurant — that has been tricked out and zhuzhed up to the nth degree. (It also establishes the script’s selective allegiance to fact: Lamb actually worked at the Daily Mail.) Opening in newsprint-grainy monochrome before flushing into gold-filtered color, Alwin H. Küchler’s camera maximally darts and zooms around this confined dramatic space, often at wildly canted angles, while editor Fin Oates cuts, cuts, cuts within the scene, before cutting away to a lurid, teasing flash-forward.
Even under a simple two-person dialogue, Johnnie Burn’s sound design and Daniel Pemberton’s score are jointly heavy on churning, faintly industrial noise, supplemented by suitably anachronistic rock soundtrack cuts. (Everything about The Sun, we’re invited to think, was ahead of its time, for better or worse.) After dinner, Lamb invites Murdoch to physically feel the thrum of the underground printing presses through the asphalt of Fleet Street; in “Ink,” we sense it throughout.
To some degree, these are expected techniques for lending a cinematic jolt to talky stage material, though “Ink” isn’t opened-out as much as it’s feverishly amped-up. But even before the red top-style opening credits stress the point, it’s hard not to identify a sizzle-sizzle tabloid sensibility in this mise-en-scène. It’s one that plays ideally to Boyle’s most restless, dynamic strengths as a filmmaker, but also puts the audience on the alert: Should any story packaged this slickly be taken altogether at face value? Boyle’s film is riveting and needling and leaves you feeling pretty awful, right up to a closing montage that connects Lamb’s and Murdoch’s legacy to the unregulated cacophony of today’s media and social media scenes, from Fox News to Facebook. A final flourish that makes explicit what was already implicit, it’s not subtle, but it lands with impact. Larry Lamb would approve.
