Guinea-Bissau voters back a sweeping power shift, boosting the president and shrinking parliament
Guinea-Bissau has voted to expand presidential powers and reduce the legislature
BISSAU, Guinea-Bissau -- BISSAU, Guinea-Bissau (AP) — Guinea-Bissau has voted in support of expanding presidential powers and trimming the country's legislature, electoral authorities announced Tuesday.
The referendum held last Sunday was to change key provisions of the West African nation's constitution ahead of December's general elections that would return the country to democracy. Opposition parties called for a boycott of the referendum, saying it would only make the president more powerful.
The region has been rocked by a series of coups since 2020. In November last year, Guinea-Bissau became one of several West African nations to be taken over by soldiers when troops seized power following a disputed election.
The changes resulting from the referendum weakened the role of the prime minister, who shared the country's top job with the president in a semipresidential system, an arrangement the ruling military government said was a source of political instability. The changes also included reducing the legislative seats from 102 to 65.
According to data released by the National Electoral Commission, 70% of voters supported the constitutional changes while 30% voted against.
The tiny country of around 2.2 million people has the highest proportion of natural wealth per capita in West Africa, according to the World Bank, but more than half of the country lives in poverty.

New immigration court tactic leads to huge lines and chaos in Miami
MIAMI — Yerandy Gonzalez looks at the line of hundreds of people in front of him and shakes his head.
He takes a step aside and lights up a cigarette.
"This is crazy, man," Gonzalez says in Spanish.
The line — which stretches across a few blocks on this humid Tuesday morning — is of people waiting to go inside Miami's immigration court. All of the people in line have a scheduled hearing – for many it's their first court appearance.
Avene Jeanite, a 52-year-old Haitian man, is among those waiting. He was here last month accompanying a friend facing deportation. But today is his appointment.
"It was not like this — you would go to the door and they'd let you in," Jeanite said. "Today is completely different."
The long lines are not a glitch. They are the result of a new Trump administration tactic, known as "mega master" calendar hearings," designed to quickly deport people.
Under the old system, each judge would handle about three dozen cases per day.
But now, judges more regularly have a docket of over 100 people, and they are seeing dozens of immigrant cases at once.
Trump administration officials say the accelerated calendar is needed to clear a massive backlog; critics call it a tactic to unfairly speed up deportations.
"It's a very unfair, but a very effective tactic," said David Wilson, the vice chair of the American Immigration Lawyers Association's immigration court committee.
He said "mega masters" create chaos because the court is cramming a lot of immigrants in one docket, making it hard for the court itself to send notices in a timely manner and for the immigrant to find legal representation.
"When that happens, it generates a significant no-show rate," Wilson said.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department said in a statement to NPR that "reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration."
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the agency that oversees immigration courts, said that as the agency continues to add immigration judges, it "will continue to make scheduling adjustments to ensure all cases are handled in a timely and lawful manner."
Since mega master calendar hearings started, in-absentia deportation orders have spiked to a record high, according to the legal tech platform bklg. In July, more than 54,000 immigrants nationwide were ordered deported for missing their court hearing. That number was similar to the 56,000 in June. Both reflect a 60% increase over the last few months.
In the Miami immigration court, the increase of in-absentia orders in July spiked from 1,383 in May to 2,886 in July — a 108% increase.
Crammed courtrooms, confusion and frustration
On this day, it's standing room only in courtroom 24. Recording is not allowed. But NPR saw Judge Xavier Racine call a group of some 30 people at once. He reads them their rights, and assigns them a new court hearing — a month from today. Other judges assign court hearings as quickly as in two weeks.
The Miami immigration court docket has exploded for three key reasons: The Trump administration is arresting a record monthly number of immigrants, it is moving up people's court dates that had been scheduled for 2027, and making people show up for cases that previous administrations deemed low priority because they have a high chance of being dismissed.
Yeriné, a 30-year-old Venezuelan mother who asked NPR to use her first name because she fears jeopardizing her immigration case, says she's concerned about being on these massive dockets. She had an appointment for May 2027 and it got rescheduled for Tuesday.
Standing in line outside the Miami immigration court, she says she's concerned about everything.
"I see this long line of people and they might not make it on time to their hearings," she said. "That scares me."
Billie Botch, a court observer with the American Friends Service Committee, a social justice group founded by the Quakers, told NPR this is causing a lot of operational issues. People are also showing up late to their court appointments because they are waiting in line for hours.
"You can't deny the correlation," Botch said. "You put more people into proceedings on shorter notice with less resources to go around to argue their case, You're going to end up with more removal orders."

Joe Rogan slams Trump’s Lake Ontario name change as ‘a distraction’
‘Who cares if it’s Lake Ontario? It’s a good name,’ Rogan told listeners
Podcaster Joe Rogan has torn into President Trump over his decision to rename Lake Ontario.
Rogan, who hosts one of the most-listened-to podcasts in the U.S., accused the man he endorsed in 2024 of attempting to distract voters from the war with Iran.
The influencer made the remarks on Tuesday’s episode of The Joe Rogan Experience amid a bitter trade war between the U.S and Canada, during which Trump has signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.
“It’s to distract you from the fact we are in a war we can’t win with Iran,” Rogan blasted. “It doesn’t make any sense.”
“Who cares if it’s Lake Ontario? It’s a good name. We’ve had that name forever.”
This is not the first time Rogan has been vocal about his opposition to Trump’s war with Iran, now into its seventh month with no end in sight.
“We might’ve f***ed up by going to Iran,” he said on his podcast in July. “Most people don’t want it, except supporters of Israel.”
“They’re the only people that seem to be thinking it’s a good idea in this country.
“Most people are horrified by the idea, because Trump was elected - one of the pillars that he stood for, apparently, was that he doesn’t want any more wars.”
In April, he even suggested that there could be a possible link between the release of the Epstein files and the launch of the war with Iran.
“Look, the Epstein files comes (sic) out - we go to war with Iran,” he said. “It’s a good way to get people to stop talking about certain things.”
Rogan’s discussion about the Lake Ontario name change came amid the U.S.’s trade war with Canada, which saw the former country imposing tariffs on some imports from the latter. In response, Canada imposed its own retaliatory tariffs on some imports from the U.S.
Then, Trump went on to announce the renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America.
During Tuesday’s podcast episode Rogan and his guest, comedian Brian Simpson, shared trivia about the Great Lakes.
Simpson joked that the renaming of the lake means that the HOMES acronym - which helps school children remember Lake Huron, Lake Ontario, Lake Michigan, Lake Erie and Lake Superior - will have to change.
“Homes?” Rogan asked. “Oh, yeah…the acronym. I didn’t learn that.”
Trump’s decision to rename Lake Ontario has been widely criticized, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney writing in a statement that the country will continue to recognise the lake’s original name.
“We know that America is changing,” he wrote. “Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms.”
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario - then, now and always.”

Vietnamese EV maker VinFast is reportedly halting its production of select cars in India to reassess costs. Reuters reported that the company has asked its suppliers to hold all activities on three programmes, including a two-door SUV called VF3, VF6 and VF7 SUVs. Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — Iran fired on U.S. allies in the Gulf early Wednesday following a night of American bombardment that Iranian officials say included a deadly strike on a wedding party.
The latest violence came after a monthlong lull in fighting. The six-month war has led to a spike in oil prices, roiled the global economy and posed increasing political problems for U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections.
Fighting has escalated since the American military hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, saying Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at American bases in Jordan that were intercepted.
American military resources are stretched and political pressure in Washington is mounting, while Iran's economy falters. Iran's currency hit another record low on Wednesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging 2.20 million rials for one U.S. dollar, a 10% hike from last week's record.
Neither side can continue indefinitely between full-scale war and a truce, said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, an international think tank.
"At some point, one of the sides may see a need to escalate in order to break this cycle," he cautioned. "So that could bring the two sides to a point that they have been trying to avoid until now, which is a full-scale war."
The struggle is focused on the Strait of Hormuz and oil prices
The latest flare-up in violence came as the standoff seemed to be shifting slightly more in the U.S.' favor, with the price of oil around $80 a barrel and Iranian leaders talking about growing economic hardships, said Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies' Middle East office in Bahrain.
Last week, U.S. Central Command's Adm. Brad Cooper said the strait had been secretly cleared of mines and that the U.S. Navy had helped nearly 1,500 commercial vessels carrying some 750 million barrels of oil pass through in recent months — still far below prewar levels.
"He basically told the world oil is flowing out and Iran is not capable of restricting the U.S.'s approach," Bruchmann said. "The U.S. is trying to reinstall some kind of confidence into the global oil markets … and the Iranians had to respond to that by reinserting insecurity and doubt."
Since the fighting resumed, the price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, has climbed to around $95, up more than 30% from the start of the war.
U.S. allies in the region fend off Iranian attacks
Following the strikes at Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain said they had also come under attack, without reporting any casualties.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy, and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," the recently appointed head of Iran's powerful Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said on X.
In Iraq, where Iranian-backed forces are active, Kurdish authorities said they had intercepted 10 drones laden with explosives in the Irbil area. Iranian television reported that American bases in Irbil had been targeted.
Israel's military also said that Iran-backed Hezbollah fired two explosive drones at its soldiers in southern Lebanon, without causing casualties.
The U.S. Central Command said Tuesday's strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defense sites, radar systems and maritime assets.
Casualties in Iran include people at a wedding party
One U.S. strike hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, a small coastal town overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media.
Four people were killed — two women and two children, aged 4 and 16 — and at least 68 were wounded, the state news agency IRNA and state TV said Wednesday. Just after the strike, Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor, had told Iranian state television that five people were killed. There was no explanation for the change.
Several heavy explosions shook Kuhestak, with fireballs that lit up the night sky, according to security camera footage carried by the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Images from Iran's semiofficial Tasnim news agency showed several hospitalized children being treated for injuries at a hospital in the nearby town of Minab, where a U.S. missile strike on the opening day of the war hit a primary school, killing more than 100 children.
Footage from the Iranian Red Crescent showed rescue workers entering a damaged home in the wake of the strike. It showed a hole in the roof of one house in a neighborhood of densely packed homes.
Experts say a "very precise" weapon appears to have been used
Two weapons experts told The Associated Press that images of fragments of a missile, which Iranian media said was used in the strike, were from a U.S.-made SLAM-ER cruise missile.
Trevor Ball, conflict researcher at the investigative group Bellingcat, said the SLAM-ER was "developed as a very precise weapon" that can be retargeted in flight by a human operator watching by infrared camera.
N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services, said the air-launched missile is also used by the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Neither has reported carrying out any recent strikes on Iran.
"Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished," Ebrahim Azizi, chairperson of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X.
U.S. Central Command spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said the U.S. military was "aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them." He would not say if CENTCOM had launched a formal investigation.
Separately, Iran has said four members of its paramilitary Revolutionary Guard and 10 members of the Guard's volunteer Basij forces died in the U.S. attacks.
The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut down
During last month's lull in fighting, the U.S. ramped up economic pressure on Iran as Washington sought to fully open the Strait of Hormuz.
About a fifth of the world's traded oil was shipped through the key waterway before Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 and Iran largely shut it down in response. Despite many pronouncements from Washington that the strait is open, only a handful of ships are making the passage each day and Iran has regularly attacked vessels.
On Wednesday, Saudi shipping company Bahri said two Filipino sailors were killed in an attack late Monday as their vessel transited the strait.
A ceasefire deal reached in June quickly fell apart amid exchanges of strikes that same month. Mediator Pakistan has been working to restart talks.
Late Tuesday, Trump said he would not force Iran to the bargaining table.
"I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump wrote on social media.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

As of 12:18 IST today, the public issue had received bids for 25.1 Lakh shares against 68.5 Lakh shares on offer, translating to a subscription of 37%. The issue was subscribed 8% on the first day and ended the second day with a subscription of 24%. Retail investors continued to lead the demand, with their reserved portion subscribed 1.23X. The category received bids for 15.4 Lakh shares against the 12.5 Lakh shares reserved for it. Meanwhile, NIIs subscribed 41% of their reserved quota, placing bids for 7.6 Lakh shares against 18.7 Lakh shares on offer. Of this, NIIs bidding for shares worth more than ₹10 Lakh subscribed 48% of their portion, placing bids for 5.9 Lakh shares against 12.5 Lakh shares on offer. Those bidding for shares worth between ₹2 Lakh and ₹10 Lakh subscribed 26% of their quota, with bids for 1.6 Lakh shares against 6.2 Lakh shares reserved for them. QIBs subscribed just 6% of the portion earmarked for them, placing bids for 2.2 Lakh shares against the 37.4 Lakh shares reserved for the category. The muted institutional demand comes despite Purple Style Labs raising ₹306 Cr from anchor investors ahead of the IPO. The company allotted 53.2 Lakh shares to anchor investors at ₹575 apiece, with Morgan Stanley and BofA Securities among the participants. The ₹680 Cr IPO, which opened for subscription on August 31, comprises entirely a fresh issue of shares, with no OFS component. The price band has been fixed at ₹546-575 per share. Of the fresh capital, ₹371.1 Cr will be used to meet the lease liabilities of Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop’s experience centre network. The company operates 12 experience centres and two back-end offices in India, along with experience centres in London and New York. Another ₹138.9 Cr has been earmarked for sales and marketing expenses till FY30, while the remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. The IPO will close today. Purple Style Labs is scheduled to list its shares on the NSE and BSE on Monday (September 7). Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury fashion company that operates Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop and owns designer brands such as Wendell Rodricks and Hemant Trivedi. The company has raised about $78 Mn from investors, including the Harish Shah Family Office and Masaba Gupta. Celebrities such as Salman Khan, Shah Rukh Khan through the Gauri Khan Family Trust, and Shraddha Kapoor are also among its investors. Its platform houses offerings from designers such as Seema Gujral, Anushree Reddy, Amit Aggarwal, and Rohit Gandhi Rahul Khanna across wedding wear, occasion wear, menswear, and accessories. On the financial front, Purple Style Labs’ net loss widened 51% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹188.4 Cr in the previous year. Its operating revenue rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25.

The newly created Department of Senior Citizens’ Welfare, one of the highlights of the first Budget of the UDF government, is in the process of becoming fully operational, with key posts being redeployed and proposals for a range of new welfare initiatives submitted to the government.
The General Administration department has issued orders redeploying posts, including those of Additional Secretary, Under Secretary, Section Officer, Assistants and Computer Assistants, from the General Administration and Personnel and Administrative Reforms departments to the new department.
The government had earmarked ₹10 crore in the State Budget for the functioning of the department and implementation of senior-citizen welfare schemes. Proposals submitted for senior citizens’ welfare include measures aimed at protection, care, healthcare, social security and productive ageing.
The creation of a dedicated department assumes significance against the backdrop of Keralam’s rapidly ageing population and the growing social, economic and healthcare challenges faced by senior citizens.
The government proposes to move beyond welfare assistance to the elderly, to create a comprehensive programme for addressing the needs of the elderly.
Silver economy, which encompasses economic activities based on the needs, purchasing power, skills, employment and entrepreneurial potential of older people, is proposed as an important component of the department’s work.
The new department has been assigned the task of administering laws and rules relating to senior citizens, implementing the State’s senior-citizen policy and centrally sponsored and State welfare schemes, managing the affairs of Kerala State Commission for Senior Citizens and that of elderly care homes.
State-level directorate
Efforts are already under way to establish a State-level directorate for senior citizens’ welfare and district-level offices and a State Governing Council to coordinate all welfare measures for senior citizens.
The government is also planning to launch a comprehensive State-wide survey on senior citizens.
24-hour helpline
The proposed 24-hour helpline for various emergency interventions on behalf of senior citizens will be coordinated at the field-level by a Rapid Response Team which will deliver the services to senior citizens. A Field Response Officer will head the RRT to ensure immediate assistance to the elderly
A State Technical Advisory Committee and Senior Citizen Facilitation Desks in all local self-government institutions have been proposed. Initiatives are also being planned to promote greater interaction and cooperation between senior citizens and those belonging to the younger generations.
A dedicated senior citizen services portal will be set up, which will establish an Elder Vulnerability Register, Kerala Care Workforce Register, Service Connect Directory and Productive Ageing Register.
The establishment of District Senior Citizen Cells in all 14 district collectorates, certification processes for senior citizen-friendly government offices, a Dementia-Friendly Keralam initiative and senior citizen-friendly health protocols and neighbourhood support networks for elderly persons with Kudumbashree support are in the final stages

In Summary
- The CMF Buds Neo are the latest TWS from Nothing’s sub-brand, CMF.
- The new buds come in attractive colors, in true CMF tradition, and punch above their price point in terms of specs and features.
- At Rs 1999, the CMF Buds Neo are the most affordable TWS in CMF’s audio portfolio, and have also been called the most accessible entry point to the CMF ecosystem. They do face a lot of competition, though.
While it is hard being a new smartphone in this tech climate, we believe it is harder being a new pair of TWS. The number of new TWS, as well as increasingly competitive prices and features across a wide range of price brackets, make it quite a task for a new pair to make its mark in the tech world. The latest addition in this lineup comes from Nothing’s sub-brand CMF, the CMF Buds Neo. Priced at Rs. 1,999, the Buds Neo are positioned as the most accessible entry to the CMF ecosystem. They come with an impressive feature list and a quirky design. But is that enough to help the CMF Buds Neo make space for itself in the TWS market?
CMF Buds Neo Appearance and Design: Typically CMF, Geometry with some flair
CMF, like its parent company Nothing, speaks a very distinct design language. A language no one else in the industry has adopted (yet) – a very smooth blend of Nothing’s industrial design combined with CMF’s bright colored flair. The CMF Buds Neo speak this language. Their square-shaped case comes with soft, rounded edges that make it sit very comfortably in one’s hands. The top left corner has a tactile, round dial. This is not just a design touch but also has some utility – it can be used to attach a lanyard that will keep your Buds Neo from getting lost.
The buds come in three different colors: Black, White, and Dark Blue. The Dark Blue and White color options bring very vibrant color contrasts with green and orange ear tips and tactile dials, respectively, while the Black is all black. The white variant, whose white case comes with a super bright orange tactile dial, is perhaps the most distinct. There is a small ‘CMF by Nothing’ badge in orange on the front as well. The cases have a matte finish while the dials are glossy.
The case has a very tiny LED light on the front and a USB Type-C port on the back. Flip the case open, and you find the buds resting nicely inside, with a ‘Buds Neo’ branding slightly above the earbuds. The buds come with a typical TWS design – a bulbous head attached to a long pill-shaped stem. The eartips bring the pop of orange to the white buds, while the texture of the overall buds is a mix of glossy and matte.
There is a small glossy dot on the head of the stem of the right bud and a thick, slightly raised circle on the stem of the left bud. The buds are comfortable to wear and come with one set of eartips attached and two others in the box. We used the medium-sized eartips, and they fit snugly. Speaking of snug fits, the buds also attach magnetically to the case.
The CMF Buds Neo case itself is quite compact – it is square, with length and breadth both at 54.3 mm, and is a little thick at 23 mm. It weighs 50.3 grams, while the buds weigh just a little over 4 grams each. The case is very pocket-friendly, and the buds are light on the ear. The buds come with an IP55 rating, making them good enough for sweaty gym sessions, while the case has an IPX rating, making it splash-proof, which is handy (most TWS cases still do not have splash resistance).
The white case does get dirty very easily (it caught dirt marks in our bag), but all in all, the design of the CMF Buds Neo is very eye-catching and definitely something not-so-usual. If you are not into pops of color, you can choose the black variant. Those who want to be right between these two extremes can go for the blue variant, with its flash of green eartips and disk.
CMF Buds Neo Specs and Controls: Very impressive at this price point
The CMF Buds Neo come with impressive specs for their price. They have 12.4 mm dynamic drivers with a 20 Hz- 20 kHz frequency response, two mics per earbud (for a total of four), Bluetooth 6.0, support for AAC and SBC codecs, and ANC of up to 35 dB. There is also support for spatial audio, and you get six EQ presets. All of these features are accessible through the NothingX App. The case comes with a 460 mAh battery with support for fast charging, and each earbud has a 45 mAh battery in it as well. The buds support Google Fast Pair, Microsoft Swift Pair, and also Dual-Device connectivity.
Pairing the CMF Buds Neo is simple: you flip the case open, wait for the buds to appear in your device’s Bluetooth list, and select them. To get the buds in pairing mode to connect with other devices, you can simply tap and hold the stem of the buds for five seconds, then select them from your device’s Bluetooth list. The controls on the buds are basically a series of taps- double-tapping on either bud will take you to the next track or reject a call; triple-tapping will take you to the previous song, while tapping and holding will let you switch between ANC and transparency mode.
No action is assigned to the double-tap-and-hold, but one can assign it to increasing or decreasing the volume or summoning the voice assistant. Apart from the call functionality, these controls can be customized using the Nothing X app. Interestingly, there is no option to map a control to a single tap, perhaps out of concern for accidental touches.
CMF Buds Neo Performance: Good audio, decent ANC and very good calling
The 12.4 mm dynamic drivers on the CMF Buds Neo come with a titanium-coated PET dome and a flexible PEEK and PU surround. This, as per Nothing, adds a bass-ful punch to the audio while ensuring vocals do not get muddied. The buds certainly deliver on both these fronts. The audio is full-bodied, and while it does focus a bit on bass, it does not drown out the treble or vocals. It is not balanced in a way that would give an audiophile an eargasm, but we seldom see that at this price anyway. On the other hand, they will impress casual listeners in a heartbeat, delivering a thoroughly enjoyable experience in pop, Bollywood, R&B, and hip-hop, and similar genres.
The Nothing X app comes with six EQ presets, and each one offers a distinct sound profile, which sometimes is not the case in this price segment. There is also the option to create an EQ based on one’s own preferences. The buds provide a reasonably spacious sound, which is usually not very easy for TWS to achieve, especially at this price point. The sound obviously does not feel as immersive as some of the high-end audio gear available on the market, but for the price, it is a hit in our books. The vocals are sharp enough to listen to hour-long podcasts or watch content.
The CMF Buds Neo also come with ANC. There are four options – low, medium, high, and adaptive. We mostly stuck to the ‘high’ setting. It will not cancel out very loud noises, but the snug fit of the buds combined with effective ANC does kill environmental noise with ease. It managed to drown out noise in a crowded cafe very effectively. We could not hear our friend sitting across from us with ANC on. The transparency mode brings back awareness to what would otherwise be a very isolating experience – the conversation we were not able to hear earlier became clear with transparency mode.
The call quality of the buds is very good as well – a pleasant surprise at this price point. We did not have any issues hearing the caller and did not get any complaints about our voice quality either. There is a low latency mode for games, but we had to turn it on manually, which was a bit of a pain.
The controls of the CMF Buds Neo are easy to remember but take some serious getting used to. We often found we had to tap harder than we are used to in order to register a command. The buds also lack wear detection, which means the audio does not automatically pause when one takes the buds (one or both) out. While this is a feature not often found at this price point, its absence was inconvenient.
Battery is another strong suit of the CMF Buds Neo. The buds promise 11 hours of listening time with ANC off, with 52 hours of total playback with ANC off, including the case. With ANC on, the numbers become 5 hours for the buds, and 30 hours with the case. We found the buds’ actual performance to be close to these numbers. With mixed use (ANC/ transparency mode on and off) at 70 percent volume, the buds easily lasted for around 9 hours. The buds also have a fast charging feature in which 10 minutes of charging gives one 5.5 hours of play time with ANC off . However, there is no cable in the box, which is a bit of a letdown.
CMF Buds Neo App: NothingX remains as clean and easy to use as ever
The NothingX app is the perfect accompaniment to the CMF Buds Neo – simple, clean and easy to use. We did have some trouble adding our Buds Neo to the app, but after a little struggle, the buds were added to the list of our other CMF devices. There is one main page, and you can scroll down to access all the functions and features. ANC, Spatial Audio, controls, bass enhancement, equalizer settings, low lag mode, dual connection, and firmware updates can all be accessed through the app. One also gets the exact charge percentage left in each earbud, although rather oddly, not that of the case. The app is easy to use and remains one of our favorites.
CMF Buds Neo Review Verdict: Superb value for the price
The CMF Buds Neo come with a price tag of Rs. 1,999, which is quite competitive for the performance and specs they offer. The similarly priced OnePlus Nord Buds 3r bring a comparable spec sheet, as do the Realme Buds T200 Lite, but both come with Bluetooth 5.4, marginally less playtime, and are not even close to the Buds Neo in the design department.
The CMF Buds Neo are near-perfect entry-level TWS options. Their audio, ANC, and battery performance give them an edge over the competition, and the distinct design is the cherry on this TWS cake. If you do not want to burn a hole in your pocket and still want a good pair of feature-packed TWS, the CMF Buds Neo are the perfect pick.
- Distinct design
- Enjoyable audio
- Good ANC
- Super call quality
- Very good companion app
- Good battery life
- Controls take some getting used to
- No charging cable in the box
- The white coloured case attracts scratches and smudges easily

I wouldn’t call it cheap, but this monitor from Asus brings proper HDR-capable video editing to creators who couldn’t previously afford an OLED display.
Attractive, thin design. Stand comes with lots of adjustability. Forward-facing buttons are convenient. Solid HDR performance for the price. 120-Hz refresh rate is a nice bonus. Great port selection.
TIRED
Not very bright in SDR. Some quirks when connected to macOS.
OLED is common in gaming monitors these days. But for those of us who don’t need gaming gear? Well, home-office and content-creation monitors have been much slower to adopt the exciting and more capable display technology. That’s unfortunate because having an OLED monitor is every bit as useful as having an OLED TV if you ever use your monitor for entertainment purposes. OLED displays are also helpful for photo editors, videographers, game developers, and other creators who might want to work in high dynamic range (HDR) for a broader range of brightness, contrast, and color.
The PA279CDV is Asus’ attempt to bring that OLED goodness to a wider demographic, at a retail price of $699, which is competitive for the technology. This monitor makes a few compromises to hit that price, but it does so without losing what makes owning a high-end OLED display feel unique.
Unique, Ergonomic, and Easy to Use
Asus is one of the few manufacturers releasing OLED monitors precisely for this non-gamer demographic, and the PA279CDV is the cheapest it's ever had in its lineup. In fact, the monitor only has one major competitor: the Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED (9/10 WIRED Recommends). The main difference between the two is the size. Dell’s model is 31.6 inches, compared to Asus’ 27 inches. Being larger gives you more screen to work with, but it's also less sharp and takes up more desk space. The Samsung 32-inch Smart Monitor M90SF (7/10 WIRED Recommends) is the only other non-gaming OLED monitor option, but that's far more expensive.
As far as the Asus’ appearance goes, the side bezels are a bit large, and the top and bottom bezels aren’t the same size, which I find visually off-putting. Nicely, though, the amount of adjustability is impressive. This stand can swivel, tilt, rotate into portrait mode, and the height can shift 5 inches. The stand has some very basic built-in cable management, with down-firing ports that help keep cords organized. Also, the flat base doesn't require much space on my desk.
Each of the two back USB-C ports has a specific purpose. One is USB-C 3.2 with DP Alt Mode, which provides 96 watts of power delivery for your laptop. The other is a USB-C 3.2 port for the KVM switch, enabling you to connect two PCs to the monitor and switch between them seamlessly. Fortunately, Asus clearly labels each port, so you know which to use for your intended purpose. The monitor also comes with two USB-A ports for accessories, a headphone jack, HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, and a DisplayPort Out for daisy-chaining monitors together. This is a solid array of port selection that gives you just about everything you need to use the ProArt PA279cdv as a workstation.
Meanwhile, the controls for the onscreen display and menu are on the right side of the front panel. I tend to prefer just a single joystick for simplicity's sake, but like the other Asus ProArt monitors, this one gives you five control buttons, plus a power button, in addition to a joystick. Once you know how to use it, though, the buttons give you quick access to switching inputs or changing brightness.
There are quite a lot of features to dig through in the menu, including a number of color modes and detailed picture-quality tweaks. There's also a Display Widget app to handle all these settings, available in Windows 11 or macOS.
The monitor includes speakers, but they sound pretty bad, which is unfortunate for a monitor designed at least partially for entertainment purposes. Keep this in mind if you plan to watch a movie on the monitor, since you’ll only want to use the speakers for basic notifications. By contrast, the Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED has a really nice set of speakers.
OLED, Oh My!
Brightness—both measured in standard dynamic range (SDR) and HDR content—is the key feature of an OLED monitor, as it determines how good at HDR the device in question truly is. OLED displays can switch off individual pixels, a capability that provides the absolute blacks this class of display is known for. But if the pixels aren't bright enough, the display still won’t produce a strong HDR performance.
Using an HDR test pattern, I was able to record 1,038 nits in a 1 percent window and 917 nits in a 4 percent window. These strong results deliver a greater sense of visual fidelity when watching movies or playing games than what you’d get with dimmer displays. Compared to the current ultimate HDR monitor, the Apple Studio Display XDR (7/10, WIRED Recommends), though, these results aren’t stunning. On the Apple monitor, I got to 1,905 nits of brightness in a 25 percent window. Even so, comparing these two monitors is hardly fair, given that the Apple costs more than $3,000 and should provide a premium quality to match. I’m providing these results to demonstrate the broad HDR landscape in monitors.
I tested the Asus visuals in a few scenarios, including HDR video test footage, Netflix streaming, and some games. Dark scenes in Cyberpunk 2077 really come to life, aided by the deep blacks and brighter highlights. The effect isn't mind-blowing, but it's definitely noticeable.
In SDR content, though—which is where you’ll spend most of your time—the results are even less stellar. According to my meter, it maxed out in SDR at 240 nits at full-screen brightness. While that's bright enough for most days, if you sit next to a window, you might find yourself wishing for an extra 100 nits. The Dell 32 Plus 4K QD-OLED has the same issue. The good news is that while the PA279CDV has a glossy display, it’s surprisingly good at resisting reflections and glare.
I also tested the color performance, as that's one of the features that Asus claims distinguishes the PA279CDV from its more expensive OLED options, such as the ProArt PA27ucdmr ($1,401). The color gamut was fantastic across the board, meaning the panel is capable of producing great color, covering 91 percent of Adobe RGB and 98 percent in Display P3. When plugged into a Windows machine, the Spyder Pro I used measured excellent color accuracy as well—far beyond what Asus claimed.
However, when plugged into a MacBook Pro, I was unable to get that same color accuracy. For whatever reason, the best I could measure was a Delta-E of around 2.0. That's not terrible, but it's not quite pro-level. Speaking of Mac compatibility, the PA279CDV has a number of features to entice Mac users. Once you install the Display Widget app, it'll match up color temperature with your MacBook and even allow you to control screen brightness from your keyboard. (It can’t control volume, though, which is a miss.) A lot of this is very similar to what BenQ offers in its own Mac-focused line of monitors, such as the BenQ 5K MA270S that I recently tested.
This doesn't solve the problem of scaling. MacOS still doesn't love the 4K resolution, so you'll need to play around with different resolutions and decide which suits your needs best. When you plug it in, it defaults to a 2560 x 1440 resolution in macOS. This doesn’t yield the same sharpness as running a native 1440p on a Windows machine, but it still looks quite sharp. If you upgrade to a 5K monitor, you won't have to deal with this, but those tend to be more expensive and often aren't available in OLED. The other macOS quirk I ran into was that I could only turn on HDR if I changed the refresh rate to 60 Hz.
Despite the macOS hiccups, the 120-Hz refresh rate is a nice touch in the PA279CDV. It's increasingly common in cheaper monitors, even appearing in the Dell 27 Plus 4K, which is often on sale for less than $300. But it nicely matches the refresh rate of the MacBook Pro and gives the screen smoother animation and motion. And while serious gamers will certainly desire a faster display, 120 Hz at least allows games to look fluid at frame rates over 60 frames per second (fps).
Hope for HDR
There's a lot to like about the PA279CDV and very few reasons for frustration. I'm thrilled to see the category of non-OLED gaming monitors grow, especially in the direction of affordability. The vast majority of laptop screens and monitors lack any meaningful HDR support. So, as these HDR-capable monitors become more accessible, the hope is that we'll see more high-quality HDR content available online. Heck, most browsers and streaming services don't even support HDR at this point. The PA279CDV is exactly what we need more of to improve the situation, and the monitor’s strong port selection makes it a solid option for a home-office workstation in its own right.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.
Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.
The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.
While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.
Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.
“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

Modding platform Nexus Mods now owns SteamDB
Nexus Mods said the community-led site will operate as it always has, while becoming stronger and better resourced.
In today's slightly unexpected acquisition news, the world's largest mod-sharing platform just bought SteamDB. Nexus Mods announced that it had acquired the Steam-focused independent database in a news post on its website, where it called SteamDB "one of the most trusted resources in PC gaming."
SteamDB was launched in 2013 by two people who go by the names of Marlamin and xPaw as little more than a hobby, but as it grew in size it became more difficult to maintain. Nexus Mods said it started talking to xPaw when the programmer — who had eventually assumed sole responsibility of managing the site — started looking for someone who could give it "the resources, development capacity, and long-term stability" he was struggling to provide alone.
Nexus Mods says it shares a lot of the same values as SteamDB, both of which were primarily built to serve a large community of hardcore PC gamers. SteamDB logs player charts, price history, updates and other data for the entire Steam catalog, and the ability to better track which version of a particular game players are installing mods into was especially appealing to Nexus Mods. Updates are notorious game-breakers when mods are involved and SteamDB's enormous amount of historical data should prove beneficial for ongoing development.
SteamDB will keep its current name and won't change much in the short-term, so you can continue to use it as you do now. The main changes, Nexus Mods says, will be behind the scenes, as a dedicated team will eventually transition into managing the database, improving its "infrastructure, security, and scalability." SteamDB has also traditionally relied on donated Steam keys for tracking game files, and while it will still lean heavily on its community going forward, Nexus Mods will also start funding keys itself.
In his own separate statement on SteamDB, xPaw reassured the community that it was in good hands with Nexus Mods, and said the aim was to invest in and help it survive rather than "change what makes the project special." He also pointed to the rise of AI in a post-COVID world contributing to the end of "the internet we once loved", and with it his own passion for continuing.
"I have full confidence the team will be able to continue improving the project for gamers, developers and publishers alike," xPaw said in a statement. "I will be helping the team ensure a smooth transition in the coming months. This project has occupied my whole adult life. Thank you to everyone who has used SteamDB, contributed to it, reported bugs, shared it with others, or simply found it useful."

What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
- Published
Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.
Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.
Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.
That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.
With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.
The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.
It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.
However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.
More involved, more shots - but a smaller sample
On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.
The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.
Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.
His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.
That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.
Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny.
During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.
Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).
Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.
There is, however, an important caveat.
Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.
Are Villa getting a different type of striker?
Both players were predominantly used as centre-forwards last season, making the comparison reasonably fair.
Watkins played 100% of his 3,837 minutes as a striker, with 92% coming as the central striker in Villa's 4-2-3-1.
Jackson spent 95% of his 1,320 minutes up front, with the remaining 5% on the left. At Bayern, 86% of his playing time came as the striker in a 4-2-3-1.
The similarity largely ends there. Jackson averaged 46.6 open-play touches per 90, compared with Watkins' 29.5, and completed almost twice as many passes - 24 per 90 to Watkins' 11.6.
He was also considerably more involved in creating and progressing attacks. Jackson averaged:
- 1.6 shot-ending carries per 90, compared with Watkins' 0.8
- 1.6 successful take-ons per 90, compared with 0.82
- 2.5 passes into the penalty area per 90, compared with 0.7.
Opta's touch maps reinforce the difference. Watkins' involvement was concentrated more heavily around the centre of the final third and penalty area, while Jackson received possession across a wider range of attacking zones.
Among a sample of 1,577 top-five European league strikers over the past 10 seasons, Jackson ranked in the 85th percentile for chances created, 77th for progressive carries and 73rd for touches.
Watkins ranked in the 28th, 53rd and eighth percentiles respectively. That points towards Villa moving from a relatively low-touch focal point to a forward who is more comfortable becoming involved in attacks earlier.
Greater intensity without the ball
There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.
Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.
His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.
The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.
Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.
Why Emery believes he can unlock Jackson
Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.
Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game.
"Unai taught me everything about football," he said,
Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move.
Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.
Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.
Jackson's ability to carry the ball was already evident too. Ten of his league goal involvements followed carries, fewer only than Vinicius Jr, despite Jackson playing substantially fewer minutes.
Chelsea subsequently signed him in 2023. He scored 30 goals and supplied 12 assists in 81 appearances for the club before spending last season on loan at Bayern.
His time in Munich was complicated by circumstances rather than simply performance.
Bayern's obligation to buy would have been triggered if he reached a demanding appearance threshold, but Harry Kane remained fit and prolific, while the displays of Luis Diaz and Michael Olise limited opportunities elsewhere across the frontline.
Jackson still produced 11 goals across all competitions, and only Kane recorded a better rate of open-play Bundesliga goals per 90.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany publicly defended him when criticism resurfaced, pointing to the quality of the forwards ahead of him and saying Jackson had trained and performed well.
A replacement - but not necessarily a replica
Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.
Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.
There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.
But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.
If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards.
They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

Iron deficiency can develop gradually, with the body’s stored iron being depleted before there is a measurable fall in haemoglobin. So, a normal haemoglobin level does not always mean that the body has adequate iron stores.
Steve Thomas A., consultant haemato-oncologist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, explains that haemoglobin and ferritin measure different things. Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, while ferritin reflects the body’s iron reserves. The body can maintain haemoglobin for some time by drawing on these reserves. As a result, iron deficiency may be present even when a routine blood test shows normal haemoglobin.
Ferritin is one of the key markers used to assess these iron stores. Gopinathan M., consultant, haemato-oncology (BMT), MGM Cancer Institute, compares ferritin to a warehouse where iron is stored for use whenever the body needs it. Iron is stored mainly in tissues such as the liver and spleen and within cells called macrophages. It is subsequently mobilised for erythropoiesis, the process through which red blood cells and haemoglobin are produced.
Iron deficiency without anaemia, therefore, can be missed if testing is limited to just haemoglobin measurement.
In India, the latest available NFHS-5 data showed that 57% of women aged 15-49 years live with anaemia.
Ferritin levels
Ferritin is an important marker of iron stores, but there is no single number that can be interpreted in isolation for everyone. Dr. Gopinathan says, along with ferritin, serum iron and total iron-binding capacity are assessed to calculate transferrin saturation. A transferrin saturation below 20% can support a diagnosis of iron deficiency, particularly when ferritin is difficult to interpret.
Dr. Thomas, however, cautions against treating ferritin cut-offs as universal rules. Age, sex, pregnancy, menstruation and a person’s clinical history can influence how the result should be interpreted.
Inflammation is particularly important. Ferritin is also an acute-phase reactant, meaning its level can rise during infection or inflammation. This can make iron stores appear better than they actually are. The World Health Organization recommends taking inflammation into account when interpreting ferritin and, where appropriate, using markers such as C-reactive protein alongside it.
This is why a ferritin value that appears to be within a laboratory’s reference range does not necessarily rule out iron deficiency in a person who has inflammation or chronic illness.
Who is affected?
Iron stores can gradually decline when iron loss continues or the body’s requirements increase. Women who have heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding are particularly vulnerable. Pregnancy also increases iron requirements. Frequent blood donors can lose significant amounts of iron through repeated donations. People who follow vegetarian diets may also be at risk because the iron in plant foods is generally less readily absorbed than haem iron from animal foods.
Chronic, unnoticed blood loss is another important cause. Experts point to conditions such as ulcers and bleeding piles as examples, while gastrointestinal blood loss can continue without obvious visible bleeding.
In such situations, ferritin may fall while haemoglobin remains normal for months. This makes a low ferritin an important finding.
What can tiredness say
Iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia can produce symptoms that are often vague and overlap with many other conditions. Headache, body and muscle aches, itching, episodes of blackout, ringing in the ears and breathlessness are among symptoms that may occur. Persistent tiredness, weakness, hair loss and poor concentration should prompt evaluation when they do not improve with adequate rest, particularly in people who have risk factors for iron deficiency.
However, these symptoms are not specific to iron deficiency. This is why symptoms alone should not be used to decide whether iron supplements are needed. A complete blood count is generally an important starting point. Ferritin and other iron parameters can then help determine whether depleted iron stores are contributing to the problem.
Causes of low ferritin
Finding a low ferritin is only part of the evaluation. The more important question is why the iron stores have fallen.
“Iron deficiency is a symptom of something else, not a disease on its own,” Dr. Thomas says. Treating the deficiency without addressing its cause can allow the problem to recur.
Experts caution against starting iron tablets simply because a report shows a low ferritin. Treatment commonly continues for several months, including after haemoglobin improves, to replenish iron stores, but the dose and duration depend on the cause and severity of the deficiency.
Seeking diagnosis
The widespread availability of iron supplements can make self-treatment tempting, particularly when symptoms such as fatigue or hair loss are attributed to low iron.
But unnecessary supplementation can cause nausea, constipation and abdominal discomfort. More importantly, it can delay the diagnosis of the underlying reason for iron loss. Excessive iron accumulation can also be harmful, particularly in people with disorders that cause increased iron absorption.
The message, experts say, is not to panic over an isolated ferritin value, but neither should a low ferritin be ignored simply because the haemoglobin is normal. Dr. Thomas says medical advice is therefore important to determine whether iron deficiency is actually present, identify its cause and decide on the appropriate treatment and duration.

Parikshit Sharma, present on yacht during Zubeen Garg's death, testifies in court
Parikshit Sharma is the first Assamese member associated with the organisation who was present aboard the yacht on September 19, 2025, when the incident occurred, to appear as a witness before the court.
Parikshit Sharma, an Assamese associated with the Assam Association in Singapore, has appeared before a fast-track court to record his testimony in the death case of celebrated singer Zubeen Garg.
Sharma is the first Assamese member associated with the organisation who was present aboard the yacht on September 19, 2025, when the incident occurred, to appear as a witness before the court.
Sharma’s testimony is significant as he was reportedly present on the yacht during the events leading up to Garg’s death.
His account is expected to shed light on what he personally witnessed that day and may form part of the evidence being examined during the ongoing trial.
A special fast-track court had earlier framed charges against seven accused in the case.
The accused include North East India Festival (NEIF) chief organiser Shyamkanu Mahanta, Garg’s manager Siddharth Sharma, band members Shekhar Jyoti Goswami and Amrit Prabha Mahanta, his cousin and Assam Police DSP Sandipan Garg, and personal security officers Nandeswar Bora and Prabin Baishya.
The accused have been booked under various provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including murder, culpable homicide not amounting to murder, criminal conspiracy and causing death by negligence. They have pleaded not guilty.
According to the prosecution, Shyamkanu Mahanta faces eight charges, Siddharth Sharma seven, Goswami and Amrit Prabha six each, while Bora and Baishya face two charges each and Sandipan Garg one.
Garg, 52, died in Singapore on September 19 last year while swimming near Lazarus Island.
He had travelled to the city-state to attend the fourth edition of the North East India Festival.
His death triggered widespread grief in Assam and subsequently led to an investigation by a Special Investigation Team of the Assam Police CID after more than 60 FIRs were registered.
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has maintained that Garg’s death was a case of murder, saying one accused killed him while others allegedly assisted.
However, the Singapore Police Force and Singapore’s Coroner’s Court found no evidence of foul play, with the latter concluding that Garg was severely intoxicated and drowned after declining a life jacket.
With witness examination now underway, Sharma’s testimony will be scrutinised alongside other evidence. More witnesses are expected to appear as the court proceeds with the trial.
