Video of Hochul in the mosque authentically shows her wearing a headscarf, with some of her hair visible.
Hochul was not wearing a traditional hijab, which is a way of life that involves practicing modesty, covering the head and all the hair.
In late August 2026, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul was criticized after she purportedly wore a head covering to a mosque.
Videos (archived) on Instagram, Facebook, and X (archived) claimed to show Hochul wearing a black head scarf or hijab while speaking at a mosque, which conservative critics claimed was disrespectful so close to the anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. Snopes readers asked us to confirm whether Hochul was wearing a hijab — a covering for the head, hair and neck that is typically worn by some Muslim women.
The above video is authentic. On Aug. 28, 2026, Hochul visited the Islamic Cultural Center of New York and covered her head as a gesture of respect as she was speaking in the prayer hall. Hochul has worn a head covering at events with Muslims before and has even spoken out in favor of Muslim women choosing to wear the hijab. She was not, however, wearing a traditional hijab. As such, we rate this claim as a mixture of true and false information.
Social media posts and media coverage often erroneously simplify the meaning of "hijab" and claim it is just a headscarf. The term "hijab" has many interpretations but broadly refers to a veil or barrier and is a practice involving modesty for both men and women. Wearing hijab involves modest clothing in an Islamic context, including a head covering. It is worn in many styles but for Muslim women today, the hijab colloquially refers to the covering that typically conceals the head, all the hair and neck while leaving the face uncovered.
In available photographs of Hochul covering her head, her hair is visible. She is wearing a headscarf, and not participating in the practice of wearing hijab, as is typically done by Muslim women.
Hochul was visiting the Islamic Cultural Center in New York City during Friday prayers. The above video shows her standing before the front wall of the mosque with the decorative glass niche behind her (visible in these videos of the Islamic Cultural Center at 0:23 and 3:29).
The official Instagram account for the Islamic Cultural Center School — which is affiliated with the Islamic Cultural Center— posted about Hochul's visit and noted that the governor joined for Friday prayers:
 
Governor Hochul joined our community at ICCNY for Friday Jumaa, where she addressed the congregation, before visiting the Islamic Cultural Center School of New York. She toured the school, stepped into our classrooms and learned more about the community we are so proud to serve.
Hochul is wearing the same outfit in the above Instagram post and in the videos being shared on social media. However, during her visit to the Islamic Cultural Center School, Hochul's head was uncovered. She covered only it when speaking at the gathering at the prayer hall.
All Muslim women cover their heads when praying or when inside the prayer hall of a mosque, with some — but not all — in hijab. Given that Hochul was in attendance for Friday prayers at the mosque, covering her head can be seen as a sign of respect.
This was not the first time Hochul covered her head at a religious gathering for Muslims. In July 2025, she covered her head when speaking at the funeral of a slain Muslim police officer. In 2020, she covered her head when speaking at the Jamaica Muslim Center.
In February 2024, Hochul posted (archived) on X in support of World Hijab Day, writing: "we stand in solidarity with our Muslim sisters who choose to wear the hijab. New York's diversity has always been its strength, and together, we will always promote respect, inclusion, and religious freedom in the face of hate."
The post also showed Hochul shaking hands with a Muslim hijabi woman while wearing a head covering. Another Muslim woman in the photograph is wearing a head covering similar to Hochul's:
Hochul has not publicly addressed the criticism as of this writing.
Snopes has previously covered examples of other leaders wearing head coverings as a sign of respect among Muslim communities, including former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern.

What is the ‘Cat in the Hat’ viral trend that is landing teens in trouble with the law?
Authorities in Kentucky and Colorado have cracked down on the trend over concerns about students’ safety
A viral social media trend has landed teens in trouble with police in at least two states as authorities warn students about threats to school safety.
The so-called Cat in the Hat trend has spread across the country as young people share AI-generated content of someone wearing a costume of the famous Dr. Seuss character and appearing to be coming after people at their schools or homes.
Authorities in Kentucky and Colorado are among those to have cracked down on the trend.
The Allen County-Scottsville Crime Task Force in Kentucky opened an investigation last Thursday after it said multiple local students reported receiving threatening messages through Snapchat and other social media platforms from someone who identified themselves as the “Cat in the Hat.”
The task force said in a Facebook post Saturday that it had identified the minor behind a TikTok account involved in the investigation and that “the matter is being handled accordingly.”
A minor linked to the “Cat in the Hat” videos targeting Allen County turned themselves in to police Saturday, WKRN reported.
The Allen County-Scottsville task force told the news outlet that the minor faces criminal charges, but avoided harsher penalties. It’s unclear whether this is the same minor that the task force referred to on Facebook.
“The ‘Cat in the Hat’ accounts are part of a viral social media trend that has spread well beyond Allen County.
“Young people have been creating accounts and using AI-generated images and videos to make it appear that the character is coming to their town, school, neighborhood, or even after specific people,” the task force explained in a statement shared by WKRN.
“What may start as an internet trend or prank can quickly cross the line when it causes students to genuinely fear for their safety.”
A 14-year-old student from Grand Junction High School in Colorado was arrested Monday in connection with the viral trend.
Last Friday, local police were made aware of a social media post referencing the “Cat in the Hat” trend on TikTok and suggesting someone may appear at a local middle school and at random houses.
“The posts are intended to cause alarm and fear in individuals,” Grand Junction Police said in a Facebook post.
The 14-year-old was charged with Interference with Staff, Faculty, or Students of Educational Institutions and Harassment and released to his parents.
“GJPD takes reports involving school safety seriously and will continue working closely with our community partners to prioritize the safety and security of our students, staff, and schools,” the Facebook post read.

Xi visits Egypt as China seeks deeper influence across the Mideast
China’s President Xi Jinping visits Egypt this week for the first time in a decade
CAIRO -- On the surface, Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt this week is a run-of-the-mill opportunity for two countries to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties.
But there is deep subtext to the meeting between Xi and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi: China, the United States’ top global rival, is cultivating an extensive relationship with one of America's key allies in the Middle East as it moves to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region.
Xi aims to present China as a stabilizer in the region and contrast it with the United States, which for decades has been militarily entangled there — its six-month war with Iran being just the latest example.
“China continues to build up its soft power reserves while the United States self-sabotages its own stock,” Amr Hamzawy, director of the Washington-based Carnegie Middle East Program, wrote in a paper earlier this year along with Kathryn Selfe, a former fellow at the program.
Xi arrived Tuesday evening at the Cairo airport, which was adorned with Chinese and Egyptian flags. El-Sissi and military guards greeted him on the tarmac with a red-carpet ceremony. The leaders are scheduled to hold talks on Wednesday, and Xi plans to visit the Grand Egyptian Museum, near the pyramids of Giza.
Xi will be in Egypt for three days. It is his first visit there in a decade, and his first trip to the region since visiting Saudi Arabia in 2022. El-Sissi has visited China multiple times in recent years.
The leaders marked 70 years of diplomatic ties by publishing friendly opinion pieces Tuesday in Egypt’s state-run newspapers.
Xi wrote that Beijing and Cairo should “expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration" through development. El-Sissi lauded China's investments in Egypt and reiterated Cairo's support of China's claim that Taiwan is part of its territory.
Egypt views its growing relationship with China as a way to diversify its strategic partnerships.
In 2023, Egypt was invited to join the BRICS bloc of nations, a grouping of major emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa and is seen as a counterbalance to Western-led institutions such as the G7.
A year later, Egypt signed agreements with China to collaborate on its Belt and Road Initiative, a signature policy of Xi’s that seeks to build power and transportation infrastructure around the world.
China has invested more than $10 billion in Egypt, building a business hub east of the capital, Cairo, and an electric rail line for industry in the Nile Delta. Annual trade between the two countries is estimated at $20 billion, according to government figures.
Trade between the U.S. and Egypt was $15.7 billion in 2025. Egypt is a crucial partner in U.S. national security priorities in the region, and the countries' leaders enjoy close ties.
In 2023, Beijing brokered a deal to reestablish diplomatic ties between Iran — its most important regional ally and oil supplier — and Saudi Arabia, a longtime U.S. ally. The agreement showcased China’s aspirations to compete with the United States for influence in the Mideast.
Popular Reads
Since then, ties between Riyadh and Tehran have frayed. Iran attacked Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries as part of its retaliation against the U.S. and Israel, which launched the war on Feb. 28.
China has cast itself as a regional mediator in other ways. It has long advocated a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which is seen by the Arab world as a linchpin to regional stability.
Shortly before Hamas militants attacked Israel in 2023 and launched the war in Gaza, Xi had hosted Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and announced a “strategic partnership” with the Palestinian Authority.
With oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz heavily disrupted by the Iran war, the Suez Canal — which is controlled by Egypt — has become an important alternative path for getting energy supplies out of the region.
“China has good reason to strengthen ties with the country that controls the route still open,” said Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat, a Middle East expert with Jakarta’s Center of Economic and Law Studies.
Xi views Egypt "as a base to reach the wider Arab and African world, at a time when the U.S. has less attention to spare there,” said Rakhmat.
In August, China and Egypt held a multiday air exercise at several bases across Egypt — the first-ever combat exercise for China’s J-16 fighter jets and Egypt’s French-made Rafale fighters.
Xi is visiting Cairo after attending a two-day conference of the 10-nation Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a political and security group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence. The leaders of Russia, India, Pakistan and Iran attended the conference in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek.
The trip also comes on the heels of the Trump administration’s “economic onslaught” on Iran’s financial connections around the world. The sanctions aim to isolate the Islamic Republic from its remaining economic partners, including China, which buys more than 80% of Iranian oil shipments, usually through indirect channels.
Beijing says its trade with Iran has always abided by international law.

Kennedy did not explicitly that hospice patients cost taxpayers too much money because they received treatment for too long. Instead, he was specifically referring to instances of suspected hospice fraud in California.
In late August 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said people in hospice care weren't dying fast enough and were costing taxpayers too much money.
For example, independent journalist Aaron Rupar shared a clip of Kennedy speaking on X and wrote, "RFK Jr complains that people in hospice aren't dying quick enough and therefore cost too much money."
Similar claims about Kennedy's alleged comments on people receiving hospice care also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Though Kennedy did speak about hospice care during an appearance on the Fox News program "Saturday in America" on Aug. 29, summaries such as Rupar's on X did not accurately reflect his words.
Kennedy did not explicitly say that hospice patients cost taxpayers money because they received treatment for too long. Rather, he said hospices in California had fraudulently received federal funds, pointing to billing for patients over multiple years instead of the typical several months as one example.
In August 2026, The Associated Press reported on one incident of fraud where a California hospice billed Medicare for a healthy 71-year-old woman.
In a recording of the "Saturday in America" town hall featuring Kennedy, he said (at 52:52):
We closed down thousands of hospices in California, they didn't have patients, they were just billing us. And the way we found them is because the patients would never die. And so, we could see, we've been paying for this guy for five years — usually, if you go to a hospice, it means you've got three months left to live — these people were never dying, they just had the patient numbers and we were being charged $6,000 a month and just paying, I think 8,000 of them, of these hospices. We're talking about tens of billions of dollars stolen every year.
Given the above, we find claims that Kennedy said hospice patients weren't dying fast enough and costing taxpayers money false. Instead, he was specifically referring to instances of suspected hospice fraud.
We contacted the Department of Health and Human Services to ask when it closed the 8,000 hospices Kennedy mentioned and how much money the department estimated hospice fraudsters had received and await a reply.
Medicare, the U.S. federal health insurance program for people 65 and older, covers hospice care for eligible patients. According to Medicare's website, a patient is eligible if one or more doctors certify they are terminally ill, with a life expectancy of six months or less — not three, as Kennedy said. The insurance program covers hospice care for two initial 90-day periods and successive unlimited 60-day periods.
The Associated Press reported in August 2026 that fraudsters opened fake hospices and tricked real patients into enrolling, or stole people's identities to bill Medicare for hospice services they did not receive.
In May 2026, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced six-month moratoriums on Medicare enrollment for hospices and home health agencies. The centers said they had worked with Vance's anti-fraud task force to suspend federal payments to 800 hospices and home health agencies suspected of fraud in Los Angeles. The suspected fraudulent companies received $1.4 billion in Medicare payments in 2025, according to the news release.
The release noted that hospice fraud was especially prevalent in Arizona, California, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.
California's Department of Justice described hospice fraud as "an epidemic" in the state. The department said it carried out its own investigations into hospice fraud within Medi-Cal, California's state-level health insurance program and that it had secured 51 "hospice related convictions" since 2021.
For further reading, Snopes routinely investigates claims about Medicare.

If you asked ChatGPT for a new phone, a family car or the best way to plan a holiday, you were probably looking for an answer, not an ad. That’s changing fast. Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Ads in India, bringing sponsored messages into conversations on the AI chatbot for the first time in one of its largest markets. It’s the latest to introduce ads into its AI tools after Gemini and Meta, signalling a shift in digital advertising and marketing. Ads will roll out to those using Free and Go tiers, while those on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Education plans will get an ad-free experience. The AI giant claims more than 50 brands are expected to go live during the initial rollout, with WPP and Omnicom as OpenAI’s first agency partners in India. Businesses will be able to access ChatGPT’s self-serve Ads Manager, with daily budgets starting at ₹725. OpenAI’s pitch to advertisers is fairly straightforward if you believe that the world is moving on beyond search engines. The company says ChatGPT is increasingly becoming a place where people don't just look for information, but think through what they want to buy. In India, the company claims more than 100 Mn weekly active users, though how many of these are on the free and Go tiers is unclear. ChatGPT Ads arrive at an interesting moment for the advertising industry. Google and Meta have already begun putting ads into their AI-powered experiences, while other AI companies are still figuring out whether advertising can coexist with the trust users place in conversational assistants. OpenAI now has to answer a harder question: will advertisers actually move money to a chatbot simply because it knows what consumers are thinking about? How ChatGPT Ads Work OpenAI's initial advertising model is deliberately closer to search advertising than traditional display advertising. But it also says that unlike a conventional search query, a conversation can reveal the user's budget, preferences, concerns and trade-offs. “People do not simply enter a few keywords into ChatGPT. They express their goals, constraints, preferences and trade-offs. That produces a much richer expression of intent than a search for ‘best family car,” said Preetham Venkky, chief digital officer, Omnicom Advertising India. Under the hood, OpenAI's ads system uses conversation context to show an ad relevant to what the user is exploring. It considers multiple signals, including the context and intent of users’ current conversation, the ad’s landing page, title, copy, advertiser-provided context hints and targeting selections. In this case, ads will appear at the end of a response by ChatGPT. Ads are labelled as sponsored messages and visually separated from ChatGPT’s response. For its rollout in India, ChatGPT is going for direct relationships with select brands and agencies to begin with. Globally, studies show that ads on AI platforms align with the topic of the query and score high on relevance metrics. A study by SE Rankings showed that only 14% of the times the ads seemed irrelevant to a query on ChatGPT. However, for specific topics such as news and politics, the figure was much higher, up to 50%, which shows that the AI ad engines have a lot of fine-tuning ahead of them. For now, brands who are experimenting with ChatGPT ads can use the company’s SaaS tool to set their own bid strategy, choose a destination URL, add context hints and target users by devices. ChatGPT automatically generates personalised and translated versions of headlines and descriptions, which may run without individual review, if the user opts for this approach. Helping marketing teams generate personalised versions of the campaign at hand is a key facet of this tool. This helps marketers instantly tailor their messaging for the conversational AI world. “Search advertising responds primarily to an explicit query. Social advertising is largely built around audiences, interests and attention. Conversational AI introduces a third signal: the broader context surrounding a decision,” Omnicom’s Venkky added. He cited the example of someone asking ChatGPT for a family car within a particular budget, suitable for city driving and with strong safety ratings as opposed to someone just asking about the best family car. The former is expressing a much more detailed need and the AI’s advantage is the ability to understand this need and add it to the context around the stage of decision-making and intent of the user. Will Ads Worsen The Data Privacy Issues? Now addressing the elephant in the room. AI chatbots have had some notorious data privacy and security issues. While OpenAI says advertisements do not influence the answer generated by the model, one would assume this behaviour will not be inflexible. The company says advertisers do not get access to conversations or personal information of the users. And while ads are selected based on the conversation's context, the content of the user's conversation is not shared with advertisers. OpenAI has also said advertisers will receive aggregate campaign-performance information, such as impressions and clicks, rather than access to individual conversations. But there are still concerns about how far OpenAI will push the ad agenda. A report by Wired showed that close to one in five conversations triggered an ad at the bottom of the output, often tailored to the most recent prompts. That said, the formatting and frequency of these ads may change with OpenAI’s new experiments. The company is also putting guardrails around where ads can appear. Ads will not be eligible alongside sensitive or regulated topics, including mental health and politics. They will also not be shown on accounts belonging to people who identify themselves as under 18 or are predicted to be minors by OpenAI’s systems. Users will also be able to dismiss ads, provide feedback, understand why an ad was shown, manage personalisation and clear the data used for advertising, according to OpenAI. Will Brands Embrace The AI Shift? OpenAI has also moved from experimentation towards a conventional advertising infrastructure. Its initial pilot used CPM, which is cost per thousand impressions, but the company subsequently added cost per click (CPC) bidding, allowing advertisers to pay based on clicks. For CPC campaigns, OpenAI recommends starting with a maximum bid of $3–$5 per click. In India, OpenAI is also preparing a self-serve ad management dashboard for brands and marketers. The minimum daily budget is ₹725, making the platform accessible beyond large agency-led campaigns. The important caveat for Indian marketers is that there is still limited public data on Indian clearing prices, conversion rates and return on ad spend. The market is too new for meaningful India-specific benchmarks. That said, experts believe that these ads are expected to work best for ‘intent’ based buys instead of brands that lean in more towards impulse or awareness-led. OpenAI’s early signals are encouraging, but there is little evidence yet that AI advertising can outperform established channels. The company said its initial US pilot delivered encouraging results, it revealed that ChatGPT Ads has reached $1 Bn in annualised revenue run rate in 200 days of launch. In another forecast report by Axios, OpenAI’s advertising revenue is expected to reach $2.5 Bn in 2026, $11 Bn in 2027 and potentially $100 Bn by 2030. But these are global figures and may not be justifiable in India till we see more data from the company. Perplexity’s experience offers a different picture of how the AI industry sees advertising. After experimenting with ads, the AI search startup shifted towards a more subscription-led model. However, a Perplexity spokesperson told Inc42, “We’re continually experimenting with advertisers that prioritise our users and how they use the internet now.” For ChatGPT, Google is the more consequential benchmark. Google Search advertising revenue rose 14.5% to $81.6 Bn in Q2, while the company has already integrated ads into AI Overviews in India and is testing them in AI Mode in the US. Existing AI Max and Performance Max campaigns can extend into these experiences through Google’s standard auction system. “Search is becoming an even deeper tool for discovery and decision-making through conversational AI. In India, 87% of surveyed users report making more confident decisions using AI Overviews and AI Mode,” a Google spokesperson told us, adding that ads can fuel brand discovery at the moment of intent. Meta is also using AI to automate targeting, creative and campaign optimisation through Advantage+, with Bernstein analysts expecting its ad revenue to surpass Google’s in 2026. Against these entrenched platforms, ChatGPT Ads are expected to remain experimental initially, according to advertising experts. For the first 12–24 months, most advertisers will treat ChatGPT Ads as a complementary channel funded through innovation, experimentation or performance-media budgets. The bigger prize will depend on whether conversational intent delivers better economics. As consumers shift more product research to AI, some budgets could move from Google Search and other lower-funnel media. But stronger conversion rates, lead quality or lower acquisition costs will need to be demonstrated before ChatGPT becomes a core channel. Brands And Industries Most Suited For GPT Ads The brands that will do well here are the ones selling into a decision, not just a purchase. Medium and high-involvement categories are likely to adopt the format first because consumers in these categories typically search, compare and evaluate before making a decision, Omnicom’s Venkky said. The automotive industry, consumer electronics, beauty and personal care, B2B technology and travel are expected to merge as natural early categories. These are categories where someone is actually asking a question and weighing options, not just scrolling. “If you're selling something people research before they buy, a mid-conversation ad sits naturally in that moment,” said Paramdeep Singh, cofounder of Shorthills AI. If it is an impulse or awareness-led brand, this format probably is not for them yet. The whole value of ChatGPT ads comes from intent, and low-intent categories won't get the premium they are paying for, the experts said. Not Everyone Wants An Ads In AI The most interesting counter-position for the ads in AI debate comes from Anthropic. In February, the company explicitly said Claude would remain ad-free. Its argument was not simply about user experience. Anthropic said advertising incentives were incompatible with its vision of Claude as a genuinely helpful assistant. It specifically ruled out sponsored links, third-party product placements and advertiser influence over Claude's responses. Just a year after Perplexity rolled out ads in 2024, it began phasing out ads, and reportedly said that it was not exploring any new ad deals at the moment. It is a noteworthy U-turn for the AI startup, which became one of the first generative AI companies to test ads on its platform in 2024. Similar to Anthropic, trust was the factor cited as the reason behind this decision. Before embracing ads, CEO Sam Altman had once called the combination of AI and advertising “uniquely unsettling” and described ads as a “last resort” business model. Now, OpenAI is betting on the very model that Altman once viewed as a last resort. Whether that becomes a major revenue engine, or remains a way to subsidise free access, will depend on whether advertisers find enough value in ChatGPT’s most valuable asset: user intent. The lack of proper roads and bridges continues to severely disrupt daily life for the Muthuvan tribal community in Edamalakkudy, Keralam’s first tribal panchayat near Munnar.
Transporting critically ill patients on makeshift bamboo stretchers across rugged forest terrain has become an alarming routine.
On Monday (August 31, 2026), a 40-year-old woman suffering from high fever had to be carried over seven kilometres through dense forests to access medical care. The woman, identified as Sumathi from the Parappayarkudy settlement, was eventually admitted to the Munnar General Hospital. This marks the fourth such incident reported in the panchayat in under a month.
‘No other option’
Edamalakkudy panchayat president Binu M. stated that Sumathi developed a severe fever, leaving villagers with no option but to transport her on a bamboo stretcher.
“There is no road between Parappayarkudy and Vellavarakkudy. The residents carried the woman from Parappayarkudy to Keppakkad near Pettimudy—the entry point to the Edamalakkudy panchayat—from where she was shifted by vehicle to the Munnar Tata Hospital. Carrying a patient through more than seven kilometres of dense forest is an arduous task,” Mr. Binu said.
Mr. Binu emphasised that these recurring emergencies reflect the dire conditions in the panchayat.
“Without roads and bridges connecting our tribal hamlets, we cannot resolve this pathetic situation. The community urgently demands proper road connectivity to ensure timely emergency medical care,” he added.
Recent incidents
According to the panchayat president, four patients have had to be carried on bamboo stretchers over the past month alone. On August 22, Rajathi, 33, a resident of the Keezhvalayamparakudy settlement who suffered from severe fever and chest pain, was carried on a bamboo stretcher for over five kilometres—crossing the Manaliyar river—to reach the primary health centre (PHC) at Edamalakkudy.
On August 14, Poomani, 50, from Meenkuthikudy, suffered from high fever for several days; when her condition worsened, villagers carried her on foot to the primary health facility at Societykudy, the panchayat’s base camp.
On August 12, Malayappan, 75, from Koodallarkudy, had to be carried nearly 10 kilometres through dense forest to Mankulam before being transferred to the Adimaly Taluk Hospital.
Similar incidents were reported last year as well. On August 21, 2025, a five-year-old boy, Karthik, developed a severe fever, forcing his family to trek through the forest with him on a stretcher towards Mankulam hospital; the child died during the journey. The next day, his family had to carry his coffin on foot back to their settlement.
In September 2025, Karthik’s grandmother, Rajakanni, also fell ill with high fever and had to be carried to Mankulam on a bamboo stretcher, surviving the trek.

Doctor found dead in Guwahati’s private hospital, suicide suspected: Police
A 41-year-old ICU physician was found dead at a Guwahati hospital, with police suspecting suicide and awaiting a postmortem report.
A 41-year-old physician working at a private hospital in Assam’s Guwahati was found dead in his chamber on Wednesday morning, with police suspecting a case of suicide.
Officer-in-charge of the police station Soroj Doley said the body was sent to Gauhati Medical College and Hospital (GMCH) for postmortem. “He injected high dose of sedative, possibly Propofol, in his veins and this could be reason for death. As per the initial investigations, this looks like a suicide but we are looking at all possible aspects,” Doley told HT on Wednesday.
Police were informed about the doctor’s death around 9:30 am on Wednesday, and a team from Bhangagarh Police Station later recovered the body, an officer said.
Also Read: Assam Police constable dies by suicide at Guwahati quarters, probe on: Police
According to the private hospital authorities, the deceased had been an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) physician for the past six years. He had arrived at the hospital around 8 pm on Tuesday and stayed overnight.
“At around 4am, he told the staff he was going to rest and asked them not to disturb him for a few hours. Around, 8am, the on-duty staff sensed something unusual and called the other doctors,” hospital authorities said.
According to the police, used syringes and vials of Propofol were found in the room where the doctor’s body was recovered, which led to the theory that he had injected the substance.
“The body has been sent for postmortem and once the report comes, they will be able to confirm if Propofol was injected in the doctor’s body,” GMCH principal Babul Kumar Bezbaruah said.
Also Read: CRPF jawan shoots dead 2 colleagues with service rifle in Assam, then kills self
Bezbaruah said that an overdose of Propofol can lead to serious health conditions, including respiratory depression, cardiovascular depression or potential cardiorespiratory arrest. “We don’t know the exact cause of death as of now and it will be clearer only after we get the PM report,” he added.
Police said that the family members of the doctor had been asked to visit GMCH and that the body would be handed over to them after mandatory medical examinations.
The investigating officials said that the doctor was reportedly going through depression for a period following his recent divorce. The family members, however, were not available to confirm this.

A US federal judge has sided with Google, ruling that the company will not have to sell its online advertising exchange (previously known as AdX). The US Department of Justice (DOJ) sought this remedy in the long-running ad tech antitrust trial, which Google lost in 2025. However, the remedies imposed upon Google for that loss are shaping up to be minimal.
In this case, the DOJ and a coalition of states sought to prove that Google leveraged its immense market power in online display ads to reduce the reach of competitors. Government lawyers argued that Google had “rigged” ad auctions to give itself an advantage. While the court agreed that Google illegally locked publishers into using its exchange, it did not agree that Google had broken the law when it came to the tools used by advertisers.
Despite the mixed ruling, the DOJ argued during the remedy phase that forcing Google to sell its ad exchange, which facilitates connections between ad buyers and sellers, was the best way to level the playing field. But that won’t happen. While the ad exchange represents a relatively small part of Google’s revenue, forcing the company to sell may have sent ripple effects through the rest of its ad business. It would also have been a powerful message to Big Tech firms, which have successfully knocked back a recent wave of antitrust cases.
That doesn’t necessarily mean Google gets off scot-free. While divesting the ad exchange would have been the most serious penalty, the government also asked for fines and court-ordered changes to Google’s business practices. It’s likely that the DOJ will get a lot of that, but we don’t know the specifics yet. Judge Leonie Brinkema has sealed the order for 14 days, giving the parties a chance to request redactions. So we’ll know the exact nature of the remedies in two weeks, but Google’s legal team will undoubtedly be celebrating today.

Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say
- Published
Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave at the end of July.
That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.
She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents.
Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.
Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.
Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.
Rojas said many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta".
The Spanish Society of Epidemiology has warned that violence against women "cannot be considered an isolated event".
Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.
The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.
The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".
Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave.
"We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."
The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave.
Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.
In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007.
He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold.
Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.
- Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues 
  - Published3 days ago
Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.
Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe".
He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".
Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.
A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.
Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.
The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.
Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): A wild animal attacked goats tied in a cattle enclosure in Hasli village in Mandsaur district on Wednesday morning, killing six and injuring four others.
Two goats were reportedly carried away by the animal, creating panic among villagers.
Farmer Nain Singh Gurjar discovered the goats lying dead and injured when he reached the enclosure in the morning. He informed the police and forest department about the incident.
Police from the Nai Abadi police station reached the spot and prepared a 'panchnama'. A forest department team also inspected the site and searched for signs of the animal, but no clear footprints were found.
Forest ranger Narendra Malviya said the attack appeared to have been carried out by a large wild animal.
According to the department, hyenas have reportedly been spotted in the area, while the presence of a leopard has not been confirmed.
Officials said a leopard generally eats its prey at the attack site, whereas a hyena may carry prey away. The fact that two goats were taken away has led officials to suspect a hyena attack, possibly involving two or three animals. The forest department has increased surveillance in the area.

How catastrophic flash flood unfolded at remote Nepal-China border point
- Published
The video lasts only seconds.
A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time.
What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.
Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August.
Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated.
"This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist.
The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.
On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.
Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.
Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.
The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.
Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.
Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.
Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day.
But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.
The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.
The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.
When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area.
"Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC.
Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration.
Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.
That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.
At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.
China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.
People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.
And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.
It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day.
"My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said.
Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.
The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.
For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.
Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done.
Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.
Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.
When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Reuters: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."
The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.
Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.
Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.
Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.
Posh Kumar Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.
Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.
Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports.
The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network.
"Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says.
"We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."
Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.
The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck.
"But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

Tiger Woods to change plea after crash arrest
- Published
Tiger Woods is to change his plea in court five months after he was arrested on a charge of driving under the influence in a rollover crash in Florida.
Court records show the change of plea hearing is set for Wednesday morning in Martin County, Florida. The golfer was arrested after the March crash, and had passed a breathalyser test but declined further testing for other drugs.
He pleaded not guilty the same month to misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence and refusal to submit to testing. Woods, 50, said he was seeking treatment after the incident.
It was not immediately clear what the change of plea would be. The BBC has contacted prosecutors and Woods' attorney.
No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.
Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.
In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom".
He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.
Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning.
He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.
Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".
Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.
Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today.
"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."
The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

The Guard That Won’t Be Changing
Massachusetts Democrats chose progressivism over relative youth.
Many Democrats of a certain age took the same message from the party’s 2024 debacle: Voters are sick of the old guard and craving younger, more aggressive leaders. Better to retire on your own terms than suffer the fate of Joe Biden, forced to stand down from his reelection campaign after a public humiliation. Nancy Pelosi, the 86-year-old former speaker, announced her exit from the House, as did her longtime lieutenant, 87-year-old Steny Hoyer. Senators Dick Durbin (81) and Jeanne Shaheen (79) passed up reelection bids this year, and so, too, did two senators merely in their late 60s.
Senator Ed Markey, 80, heeded no such warning, and evidently, he didn’t need to. The Massachusetts Democrat is one of just two current senators whose tenures in Congress date to the presidency of Gerald Ford. But tonight, the oldest Democratic senator on the ballot this year trounced his much younger primary opponent, Representative Seth Moulton. The AP called the race a half hour after polls closed, with Markey leading by nearly 50 points.
In a race that pitted ideology against age, Massachusetts Democrats opted for a progressive stalwart who will be 86 at the end of another six-year term over a more moderate 47-year-old challenger. Moulton, an Iraq War veteran who is concluding his sixth term in the House, moved left to appeal to a statewide primary electorate. But he could not hope to outflank Markey, who won support from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Instead, Moulton urged voters to embrace “a new generation of leadership” and argued that he could more effectively fight for liberal causes than an incumbent in the twilight of his career.
Markey had already faced that kind of challenge before, and won. Six years ago, he handily defeated then-Representative Joe Kennedy III, a grandson of Robert F. Kennedy who contended that the incumbent, after so many decades in office, was no longer up to the task. Young progressives, unimpressed with what remained of the Kennedy aura and appreciative of Markey’s record championing the Green New Deal, rallied to Markey’s side. But that race preceded Biden’s flameout in 2024 and the reckoning over the Democratic Party’s gerontocracy.
Some Massachusetts Democrats believed that Markey could be newly vulnerable, especially if a popular progressive such as Representative Ayanna Pressley, who is 52, decided to challenge him. Mary Anne Marsh, a longtime Democratic strategist in the state, told me that after seeing the reception Pressley received at a party convention last year, she became convinced that “if Ayanna runs, she wins.” But Pressley opted to run for reelection to the House, leaving Moulton to challenge Markey.
Moulton has never lacked ambition—he led a failed bid to oust Pelosi as party leader in 2018 and waged a short-lived presidential campaign the following year—but he’s neither as progressive as Pressley nor as well liked. He built a reputation as a moderate in the House Democratic caucus, and after President Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024, Moulton angered many on the left by accusing his party of being “afraid” to say that transgender athletes should not play women’s sports. He has since offered a partial apology to the transgender community, but the line became fodder for Markey, who said that he’d thrown “trans kids under the bus.” The issue was emblematic of Moulton’s struggle to convince progressives in Massachusetts that he shared their values. “He’s tried to become a progressive, but he does it by defining progressive in a way that nobody believes,” Marsh said. “He tried to become something that he’s not.”
The Massachusetts race was a rare Democratic primary this year in which U.S. policy toward Israel did not become a flash point, as both candidates criticized Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and opposed new military aid to Israel. (Moulton announced last year that he would return donations from AIPAC.)
Both public polling and Markey’s internal surveys showed a closer race until earlier this summer, when the incumbent began to pull away. A Markey adviser told me that voters had not really tuned in to the campaign yet, and media attention was focused on higher-profile Democratic primaries elsewhere. Markey’s age also did not become a big factor, perhaps because the years since 2020 have been kinder to him than they were to Biden. His support reflected a frequently overlooked nuance in the debate over whether the party needs new leadership: Older progressive leaders, particularly the 84-year-old Sanders, remain popular. “There’s a difference between being old and being part of the old guard,” the Markey adviser, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said. “Younger voters love Ed Markey, younger voters love Bernie Sanders, younger voters love Elizabeth Warren, and I think that has a lot to do with the fact that they take younger voters seriously.”
Moulton tried to align Markey with a Democratic establishment that he said has failed to deliver progressive wins. He frequently invoked the name of Senator Chuck Schumer, vowing to oppose the New Yorker if he seeks to remain the Democratic leader. And Moulton even accused Markey of having ties to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, an attack that, according to Marsh, backfired so badly that it might have sealed Moulton’s defeat. (Markey denied any affiliation with Epstein.)
In the end, Massachusetts Democrats preferred Markey’s progressivism over Moulton’s relative youth. Markey might have been helped by the fact that the stakes in this primary were not as high as they were elsewhere this year—and certainly much lower than when the party pushed Biden to withdraw in 2024. Massachusetts is not in danger of going Republican in November. Democratic voters wanted a trusted fighter to wage battle against Trump for the next two years and—they hope—for transformative progressive policies in the four years after that. They didn’t seem to care much that the fighter they chose happens to be 80 years old.

Are all TVs at risk from burn-in? Here's how to avoid the problem altogether
OLED screens run the biggest risk, but with a little common sense you can mitigate the issue.
If you're shopping for a new TV or monitor, you may have heard that OLED offers some of the best picture quality available today. While OLED TVs often cost a premium compared to budget and even mid-range LCDs, you get excellent contrast, vivid colors and deep blacks in return. However, there can be one major caveat to the display technology: the possibility of permanent image retention or burn-in.
While the term burn-in may sound alarming, especially if you're on the verge of spending hundreds or thousands of dollars, it's not something you need to worry about immediately. And even though it's inevitable, burn-in remains unnoticeable in many cases and takes years to appear even if it does. Better yet, you can take some simple precautions to significantly reduce the risk and extend the lifespan of an OLED display to keep burn-in at bay until it's time to upgrade.
So, what exactly is burn-in, what causes it on modern TVs and how can you minimize the risk? Here's a quick rundown.
What is burn-in and what causes it?
An OLED display is made up of millions of tiny organic light-emitting diodes — hence the name OLED. This is unlike an LCD, which relies on a backlight to illuminate its pixels. This means that each pixel in an OLED generates its own light and can be dimmed or turned off independently. But while this granular control provides excellent contrast and deep blacks, it also means that individual pixels can wear out independently of each other.
Each time you use an OLED display, these individual pixels undergo some infinitesimal amount of degradation. In the real-world, this wear translates to a dimmer light output. To further complicate matters, each pixel is actually made up of several smaller sub-pixels that produce different colors, typically red, green and blue. These sub-pixels don't necessarily age at the same rate, either.
Practically speaking, the OLED display is continuously varying the brightness of each pixel and sub-pixel to reproduce the colors you see on the screen. Over time, though, this can cause some pixels can experience more wear than others and become dimmer. Eventually, the difference in brightness can become noticeable enough to our eyes.
Put simply, burn-in occurs when some pixels appear brighter than those that have experienced greater wear, creating a persistent outline or ghosting of previously displayed content.
Static elements like channel logos have a higher potential to cause OLED burn-in, since the sub-pixels in that region wear out unevenly. This is why OLED displays aren't the best choice if you exclusively watch news or sports channels for several hours each day. Playing the same game for hundreds of hours can also have the same effect, as on-screen text and other fixed elements can accelerate burn-in in certain localized spots.
Is burn-in still a risk for modern OLED TVs?
If you end up buying an OLED TV, you can still take several steps to prevent rapid burn-in. Besides turning off the display when you're not actively watching content, one of the most consequential accelerators for burn-in is brightness. High brightness levels place greater strain on the LEDs that make up the display, which can cause premature wear. The organic material used in an OLED panel also degrades faster when exposed to heat, with higher brightness levels exacerbating this effect. This is one reason OLED manufacturers have historically been more conservative with sustained brightness, although newer generations have pushed the envelope in this area.
Still, running an OLED display at maximum brightness for extended periods of time can result in noticeable burn-in. The solution is simple: head into the TV or monitor's settings menu and lower the brightness setting. This will lengthen the lifespan of each pixel, which should keep burn-in at bay for a long time.
Having said that, I wouldn't worry about image retention if you only use your OLED display for a few hours each day, especially if it's mostly to watch varied content with no static elements like channel logos. Modern OLED displays have plenty of burn-in mitigation features, ranging from pixel shifting and refreshing to automatic dimming in bright scenes. I've owned the same OLED TV for five years and haven't noticed any burn-in even though I frequently watch HDR or high-brightness content.
Do LCD TVs suffer from burn-in?
If you'd like to avoid the risk of permanent burn-in altogether, a modern LCD TV can be a great alternative to OLED. Since LCD panels don't use self-emissive pixels, they don't suffer from OLED-style burn-in caused by uneven pixel degradation. While LCD backlights can and do sometimes fail with age, you can watch content with static elements like news channels without worrying about wearing out specific areas of the display.
Having said that, LCD panels can also exhibit temporary image retention after displaying static content for long periods of time. This is less of a concern for LCD than OLED, as the image retention typically recedes on its own as you switch over to more varied content.
Modern LCD TVs with Mini LED backlighting technology can offer excellent black levels and contrast, although they cannot match OLED's perfect pixel-level control. High-end models can also get significantly brighter than OLED since they don't rely on organic light-emitting material. This makes high-end LCD TVs a perfect choice for bright, sun-filled rooms or if you don't want to think about the risk of image retention at all.

The Women Obsessed With Lindsay Clancy
Horrific crimes have always attracted attention, but the women who have filled the courtroom are seeking something beyond spectacle.
Updated at 7:35 p.m. ET on August 31, 2026
On one of the final days of the trial, dozens of women streamed into the back of a Plymouth, Massachusetts, courtroom, filling two long rows of wooden benches. They stood and watched the judge and jury take their seats. Then they strained for a view as a nurse wheeled in the defendant, Lindsay Clancy, who has admitted to strangling her three young children to death in her suburban Boston home in January 2023, before swallowing prescription pills, slashing her wrists and neck, and throwing herself out of a bedroom window headfirst.
Seeing her there in a wheelchair, one woman crossed herself and whispered, “Please, God.” As an officer gaveled the court into session, others pulled out notebooks, folders, and scraps of paper. “WHY,” Marta Quijano wrote as a prosecutor called a psychiatrist to the stand. “Motivation,” she added, starring the word as the doctor began explaining his opinion that Clancy was not in the throes of psychosis on the night of the killings, as her defense has argued, but deeply suicidal and still capable of knowing right from wrong. In the back row, a woman who had flown in from Cleveland shook her head. She had a true-crime novel in her lap and turned to a blank page at the end. “Stupid experts,” she wrote.
Americans have long been obsessed with murder trials, especially those involving the primal nightmare of mothers who kill their children. The public loves to watch mothers on trial and partake in their judgment. There was Susan Smith, who had drowned her three children in a South Carolina lake and was found guilty of murder in 1995, despite having a history of trauma and sexual abuse. And there was Andrea Yates, who had drowned her five children in a bathtub and was convicted of capital murder in 2002 and then retried in 2006, when she was found not guilty by reason of insanity after witnesses testified that Yates had experienced severe postpartum psychosis and schizophrenia.
The Clancy trial is now part of this sadistic American tradition, but it has also become something else for the women who have been showing up in person. It was not enough for them to watch the proceedings on television, or listen to some lawyer on YouTube, or even stand outside the courthouse wearing pink and waving signs in support of Clancy, as hundreds of women did one day earlier this month. They did not want to be outside rendering judgment; they wanted to be inside, on the third floor, sitting on the wooden benches, as close as possible, in case they could notice some detail, some gesture, some pause or expression or word that might reveal a truth they could recognize from their own experience. Each was there for their own reasons.
A jury of nine women and three men will decide in the coming days whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor-and-delivery nurse, is criminally responsible for killing her children or not guilty by reason of insanity. The two prosecutors have argued that the killings were the premeditated decision of an entitled and controlling woman who had been frustrated that she could not master her worsening depression and sought a way out of a life that she no longer wanted. Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has cast her as a loving mother failed by a fragmented mental-health system even as she repeatedly sought help for intensifying depression, anxiety, and insomnia after giving birth to her third child.
Clancy saw her psychiatrist 14 times, tried 13 different medications, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room, tried to enroll in an inpatient program, and confided to her husband that she’d had thoughts of harming her children. Defense experts testified that doctors had missed an underlying bipolar disorder and prescribed pills that made Clancy’s symptoms worse, starting a downward spiral that culminated in a rare condition called postpartum psychosis that can cause hallucinations. Clancy has said that she heard a male voice telling her to kill her children, Cora, Dawson, and Callan, on January 24, 2023.
After being resuscitated following her suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed from the waist down, Clancy was handcuffed, placed under armed guard, and arraigned from her hospital bed. A judge allowed the moment to be livestreamed from the courtroom; a video screen showed her unblinking eyes above a white surgical mask. The trial itself has also been livestreamed, fueling conspiracy theories that have tended to blame the killings on Clancy’s husband or an intruder, attempting to find clarity where there is little, as many women at the trial already understood. At first, only a few showed up. By last Monday, they were waiting in an hour-long line to get into the courthouse, and another that stretched down a bright hallway to the courtroom doors.
“I can’t imagine what’s going through her head,” one woman was saying to her friend.
“It’s not just cold-blooded murder,” the friend said.
“I had suicidal thoughts, clear as a bell,” a retired teacher named Dottie Kiley told another woman in line, explaining her experience with antidepressants. “So bad I called the police and told them, and they had a cop come down and sit with me. It was a small town, and they had time to do that.”
The woman behind her nodded. “She could be any one of us,” she said as the courtroom doors opened.
Inside, the women listened to Avram Mack, a psychiatrist and prosecution witness, explain his clinical opinion that Clancy, having made up her mind to kill herself, then made the decision to kill her children to prevent their suffering a life without her—a theory called “altruistic filicide.” Quijano leaned over to the woman sitting next to her.
“What is the validity of this three years later?” she whispered, shaking her head.
After the morning break, she stood in line again for the afternoon session.
“With my first daughter, because it was so difficult breastfeeding, I had insomnia and anxiety—I was worried the baby is hungry,” Quijano told a woman she had just met. “I remember one time—she was a cranky baby—and I remember not so much shaking her but going like this,” she said, demonstrating how she squeezed her daughter’s shoulders and screamed. “They are called intrusive thoughts because your brain says something, and you don’t recognize it.”
Ashlyn Rizzo, who’d been attending the trial for two weeks straight, nodded.
“I had been planning to run away,” Rizzo said, referring to a moment after her first child was born. “I liquidated all my 401(k) and squirreled the money away. I was going to go without the baby. I figured everyone was better off without me. I had delusions. I couldn’t tell wake from sleep. I didn’t confide to anyone. I wrote a note.”
“My cousin had a plan,” Quijano said, not needing to finish.
“I was just going to start driving,” Rizzo continued. “Stay in hotels.”
As it happened, Rizzo said, she had called her psychiatrist, who that very day got her into the same specialized program in Rhode Island that had rejected Clancy one month before she killed her children. “Saved my life,” Rizzo said.
On Tuesday, the line was longer.
“I wonder, what does justice look like in this case?” a retired teacher named Lisa was saying. She had been keeping the livestream of the trial on in the background of her daily life all month, until she decided to come to see it for herself. She had driven up from Virginia.
“My daughter had a moment,” Lisa, who didn’t give her last name, told the woman standing behind her, referring to postpartum depression. “I’ve been there, trying to get psychiatric appointments.”
“I had a miscarriage in the second trimester and drifted into depression,” Sheila Sullivan replied, explaining that she’d wound up committed to a psychiatric facility in the 1970s. “They gave me shock treatment. Back then, they didn’t know.”
“I’m sorry,” Lisa said, hugging her.
“Thank you,” Sullivan said.
“They don’t do any research on how hormones affect mental health,” Lisa said.
“She didn’t have any symptoms until they put her on the drugs,” Sullivan said.
“It’s all interconnected,” Lisa said as the courtroom doors opened and the women filled the back benches.
“Can you tell us what peritraumatic disassociation is?” a prosecutor asked an FBI forensic psychiatrist, Gregory Saathoff.
“It’s when you feel things are unreal, not you—like you’re watching yourself,” Saathoff began.
A woman wrote down, “Witness staring at jury,” and whispered, “I think that’s weird.”
Sullivan took out her notebook.
“Moral judgement??” she wrote.
She listened as Reddington, the defense attorney, questioned Saathoff, going through his 75-page résumé and pointing out that he had treated only two women with postpartum depression, and that that had been decades ago. Reddington went over the times that Clancy had described feeling “like a zombie” and had been in a “disassociated state,” and asked why health-care providers had not asked more questions when Clancy indicated that she was suicidal.
“She was trying hard to get help,” the doctor acknowledged.
“I can relate to all of this,” Jodi Fournier said as she stood in line later that afternoon. “Not at the extreme, but I can understand.”
For several days, she had been driving to court with two friends from a town 30 minutes away.
“The other thing is, when you work in health care, you learn not to trust the doctors,” her friend Susan Hatfield said. “She was questioning her doctors. She didn’t trust them, and neither did I.”
“See that woman over there?” Fournier said, noticing a blond woman standing by herself and praying at a window outside the courtroom.
“She’s does it every day,” Hatfield said.
Sullivan joined the line behind them.
“I had a miscarriage, then depression, then thoughts of suicide,” she began, retelling her story, and soon they went inside.
Every day, the court officer gaveled in the session, a call to order that ended with the phrase “You will be heard.” Every day, a nurse wheeled in Lindsay Clancy.
“That’s her,” Fournier whispered.
On Tuesday afternoon, Reddington continued questioning Saathoff. “Do you remember Linsday talking about how she can’t feel love? She can’t feel fear?” Then he quoted from Clancy’s journal: “It takes all the effort in the world just to breathe,” she had written, as well as “I want help” and “I want to be well.”
In the back benches, the women leaned forward so they could hear. They pulled out notebooks.
“WTF,” one woman wrote as Reddington went over Clancy’s medication list.
“I am afraid,” another woman wrote down on Wednesday, quoting something Clancy had said.
Rebecca Olszewski, a pharmacist and mother of three, had flown in from Cleveland to attend the trial. She told me that she was recovering from anorexia, bulimia, and generalized anxiety disorder, all of which she said she had learned to mask, as Clancy had apparently done at times. Prosecutors submitted into evidence photos of her smiling with her kids. “There would be outings, and my mom would be like, ‘You seem in good spirits,’” Olszewski said. “And I’d say, ‘Mom, I’m just here going through motions.’”
She wrote down a list of questions: Why hadn’t the people who’d answered the suicide hotline asked Clancy more questions about her suicidal thoughts—not simply whether she had a plan at that moment, but whether she’d ever had a plan? Why hadn’t doctors placed her in an inpatient program? Why hadn’t they paid closer attention?
Now Olszewski sat on the wooden bench, studying the jury to see whether they were paying attention. Then she watched the judge, noticing how he looked at Clancy and the witnesses.
On Thursday, the day of closing arguments, the line was longer than it had been all week. Not everyone could get into the main courtroom, so another one was made available, and women filled more wooden benches, including Joni Villemez-Comeaux, a mental-health counselor there from Texas.
“This is shining a very poor light on our field, and it needs to,” she was saying, and now several women began asking her about how she would have handled Clancy—which sorts of details mattered, and which didn’t. “Every fucking thing matters,” Villemez-Comeaux said, and soon the courtroom was quiet.
In closing, Reddington once again went over all the ways that Clancy had sought help. The medications. The psychiatrist visits. The journal in which she’d chronicled her worsening symptoms until her handwriting had turned into what he described as “chicken scratch.”
“My God, what does she have to do?” Reddington said, and when he finished, women clapped and cheered, and then listened as the prosecutor for the Commonwealth, Jennifer Sprague, delivered her closing argument.
“This case is not about the mental-health system,” she began.
On the wooden benches, a woman quietly said to herself, “Yes, it is.”
After that, Sprague continued for nearly an hour. She talked about how depressed and suicidal Clancy had been but emphasized how much support she’d had. Her parents, a nanny, health insurance. “She had more access to care and treatment and support than most people do.” She once again painted Clancy as an entitled woman who’d known that what she was doing was wrong, who’d decided to strangle her children anyway, leaving them “discarded on the basement floor like broken toys because she was done playing the game.”
By the time she spoke those words, though, many of the women who’d stood in line and listened to days of testimony had already left the courtroom. They had heard enough.
