For the first time in more than 30 years, NASA has no firm plans to send any new landers or rovers to Mars. Instead, the agency’s near-term focus at the red planet is on aerial drones, a pioneering mode of exploration that didn’t seem realistic until a few years ago.
The first real use of drones for science at Mars will come with the SkyFall mission, a fleet of three helicopters set for launch as soon as late 2028. SkyFall’s helicopters will ride to the red planet with NASA’s Space Reactor-1 “Freedom” mission, which has the primary objective of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space.
The launch schedule is aggressive for SR-1 Freedom and SkyFall, projects that didn’t even exist in NASA’s portfolio six months ago. NASA’s plan for the SR-1 Freedom mission, estimated to cost $2.1 billion, calls for repurposing the core module of the canceled Gateway lunar space station into a testbed for nuclear electric propulsion. SkyFall will build on NASA’s success with the Ingenuity helicopter, an experimental vehicle that became the first rotorcraft to fly on another world in 2021.
NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory is partnering with AeroVironment, a developer of high-altitude drones, to design and build the three SkyFall helicopters, plus one spare. The same team was behind the Ingenuity helicopter that landed on Mars with NASA’s Perseverance rover five years ago.
Development underway
AeroVironment announced last week that it received a contract from JPL to “co-design and co-manufacture” the three SkyFall helicopters. Ingenuity flew 72 times before a crash landing in early 2024, far exceeding the mission’s original plan of five test flights. Engineers are building on the Ingenuity design for the SkyFall helicopters. The new vehicles will be somewhat larger than Ingenuity—about 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) instead of 1.8 kilograms (4 pounds)—with upgraded rotors to handle a heavier payload.
SkyFall will show that “Mars helicopters can be built as a repeatable product line, not a one‑off delivery,” said Jeff Rodrian, head of AeroVironment’s MacCready Works division, the company’s advanced research and development organization.
AeroVironment is responsible for the helicopters’ rotor systems, airframes, structures, avionics integration, and accommodation for science payloads, the company said in a press release. JPL will develop the power system, electronics, algorithms, and software, along with a ground-penetrating radar to search for shallow subsurface ice below the Martian surface. Each helicopter will also carry a suite of cameras and sensors to gather data on the Martian atmosphere.
This is an upgrade over Ingenuity, which carried two cameras but lacked any sophisticated scientific instruments. Ingenuity’s range was limited by a requirement to communicate through a base station on the Perseverance rover, while SkyFall will be capable of transmitting and receiving data through communications relay orbiters flying overhead.

The doors to Europe’s largest consumer tech show haven’t opened to the public yet, but there’s already plenty of news coming out of IFA 2026 in Berlin, Germany. If you’re already struggling to keep up with what has been announced, here are some of the best new gadgets and upgrades from the show — including more competition for Apple’s MacBook Neo, an excellent portable controller for gaming-on-the-go, and a concept handheld designed to balance work and play.
The best tech and gadgets announced at IFA so far
A gaming handheld you can use for work, a robovac that seals itself to floors, and more laptops you can repair yourself.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
To catch up on everything announced at IFA 2026 you can follow The Verge’s complete coverage right here.
Flipping the gaming laptop script, Acer’s latest concept is a Windows-based gaming handheld, similar to its Predator Atlas 8, that can transform into a tiny portable PC thanks to a swiveling design that repositions its screen atop a mini keyboard. The DualPlay Mini’s display is just 8-inches in size, which could make productivity a challenge if work involves sprawling spreadsheets, but the concept could be used for answering emails during a daily commute and then connected to a larger display at work for more demanding tasks.
The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or light as its recently launched XPS 13, but the company is looking to make this model even more accessible for students or others on a tighter budget. The laptop starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and those specs can be bumped to 16GB/1TB. It features a 1080P webcam with face unlock support, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and like Apple’s MacBook Neo, will be available in four bright color options: linen, dusty rose, washed denim, and velvet green.
The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is iRobot’s latest flagship floor cleaner and introduces a new feature the company calls “SealForce.” When it detects it’s cleaning carpeting, the robovac lowers a skirt around the cleaning head to create a better seal that increases suction for a deeper clean. The Max 875 also offers up to 35,000 Pa of suction power, mopping capabilities, lidar and camera-based autonomous navigation, and the ability to climb over obstacles and thresholds up to 3.5cm tall.
Released under Jsaux’s new Voidjoy brand, the $49.99 SkyLark S1 Pro is a compact portable controller that appears to do a lot of things right. It’s got drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks that are recessed so they won’t get snagged on other devices in your bag, a pair of analog triggers ideal for racing games, and three different ways to connect to devices and consoles: Bluetooth, USB-C, and 2.4GHz. If you opt for a 2.4GHz connection, you can also pair two S1 Pros to a single transmitter and swap back-and-forth between what character you’re controlling in a multiplayer game, making it useful for parents playing with a kid who may struggle with some challenges.
Is Framework’s approach to easily repairable and upgradeable laptops finally rubbing off on other companies? Acer’s 16-inch Vero 16 offers tool-free access to several internal components including its user-replaceable SSD and battery. The company says the laptop’s processor can also be upgraded down the line, but that will require it to be sent in to an Acer service center. Pricing is still unknown, but the Vero 16 is expected to launch early next year outside North America.
If you’re lucky enough to have an original Nintendo Switch Pro controller that hasn’t succumbed to joystick drift and want to expand its capabilities, Jsaux’s new Elite Extender is an easy aftermarket upgrade. For $39.99 it attaches to the back of the controller and adds four mappable buttons that can be programmed to reproduce multiple button presses. It’s got its own rechargeable battery, but does hinder Amiibo functionality while it’s piggybacking.

Chinese research team may have cracked secret to crossbreeding Asian and African rice
Scientists identified three genes that make it hard to combine the two varieties – and also highlighted a possible solution
While both Asian and African cultivated rice varieties have distinct strengths, crossing them often produces offspring with sterile pollen and low yields.
A research team has now identified three genes that act as a barrier to reproduction – and also a possible way round the problem.
“This discovery provides an important theoretical foundation and valuable genetic resources for breaking the reproductive barrier between rice species and breeding new, ultra-high-yielding hybrid rice varieties,” the official China Science Daily reported last Friday.
Such Asian-African crosses “could potentially increase yields by more than 10 per cent compared with existing Asian hybrid rice varieties”, one of the authors of the study told the newspaper.
The research, conducted by a team led by Wan Jianmin at Nanjing Agricultural University’s State Key Laboratory for Crop Genetics and Germplasm Enhancement and Utilisation, was published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on 28 August.
African and Asian rice are the only two species out of the 24 in the Oryza genus that have been domesticated to produce food for humans.
Asian rice offers high yields and excellent eating quality, making it a global staple.

A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border.
On Monday night Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor.
However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base.
Its subjects are not members of Canada’s front-line military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18.
The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense.
Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to deescalate trade tensions.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said.
David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said.

Authorities in the Thai resort city of Pattaya have stepped up security as they prepare to welcome thousands of sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln who have spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea.
“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP.
The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran.
It left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, have made headlines in the US and provoked criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the carrier would dock just after midnight on Wednesday (about 5pm GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. About 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups before the carrier departs on Sunday.
After meeting US officials on Monday, Poramase said service members would be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and cannabis use. Medical cannabis was legalised in Thailand in 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities.
Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam war in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation.
The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied this was linked to the US arrivals.
Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge US sailors, and Poramase said there would be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya beach and Walking Street.
The city’s police chief, Anek Srathongyoo, said law enforcements agencies had been ordered to step up security measures to prevent undesirable situations. He said that if any US service members broke Thai law, they would be prosecuted accordingly.
Local business owners feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war are eager for the new arrivals. A banner hung over a local bar near a beach read: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”
Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee, said she had seen US service members during past visits but she did not expect many from this crew. “They said 5,000 people will come here but how many will reach us?” she said.
Earlier in August, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East. The Lincoln, one of the US navy’s largest warships, was part of American efforts in the Iran war, which flared back up over the weekend for the first time in a month.
The deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 270 days. Trump downplayed concerns over conditions onboard and said the deployment was “not nearly long enough”.
Thai officials have said the Lincoln will return to the US after its port call in Thailand.
Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reporting

Paul Pogba, 33 (Last club: Monaco)
Former Manchester United midfielder Pogba has played very little football since his 18 month doping ban ended in March 2025. The Frenchman made just six appearances for Monaco after joining them last summer and, after a series of injuries, the French club terminated his contract last month - one year before it was due to end.

French striker Benzema has been plying his trade in Saudi Arabia since leaving Real Madrid in 2023, spending three years with Al Ittihad. ‘Stop trying to be tough’: Carney fires back at Trump as US-Canada trade fight escalates
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Trump administration needs to “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough.”
TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the Trump administration Tuesday to “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough,” as he pushed back against a fresh wave of attacks from Washington.
Carney said U.S.-Canada trade talks could resume if Washington became serious about negotiations, but he also accused the United States of pursuing terms that he said could leave Canadian industries “gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out.”
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney said. “It’s not constructive, but that’s their democracy.”
His comments came after a new barrage from Washington since trade talks collapsed Aug. 21, including Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” and social media posts taunting Canada. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Canada could not go “tit for tat” with a U.S. economy 13 times larger, while U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth mocked female Canadian cadets online.
Hegseth on Monday posted an image from a cadet training center in British Columbia showing two young women in uniform, adding “this is real” alongside a Canadian flag. Carney called the post “beneath their office.”
The Pentagon stood by it Tuesday, with deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss saying, “The X post speaks for itself.”
Carney said the U.S. approach in the talks would have left Canadian industries effectively as subsidiaries of American companies or imposed terms under which they would be “gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out.”
“We’re not going to — of course, we’re not going to accept those terms,” Carney said.
Carney said Washington sought an “uncompetitive” deal for key industries, including autos, while pushing changes affecting French-language and cultural protections. He said any of those issues was enough to block an agreement.
Carney said Washington also sought limits on Canada’s future trade deals. “Canada is a sovereign state. We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals,” he said.
Carney was also buoyed by Monday's Liberal sweep of three special elections, including a decisive win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Quebec, where the Conservatives fell to third place.
The victories brought the Liberals to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons and reinforced Carney’s position as he confronts Trump over trade and Canadian sovereignty.
Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Toronto, said Trump’s annexation threats carry particular weight in Quebec. “Quebecers have the most to lose in an apocalyptic scenario where the U.S. absorbs Canada, and the status of the French language disappears,” he said.
U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed after the two sides failed to reach a deal, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods. Canada responded with plans for tariffs on U.S. products.
Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st state.

The Backlash Against Polyester Has Gone Too Far
Clothing made from natural fibers isn’t always better.
Lately, the men of the internet who are obsessed with self-optimization have found a new fixation: their underwear. Many standard pairs use polyester or spandex, or sometimes both. What are they doing to the environment and their bodies, wearing clothes that shed all of those microplastics and leach forever chemicals? They want the underwear of their ancestors—underwear made from natural fibers. On Reddit forums such as r/PlasticFreeLiving and r/SustainableFashion, people trade strategies for breaking up with polyester boxer briefs: “Any recs or leads to find linen cloth for making my own underwear?” one exasperated user wondered. Another wanted recommendations for all-natural underwear that would also be formfitting. He knew about organic cotton and hemp, he explained, but the problem was, they chafed.
Seemingly everyone is interested in natural fibers. Whitney Crutchfield, who teaches textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology, told me that she first noticed natural-fiber mania brewing among her sustainability-minded students. Then, a year or two ago, she sensed the discourse shifting to regular consumers. Across the internet, people are purging their closets of synthetics, swearing allegiance to only natural fibers from now on. The enthusiasm seems to cut across gender, culture, and politics. “I need my workout clothes to show my nasty sweat!” the fashion journalist Liana Satenstein wrote last year, praising the emergence of a new generation of natural-fiber workout wear amid posts about French pedicures and vintage Prada thongs. “Make all clothes natural fibers again,” posted Carnivore Aurelius, an anonymous wellness influencer who sells “beef collagen peptides.”
Natural fibers are indeed pretty great. Silk, wool, hemp, linen, cotton, and the like—all of which come directly from either plants or animals—don’t carry the baggage of their artificial competitors. They don’t shed microplastics. They’re generally understood to be biodegradable. And although the research is far from settled, synthetics have been linked to adverse hormonal effects. When I visited the website for a natural-underwear brand, a pop-up asked me what I looked for in my underwear: “Fertility health” and “supporting low T” were among the options.
Natural fibers have also become an easy way to gauge the quality of a garment. Cotton, wool, and linen generally cost more than polyester and acrylic do, and they can look and feel luxurious in a way that many synthetics don’t. The reason finding a decent sweater these days is so hard is that so many of them are blended with synthetics, and one major reason for all of that blending is reduced production costs. Earlier this summer, when Gap released a reimagined version of a classic sweater from the early 2000s, fans revolted. What had originally been a chunky, cotton-blend knit turtleneck was now an entirely synthetic printed mesh. The anti-synthetic zeitgeist has transcended clothing; it is an attitude. Gen Z apparently now uses polyester as an insult meaning “cheap” and “inauthentic.”
But the frenzy has gone too far. Are you really sure it’s always better to buy cotton or wool over a nylon blend? The whole point of man-made fibers is that they can have properties that specifically don’t exist in nature. “There are reasons that these things were produced in the first place,” Crutchfield said. When DuPont unveiled nylon—the world’s first synthetic fiber—to the public at the 1939 World’s Fair, it was a revelation. In the dawning era of synthetics, people would no longer be beholden to the limits of nature; instead, we had chemistry, which was going to free women from the drudgery of endless laundering and usher in an age of universal luxury. This did not, perhaps, play out exactly as one might have hoped, but even today, synthetic fabrics have plenty of benefits.
Synthetics can enhance the performance of a garment, or the feel, or the durability, all of which contribute to a garment’s lifespan. The better it serves its intended purpose, the less likely you are to replace it with something new. A beautiful, all-natural raincoat isn’t an especially virtuous purchase if it doesn’t repel rain. On the whole, clothing with some percentage of made-made fiber requires less care than an item made with wool or silk or linen does—no hand-washing, no ironing, no reason to worry that moths might eat your favorite sweater.
Sometimes, they really are the best materials for the job. The designer Issey Miyake’s famous pleated pieces are polyester because, as one textile expert explained to NPR, their thermoplastic qualities are what helps them keep their shape. Polyester actively repels moisture and dries quickly, which is why it’s used in so much athletic gear. Wool is stronger and more durable when it’s blended with a bit of nylon—not important for sweaters, crucial for hiking socks. A little spandex can help a pair of cotton leggings keep their shape. If we want the forgiving comforts of stretch denim and athleisure, “we have to make peace with the fact that synthetic fibers are going to be incorporated into our clothes,” Nancy Deihl, a fashion historian at NYU, told me. Yes, synthetic clothing can release microplastics—bad—but it isn’t clear how much swapping out your stretch pants does to meaningfully reduce your exposure.
There is another problem with the natural-fiber obsession: Plenty of common fibers are neither synthetic nor natural. Semi-synthetics such as Tencel (the brand name for lyocell), modal, and rayon (otherwise known as bamboo) are made from natural plant material that’s been chemically dissolved and then reconstituted, a process that can be staggeringly toxic or ecologically responsible. Conventional cotton, for example, takes significantly more water to produce than lyocell and modal do.
Further complicating matters, although terms such as organic cotton, regenerative cotton, and recycled cotton tell you something about the production of fibers, they do not tell you something about the quality of a garment. Yarn spun from longer cotton fibers is stronger and wears better than yarn spun from shorter ones, but fiber length is a result of the type of cotton plant, or the growing conditions, or how the fibers have been processed. “You can compare the fiber quality of three different cotton fibers, all making the same exact T-shirt,”—same weight of yarn, same knitting machinery, same pattern, same sewing process—“and those three T-shirts can, depending on fiber quality, last wildly different amounts of time,” Crutchfield said. Fiber quality is one reason a 100 percent cashmere sweater can be $50 or upwards of $500. “You must investigate the context and the nuance,” she told me.
And fiber, natural or otherwise, is only one of a matrix of concerns that determine whether your clothing is ethical and well made. “Synthetics and natural fibers can both last a long time, but it depends on how they’re used, how they’re worn, and the quality of the garment they were made into,” Deihl said. The look and performance of any given garment are products of the fibers but also of the fabric weight, the weave, the cut, the construction, and the care instructions—all of which require at least some knowledge to assess, and none of which is easy to evaluate online.
In a dizzying consumer landscape of infinite options, it is understandable, even admirable, to want some kind of universal rubric to guide your purchasing. This can’t be cost, which may or may not correspond with quality, and there is no single label guaranteeing sustainability or ethics. You probably don’t know where a fiber was farmed and how it was harvested and processed—whether it’s been bleached and how it’s dyed, and the conditions under which a garment has been constructed—and the people selling it might not, either. Fiber content, though, is listed on the label: therefore, natural fibers! But natural isn’t a reliable shorthand for good—no matter how much you pay for your all-cashmere pants.

Bharti Group-backed satcom services provider Eutelsat OneWeb has sought the immediate grant of security approval for its low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellation, which would take it closer to commercially launching its services in India. Many of OneWeb’s satellites are nearing the end of their operational lives and could become useless if there are further delays in launching its services in India, the Economic Times reported, citing sources. The company has been awaiting security approval for more than 18 months after conducting its security compliance demonstration in January 2025. OneWeb has informed the DoT that it submitted all the required data and information related to the security demonstration and responded to additional queries raised by law enforcement agencies. However, the approval is yet to come, the report said. Questions sent to OneWeb remained unanswered till the time of publication. The story will be updated on receiving a response. The clearance covers requirements related to lawful interception, network monitoring, and the localisation of critical network functions. OneWeb’s Long Wait OneWeb was the first satcom operator to secure a GMPCS licence in India, receiving the permit from the DoT in August 2021. The company was initially looking to launch its services in the country in 2022. However, its rollout has faced repeated delays due to the Russia-Ukraine war, which disrupted the launch of its satellites, and the wait for approvals from Indian authorities, the report said. The company subsequently received authorisation from IN-SPACe in November 2023 to provide the capacity of its satellite constellation in India. OneWeb has established the necessary ground infrastructure, including gateways in Mehsana, Gujarat, and Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, as well as two points of presence in Mumbai and Chennai. The gateways will connect with OneWeb’s global LEO satellite constellation and enable the delivery of satellite broadband services in India. OneWeb operates a global constellation of more than 600 LEO satellites. ISRO launched 72 OneWeb satellites across two dedicated LVM3 missions in October 2022 and March 2023. The report said OneWeb is replacing some satellites that have completed their operational lives. However, the number of operational satellites in its existing constellation could decline as more reach the end of their lives. Even after securing security approval, OneWeb will require spectrum assignment before it can commercially launch services in India. India’s Satcom Race Elon Musk-led Starlink and Jio Satellite are also awaiting security clearance to commercially launch their satcom services in India. However, the three companies are targeting different customer segments. OneWeb plans to cater primarily to businesses, while Starlink intends to offer services directly to retail consumers. Jio Satellite, meanwhile, plans to offer services through Reliance Jio’s joint venture with Luxembourg-based SES, which operates a medium Earth orbit satellite constellation. Reliance Industries is also said to be evaluating a multi-billion-dollar investment in its own LEO satellite constellation. The conglomerate is exploring both organic and inorganic expansion opportunities, including possible acquisitions of satellite companies with existing orbital slots and infrastructure. Last month, Starlink reapplied to IN-SPACe for authorisation for its second-generation constellation comprising nearly 30,000 satellites, which will include direct-to-device connectivity capabilities.

A video showing Union defence minister Rajnath Singh and his Japanese counterpart Shinjiro Koizumi signing what appears to be a diplomatic agreement has gone viral on social media. Users have circulated this clip with the claim that India and Japan have signed a contract to allow for “50 million Hindus to settle in Japan.”
X user @CoinMarginalX posted the viral claim on August 21. (Archive)
NEW: Japan and India signed a contract to allow 50 millions Hindus to settle in Japan.🇯🇵🇮🇳 pic.twitter.com/cHao8wTGC9
— CoinMarginalX (@CoinMarginalX) August 21, 2026
Another X user, Hindu hero, (@SuperBrahmin) posted the same claim. (Archive)
Shesh Paul Vaid (@spvaid), the former director general of police (DGP) of Jammu and Kashmir, amplified this viral claim, calling it an unique agreement. His tweet was viewed 92,000 times at the time of publication. However, it was later deleted by the user.
Fact Check
First, we ran relevant keyword searches to see if there were any credible news reports on the alleged contract, but could find none.
Instead, the keyword search led us to this article published by Business Standard on August 20. It reports that Indian defence minister Rajnath Singh had met his Japanese counterpart, Shinjiro Koizumi, in New Delhi, to discuss bilateral strategic partnership. The discussion was largely focused on the Indo-Pacific region, and saw the two signed a “memorandum of arrangement” on maritime security. The report does not mention any “contract” that allows 50 million Hindus to settle in Japan.
News on Air, the news service of All India Radio, also reported on the meeting, on August 20. Citing growing vulnerabilities and efforts to stifle freedom of navigation, the memorandum had reportedly been signed as a strategic imperative between the two countries to ensure co-operation in the Indo-Pacific region.
On further investigation, Alt News came across an Associated Press report, published in August 2025, which states that at the India-Japan Economic Forum in Tokyo, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had signed a total of 11 documents, and released a “joint vision” of cooperation for the next decade in areas spanning security, defense, clean energy, technology and space.
Further, the Union ministry of external affairs (MEA) also published a media release on the discussed points on August 29, titled “Action Plan for India — Japan Human Resource Exchange and Cooperation”. Reportedly, the MEA and the Japanese foreign ministry agreed to promote the efforts of various entities in government, industry, and academia to “…increase the number of skilled personnel and potential talents from India to Japan by 50,000 over the next five years.” The proposed plan covers students, researches, skilled professionals, easing worker visas, boosting Japanese-language training in India, and setting up support systems for Indians in Japan.
Nowhere in the AP report or in the press release is it mentioned that the two countries had signed a “contract” allowing 50 million Hindus to settle in Japan. In other words, a video from the aforementioned meeting between Singh and Koizumi is being circulated with an entirely fabricated claim.

Monza memories - Italian GP in pictures through the years
ByAlan Jewell

The Italian Grand Prix takes place this weekend at Monza, arguably the most historic venue on the calendar.
Monza has hosted Formula 1 races more times than any other circuit, staging grands prix in all but one year since the inaugural season in 1950.
The only time Monza was absent was 1980, when it was being renovated.
Located in a royal park and surrounded by woodland, it is known as the 'cathedral of speed'. It is the spiritual home of Ferrari and the devoted tifosi who adore the Italian team.
It is all but impossible to imagine F1 without Monza - it was where the first world championship was decided 76 years ago and where, last year, Red Bull's Max Verstappen set the fastest lap in F1 history during qualifying.
Throughout the years, Monza has been the scene of thrilling finishes, Ferrari glory, title wins, controversy and tragedy. Its story is F1's story.
Here is a selection of images through the years...

I think automakers are finally getting the memo. Rather than try to reinvent the wheel with its new electric vehicle, Range Rover just made one that looks nearly identical to its lineup of gas-powered SUVs. They didn’t try to pass off some sleek, spaceship-looking pod as a Range Rover. Sometimes familiar designs are the way to go.
Range Rover’s new EV looks just like a regular Range Rover — that’s refreshing
Range Rover’s first EV is a little late to the party, but it arrives looking refreshingly similar to the automaker’s gas-powered models.
Of course, under the surface the Range Rover Electric is nothing like its internal combustion engine sporting brethren. Twin permanent magnet 260kW electric motors are powered by a double-stacked 118.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, with an estimated range of 330 real-world miles.
The all-wheel drive system puts out 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque, which Range Rover describes as “V8 levels of power.” An 800-volt architecture enables DC fast charging from 10–80 percent in just 22 minutes, or about 137 miles in 10 minutes, when plugged into a 350 kW charger. A zero to 60 mph time of 4.3 seconds won’t win it any awards, especially compared to EV rivals like Lucid and Rivian. But this Range Rover probably doesn’t need to blow up any records to make its mark. With a familiar design and decent enough specs, it should be more than sufficient for anyone who has been pining for a touch of British sophistication in their EV shopping.
The wait has certainly stretched on longer than it should have. Range Rover first announced it was working on an electric model over five years ago. It first opened preorders in 2023, promising that customer deliveries would begin a year later. The Jaguar Land Rover–owned brand took its sweet time fulfilling these promises, but now that the cover has been lifted, the automaker is taking orders at a starting price of £154,070 in the UK (or about $140,450 in the US).
JLR says it will produce the Range Rover Electric at its Solihull factory, alongside gas and hybrid models. It’s also touting the number of patents submitted for this EV — 300 — making it the most technologically custom-built Range Rover ever.
How technologically advanced? Try lightning-fast grip control. Instead of waiting for mechanical gears to adjust when tires slip, the electric motors adjust power in 50 milliseconds — 100 times faster than a gas car. This gives instant control on ice, mud, or loose gravel. The one-pedal drive system is tuned for super steep slopes of up to 45 degrees, so you can climb mountains or crawl over obstacles using just the accelerator. And the battery and motors are fully sealed, allowing you to drive through nearly 3 feet of water (900mm) without damaging the vehicle. Lastly, a built-in heat pump reuses waste heat to warm the cabin and keep the battery at the right temperature, preserving up to 25 extra miles of driving range in freezing weather.
All of this sounds great on paper. Stacked up against rivals like the Porsche Macan EV or the Lotus Eletre, the SUV may look even better — especially for those car buyers who still prefer a familiar face on their electric vehicle.
Images by Range Rover

- A rumor circulating in late August 2026 claimed crews cut down dozens of cherry trees to pave the way for U.S. President Donald Trump's plans to renovate a Washington, D.C., golf course.
- As of this writing on Sept. 1, we've found no evidence to support the claim dozens of cherry trees had been removed as part of the project.
- The gold course makeover, which Trump said would begin on Sept. 1, aims to create a championship-style site by overhauling the East Potomac Golf Links property inside East Potomac Park.
- The rumor about cherry trees appeared to have originated with readers misunderstanding or misrepresenting an Aug. 28 Washington Post article reporting that an informal count found roughly 60 trees had been removed. Out of those 60, only one was a cherry tree.
- An Interior Department spokesperson told Snopes arborists recommend the removal of dying, declining or hazardous trees as a part of routine maintenance. For example, during the Biden administration, the National Park Service reportedly removed 300 trees (including 140 cherry trees) from the Tidal Basin area north of East Potomac Park as part of a three-year project capped off by the replanting of 277 cherry trees.
In late August 2026, Snopes received emails and searches asking if it was true crews cut down dozens of cherry trees to pave the way for U.S. President Donald Trump's Washington, D.C., golf course renovations, specifically the East Potomac Golf Links property inside East Potomac Park, the site of the nation's first cherry blossom planting.
Earlier in the year, the Trump administration revealed visual plans to overhaul the property into a championship-style golf course. Then, Trump announced on Truth Social that work on the golf course would begin Sept. 1. Earlier in the year, the DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit challenging the project, including citing crews dumping White House East Wing debris at the site.
Readers specifically asked if a rumor that between 60 and 158 cherry trees were chopped down was true, and whether the administration violated a court order by doing so. They also wanted to know if the alleged tree removal impacted the cherry tree collections gifted to the U.S. by Japan in 1910 and 1912.
For example, one reader emailed, "Despite court orders, Trump is moving forward with plans to remove 158 iconic cherry trees near the Tidal Basin and 60 have already been cut down."
Another email read, "Has Trump ordered the removal of dozens of cherry trees in DC that were a gift from Japan?"
Social media users shared variants of this claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived), among other platforms.
(X user @adamemedia1)
In sum, as of this writing on Sept. 1, we have found no evidence to support the claim, nor any examples of news media outlets reporting that dozens of cherry trees were removed from East Potomac Park, including any that arrived from Japan in 1910 or 1912.
Regarding court orders, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes reportedly said on May 4 the court must be told if the renovation plans called for the removal of more than 10 trees.
We haven't given this multipart claim a true or false rating given the lack of conclusive evidence either way and the fact that it remains an ongoing situation.
One popular Facebook post (archived) indicated the rumor stems at least in part from people misrepresenting an Aug. 28 Washington Post report. That story, headlined "Trees are coming down by the dozen as Trump's D.C. golf makeover nears," tells of "newly cut stumps and bare patches of dirt [marking] the places where dozens of trees recently stood" and says an informal count found that 60 trees "appeared to have been removed in recent weeks." The Post mentions noticing at least one removed cherry tree near the 14th green of the blue course, as well as two large sycamores removed around another area.
An Interior Department spokesperson provided the same statement the Post published, saying arborists recommended recent removals of dying, declining or hazardous trees as a part of routine maintenance:
Arborists are doing routine maintenance at East Potomac Park with selective removal of hazard trees, non-native invasive trees and declining and dying trees that cannot be brought back to good health through any degree of intervention. Trees throughout the park are regularly monitored for potential safety impacts to visitors, and when a tree is determined to be dying, declining or hazardous our arborists may make the decision to remove it.
In response to the department's statement, we requested numbers of removed trees from previous years for comparison.
For example, in March 2024, when former President Joe Biden was in office, the NPS reportedly announced a $133 million project to rebuild and reinforce the sea wall of the Tidal Basin, an area located north of East Potomac Park. The work, scheduled at the time to last three years, featured the removal of 140 cherry trees out of 300 total trees, as well as the replanting of 277 cherry trees at the project's conclusion. Those removals included a beloved tree named "Stumpy."
According to an NPS article last updated in 2019, fewer than 100 of the cherry trees Japan gifted the U.S. in the early 1900s remain to this day and are planted along the Tidal Basin and around the park and the city. Those few remaining trees make up only a small portion of "the nearly 4,000 cherry trees growing in West and East Potomac Parks, on the Washington Monument grounds, and in several other park locations."
Officials reportedly burned most of Japan's 1910 cherry-tree shipment after arrival upon finding they were infested with insects and disease, with the 1912 shipment proving more successful. In 2009, the Post, citing century-old reporting, told of some of the 1910 trees possibly being saved and planted in an "experimental plot" — a gathering possibly remaining to this day, located at the southern tip of the park in Hains Point.
We reached out to the White House, which referred us to the Interior Department, as well as the DC Preservation League and the National Park Service for further comment, and will update this article if we receive further information. We also contacted Post writer Rick Maese, who posted on X, "It doesn't seem like any cherry trees from the historic grove have been impacted thus far." Another journalist responded to the post, bringing up the 2009 Post article about officials possibly planting a small number of Japan's 1910 shipment.
An online booking search for East Potomac Golf Links tee times showed availability continuing into the first days of September, with no sign of any potential closures.
Tree care company denies axing cherry trees
During the Post's Aug. 27 visit to the property — a site Snopes has not visited firsthand — the writer reported seeing a company named RTEC Treecare cutting trees, including a large tree that showed "clear signs of decay." The writer also mentioned noticing white dots and yellow ribbons on some trees, marked for purposes not known to the Post.
The RTEC Treecare website displays a message addressing the cherry tree rumor, reading in part as follows (bolded emphasis theirs):
RTEC Treecare is currently performing hazard tree pruning and removal services for the National Park Service at East Potomac Park Golf Course. The trees assigned for treatment have been evaluated and selected by National Park Service arborists based on established hazard assessment criteria.
We want to be clear: RTEC Treecare has not removed any cherry trees at East Potomac Park Golf Course. Our work has been limited to trees identified by the National Park Service as hazardous, non-native, or invasive.
We contacted RTEC Treecare to ask if they were aware of who chopped down the cherry tree the Post reported about and will update this story if we receive more details.
DC eyewitness reports from East Potomac Park
On Aug. 31, Threads user @drybrarian, whose bio identifies him as "Kennedy Center Bike Guy," posted (archived) photos purporting to show the current state of East Potomac Park, including one displaying a newspaper with the day's date as evidence of when he captured the images. The thread of posts, featuring more than the post embedded below, reported that the user witnessed some trees being cut down, adding, "there has NOT been a wholesale Cherry Blossom Massacre," as well as that "the VAST majority of the trees are still there."
We messaged the user to ask for further information and will update this story accordingly.
For further reading, we previously reported in July about similar rumors of the Trump administration planning to chop down cherry trees.

Uganda names its crude oil blend 'Pearl Sweet' ahead of commercial production
Ugandan authorities have named the country's prospective crude oil blend "Pearl Sweet," marking a milestone as Uganda prepares for commercial production by the end of the year
MBALE, Uganda -- Ugandan authorities on Wednesday named the country’s prospective crude oil blend “Pearl Sweet,” marking a milestone as the East African country gears up for commercial production by the end of the year.
Officials announced the name at a remote oil infrastructure site, celebrating Uganda’s emergence as an oil producer.
The name chosen for Uganda’s crude oil blend is a nod to Winston Churchill’s description of Uganda in the last century as “the pearl of Africa,” and officials said the “sweet” in the nomenclature reflects the crude blend’s low sulfur content.
“The name combines national identity with a commercial description,” the Ministry of Energy said in a statement. “Naming supports future crude marketing activities and engagement with potential buyers.”
Uganda is estimated to have recoverable oil reserves of roughly 1.6 billion barrels. The investors are French oil company TotalEnergies, which owns the largest stake, and China National Offshore Oil Corporation, or CNOOC. The Ugandan people, through the Uganda National Oil Company, own 15% of the projects.
"This marks an important milestone in our journey to develop Uganda’s oil and gas resources for value addition and economic transformation," Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni said. "Through refining, petrochemical industries and the use of associated gas for electricity generation, we shall maximize the value of our resources here at home and reduce dependence on imported petroleum products.”
Production is expected to plateau at about 230,000 barrels per day, with blended crude exports emerging from separate projects by CNOOC and TotalEnergies.
Wednesday’s event in Kikuube, the site of a CNOOC project known as Kingfisher, signals progress despite legal and other setbacks since the discovery two decades ago of commercially viable quantities of crude deposits.
The oil development projects are linked to the controversial construction of a heated pipeline linking Uganda’s oil fields near Lake Albert to a port in Tanzania. Environmentalists and others have opposed the pipeline, saying it runs afoul of the Paris Climate Agreement.
Most efforts by climate watchdogs seeking to stop Uganda’s oil projects have focused on TotalEnergies, which has been sued in France at least twice by groups and individuals alleging food and land rights violations.
Oil wells are being drilled within western Uganda’s Murchison Falls National Park, where the Nile River plummets 130 feet (40 meters) through a gap just 20 feet (6 meters) wide and the surrounding wilderness is home to hippos, egrets, giraffes and antelope. The pipeline is to pass through forest reserves and game parks, running alongside Lake Victoria, a source of fresh water for 40 million people.
That ecological fragility is one reason why some activists oppose the project despite assurances from TotalEnergies that the pipeline’s state-of-the-art design will ensure safety for decades.
Ugandan officials expressed anger toward opposition to the pipeline, saying climate campaigns verged on interference in the internal affairs of a sovereign country. They say oil wealth can lift millions out of poverty.

August turned out to be yet another eventful month for the Indian startup ecosystem. The month marked multiple mega rounds, including River Mobility’s $120 Mn infusion and Navi’s $100 Mn maiden institutional fundraise. AstroTalk also joined the unicorn club, becoming India's 133rd unicorn. August also underscored the growing investor interest in AI and advanced hardware, with both sectors featuring prominently across the funding activity. Overall, Indian startups raised $857.4 Mn last month, as funding activity remained concentrated around growth and early stage bets. Beyond funding, August also saw IPO activity gather pace, with startups increasingly moving towards public markets. Atomberg filed its DRHP and Shiprocket listed on the bourses, while SEBI cleared the IPOs of Garuda Aerospace, PlaySimple Games and Rediff. Simultaneously, policy support continued to shape opportunities for India's deeptech and technology startups. The Centre notified the ₹1.28 Lakh Cr Semicon 2.0 scheme while stepping up support for early-stage deeptech ventures through MeitY's GENESIS Entrepreneur-in-Residence programme. However, the month also brought forth its own set of challenges. The government's ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund came under the spotlight after questions were raised over its first allocation, highlighting the growing role of public capital in funding India's deeptech ambitions. Against this backdrop, Inc42 is back with the latest edition of its flagship “30 Startups To Watch” series, where we spotlight promising early stage ventures that caught our eye this month. As India celebrated its 80th I-Day in August, Inc42’s 74th edition of 30 Startups To Watch, brings together startups working across sectors such as AI, deeptech, spacetech, climate tech, defence, EVs, consumer and enterprise tech. From companies using microgravity for pharmaceutical manufacturing to startups building AI companions, autonomous drone infrastructure and new-age consumer brands, these ventures are tackling problems across some of India's fastest-evolving markets. So, without further ado, here are the new-age companies that made the cut for this edition of Inc42's 30 Startups To Watch. Editor’s Note: The list below is not a ranking of any kind. We have listed the startups alphabetically. Acres of Ice | Building Seasonal Ice Reservoirs In Ladakh, water is abundant when farmers do not need it and scarce when they do. Winter snowfall and glacial flows provide water during the colder months, but by spring, which is when farmers begin sowing, rising temperatures, erratic snowfall and retreating glaciers can leave mountain communities without enough water for irrigation. The challenge is particularly acute in high-altitude regions where conventional water-storage infrastructure can be expensive and difficult to build. Founded in 2023 by Suryanarayanan Balasubramanian and Basit Afzal, Leh-based Acres of Ice is building technology to bridge this seasonal gap. Its Automated Ice Reservoirs (AIRs) channel winter water through gravity-fed pipelines, freeze it into large monitored ice structures and release the meltwater during the spring and summer growing season. Sensors and automated controls help optimise freezing and monitor reservoirs remotely. The startup has also expanded into automated micro-irrigation, using weather, soil and water sensors to schedule irrigation and control pumps and valves. The startup claims that its AIR systems stored 18.4 Mn litres across seven sites in Ladakh during the 2024-25 season, while its irrigation systems have achieved 60-70% water savings and 70-80% labour reduction. The opportunity extends beyond Ladakh: Acres of Ice estimates that around 14 Mn people across more than 14,000 villages in 16 countries face similar water-security challenges in high-altitude regions. With deployments envisioned across the Hindu Kush Himalayas, the Andes, and the Alps, the startup is effectively turning an indigenous water-storage practice into a data-driven, replicable climate-adaptation system. AlgoFET | Autonomous Docking Stations For Drones Drones may be getting smarter and more autonomous, but tactical drones used for surveillance, infrastructure inspection or agriculture still need to land, recharge or swap batteries before taking off again. These processes require human intervention, creating a bottleneck for operators looking to run fleets continuously and remotely. Founded in 2023 by Ankit Mishra, Bengaluru-based deeptech startup AlgoFET is building the ground infrastructure needed to keep industrial drones operational with minimal human intervention. Its technology stack includes autonomous docking stations, intelligent battery management systems, high-power charging infrastructure, embedded electronics and cloud-based fleet monitoring. Its AlgoDOCK enables drones to land and recharge autonomously, while AlgoBMS provides real-time battery health and diagnostics. Incubated at ARTPARK, IISc, AlgoFET claims to have deployed 2,000+ units. It has an order pipeline of more than 4,000 units and an order book worth around ₹100 Cr. The dronetech startup counts drone manufacturers and the Indian Army among its customers. In August 2026, the startup raised ₹15 Cr, which it plans to use for product development, manufacturing, IP and expansion into defence, enterprise and international markets. India’s drone ecosystem is expanding across defence, agriculture, surveillance, logistics and infrastructure, with the drone market projected to reach $3.2 Bn by 2030. With companies such as Skylark Labs, Raphe mPhibr, and ideaForge building drone hardware and autonomous systems, AlgoFET is targeting the layer beneath to enable those fleets to operate around the clock. Antimattr | Betting On A Screenless AI Future AI assistants are becoming increasingly capable, but using them in the real world still largely means pulling out a phone or sitting in front of a computer. For the founders of Bengaluru-based Antimattr, the problem became obvious while building voice agents: the AI worked, but noisy environments such as cafés, airports and open offices made voice interactions unreliable. Founded in 2025 by Sridipto Ghosh and Sirsho Chakraborty, Antimattr is building Project Mnemosyne, a voice-first computing system designed around memory and productivity. The hardware combines a smart ring with a pair of voice-isolation earphones. The ring can capture thoughts, record and summarise conversations and control AI agents, while the earphones use six microphones and proprietary voice-isolation technology to enable clearer conversations and dictation in noisy environments. It has already attracted backing from Y Combinator, which invested $500K in the startup, along with Nikhil Kamath’s WTFund and gener8tor, and it recently joined YC's Fall 2026 batch. In India’s AI wearable market, projected to reach $19.1 Bn by 2033, Antimattr is betting that voice can become the primary interface to AI without putting a screen between the user and the machine. Its longer-term roadmap extends beyond Mnemosyne to a privacy-focused AI computer and eventually an AI-native vehicle. Auxobit Aerospace | Autonomous Systems For Defence Modern warfare is increasingly shifting from large, human-operated platforms towards smaller, autonomous and networked systems that can provide surveillance, deliver tactical payloads and operate in environments where putting personnel at risk is difficult. India’s push for indigenous defence technology is creating room for startups to build these systems locally. Founded in 2023, Maharashtra-based Auxobit Aerospace develops unmanned systems for aerospace and defence applications, spanning aerial drones, autonomous surface vehicles, counter-drone systems and swarm technologies. The startup's portfolio includes Hell Fire, a swarm-enabled aerial platform designed for tactical payload delivery; Mystic One, an autonomous surface vehicle for hydrographic and bathymetric surveys; and other kinds of autonomous aerial platforms. The startup claims to be building capabilities across unmanned surface vehicles, submersibles, helicopters, counter-drone systems and loitering-munition swarms. The opportunity is expanding as India builds out its domestic defence-drone ecosystem, with demand coming from surveillance, border security, tactical operations and maritime applications. Auxobit is entering a competitive field that includes ideaForge, NewSpace Research & Technologies, Raphe mPhibr and Garuda Aerospace, but its broader focus across air, surface and autonomous defence systems gives it a different moat. base14 | Dedicated Performance Dashboard For AI Teams As software systems become more complex, engineering teams often use multiple tools to monitor logs, metrics, performance and traces. This creates fragmented data, increases costs and makes it harder to find the root cause of problems. Bengaluru-based base14 is building a unified observability platform to give engineering teams a single view of their software infrastructure. Founded in 2024 by Nilakanta Mallick, Ranjan Sakalley and Irfan Shah, the startup brings logs, metrics, traces, APM and LLM telemetry into a single data lake through an OpenTelemetry-native architecture. Its flagship product, Scout, uses this unified data layer to help teams monitor applications, identify anomalies and debug production issues. The platform claims to offer full-cardinality data without sampling while reducing observability costs significantly compared with legacy platforms. The startup is also expanding into AI-native developer infrastructure with Scope, a prompt-management and evaluation platform that lets teams version, test and deploy prompts while tracking latency, cost and output quality. With early customers, including Glomo, DPDZero and Zinc Learning Labs, base14 is tapping the growing application performance management market in India, which generated $291.1 Mn in revenue in 2024 and is expected to reach $723.4 Mn by 2030 as AI scales, driving demand for observability and granular data insights. Bruno Milano | Building India’s Affordable Premium Watch Market For a generation of consumers increasingly buying fashion and lifestyle products online, watches are becoming as much about design and self-expression as they are about telling time. Yet the affordable end of the market is crowded with mass-market brands, while premium international labels can quickly push prices out of reach. Bruno Milano is trying to occupy the space in between with design-led watches at accessible price points. Founded in 2024 by Rachit Jain and Saurabh Agarwal, Noida-based Bruno Milano is a D2C watch brand offering hand-finished quartz and chronograph timepieces, generally priced between ₹2,000 and ₹5,000. Its watches use Japanese quartz movements, with collections including Vittorio Chrono, Ambrosiana Chic and Duomo Heritage. The brand sells through its website as well as ecommerce and quick commerce platforms. It also offers customised watches for corporate gifting. The startup raised ₹7.5 Cr in August to expand across India, launch new collections, and strengthen ecommerce and quick commerce distribution. India’s watch market is projected to reach $7.52 Bn by 2031. While the mass segment currently accounts for nearly three-fourths of this opportunity, premiumisation and online shopping are creating room for new brands to target younger consumers with design-led products. CNN Foods | Traditional Desi Beverages Get A Gen Z Makeover The great Indian beverage aisle is packed with colas, juices, energy drinks and an expanding crop of better-for-you beverages, but traditional Indian flavours have often remained confined to local and regional formats. CNN Foods is trying to bring those flavours into contemporary packaging and formats while keeping them accessible to mass-market consumers. Founded in 2024 by Chirag Wadhwa, Delhi-based CNN Foods is building a portfolio of beverage brands centred on familiar Indian flavours and unconventional formats. Its flagship Phirki Zero is a zero-sugar, zero-calorie, zero-caffeine take on jeera masala soda, made with real lemon, while Papa Nata combines a fruit drink with coconut jelly for a drink-and-snack proposition. The early traction has been notable. Phirki Zero, launched in March 2026, sold roughly 2.5 Lakh cans in its first two months, with around 80% of sales coming through quick commerce platforms. The brand has since expanded onto Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, alongside modern trade and kirana outlets. India’s non-alcoholic beverages market is estimated at $34.7 Bn in 2025 and is projected to reach $69 Bn by 2034, growing at a 7.9% CAGR. CopperPilot | Bringing AI To The Hardware Design Process Building a new electronic product can involve weeks of repetitive engineering work before a prototype is even ready. 'Like fighting a dinosaur': Sydney woman recalls how she punched shark during attack
- Published
A Sydney woman who survived a shark attack has described the moment she came face-to-face with a 4m great white before repeatedly punching it.
Leah Stewart, 34, was dragged under the water at Coogee Beach in June as the shark bit into her thigh and arms, leaving her with extreme blood loss and injuries so severe that doctors had to amputate her left arm.
In an interview which aired on Sunday, the mother-of-one said she was determined to live for the sake of her baby daughter.
"In my head, I was like, ... 'You are not taking me away from my daughter', and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again - it was like fighting a dinosaur".
Moments earlier, Stewart had just finished her regular Saturday morning swim and was heading back to shore when she was alerted to danger.
"I heard a girl behind me… a shrill shriek. I turned and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive," she told Nine Network's 60 Minutes.
"I looked at the size of it and I realised that's not a dolphin."
Stewart turned around and realised the shark was "right there … and it just was getting closer and closer and closer."
The shark's face was "horrific" with "black little beady eyes" and its "teeth and its mouth was massive".
"We were looking face-to-face," Stewart said, and at one point, the shark was just 30cm from her own.
Even in that moment, Stewart's thoughts remained calm.
"I'm right-handed, so I thought 'let's do a left hook'," she said.
"I just kind of throw my left arm and it just grabs onto my forearm and rips, rips away my skin, my muscle, everything... there's a big gap between my forearm and the hand."
The shark started to pull Stewart under the water, grabbing her leg.
"I had the thought, 'this is it, this is how I die' and then I just thought of [my daughter] August and I thought she's not going to have a mum, she's gonna grow up without a mum," she said, fighting back tears.
"I just knew I couldn't leave her... I know it sounds strange but I sort of willed myself back."
Fighting the shark felt "like punching a brick wall" but she kept going.
"I must have got a really good one in and so it let me go. It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there."
Stewart was pulled to the shore by other swimmers and rushed to hospital, where she was placed in an induced coma and underwent almost a dozen surgeries.
Despite her harrowing experience, Stewart said she doesn't want to be remembered as "a girl that got mauled on the beach".
"I'm the woman that punched the shark in the face," she said.

How Everton's deadline day debacle leaves owners facing fan mutiny
- Published
Everton's shambolic end to the transfer window has resulted in open revolt from supporters that places fierce scrutiny on owners The Friedkin Group and chief executive Angus Kinnear.
The last straw for fans already infuriated by the controversial proposed sale of home-grown youngster Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest - the deal was eventually blocked by Everton's board in the face of the toxic reaction from the fanbase - was the bungled final day before the window closed.
Folarin Balogun's proposed £40m move from AS Monaco descended into high farce in the early hours of Wednesday morning after the original deal was renegotiated when issues arose with his medical, ending with the United States striker deciding to walk away from Everton's Finch Farm training base without signing.
And all after Balogun, 25, and both clubs had signed the deal sheet allowing the move to be completed after Tuesday's 23.00 BST transfer deadline.
Everton had scheduled an 8am flight to bring Balogun to Merseyside, but he was unable to arrive until later in the day. Everton were also frustrated at a delay in receiving documents related to the deal from Monaco.
When the problem with his medical cropped up, it prompted Everton to pursue a loan deal for Manchester United's Joshua Zirkzee, who was happy to sign but was not allowed to leave Old Trafford. A move was also made for Aston Villa's Tammy Abraham but did not progress as the striker wished to remain at Villa Park.
After failing to sign an alternative, a deal was eventually agreed with Monaco, minutes before the deadline, which would have resulted in a smaller up-front payment and a series of triggered payments based on how he progressed. The player's personal terms were unchanged.
It was only then that the former Arsenal striker had his change of heart, leaving Finch Farm with Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro telling journalists at a news conference on Wednesday that Balogun was "not comfortable" with how Everton treated him during his medical.
Everton believe they supported Balogun throughout the process, while being open about the issues identified. The club also made clear to the player they would work with Monaco to explore a solution that could still enable the transfer to be completed.
To make matters worse, and to shed an even more unflattering light on the club's strategy and operation, it all came after hours after Everton had sanctioned striker Beto's £15.5m move to Fiorentina.
Events unfolded as Everton's most creative player Iliman Ndiaye was completing his £65m move to Manchester City.
Everton could point to the fact Balogun took a personal decision they could not reverse, but the bigger question is why they took until the final day of the window to address glaring long-term issues?
Kinnear, in what must now be looked upon as an ill-fated recent interview with BBC Radio Merseyside, announced Everton's squad was "in a good place", adding: "The challenge is we want to get the absolute best player we can in their position. Our metric is that by the close of the transfer window we have achieved that."
He also relayed the views of Everton's American owners that they regarded missing out on Europe last season as "failure". It was an announcement manager David Moyes admitted came as a "surprise".
After the events of recent days, the word "failure" is being applied to the owners and chief executive, not Moyes. And there will be no hiding place for TFG and Kinnear should things now go wrong.
The "good place" Kinnear spoke about has eventually amounted to leaving Moyes with just one striker in the raw Thierno Barry and only 18 senior, outfield players, a parlous state of affairs for the 63-year-old Scot, who has at times found it hard to disguise his dissatisfaction with the extent of the summer's transfer business.
Everton may have re-signed Jack Grealish on loan, and finally solved a right-back problem stretching back years by signing Ashley Maitland-Niles from Lyon for £3m, but the over-riding verdict on the club's transfer window has to be one of huge embarrassment for TFG and Kinnear.
Even the search for a right-back, a problem from last summer and further back, was not smooth, with Maitland-Niles being officially announced shortly after midnight after a £9.4m deal for Fulham's Kenny Tete was shelved when the Cottagers could not find a suitable replacement.
As well as only one striker in Barry, Everton's squad now has just one recognised right-back in Maitland-Niles and one left-back in Vitaliy Mykolenko after youngster Adam Aznou was allowed to join Malaga on loan.
The last few days have seen one major PR catastrophe narrowly avoided by pulling out of the sale of 19-year-old Armstrong, arguably Everton's most promising academy product since Wayne Rooney, only to walk straight into another, highly damaging one.
After the Carabao Cup second-round win at Preston North End, Moyes said: "I still think we have got a lot of work to do. We need more players. Our squad is not big enough and we need to get more quality in some areas if we can do."
Moyes' thoughts will be worth much more than a penny, should he choose to air them publicly, while fans' groups have wasted no time in expressing their undisguised anger, with a petition even set up calling for Kinnear's resignation.
"The Everton Fans' Forum" issued a lengthy statement featuring widescale criticism of the club, saying the Toffees' squad had been left "dangerously short" in key areas.
It added: "The conclusion of this summer's transfer window leaves Everton supporters with serious questions about the club's planning, recruitment and decision-making.
"This is not about demanding that Everton spend recklessly. Supporters understand the financial restrictions the club operates under. We are not demanding marquee signings simply for the sake of it.
"We are demanding competence, preparation and accountability."
And the influential group "The 1878s", volunteers who have created huge flags, banners and tifos to enhance the atmosphere at Everton's new Hill Dickinson Stadium, and whose efforts were described as "unbelievable" by Moyes, has responded to deadline day in similar vein.
In a statement it said it is "standing down for the foreseeable future" in protest, saying: "Like the rest of our fanbase, we are utterly disappointed and disgusted with how this transfer window has gone, especially the end of it.
"Also for fans asking, just to reiterate - when we design flags, there are rules and regulations that we have to adhere to regarding the wording on our flags during displays, we are not allowed derogatory or offensive wording or images.
"If we were able to get a load of flags in the ground to show our feelings of discontent, disappointment and anger over this whole situation, believe us, we would, but this is something that simply wouldn't be allowed."
As well as the last-day signings of Grealish and Maitland-Niles, Everton did make other acquisitions during the window, bringing in PFA Championship Player of the Year Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough.
Christian Norgaard was signed from Arsenal - although the 32-year-old Dane is currently injured with no comeback date - as a replacement for departed veteran Idrissa Gueye.
Deals for young German Merlin Rohl and England Under-21 winger Tyrique George, on loan last season, were confirmed. Brennan Johnson arrived from Crystal Palace in a straight swap with Dwight McNeil.
All this, however, has been overshadowed by a transfer deadline day that ended as nothing short of a debacle. In reality, they have ended this transfer markedly weaker than when they started it.
Everton are yet to issue any public statement on the events that have led to such damning criticism, fan rebellion and a loss of credibility for owners TFG - but there are many fences to be mended.
If that can be done successfully remains to be seen.

The Trump Administration just took OpenAI’s side in the artificial intelligence company’s legal battle with the New York Times.
The media juggernaut sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, alleging that the companies had violated copyright law by training their AI tools on its articles without permission. Now, the government has stepped in, arguing that OpenAI’s actions were within bounds.
On Tuesday, the federal government submitted a letter to the court stating that the United States has a “strong interest” in whether AI training on copyright works is considered “fair use,” because it connects to whether the country’s AI industry can “retain global leadership in artificial intelligence.” (The “fair use” rule shields certain uses of copyrighted materials.)
The letter argued that the Times’ definition of fair use is “inconsistent” with current copyright law, and that a win for the paper could have disastrous consequences. “Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility,” lawyers for the government wrote.
While the letter focuses on the New York Times and OpenAI, the government noted that its arguments apply to all of the parties in this case and related cases, including other publishers and authors.
Training LLMs on copyrighted works is considered “extraordinarily transformative,” meaning that these systems meaningfully change their inputs, the administration argued. The administration also wrote that OpenAI’s LLMs do not significantly compete with The New York Times’ articles. Courts consider both of these conditions, as well as others, when deciding if the fair use doctrine is met.
Conflating AI training with what artificial intelligence tools produce would lead to “problematic implications for copyright law generally” by implying that it would be similarly illegal for human writers to practice their craft by training on the words of others, per the letter. (The lawyers compared it to how a teenage Joan Didion typed out Ernest Hemingway’s stories to figure out how to write.)
Evan Brown, an intellectual property lawyer with the firm Neal & McDevitt, tells WIRED that the US district judge overseeing this case, Sidney H. Stein, is not obliged to let this letter influence his ultimate decision. However, Brown says that Stein and other judges overseeing cases like this will almost certainly “take it quite seriously because it comes from the Department of Justice, and inherently carries a lot of weight.”
Pamela Samuelson, a copyright lawyer who codirects the Berkeley Center For Law & Technology, tells WIRED that the government’s brief is a “significant development,” and one which is consistent with AI copyright rulings thus far.
“The Administration is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells WIRED. “Both AI and creators can thrive–AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires.”
OpenAI and Microsoft did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Other plaintiffs are unhappy at the government’s incursion. Mary Rasenberger, the chief executive of the Author’s Guild—which filed its own lawsuit against OpenAI in 2023—tells WIRED that the nonprofit is “extremely disappointed” about the letter, which she calls ”replete with faulty arguments and a gross misunderstanding of the fair use doctrine and copyright law.”
There are dozens of ongoing, high-profile lawsuits over the legality of AI companies training their tools on copyrighted work. The two biggest decisions so far took place last year. Meta technically won its copyright case, Kadrey v. Meta, although the judge noted that the plaintiffs did not produce enough evidence that the training caused them harm while stressing that in other circumstances, training on copyrighted materials without permission might indeed be illegal.
Anthropic, meanwhile, lost its case, and must pay authors $1.5 billion in damages, the largest copyright settlement in national history. The judge in that case carved out an important caveat, ruling that the AI training itself was fair use, but that the authors were owed damages because the AI giant had pirated their books.
Meanwhile, the larger fight over copyright rages on. New lawsuits are still rolling in; late last week, Sony and Warner Music sued Anthropic, following another suit from other music giants like Universal Music Group, in which Anthropic is mounting a fair use defense. In both cases, the companies allege that their copyrighted material was stolen to train Claude, the company’s popular AI tool.

Police arrest 34 after a fatal shooting in a rural Dutch village
Police in the Netherlands have arrested 34 suspects after a fatal shooting in Overasselt, southeast of Amsterdam
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Police arrested 34 suspects in a huge manhunt Tuesday after a person was fatally shot and two police officers were wounded in what appeared to be a gangland attack that involved some 30 masked men walking down a street in a rural village.
The shooting happened in the early hours of the morning in Overasselt, some 135 kilometers (85 miles) southeast of Amsterdam. Hours later, police urged local residents to stay indoors as officers investigated.
The two wounded police officers were recovering in hospital. Details of their injuries were not released.
Security camera footage broadcast by Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf showed some 30 people, many wearing ski masks and carrying weapons, walking down a street before fleeing after an apparent shooting. Police said their investigation includes analyzing the video images.
Mayor Joerie Minses said that Overasselt “was shaken last night by a form of extreme violence that is completely unacceptable.”
National police chief Janny Knol said in a message on X that officers from across the country were investigating and had already detained “a large number” of suspects. She called the violence “unprecedented.”
Prosecutors and police declined to comment on a possible motive.
Police said that the 34 people detained included people from the Netherlands, France, Belgium and Algeria. Their identities were not released and there were no immediate details of charges.
The Netherlands is a major destination for cocaine that arrives in ports large and small across the country. That has created an increasingly violent underworld of gangs. Criminal gangs operating in the country are also major producers of synthetic drugs.

- The claim that authorities in Florida rescued 163 missing children is still under investigation pending the release of more detailed information.
