In Summary
- A decade ago, Indian brands commanded a large chunk of the Indian smartphone market. In Q2 2016, three of the top five smartphone brands were Indian ones.
- The arrival of Chinese brands and changes in the market led to the decline and exit of many Indian phone brands. Today, while brands like Lava and AI+ exist, their market shares are nothing compared to Indian brands of the past.
- Rising smartphone prices and memory costs seem to have opened the door for Indian smartphone brands, with new brands emerging and old ones looking to make a comeback, with encouragement and support from the Government. But is this just a temporary phase, or will Indian brands win back the market dominance they lost almost a decade ago?
When I first started covering technology, the Indian smartphone market looked extremely different from what it does today. Today, there are barely any Indian brands among the major smartphone brands in the Indian market – Counterpoint’s report on Q2 2026 showed not a single Indian brand among the top eight smartphone brands in the Indian market. Yes, some Indian smartphone brands do exist, such as the persistent Lava and the newcomer AI+, but they do not command significant market shares.
The story was extremely different a decade ago.
It may be hard to believe, especially for those who have started following smartphone trends in India since 2017, but in mid-2016, Indian tech brands were not just surviving but ruling the smartphone charts. IDC’s report for Q2 2016 placed three Indian brands in the top five smartphone brands in the country – Micromax, Intex and Reliance Jio (this was around the time of the 4G revolution).
And this was not because of a lack of competition. The Indian market was home to a number of high-profile foreign smartphone players like Apple, Samsung, HTC, BlackBerry, LG, Sony, and Motorola were very much present in the Indian market, and the likes of OnePlus, Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo had also arrived in the market. Still, Indian brands like Micromax, Intex, Spice, and Karbonn dominated sales charts for multiple and sometimes even consecutive quarters. In fact, in Q2 2014, Micromax even overtook Samsung to be the number one smartphone brand in the country in terms of shipments. It was a time when we carried a story on how Micromax deserved to be shown more respect.
Ghosts of the Indian smartphone market past: Why Indian brands ruled, and how the Chinese brands beat them
There was a reason for this dominance. At that point of time, Indian smartphone brands mainly catered to the budget segment, mostly under Rs. 15,000 (or even Rs 10,000), which comprised a large chunk of the smartphone market. While international brands had tried to enter this segment, they had very limited success, as they could not match the price-to-spec ratio that the Indian brands were offering. Big displays, big batteries, and decent processors (often from the more affordable MediaTek) and a small price tag made phones from the likes of Micromax, Intex, and Karbonn the perfect pick for anyone looking to pick up an entry-level smartphone. The likes of Apple, Samsung, HTC, Sony, and BlackBerry were largely operating in the mid/ upper mid and premium segment.
The tech climate changed as Chinese brands began to make their presence felt. Xiaomi, OnePlus, Vivo, and Oppo all stepped into the Indian market in 2014. Oppo and Vivo seemed to be playing in the premium segment, while brands like Xiaomi and OnePlus initially seemed to focus on flagship killers (a term OnePlus popularised). However, given India’s demography, it did not take a long time for these brands to realize that real numbers were actually in the budget and mid segment.
Even as Indian brands struggled with inventory issues as the 4G revolution hit India, the Chinese brands shifted focus and brought in smartphones with prices and spec combinations that matched and, in many cases, even eclipsed what Indian brands were offering. That was not all.
With the mobile Internet becoming more accessible thanks to extremely affordable 4G rates (pioneered mainly by Reliance Jio), these brands also opted for a very unconventional plan of action, going for flash sales, online only sales, often with little to no advertising in mainstream media, and building communities online. These not only cut expenses, but built greater brand loyalty (something Indian brands had been unable to do, as they had focused mainly on price). This combination of pricing and communications affected all the other brands in the market, but hit the Indian brands particularly hard, as it took away their biggest USP – a low price tag. The years that followed saw not just Indian brands fade, but even the likes of LG, Sony and HTC bid farewell to the Indian market.
The Indian Smartphone Market Today: Rocked by a steep price rise
In the last ten years, the Indian smartphone market has changed completely. Many Indian brands that had seemed almost invincible have packed their bags and left, although some like Lava have managed to stick around, in spite of not being the force they once were. But the tech stars in the tech universe move in different ways, and the way in which they have been aligning in recent times makes me think that the time is ripe for Indian smartphone brands to make a comeback in their own market.
Hear me out before you think I am talking through my hat. We have seen a very steady shift happening in the tech world in 2026. Many brands that earlier ruled the budget, mid, and lower-mid segments have been climbing up the price ladder for a while now, seeking larger profit margins. Indeed, the number of phones available in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment has been shrinking in recent times, with many brands seemingly inching towards vacating it altogether.
The likes of Motorola, OnePlus and Xiaomi are also no longer organizations with lean portfolios and small, focused teams but have become tech behemoths with large-scale operations, huge marketing budgets, multiple sub-brands and extensive product portfolios. This has, of course, affected their ability to offer the extremely competitive price-spec combo that made them popular in the first place.
The dramatic increase in the price of memory has now made it even more difficult for existing brands to offer good devices at lower price points. Devices with specs that used to be seen in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment are now being seen at prices in the range of Rs 25,000 or more. Options at lower price points are either vanishing or are coming with relatively modest specs.
And Indian brands are suddenly appearing on the horizon again.
Guess who’s back, back again… Indian smartphone brands
White Lava had never left; it seems to have got a new lease of life. AI+ is increasingly aggressive, and Fire-Boltt, a brand known more for its wearables and hearables, has entered the smartphone market. Even as this is being written, Mivi, a mainly audio brand, has announced plans for a smartphone with a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor for under Rs 15,000, and there is also talk of Micromax returning to the market, and Boat (which, like Fire-Boltt, is known mainly for audio and wearable products) is also planning to sail in smartphone waters. And from what we know, all these brands are targeting the sub-Rs 15,000 market, from which many brands have moved products to higher price points and/ or releasing new devices with much more modest specs in the past.
The Indian Government is also making efforts to build a smartphone brand that it can call its own. On August 21, it officially sent out a notification, as per which the Union Cabinet approved a budget of Rs. 62,500 crore for a Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) to build globally competitive, native smartphone brands. The scheme offers a number of incentives and rewards for Indian brands. To qualify, a company must be registered in India, keep its ownership and trademarks in India, have more than 51 percent Indian shareholding, be controlled in India, and have its products designed locally without outsourcing. This is a massive push and is likely to encourage more Indian entrepreneurs to enter the smartphone market.
Welcome back, Indian brands, but this time, please stay!
But making a comeback will not be enough. The smartphone world has changed a fair bit since the time Indian brands ruled the charts. And the new ones or those making a comeback would need to adopt a fundamentally different approach to ensure that the second innings of Indian brands in the smartphone market is a long one, and does not end as abruptly as the first. Being an ‘Indian brand’ has to have a different connotation than it did in the past.
Indian brands have struggled with offering good after-sales service and good software, and have tended to compete mainly on price and specs. That needs to change. The new and not-so-new native brands have to ensure they not just deliver a smartphone at a competitive price, but follow through on the whole process that comes after. Easy access to repairs and spare parts, timely OS updates, and improved, new-age marketing strategies are all necessities for these brands to actually establish themselves in this competitive market for the long run.
Native brands also need to shed their image of merely assembling and/or importing devices from outside and rebranding them for the Indian market. Authentic and good quality products backed up with a solid sales and service system are both needed to make consumers associate Indian brands not just with low prices, but also with high quality.
As of now, Indian brands are knocking on the door of their nation’s smartphone market once again. Just how well they will do, only time will tell. While I am hoping their second coming will be a successful one and they will win back lost ground (more local brands are always welcome in any market, and the big five out there need competition), there is no way of knowing how things will actually work out. Who knows, if I am still here, covering tech a decade later, I might be telling you a completely different story altogether.
A decade is a VERY long time in tech. Stay tuned.

A Palestinian Australian man who alleges he was punched in the face when trying to stop police from harassing Muslim men praying during an anti–Isaac Herzog protest is suing New South Wales over “a series of false accusations”.
Eyad Shadid has launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall.
The Palestine Action Group member, in his statement of claim, says NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.
“I attended the protest to object to our government rolling out the red carpet for Isaac Herzog, president of a state that has been found by United Nations commissioners and most major human rights organisations to be perpetrating a genocide,” Shadid told Guardian Australia.
“The right to protest in this state must mean more than words on paper and, if we must go to court to prove that, then so be it. I did not go to town hall looking for trouble. I went to be counted.”
Shadid, 26, was looking for his mother – who, like his father, is from Palestine – after they became separated during the protest on the evening of 9 February.
He found himself between a group of Muslim men praying and advancing police when, according to his statement of claim, he told officers: “Stop, they are praying.”
Const Daniel Stewart then allegedly dragged Shadid, who had travelled from Parramatta, to the ground and punched him in the face and twisted his wrist. Another officer kneeled on his head, the documents allege.
Shadid alleges that when on the ground another officer handcuffed him and he was taken into custody. He was charged with failing to comply with a police direction and resisting arrest.
In May, NSW police dropped the charges. Since then, three others charged after the protest have had their charges withdrawn. More than 20 protesters are due to face a joint trial in mid-2027.
Shadid alleges in court documents that Stewart failed to tell another officer deciding whether to charge him that the police line had been advancing towards people praying – and he’d requested the police stop because of that.
He claimed the omission was “deliberate” and that Stewart falsely alleged Shadid threatened him with words to the effect of: “Mate, I’d fuckin’ drop you.”
In his police statement, Stewart wrote the group of men “began” to pray as the police line moved forward and he was acting in the lawful execution of his duty when he arrested Shadid.
Shadid claims that allegation was “dishonest” and designed to make it look like the prayer was a “cynical ploy” to frustrate officers.
NSW police issued a statement three days after the protest confirming the prayer had been authorised, but claimed that message was not passed on to officers. The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, apologised “for any offence that may have been taken” after officers dragged away those praying.
After Shadid’s charges were dropped, the police prosecutor agreed officers had not given him a move-on direction. The 26-year-old was awarded costs.
“As a consequence of the matters pleaded herein, the plaintiff was assaulted, battered, falsely imprisoned, subjected to a misfeasance in public office, and maliciously prosecuted,” his statement of claim argues.
Shadid, a social services worker, is seeking aggravated and exemplary damages, arguing there was an “oppressive abuse of police powers” and he was prosecuted for “exercising a lawful democratic right to engage in peaceful protest”.
Shadid said after he was charged his name was published in media reports and he lost business clients.
Shadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna, said the case involved “very troubling allegations of police misconduct”.
“We claim that Mr Shadid was violently assaulted and arrested without any lawful basis and then charged and prosecuted on the basis of a series of false accusations and misleading omissions,” Hanna said.
The defence is yet to file its response to Shadid’s statement of claim. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, and NSW police declined to comment while the matter was before the court.
Minns said after the rally that police were “put in an impossible situation” after protesters attempted to defy the public assembly restriction declaration (Pard) law. He refused to apologise to the prayer group or for the police’s conduct.
In April, the state’s court of appeal found that law unconstitutional, ruling in favour of the Palestine Action Group and Blak Caucus.
Derek Jones, who became known as “white shirt guy”, said in May he intended to launch legal action in the supreme court against police regarding their conduct at the Herzog rally.
“It was completely unprovoked, unwarranted, excessive, crazy,” the 56-year-old finance worker told Guardian Australia at the time.
The February protest is the subject of a police watchdog investigation after allegations of widespread police brutality. Footage emerged earlier this week of a separate incident in which an officer boasted about punching a protester.
The police commissioner, when asked about the video on Wednesday, said: “The language is something that I don’t condone, but I need to understand the context of it.”

Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?
- Published
"Very ambitious, very fast, and very smart."
That was manager Mikel Arteta's aim for Arsenal's transfer dealings following their defeat by Paris St-Germain in the Champions League final in May.
The Gunners won their first title in 22 years last season by seven points and did not lose a game in the Champions League during normal time, with their only loss in the competition coming to Luis Enrique's side on penalties.
But it was clear coming into the summer transfer window that the club were looking for a game-changing attacker to lift their forward line.
Viktor Gyokeres - a £64m signing last summer from Portuguese side Sporting - scored 21 goals in his first season for Arsenal but his performances still raised questions about whether he is the best fit for Arteta's side going forward.
The same debate was posed on the left wing with Leandro Trossard's form dipping after starting the season well and Gabriel Martinelli, despite scoring six goals in the Champions League campaign, scoring just once in the league.
And now both of those players have left the club.
But finding an attacker who could elevate a squad that almost won a domestic and European double proved difficult.
Hunt for a forward
Arsenal want to be one of the best clubs in the world.
In an interview with the Times, chief executive Richard Garlick said that joining the world's super-clubs is "the goal - that's the ambition".
In that same interview, Garlick acknowledged that the "pool of players is smaller now than it was a few years ago if we're going to improve".
And unfortunately for the Gunners, they have found that out this summer.
Sporting director Andrea Berta is known for speaking to multiple targets at once while preparing the deals simultaneously.
The Gunners went into this window with interest in Morgan Rogers, Bradley Barcola, Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr.
They didn't sign any of them.
Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius Jr turned public and was shaped around his contract situation at Real Madrid.
Ultimately, the Spanish club offered him a bigger package than they had done before Arsenal's interest stepped up.
But inside the club, there was a period where they thought they were going to be successful in bringing one of the best wingers in world football to north London.
Questions will be posed as to why the club did not go big for Rogers, but Arsenal stuck to their valuation of £80m before Chelsea then paid £117m for the former Aston Villa forward.
That left Julian Alvarez as the only available target in the window after Liverpool succeeded in bringing in Bradley Barcola.
Arsenal always had reservations about paying the fee needed to get Barcola too.
It appeared Alvarez's only way out of Atletico Madrid was Arsenal, after Atleti were adamant that they would not negotiate with Barcelona.
However, Alvarez returned to training with the Spanish side and, despite Arteta's best efforts laying out plans to the player, the deal did not come off.

Who did they bring in?

Guimaraes is being described by some as one of the signings of the window, and Konsa was statistically the best defender in the league for ground duel success (73.1%) and passing accuracy (95%) last season.
Konsa, although he brings the number of senior defenders in Arsenal's squad to eight, was brought in because of the injuries to William Saliba and Jurrien Timber.
A big part of Arsenal's window has been who they have let go too.
Gabriel Martinelli is close to completing a move for around £60m to Al-Hilal, which would be a record sale for the club.
Leandro Trossard has moved to Besiktas (£15.3m), while Christian Norgaard was sold to Everton (£7m).
The main worry from supporters is that they have let two forwards go who play on the left wing and brought in just one to replace them.
Are they better?
There is no denying that Arsenal wanted a game-changing attacker this summer - if there was one available.
Not signing one this window does leave them with the chance to act again in January or wait completely until next summer to try to bring in a new forward.
But there will be uncomfortable conversations about why there hasn't been one during this window, even if the football leadership team are content with the business the club has done.
Questions will of course be asked of Arteta, Berta and co-chair Josh Kroenke as to why, after Arsenal's success, such an attractive club weren't able to get one of their targets over the line.
However, there is no denying that Arsenal's squad is one of the best in Europe. Their bench for the win over Aston Villa contained nine full internationals with two of those - Merino and Zubimendi - World Cup winners.
Gabriel Jesus has moved to Barcelona for £12.8m, and although he was not an integral part of Arsenal's team because of selection and fitness issues, he still made 27 appearances in all competitions, scoring six goals.

It is also intriguing that Gyokeres has not played a minute of the opening two Premier League matches so far.
Arsenal are still looking like the early season favourites and have the potential to defend their title, but criticism surrounding the lack of a new forward will be tough to avoid if goals start to become hard to come by.

Star Wars Zero Company is a great game that's busted and may never be fixed
It's hard to be confident about the game's future after the studio that made it furloughed most of its staff.
If you're on the fence about Star Wars Zero Company, you should know what you might be getting into. The game currently has an aggregate critic score of 85 on Metacritic, making it one of the best reviewed Star Wars games in recent memory. When it comes to story and gameplay, it's a masterfully executed tactics game in the style of X-COM with memorable characters. What none of the reviews I read or watched mentioned is that Zero Company is also something of a technical mess.
On PC, the game has all the trademarks of a janky Unreal Engine 5 release. I'm running a system with a Ryzen 7 5800X3D, RTX 5060 Ti and 16GB of RAM, and I'm getting constant traversal stutter and input lag when I try to play the game with a mouse and keyboard. I've also encountered a bug that forced me to restart the same mission twice. Yes, you might say I'm running the game on a glorified RTX 3070, but even those with more powerful GPUs like the RTX 5090 are complaining of poor performance. On Steam, the game has a "mostly positive" rating across nearly 9,000 reviews, and yet almost every one of those reviews mentions stuttering, game-breaking bugs and crashes.
"Started off having a great time," one negative review starts. "Then came the crashes. Crashed almost every hour, so needed to save every few minutes. On the times I forgot to save, I had to replay the entire section again. Of course it only ever crashed as I was about to complete a mission." Over on Reddit, console players are complaining of their own set of issues. YouTuber Daniel Owen has also made a video about the game's PC issues. While I haven't played the Xbox Series or PlayStation 5 ports, there are similar reports of crashes and stutters floating around the internet for each.
The experience of playing Zero Company is frustratingly similar to that of another recent UE5 Star Wars game, Jedi: Survivor. As I wrote about in 2023, that game was broken on release. It suffered from constant traversal and shader compilation stutter on PC, meaning the game would constantly hitch even on high-end systems. For NVIDIA users, the game also shipped without DLSS support. Even after nearly a dozen major patches, Jedi: Survivor still stutters on PC. At this point, I've given up hope that the game will ever play smoothly; Respawn Entertainment, Jedi: Survivor's developer, hasn't released a new patch in nearly two years.
Unfortunately, I can't confidently say Zero Company will receive even a fraction of the post-release support that Jedi: Survivor got from Respawn. That's because while Electronic Arts published both games, the new one was made by an independent studio named Bit Reactor, not a direct subsidiary, and its future depends on whether Zero Company sells enough copies.
On Monday, Game File's Stephen Totilo reported that Bit Reactor had furloughed the majority of its staff just weeks before Zero Company's release on August 27. One source told Totilo that as much as 80 percent of the studio's employees aren't being paid right now. Another source told him that only a skeleton crew remains, "ready to address any of Zero Company's post-launch bugs." A spokesperson for Bit Reactor told Totilo that the studio hopes to bring the furloughed workers back with restored pay, a promise the employees he spoke to said they weren't confident it would be able to deliver on, even if the game is a commercial success. The studio is also embroiled in a legal dispute between its co-founders that won't go to trial until early 2027.
If what remains of Bit Reactor is working to address Zero Company's many bugs and performance issues, the one public statement the studio has made on the subject isn't reassuring. On the day of the game's release, it simply said on Steam's Community forums it was aware of "emerging issues (crashes and CPU threading)," and that it was working on implementing fixes. "We'll let you know when we're able to provide an update," it added.
On the face of it, that's a fine enough statement, but it was issued before the news about its staffing levels came out, and it hasn't said anything since. EA and Bit Reactor did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request, asking what, if any, post-release support the game will receive.
If you're thinking about buying Zero Company, just know that it might not get to a better state than it is right now. You might think I'm being overly pessimistic, but I'll point out it took Respawn, a studio with the full financial backing of EA, a year-and-a-half to get Jedi: Survivor to its current state. Another comparison here is just as illustrative. Cold Symmetry, the indie studio behind Mortal Shell II this past Saturday announced a hefty "Week One" update for its new game, which it released just seven days before Zero Company. Those two comparisons give a sense of the potential difficult road ahead for Bit Reactor, but also what an indie studio can do when it's fully staffed. Right now, Zero Company doesn't that have going for it.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Teri Williams, president and chief operating officer of OneUnited Bank. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Growing up in Indiantown, Florida, I used to follow my great-grandmother around, whom I called Ma Honey. Ma Honey owned a penny candy store, a barbecue place, and a juke joint, where I learned how to play pool. She also owned rental properties, and I'd go with her to collect the rents.
Ma Honey's businesses shielded her family from the dangers of a segregated southern town. Her money also gave our family opportunities: she paid for my grandparents to move so that my father could attend high school, since there wasn't a Black high school in their town. She also built houses, one of which my parents and I still lived in when I was growing up.
But they say wealth lasts for three generations, and I was the fourth. By the time I went to college at Brown University, I was on a scholarship, and I felt embarrassed about Ma Honey and my small-town Southern roots.
I started running a bank while raising kids
I didn't think about Ma Honey as a businesswoman until I was in my 50s. But looking back, I can see that her spirit shaped my success. I went to Brown, then Harvard Business School, before working for major national banks.
In the mid-90s, my husband Kevin and I consolidated four banks in Boston, Los Angeles, and Miami to form OneUnited Bank. The banks we consolidated were serving the Black community, and that's what we've done since.
Kevin and I were growing the bank — he as chairman and CEO, me as president and chief operating officer — while we were raising our kids, who are now 30 and 32.
I taught my kids to prioritize savings
I'm curious if my kids thought about us as bankers or just accepted the environment they were raised in without questioning too much, as I did with Ma Honey.
The lifestyle of bankers isn't what people might think. In our house, being bankers meant prioritizing savings. One of the most important things we've taught our kids is to save, save, save.
I explain it like this: savings allows you to take risks. And to succeed, you need to take those risks — even more mainstream ones, like owning a home. The higher the risk, the higher the reward, and having a healthy savings account gives you a cushion for when mistakes and pitfalls inevitably happen.
Financial literacy is hard, even in my family
Building financial literacy was also very important — not just for my kids, but for the wider Black community. I wrote a children's book that addressed some of the issues in the Black community, such as check cashers and payday loans. At OneUnited, we've integrated these terms into our financial literacy programs in schools.
All the financial terms can still be overwhelming. One of my children called me when she was a young adult. She was confused about the balance on her credit card. In talking, I realized that she thought her balance was what she had available. I had to tell her it was what she owed.
I almost fell off my chair, thinking, "Where did I go wrong?" Then I reminded myself that financial terms can be complicated. There's no embarrassment or shame in not understanding terms that aren't easy to comprehend at first glance.
My kids use money differently from me
I tried to remember that as my children transitioned into adulthood. We had talked with them about money a lot. And yet, when you're suddenly dealing with your own paycheck, taxes, bills, and credit cards — well, that's a road that's different once you're actually traveling it.
My kids handle money differently from the way I did. I invested mostly in mutual funds, whereas they often chose individual stocks. They invested in crypto, which I wouldn't do. It's natural for financial decisions to change over time, so this doesn't worry me too much.
I hope this next generation thinks bigger. Ma Honey was able to serve her town, and through OneUnited, my husband and I now serve all 50 states. I hope my children, or my children's children, might be able to serve the world.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

Madagascar ex-Senate chief sentenced to hard labour over deadly Gen Z protest crackdown
- Published
Madagascar's former Senate president has been sentenced to 10 years of hard labour over his alleged role in the violent crackdown on youth-led protests that helped bring down the previous government last year.
Richard Ravalomanana, a retired general and close ally of former President Andry Rajoelina, was found guilty of complicity in murder by a court in the capital, Antananarivo, on Tuesday.
Prosecutors accused him of giving instructions to security forces to use violence against demonstrators during the so-called Gen Z protests in September and October 2025.
Ravalomanana denied the allegations and said he would appeal against the judgement.
- From prison to presidential palace: Who is Madagascar's new military ruler? 
  - Published17 October 2025
The protests began a year ago, initially sparked by anger over persistent power and water shortages, before developing into a broader movement against Rajoelina's government.
At least 22 people were killed and more than 100 injured during the unrest, according to UN figures cited by local media.
The protests eventually triggered a political crisis that led to Rajoelina's removal from power and the installation of a new administration led by Col Michael Randrianirina.
The crackdown was led by the gendarmerie, where Ravalomanana retained considerable influence at the time.
He "directed violent actions to suppress the demonstrations", a state prosecutor said in December 2025.
Ravalomanana was removed as Senate president in October, shortly after the protests, and was arrested at his home in December after failing to respond to a summons from the gendarmerie.
He was later placed in pre-trial detention at the high-security Imerintsiatosika prison outside Antananarivo, where he has spent the past seven months.
He is among several senior figures associated with Rajoelina's former government who have faced legal proceedings since the change of power. Ravalomanana is also facing a separate corruption investigation.
A former national police chief who testified at the trial backed his account, saying Ravalomanana was not part of the operational chain of command and had issued no orders to police, gendarmes or soldiers deployed during the unrest.
His lawyer questioned the evidence linking him directly to the violence.
"Is there confirmed written or verbal evidence... to accuse him?" he asked the court, arguing that prosecutors had failed to produce proof that security officers had received orders from his client.
Ravalomanana's defence team said it would challenge the verdict in a higher court.
The court dropped a separate allegation of making a death threat after ruling that the case was too old to prosecute.
Known for wearing a cowboy hat and displaying his military medals, Ravalomanana was viewed by protesters as a symbol of authoritarian power.

Edmonton woman says she was ‘unpersoned’ by church after Orthodox clergyman charged with sexual assault
Edmonton clergyman remains listed as active protodeacon after criminal charge
A member of the clergy with an Orthodox church in Edmonton has been accused of sexually assaulting a woman more than two decades ago, and the complainant in the case says she was ostracized from the church after reporting the alleged crime.
Jesse Isaac, 43, was charged by the Edmonton Police Service (EPS) in July in connection with an alleged sexual assault in October 2004. The allegations have not been proven in court.
According to the website for St. Olga of Alaska Orthodox Church, Isaac serves as a protodeacon at the south Edmonton church. The church is part of the Orthodox Church in America (OCA), which includes hundreds of parishes across Canada, the United States and Mexico.
At the time of the alleged assault, Isaac was serving at the St. Herman of Alaska Orthodox Church, which also belongs to the OCA.
As of Tuesday afternoon, Isaac remained listed on the OCA’s Archdiocese of Canada website as an active member of its clergy, more than six weeks after the charge of sexual assault was laid against him.
Protodeacon is a senior rank bestowed on married deacons for dedicated service and they serve the church by assisting a bishop or priest during services, as well as leading congregations in prayer.
During a hearing in the Edmonton Court of Justice Wednesday, Isaac pleaded not guilty to the charge of sexual assault and elected that his trial be heard by a judge and jury.
The case will now proceed in the Court of King's Bench of Alberta with the next appearance in Edmonton scheduled for November 27.
'So broken'
The woman who alleges Isaac assaulted her has been granted a court-ordered publication ban, but shared her story with CBC News, along with emails and messages that document her attempts to have her claims investigated by the church.
She said she felt compelled to report what happened to police, years later, in May 2025 out of a desire for justice and healing.
She said Isaac has remained in his position long after church leaders became aware of her allegation, making her feel like a criminal investigation was her only remaining recourse.
“I was so broken,” she said. “I was seeking accountability.”
In response to a request for comment, CBC News received a statement from a lawyer representing the OCA.
“The church takes allegations of criminal wrongdoing very seriously in every instance and fully co-operated with the Edmonton police,” wrote Mark Hamilton of Eckert Seamans Cherin & Mellott, LLC.
“Yet other than to offer prayers for the welfare and healing of all those involved, the church does not comment on ongoing police investigations or criminal proceedings.”
Church officials declined to answer CBC News’ questions about the internal investigation or Isaac’s future with its congregations, citing the ongoing court case.
Isaac has not responded directly to requests for comment. In a statement to CBC News, his criminal defence lawyer declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing court proceedings.
According to his profile on the church website, Isaac was ordained as a deacon in 2011 and elevated to the rank of protodeacon in 2015. He spent many years serving at the St. Herman of Alaska Orthodox Church in Edmonton but was transferred in 2025 to St. Olga’s Mission, a newer mission church established by St. Herman's.
EPS has declined to provide specific details about its investigation, the evidence gathered against Isaac or the relationship between the accused and the complainant.
Court records show Isaac was arrested on July 18, 2026, and has since been released on bail with conditions.
The case will be prosecuted by indictment, a process reserved for more serious offences, which means a conviction could result in a sentence of up to 10 years in prison.
Documents, including emails and text messages the complainant shared with CBC News, show it has been more than 17 months since she formally shared her allegation of sexual assault with church officials.
The complainant was a young woman at the time of the alleged assault. She told CBC News she had just moved to Edmonton and joined an OCA congregation after converting to the Orthodox faith.
She said that by spring of 2025, the memory of what happened to her had become an unbearable burden, leading her to confide in a few close friends within the congregation.
She said word of her allegations soon spread and reached church officials, in what she characterized as a betrayal of her trust that resulted in her being ostracized.
“I was robbed of the chance to heal quietly,” she said.
Internal investigation
Documents she shared with CBC News show that after being questioned by church officials, she later detailed her allegations to OCA leadership in March 2025, and her complaint was referred to the Office for Review of Sexual Misconduct Allegations (ORSMA).
ORSMA is a dedicated body within the church responsible for tracking and assisting with investigations into allegations of sexual misconduct.
Correspondence shared with CBC News shows that ORSMA was formally informed of the allegations on April 3, 2025, after local church leaders became aware of the alleged sexual assault and filed a formal report.
Documents show Isaac served a 10-day suspension from his role with the church, from April 3 to April 13, 2025. The church announced the suspension on its website but did not provide a reason to its parishioners.
'Like losing a family'
Correspondence shared with CBC News indicates ORSMA later determined the allegation fell outside its purview because the alleged assault occurred before Isaac was ordained as a deacon.
The complainant said she repeatedly called for further investigation and repercussions, but felt her demands went unheard. Documents she shared with CBC News show she messaged and emailed church leaders repeatedly and sent parish-wide emails sharing her concerns.
After weeks of sharing her complaints, she said she was told to leave the congregation outright.
In late April 2025, according to an email she shared with CBC News, she was informed that she no longer had the “blessing” of church leaders to attend services or receive sacraments at St. Herman’s or St. Olga’s.
In the email, church officials told her she was no longer welcome, that due to her allegations against church leadership, they could no longer give her the spiritual guidance she needed.
The email also stated the ORSMA investigation had concluded after determining the “incident, if true,” occurred prior to Isaac’s ordination.
The complainant said there is no clear mechanism for victims to seek accountability within their church communities. She said the parish she attended for 20 years no longer feels like a safe place to practise her faith.
“It’s like losing a family,” she said. “They unpersoned me.
“I still have faith … but it killed my spirit.”

Bancroft Hall at the US Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, is named for former Navy Secretary George Bancroft, but to the midshipmen who call the dormitory home, it is affectionately known as "Mother B."
The largest single college dormitory in the world, Bancroft Hall, houses all roughly 4,400 midshipmen throughout their four years of study at the elite military academy.
Bancroft Hall's center section and first two wings, designed by Ernest Flagg, a Beaux-Arts architect known for his grand, classical designs, were completed in 1908. The dormitory was expanded in 1921, 1941, and 1961 and now features eight wings.
The enormous 1.4-million-square-foot complex houses 1,639 dorm rooms and 4,663 beds, and contains 33 acres of floor space and 4.8 miles of hallways, which midshipmen refer to by their maritime term, "passageways." The dorm is so big that its internal post office uses the unique ZIP code, 21412.
Incoming freshmen, known as "plebes," march into Bancroft Hall through the center doors after their Oath of Office Ceremony on Induction Day, the first official day of Plebe Summer before the academic year begins. From then on, midshipmen are not permitted to walk through the center doors until after graduation. (Civilians, officers, and non-midshipmen are allowed to use the center doors.)
The front doors of Bancroft Hall open into a decorative rotunda accessible to visitors. Memorial Hall, a space honoring fallen alumni of the US Naval Academy, is publicly accessible through the staircase in the rotunda.
Bancroft Hall also features student services, including gyms, a uniform store, a bookstore, a tailor, a cobbler, laundry rooms, and dental and medical facilities.
The greater Bancroft Hall complex also includes Mitscher Hall, located in the courtyard, which houses an auditorium and a small chapel. The Levy Center inside Mitscher Hall includes a synagogue, conference rooms, and the Honor Court, a midshipman-led body that investigates alleged violations of the USNA Honor Concept.
Midshipmen keep their dorm rooms shipshape
Attending the US Naval Academy requires adherence to strict rules, including in the dorms. Uniforms and shoes must be stored in order from light to dark, and beds must be neatly made with hospital corners each day. Rooms are also inspected regularly.
The rooms, housing at least two people, are single-sex. Each room includes a twin bed above a desk, a closet, storage, and its own shower and sink. Communal toilets are located in the halls. The dormitory is co-ed. As of 2024, the student body was around 70% male and 30% female.
Rooming assignments are organized by the roughly 150-person companies that midshipmen are placed in upon arrival. The companies also eat and study together, and compete for points each semester that earn special distinctions.
Meals are served in King Hall, which was completed in 1953 and is located within Bancroft Hall. At breakfast, lunch, and dinner, the Naval Academy serves 4,500 meals at once in less than 10 minutes — enough for virtually every midshipman to eat at the same time. In total, it serves 13,500 meals a day.
Aside from housing the entire student body, Bancroft Hall's most important role, US Naval Academy public affairs officer Lieutenant Commander Kara Handley told Business Insider, is shaping future leaders.
"For over 120 years, the US Naval Academy has built warfighters behind the doors of Bancroft Hall," Handley said. "Serving as the structural heart of the Yard, Bancroft Hall not only houses the Brigade of Midshipmen as the largest, single dormitory complex in the world but also provides a training ground to reinforce military discipline, unit cohesion, high standards, and accountability."

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

Whatever happened to the U.S. famine alert system that Trump shut down, then reopened
In February 2025, we reported that "A respected U.S. famine warning system is 'currently unavailable.' " That system is known as FEWS NET and ran a database that could pinpoint areas where the risk of famine is high, enabling aid groups to prepare for relief. As NPR noted: "The website that once served up detailed, color-coded maps of hunger hot spots around the world now bears a stark message: The site and its data are "currently unavailable."
Over the next week, we'll be looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
FEWS NET did eventually come back online. But now there have been some new developments. This is the first story in our annual series of follow-ups.
Jeremy Konyndyk was on a flight to Somalia in early August, when he checked a U.S. database routinely used by aid workers to predict and respond to hunger crises across the globe: The Famine Early Warning System (FEWS NET).
To his surprise, a map of East Africa on the website's landing page showed a gray outline where Somalia's color-coded famine report should be.
"I was reading this stuff on the flight over, and I thought oh that's weird – why isn't there anything since June?" Konyndyk says.
Despite Somalia's worsening food crisis affecting an estimated 6.5 million people, the country's profile did not show any updates after July. Additionally, Somalia as well as Afghanistan and Yemen were eliminated from a regular "Peak Food Assistance Needs Outlook Brief," published on August 14, 2026.
The Trump administration previously slashed aid funding to all three countries; despite all three experiencing widespread food insecurity.
"Somalia is probably the country that FEWS NET has historically reported on more than any other," says Konyndyk, president of Refugees International and a former top official at USAID, the U.S. foreign agency that is now shuttered. "The conditions are extremely dangerous, extremely precarious, and now is the moment where you really need that sort of reporting."
In a statement to NPR on Monday, the State Department said that FEWS NET's reporting for specific countries has historically "increased or decreased based on shifts in need, policy priorities, access, cost-efficiency, and other factors."
The pause in reporting led several organizations, including the Rockefeller Foundation, as well as former USAID employees to speak out against it.
"If they allow FEWS Net to continue reporting, they're basically documenting the damage of their own decisions," Konyndyk said. "I think they don't want the world to see, they don't want their own systems to tell them the damage of what they're doing."
A reversal
However, the State Department told NPR on Monday afternoon that FEWS NET will resume reporting on those three countries in September.
Their statement noted: "The Department will continue to evaluate that all programming appropriately uses limited resources to address foreign policy priorities."
This is not the first time that FEWS NET has faced the chopping block. Before the Trump administration, the service was run by a private contractor and funded by USAID. It was suspended for six months in early 2025, as part of Trump's unilateral freeze on foreign assistance.
Piecemeal stoppages of reporting on specific areas are not new, either: FEWS NET has not reported on the hunger crisis in Gaza, since the fall of last year.
The role of FEWS NET
Developed 40 years ago to help USAID respond to crises, FEWS NET is widely used by international aid groups to strategically preposition donations and time their responses. Its analysts pull in crop reports, market data and satellite images to create hyperlocalized information, often predicting major crises up to nine months in advance. That window allows governments and aid groups to ship supplies, arrange transportation and prevent famines.
Five million Yemenis — nearly half of the country's population — are facing acute food insecurity, according to the U.N. In Afghanistan, the U.N. estimates that 14 million people are facing acute hunger.
This summer's pause in data reporting for Somalia came at a particularly precarious time.
Approximately a third of Somalis — 6.5 million people — are facing acute food insecurity, according to the U.N. A survey by Doctors Without Borders found that half of children under age 5 in camps near the city of Baidoa were malnourished.
"When we went there, we were seeing that a lot of children even over the age of five had distended stomachs and discolored hair, indicative of malnutrition," saysid Chenoa Sankar, an epidemiologist for Doctors Without Borders.
A third of nearly 900 families who were interviewed said they were surviving on just one meal a day. In just two months this summer, Doctors Without Borders treated 2,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women for malnutrition.
"Because of the extended drought and the multiple missed rainy seasons, there's this huge influx of people coming in," Sankar says. "When you sit down with people, the main complaint is there is simply no food."
Mukhtar Sirat Mahdi, an aid worker coordinating treatment centers for malnourished children, recalls the face of a starving 11-month old baby.
In June, the child arrived with her family in a camp for internally displaced refugees after being forced off their farm by Somalia's multi-year drought.
"The child was very weak," Mahdi says. "Between death and life."
After six weeks of treatment, the baby recovered. But close calls like this, Mahdi says, are happening more often.
Efforts to prevent famine have been hampered by the January decision of the United States, once Somalia's largest donor, to freeze nearly all of the country's humanitarian aid. Assistance had reached $770 million during the Biden administration. But in early January, the Trump administration accused Somali officials of seizing food aid and destroying a U.S.-funded warehouse used by the World Food Program. Other Western countries have also cut assistance, leaving a patchwork of aid programs to fill the gap.
Previously U.S. funding helped the World Food Program feed about 2 million Somalis every month. That's now down to 350,000, and those families are only receiving half rations, said Konyndyk from Refugees International. Additionally, 205 clinics used to feed malnourished kids have closed due to a lack of funding, according to UNICEF.
"When you close facilities you create longer journeys for mums and their babies — which means later treatment, and later means a greater risk of preventable death," UNICEF spokesman James Elder tells NPR.
Data that makes a difference
Whether or not Somalia reaches the international threshold for famine depends largely on outcomes of the next growing season and the success of food aid programs. Now, aid workers say, is when FEWS NET data is most critical.
"If you can't get to the place, you can't deliver the food," says Colin Thomas-Jensen of the Aurora Humanitarian Initiative. "This is effectively a global public good. This is a publicly available data set that is rigorous, that has historically predicted pockets of extreme food insecurity."
Thomas-Jensen was a national security adviser to USAID in 2024, when FEWS NET reports played a critical role to help USAID organize airdrops of food aid into Sudan's Nuba Mountains. Because the system's forecasts can anticipate crises six to nine months out, humanitarian workers were able to coordinate with foreign governments and target the highest-risk communities.
"The FEWS NET data allowed us to target specific towns and counties [where] we could drop the food to reach the most acutely affected populations," Thomas-Jensen says.
Top quality
The U.N. also maintains data on food insecurity, known as the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). The World Food Program also publishes its own data, which it calls HungerMap.
However, aid workers and experts who use FEWS NET say it stands out as the highest-quality indicator available for their work. Governments are often reluctant to label a food crisis in their country as a famine; fearing losses to investment and other economic implications.
"If governments are allowed to put their thumb on the scale of these systems, including where data is allowed to be collected, the system itself loses its credibility," says Michelle Jurkovich, an expert on food aid policy at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

More than 900 killed in Gaza this year despite ceasefire, Hamas-run health ministry says
- Published
More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.
It brings the total number of people killed in the Strip since the 10 October ceasefire was declared to more than 1,300, including 301 children, the ministry says.
Hamas and Israel agreed to halt the war after accepting US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan. That plan included a suspension of "all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment".
Since then, BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos which show the impact of Israeli strikes on locations including a beachside cafe, tents where displaced people have been sheltering, and a reported funeral procession in central Gaza.
Recent months have been some of the most deadly according to the figures, with more than 100 people recorded killed each month between April and August.
The health ministry attributes the deaths directly to Israeli military action, but does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
The UN considers the figures reliable, and experts have told BBC Verify that their independent analysis is consistent with the ministry's data.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) disputes the ministry's figures. It told BBC Verify there is "no basis to assume" that all those listed were killed as a result of IDF activity.
It said it operates in "a precise manner to remove threats and protect its troops and Israeli civilians, in accordance with the agreement", and that it works to mitigate any civilian harm "to the greatest extent possible".
At the start of this year Israeli media reported that an Israeli security official acknowledged more than 70,000 people had been killed in the Gaza war, which it said included more than 20,000 combatants.
'Ceasefire in name only'
From the start of the ceasefire agreement on 10 October to the end of that month, the ministry recorded 251 deaths. Since then the deadly Israeli attacks have continued every month. The highest monthly death toll this year was recorded in July, when 152 people were killed including 21 children, according to the figures.
The IDF says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".
It also says it has killed hundreds of military operatives since October.
Conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (Acled), which uses official statements, media reports and social media to verify attacks, says it has recorded around 200 Israeli strikes during the ceasefire that have reportedly killed Hamas operatives or other armed "militants" in targeted strikes.
Acled said this includes commanders involved in planning the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the war and killed around 1,200 people with 251 taken hostage.
Hugh Lovatt, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, said "Gaza has seen a ceasefire in name only" since last October. He said the Israeli military has continued its almost daily air and drone strikes, and "though it claims to be targeting Hamas or imminent threats, it is Gaza's civilians that have continued to bear the brunt".
This could now be a "central stumbling block" in international efforts to implement Trump's ceasefire deal, he added.
The IDF told BBC Verify it "remains committed" to the ceasefire agreement and that there have been "continued violations and threats posed by Hamas and other terror organizations" in Gaza.
Summer of deadly incidents
Warning: The following segment of this story contains graphic content which some readers might find distressing.
BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos of attacks in Gaza carried out since the ceasefire.
In one, emergency services are seen attending to people in the aftermath of a strike at a beachside cafe in Gaza City on 18 August, where six people were killed, according to the health ministry. The next day nine people, including a 13-year-old, were reportedly killed in a strike on a police headquarters in the al-Tuffah neighbourhood.
The IDF said it was targeting Hamas commanders and terrorists in the two incidents and that "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".
One of the deadliest single incidents in July was a strike on a reported funeral procession in Nuseirat. Seven people were killed and 22 injured, according to the Al-Awda Hospital where casualties were taken. Several verified images show nine people covered in blood lying on the street. Two people appear to still be alive and are being treated by bystanders.
The IDF said it was targeting a "significant military operative" of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad group who was involved in the 7 October 2023 attacks.
In a strike on an apartment block on the western edge of Gaza City overnight on 1 August, a pregnant woman, her husband and their young son were killed, according to local reports. Verified footage showed the body of an unborn baby in the rubble.
A man searching the ruins said he had heard a strike overnight and saw smoke coming from the building. "I broke the door and went up and I found dead bodies scattered," he said. The IDF said it had targeted an acting Hamas commander.
Child deaths 'absurd and devastating'
UN agency Unicef has also reported more than 300 children have been killed since the ceasefire. The aid organisation has been tracking all available reports of incidents affecting children in Gaza, including via UN personnel on the ground.
James Elder, Unicef global spokesperson, said the number of child deaths was "absurd and devastating".
He added that hundreds more have been injured. "A ceasefire that paints such a grim picture can only be failing children."
Unicef and other humanitarian organisations operating inside Gaza have also reported Israeli strikes on their workers since the ceasefire. This includes two water truck drivers contracted by Unicef killed in April by Israeli fire at the Mansoura water filling point in northern Gaza.
The IDF said its soldiers "identified suspects approaching" the Yellow Line area during the incident, who were later identified as UN contractors who had not "coordinated in advance". Unicef said the drivers were carrying out routine water trucking operations with "no changes in movement or procedures".
Aid Worker Security Database, whose figures have been cited by the UN and UK government, told BBC Verify it has recorded 22 aid workers killed in Gaza since 10 October 2025.
Independent research group Airwars works to identify civilian deaths from a range of open sources including news agencies, NGOs and social media, matching names it finds to those published by the health ministry.
Director Emily Tripp told BBC Verify the ministry's data on death tolls is consistent with its own tracking and research, and that it recorded more than 60 deadly incidents in July.
"This is the highest number of fatal incidents we've seen in a month since the ceasefire," Tripp said. "Our own findings point to an increasing number of civilian harm incidents a month."

  - Published16 November 2023
Professor Michael Spagat from Royal Holloway, University of London, is the chair of Every Casualty Counts, a charity that studies death tolls in wars. He told BBC Verify that the figures recorded by the health ministry are "testable" because it publishes names, ages and ID numbers of the dead.
He said that since April, the monthly death toll in Gaza has been roughly double what was seen in December. "July was the worst month but even August's lower toll is still high compared with the November to March period," he added.

The first joint field-level study by the Keralam Health Department and experts from ICMR’s National Institute of Epidemiology in Chennai to describe the epidemiology of amoebic meningoencephalitis (AME) cases reported in Kerala in 2025 has identified exposure to natural water bodies and the use of non-chlorinated water for bathing and other domestic purposes as significant risk factors, providing the first epidemiological evidence from the State on potentially modifiable exposures linked to amoebic meningoencephalitis.
The case-control study is the first scientific proof of the questionable quality of well water in Keralam, on which a significant section of the population depends for bathing and other domestic use.
It has already been well explained by the scientific community that certain risky behaviours — exposure to natural water bodies (especially diving into water and snorting water into the nostrils), a history of previous facial or nasal injury, and entering natural water bodies when there are ulcers or skin wounds — predispose one to AME caused by Acanthamoeba, which can enter the body through tissue or the respiratory tract.
“The finding that the use of non-chlorinated water, or well water, for domestic purposes is independently associated with AME caused by Acanthamoeba is quite relevant for Kerala, where only a tiny fraction of the population has access to chlorinated, safe, piped water supply. Our study results showed that people using well water for bathing or washing their face had 2.95 times higher odds of getting AME,” points out R. Aravind, Head of Infectious Diseases, Thiruvananthapuram Government Medical College, and one of the key researchers involved in the study.
“The estimated population attributable fraction (PAF) was 34.2%. This means that 34.2% of the cases of AME caused by Acanthamoeba in the population would not occur if non-chlorinated well water, as a specific risk factor, was removed,” Dr. Aravind pointed out.
(PAF is an epidemiological measure that estimates the proportion of disease cases in a population that would not occur if a specific risk factor were removed.)
It should be noted that domestic water use referred to activities involving direct contact with the face, head, skin, or body, such as bathing or washing the face or hair, and did not refer to ingestion.
Many households in Kerala depend on individual or public wells. Heavy rainfall, flooding, sewage contamination, organic matter, and algal growth might contribute to the contamination of, or proliferation of free-living amoebae (FLAs) in, poorly maintained wells.
This case-control study is the highest level of scientific evidence that water quality is going to be a key public health issue in which the State will have to invest in the immediate future. Water quality surveillance, along with periodic chlorination and maintenance of wells, has to be a year-round activity through local self-governments so that the risk of people contracting AME can be minimised.
In a State where there are a large number of water bodies, the focus of public health messaging about AME should be on reducing high-risk exposures, particularly during the monsoon and post-monsoon period, along with routine chlorination of domestic water sources.
The study, “Epidemiology of and Risk Factors for Amoebic Meningoencephalitis, Kerala 2025”, published in the latest issue of Emerging Infectious Diseases, the journal of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, analysed 159 AME cases reported in Kerala between January 1 and November 11, 2025. Of these, 76 were confirmed by real-time PCR and 83 by microscopic examination of cerebrospinal fluid.
Among the PCR-confirmed cases, 67 (88.2%) were caused by Acanthamoeba species and nine (11.8%) by Naegleria fowleri.
This is significant because popular perception, and even international media attention, centred on the “epidemic” of “brain-eating amoeba” (N. fowleri) infections in Kerala, when, in fact, an overwhelming majority of AME cases in the State in 2025 were granulomatous amoebic encephalitis caused by Acanthamoeba.
Among the 159 case-patients, 41 died, giving a case fatality rate of 25.8%. Seventeen of the 67 patients with PCR-confirmed Acanthamoeba infection died (25.4%), while four of the nine N. fowleri patients died (44.4%).
The researchers noted that between 2016 and 2024, Kerala had reported only 45 AME cases and 15 deaths. Increased clinical awareness, wider availability of molecular diagnostics, and improved surveillance could have contributed to the sharp increase in laboratory-confirmed AME cases in 2025.
To identify possible risk factors, the researchers conducted a matched case-control study restricted to 43 PCR-confirmed Acanthamoeba patients and 129 apparently healthy controls from Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Kozhikode, and Malappuram. Three controls were selected for each case and matched for age, sex, and place of residence.
Exposure to natural water bodies — swimming or diving in ponds and canals during the preceding three months, especially among persons with a history of maxillofacial injury or nasal surgery — was associated with 4.7 times higher odds of disease.
Exposing skin wounds or ulcers to natural water bodies had one of the strongest associations with AME. The odds of AME in this group were 25.4 times higher. This is consistent with the known ability of Acanthamoeba to enter through breaks in the skin and subsequently disseminate to the central nervous system.
Public health communication should therefore specifically advise persons with previous facial or head injuries, and those with wounds or skin ulcers, against entering natural water bodies, especially during the monsoon and post-monsoon season.
The researchers make an important distinction: while the entry of contaminated water through the nose is an established route of transmission for N. fowleri, it has not been established as a route of transmission for AME caused by Acanthamoeba.
Although Acanthamoeba AME has traditionally been associated with immunocompromised individuals, in the Kerala study, most PCR-confirmed Acanthamoeba AME cases did not have documented immunocompromising conditions, according to records.
The researchers say that host susceptibility remains important, but it cannot by itself explain the pattern of AME seen in Kerala.
They also make a clear distinction that the associations between Acanthamoeba AME and exposure to natural water bodies or non-chlorinated water are epidemiological associations and do not prove that water exposure led directly to neuroinvasion. Further environmental, clinical, and microbiological studies would be needed to determine whether these associations reflect a route through which the disease was acquired.
Lower socioeconomic status was associated with AME in this study, which might influence the behavioural exposures identified by the researchers. Low socioeconomic status could affect access to safe domestic water and increase reliance on non-chlorinated wells. This is also why most AME cases are reported by public hospitals.
Risk communication on AME should therefore prioritise socioeconomically vulnerable communities, the study notes.
