OpenAI announced Tuesday that its forthcoming AI model, Astra, is its first to reach the company’s threshold for what it calls “critical” cyber capabilities. OpenAI says it plans to publicly release a version of Astra “soon,” but will make the model’s advanced cyber capabilities available only to select partners in its Daybreak Blue early-access program at launch.
In a briefing with reporters, OpenAI safety and security leaders said the company has concluded that Astra reaches the critical cybersecurity capabilities outlined in its preparedness framework, which sets thresholds and protocols for when its AI models pose new levels of risk. The company says an AI model has reached its critical cyber threshold when it can independently find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world software. OpenAI leaders said the company has followed its procedure for this situation, which is to halt further development until appropriate safeguards and security measures can be implemented.
OpenAI previously said that it paused some training workloads related to the development of Astra and a future AI model for several weeks. Executives say the company has now resumed said work on Astra, and the future AI model, after putting additional safety and security controls in place. OpenAI says the multi-week pause was productive, and it is now confident that it can release Astra broadly in a safe way.
The announcement comes as Silicon Valley grapples with the advanced cybersecurity capabilities of cutting-edge AI models, and tries to assure users, lawmakers, and other companies that it can keep them under control. In July, OpenAI disclosed an incident in which agents running two of its models exploited vulnerabilities in what was supposed to be a siloed testing environment, gaining access to the internet and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face. (OpenAI notes that Astra was not one of the models involved in this case.)
Other AI companies, such as Anthropic and Meta, have disclosed similar incidents in recent weeks. On Monday, Anthropic also said it has paused some AI training workloads while it hardens its safety and security practices.
OpenAI says it’s implementing a multi-step approach to limit everyday users from accessing Astra’s advanced cyber capabilities, including a new “misalignment monitor.” If someone asks Astra to help them find an exploit in a real-world software system, for example, the model is supposed to refuse to answer. OpenAI says it has also made Astra more robust to jailbreaking attempts, and in tests it successfully refused unsafe queries at a significantly higher rate than previous models.
However, OpenAI notes in a blog post that its misalignment monitor may “occasionally flag legitimate activity as potential cyber misuse or unauthorized behavior, leading to it inadvertently being slowed, paused, or stopped.” OpenAI says the guardrail can be triggered in some cases even when a user is engaging in activities that don’t appear related to cybersecurity. When this happens, ChatGPT and Codex users may be asked to review the model’s action before proceeding, OpenAI said.
Partners in OpenAI’s Daybreak program—which includes digital infrastructure providers like Cisco, Cloudflare, and Palo Alto Networks—will get early access to a less restricted version of Astra with more robust cyber capabilities. The goal of the program is to ensure these companies can use advanced AI models like Astra to harden their defenses before similarly capable models are made broadly available. OpenAI leaders also said the company has been working closely with government partners to ensure they’re aware of Astra’s cyber skills and can get access to them.
Astra is not only capable of finding novel software vulnerabilities and developing ways to exploit them for hacking, but is also able to “chain” multiple exploits together, a technique used to bore deeper and deeper into a target system and gain access that wouldn’t be attainable using just one vulnerability.
According to figures from OpenAI, Astra outperforms industry leading AI models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic’s Mythos on cybersecurity benchmarks such as ExploitBench, which Astra scored 100 percent on. However, these capabilities are broadly in line with the rising hacking abilities of AI models that OpenAI and Anthropic have been forecasting for months. In April, for example, Anthropic emphasized that Mythos Preview was able to autonomously develop exploit chains.
As the AI and cybersecurity industries have scrambled to adapt, though, many cybersecurity experts have emphasized that key digital security defenses and longstanding best practices are still durable. However, AI puts organizations and systems that haven’t fully implemented these protections at even more urgent risk.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.

WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

The battle that made Canada bleed: Operation Medusa, 20 years later
Over 1,000 Canadians took part in battle that was military's largest since Korean War
As Canadian troops crossed the Arghandab River, the first indication to former corporal Bruce Moncur that something was amiss came with the sight of a green pen flare shooting across the sky.
"I remember looking at it thinking, well, that's weird," said Moncur, who realized that since NATO troops in Afghanistan fired red flares, green must have belonged to the Taliban.
"That was an indication that we had walked far enough into the trap."
The Taliban had waited until he and his section of troops had dismounted from the protection of their armoured vehicles before springing their three-sided ambush.
Moncur recalls every detail of that day 20 years ago with a stark, blinding clarity.
It was the opening phase of Operation Medusa, a savage, close-quarters battle in the vineyards and dusty villages of Kandahar.
The battle began on Sept. 2, 2006, with an artillery and air bombardment.
A day later, Moncur's unit set off to cross the river.
The Canadians ran into a deeply entrenched enemy that was firing machine guns, rocket-propelled grenades and small arms.
The battle was different in the sense the Taliban force had chosen, unusually, to stand and fight.
More than 2,000 NATO troops, including over 1,000 Canadians, took part, alongside Afghan forces and American, British, Dutch and Danish elements.
It would be the biggest battle Canadians had fought since Korea and their largest conventional operation of the Afghan war.
Moncur's unit, Charles Company, 1st Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment (1RCR), had been drawn into the insurgent ambush after crossing the river as they were pushing toward their objective, a little white school house the Taliban had occupied.
The firefight lasted five hours. Four Canadian soldiers were killed: Warrant Officer Frank Mellish, Warrant Officer Richard Nolan, Sgt. Shane Stachnik and Pte. William Cushley. An additional 16 troops were wounded before the order was given to retreat.
"In that firefight, I was all over the battlefield. Some vehicles were stuck and left behind, and we had to try to salvage them," Moncur said. "One soldier was left behind. We obviously don't leave anyone behind. So, we had to go and rescue his body."
In an interview given to reporters at the time, the commander of Bravo Company 1 RCR said the depth and strength of the Taliban force, which were later estimated at a total of 1,000 insurgents, was not something the Canadians expected.

"Truthfully, I was surprised by the resistance they put up," the commander, Maj. Geoff Abthorpe, said. "We came at them with what I perceived to be a pretty heavy fist."
"I think closer to about 400 Taliban fighters and men that had fought all their lives versus 80 Canadians that had … this is their first time at combat, first time in a real firefight," said Moncur.
In the late summer of 2006 prior to the battle, hundreds of insurgents had massed in the Panjwai and Zhari districts, roughly 30 kilometres west of Kandahar city, the provincial capital.
They had dug trenches, fortified compounds, planted mines and improvised explosive devices and established defensive positions around the nearby village of Pashmul.
The timing was deliberate. NATO had only recently taken responsibility for southern Afghanistan from the U.S.-led coalition, and the Taliban appeared determined to test whether the alliance had the stomach for a serious fight.
Sean Maloney, a historian at the Royal Military College of Canada, said all throughout the spring and summer of 2006 Canadian troops had been fighting running battles with the Taliban.
The ones that decided to fight in Pashmul were different. They were better trained, more co-ordinated and better equipped.
There has been a long running debate in Canadian and U.S. military circles about whether Pakistan's notorious intelligence service had contributed — in some way — to the sophistication of the insurgents who fought NATO forces.
"They're definitely a major factor in this," said Maloney.
A U.S. military study of insurgent tactics, written long after the battle in 2018, also pointed to potential Pakistani involvement, including the redirection of foreign fighters to bolster the ranks of local Taliban.
The report noted how the insurgents mounted planned ambushes and counterattacks and, when NATO firepower became overwhelming, conducted what the study calls a "disciplined retreat."
Several weeks after the operation, Pakistani journalist and noted Taliban expert Ahmed Rashid wrote a piece quoting NATO commanders, who believed the battle had exposed the Taliban’s support structure in Pakistan to an "extraordinary degree."
Friendly fire
After the failed river crossing on the second day of the battle, disaster struck Moncur's unit again.
An American A-10 mistakenly strafed Canadian positions, killing Pte. Mark Graham and wounding more than 30 others, including Moncur, who suffered a major head injury.
"I'm sitting there eating, and my fire team partner comes to sit next to me,' said Moncur, who compared the sensation of being strafed to being electrocuted. "I just remember being tossed in the air like a rag doll…. I remember feeling like my body was being, like I touched a socket or something."
He tumbled down a rocky slope before losing consciousness. When Moncur came to, he knew his head was bleeding.
"If you've ever washed your face in a basin and just filled up and splashed yourself with water, that's how much blood ended up filling in my hands," Moncur said.
He crawled to a nearby medic, who was also wounded, before passing out again.

"I basically made peace with this. That was going to be the final moments of my life," Moncur said.
But it wasn't.
He was rushed to the military hospital at Kandahar Airfield before being evacuated to a U.S. military trauma centre in Germany, where he faced a long, painful road to recovery.
Following the friendly fire attack, Charles Company was effectively removed from the battle.
The commanders — Brig.-Gen. David Fraser and Lt.-Col. Omer Lavoie — shifted the axis of the main attack to the north.
The battered remnants of Charles Company remained in the south, helping convince the Taliban another river assault was coming, while Canadian forces pushed down from Highway 1.
The operation lasted another two weeks and ended with hundreds of insurgents killed.
Maloney said it was a pivotal moment in the war. The intention of the Taliban, at the time, was to eventually push into Kandahar city.
The decisive defeat forced them to switch back to hit-and-run tactics of improvised explosives and ambushes.
It was also an important political moment.
"That's when the Afghans realized, yeah, we're going to fight," Maloney said. "And as one of them walked up to our people and said — in shock — you're willing to bleed for us."
